title: Çiğdem Doğu: Young people no longer accept the life imposed by capitalism
content:
Kurdistan Women's Communities (KJK) Executive Council member Çiğdem Doğu appeared on a special program broadcast by Medya Haber television, where she discussed the Peace and Democratic Society Process initiated by Leader Apo (Abdullah Öcalan) and violence against women.




The first part of this in-depth interview can be read 

here

.




Looking beyond the Middle East region to world politics, Trump has not fallen, but he has become increasingly surrounded. Democrats and Republicans have clashed, and electoral balances have shifted. Meanwhile, youth-led resistance and uprisings are taking place in Spain, France and Italy. How should we interpret these developments? What direction are these changing balances giving to the broader process?




There was also an election in Brazil, where Lula won. He represents a more democratic and somewhat more left-leaning position. There was also an election in Serbia. This was a very important experience. A candidate list was formed under the leadership of the student youth movement. The students themselves were not on the list, but they supported democratic and honest politicians whom they believed in. That list won. This provides a very important indication for evaluating certain developments.




There was also a recent election in the United States. We cannot simply conclude that the peoples won or that the Democrats won in a broader democratic sense. But certain signals emerged, and it is important to evaluate them. We all know Trump. The peoples of the world know him. He emerged as a model of imperial leadership. He was perhaps the clearest example of the type described by the Kurdish People's Leader in the manifesto as a "murderous, hierarchical" personality. He disregarded everyone and paid no attention whatsoever to the peoples.




This tendency already exists within the capitalist system. At least when nation-states first emerged, there was a legal system, even if it was never fully implemented. Trump and leaders like him, however, adopted an approach that recognized no legal, moral or ethical boundaries. They put this approach into practice. People speak of a Third World War as though it has yet to begin, but it has already begun. Trump was one of those leading it. He waged war against Iran. There are other wars taking place around the world. He claims to have resolved numerous conflicts, but in reality, he played a role in provoking and escalating wars. Naturally, this has produced social, economic and humanitarian consequences. The American people have also paid a price for these policies. In this sense, the American public delivered a response, saying that such leadership could not continue and that one person could not govern in this manner.




I want my words to be understood correctly. We are people who hold a socialist ideology. Our standards and expectations are therefore much higher. Nevertheless, peoples send messages through elections. It is very important to understand the sociological dynamics behind these developments and interpret what elections reveal. This does not mean that powerful socialist movements have emerged or that the Democrats are necessarily better simply because they won. Such a comparison would not be accurate or objective. What matters is understanding what the people are saying. From this perspective, the American public has delivered a response. The message was that the escalation of wars, the refusal to recognize the will of peoples and the unilateral decisions affecting the Palestinian people and the peoples of the Middle East were not accepted. It is important to recognize this as a positive message.




'

Young people no longer accept the life imposed by capitalism'




Why is this important? Because perceptions are also being manufactured. We frequently hear claims that "the right is advancing" or "the far right is on the rise." This is also a form of psychological warfare. We must evaluate everything sociologically. We need to carefully analyze what social tendencies are telling us and what realities they express. We are leading figures within a socialist movement, and we must therefore approach these developments through sociological analysis.




The example of Brazil is important in this respect. The student movement in Serbia generated significant mobilization, struggle and rebellion. Youth movements have also become increasingly active in Paris and other French cities, as well as in Italy, Germany and various other countries. These developments tell us a great deal. They show that young people reject the imperialist-capitalist world, the capitalist system, the nation-state, industrialism and the male-dominated system. Young people have demonstrated that they no longer accept this way of life, that they refuse to be condemned to such a fate and that they are prepared to struggle against it. This is extremely important. Youth struggles also have the capacity to inspire and reinforce one another.




Serbia provides a particularly significant example. I have read some articles in which socialist and left-wing circles argue that the movement lacks a plan or program. There may be some truth to this, and I do not reject that possibility. However, this also reveals a weakness among leftist and socialist forces: our ability to understand the tendencies emerging among peoples, young people and women. The tendency toward democratic society is already expressing itself everywhere. Even in the most fascist country, society continues to preserve certain democratic values through its everyday life. These values may not be fully developed or expressed at an ideal level, but they exist. A youth movement emerged in Serbia. If I remember correctly, a wall collapsed in a Serbian city about two years ago, killing approximately 16 people. For two years, young people struggled against the government over this incident and demanded accountability. They did not limit their struggle to students. They reached out to every section of society, visiting villages, towns and cities. Young people entered society, organized within it and demanded accountability from those in power. The government fell. Through their struggle, young people brought down the government, and the list they supported won.




'Youth movements are showing the way forward'




This tells us something important. It gives us hope. But it does more than offer hope. It shows us a path forward. If young people genuinely become part of society and develop and strengthen their struggle from within it, they can unleash a force capable of bringing down even a government. That is how we must understand these developments.




Ideally, of course, it would have been better if the movement had a clear program and strategy. Nevertheless, the struggle has produced results. We must examine those results, better understand the struggle of young people and the revolutionary potential of the peoples, and listen carefully to what they are saying. We should strengthen our strategies, programs and plans on that basis rather than simply declaring that the right is rising. Leftist and socialist forces, ecological, feminist and cultural movements, and even democratic religious movements are engaged in struggles throughout the world.




We must recognize and understand these developments. Through collective action, we can bring about the rise of the left. We therefore need to look at the situation from another perspective. The issue is not simply that the right is becoming stronger.




Rather, the balance is shifting because leftist, socialist, feminist, ecological, anarchist and other movements have not yet developed sufficiently strong forms of organization. We must strengthen the weaker side of this balance. We need to organize more effectively, overcome fragmented approaches and build stronger democratic alliances. I therefore believe we should examine global developments with hope, understanding them more deeply through sociological, strategic and political analysis, and take action accordingly.




The 31st Conference of the Parties to the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (COP31) is being held in Antalya. Climate summits are organized repeatedly, and many issues concerning climate change and ecological balance are discussed. Those responsible for disrupting the climate gather to seek solutions. Some regard these summits as a kind of conspiracy or trap set by nation-states. Climate disruption also has serious consequences for violence against women and unemployment. How do you assess this?




First, I would like to say that COP31 and many other initiatives around the world address ecological problems. However, there is considerable hypocrisy and an effort to conceal reality. Perhaps the capitalist system's greatest skill is doing the worst things while marketing them as the best. This seems to be a particular characteristic of capitalism. It disguises its actions and conceals its responsibility for their consequences, presenting itself as though it bears no responsibility. International organizations and gatherings of this kind can also serve this purpose. I do not want to suggest that we oppose such initiatives altogether. But how realistic are they? To what extent do they genuinely discuss the systemic causes of ecological problems and develop a framework for struggling against them? That is the essential question.




Organizing such gatherings and discussing climate problems is positive. But how will these issues be discussed? The summit is being held in Antalya, Turkey. Some of the greatest ecological problems are caused by construction and pollution. These problems exist in Antalya, throughout Kurdistan and across Turkey. People are already engaged in ecological struggles everywhere. There are mining companies, hydroelectric power plants, dams and numerous other projects. Air pollution has reached alarming levels, and living beings are being destroyed. All these developments now pose serious threats not only to human life but to the lives of all living beings. If this continues, the planet itself will not have much time left. Why? Because the issue is not simply whether I throw rubbish somewhere. Of course, this is a moral and ethical matter. I should not litter. I should think and live ecologically in every aspect of my life. But the global climate crisis is not caused merely by an individual throwing rubbish on the ground. There is a much deeper systemic problem. We call this industrialism. These are the consequences of capitalist capital using technology in a manner completely detached from morality and conscience.




Will COP31 take a position against industrialism? Will it take a position against mining companies? Will restrictions be imposed on them? Will the views of local communities be taken into account? I consider this extremely important. This is a fundamental aspect of our strategy for democratic society, the democratic republic and democratic integration. A democratic society is one in which people organize locally and make decisions concerning their own lives. For example, a community should be able to say, "We do not permit this mining company to operate here." The people and women living in that area should be able to say, "We do not permit this because it leaves us without a living environment." Is there a system that allows them to make such decisions? Is there a legal framework recognizing this right? There is not.




Summits and conferences of this kind should therefore provide opportunities for local communities and local democracy to express themselves, present their views and make decisions that are respected. Instead, a certain number of people gather, meet and discuss these matters. But what benefit does this bring to the people living in the affected areas? For example, climate change has caused severe drought and famine in parts of Africa. Epidemics are also a serious problem. Women bear the heaviest burden of these consequences.




It also lowers the age of marriage.




Yes. In Africa, poverty drives families to sell young girls, including children, or forces them into early marriages. Rape and sexual harassment are connected to these circumstances. Women are responsible for household care and looking after children. Many women have to travel long distances to collect water, and dozens, even hundreds, are subjected to rape during these journeys. Poverty is also increasing dramatically. There are deaths caused by diseases and complications related to childbirth and women's reproductive health. These conditions have severe consequences for women, children and society as a whole. If we consider the situation globally, we are exposed to numerous chemicals simply by breathing.




These substances cause cancer and other serious illnesses, threatening physical and mental health. We are facing a very serious assault. It is an assault produced by industrialism. We frequently speak of the Third World War. When people hear the wes fighting one another, with thousands of soldiers on battlefields. But another important dimension of the Third World War is industrial warfare. It has not been named as such. You cannot see it, and there are no soldiers standing before you. Yet air pollution, climate disruption and broader ecological problems cause millions of deaths. Some are documented, while others remain unrecorded. If this is not war, what is it?




Climate and ecological discussions must therefore also be approached as a struggle against a form of warfare. They must be taken extremely seriously. Societies themselves must be at the center of these discussions. Rather than speaking only of Indigenous peoples, I would emphasize that people living in their own communities must discuss these problems and develop their own solutions. The people living there, including women and children, must have the power to make decisions. They must be able to take a position, organize protests and develop practical measures to protect their lives. Establishing this decision-making power is extremely important. If this summit genuinely discusses the fundamental problems, develops solutions and establishes plans to implement them, then it can have meaning. Otherwise, it will amount to little more than an exercise in disguising reality, concealing responsibility and delaying action.

title: YJK-E and KON-MED: Justice for Vesile Akın
content:
The Union of Kurdish Women in Germany (YJK-E) and the Confederation of Democratic Kurdish Communities in Germany (KON-MED) said in a written statement: “We learned with profound anger and sorrow that Vesile Akın, a 35-year-old mother of five, was stabbed to death on 9 November in the German city of Düren by her estranged husband.”




The statement continued: “Only recently, we raised our voices against the murder of Enda in Coesfeld. Today, once again, we are witnessing a woman being deprived of her right to life. The names and cities change, but male violence and the suffering endured by women remain the same.”




The statement, which emphasised that “violence against women is not only a women’s issue but a problem affecting society as a whole”, continued: “The murder of a woman is also an attack on the future of society and on our shared life together. According to information reported in the media, Vesile Akın had previously contacted the police, citing threats against her, and had requested protection. It has been reported that the threats continued despite restraining measures being imposed. Yet Vesile could not be protected. Today, five children have been left without their mother.




When a woman reports that she is being threatened, asks for help and turns to the state for protection, what more needs to happen to prevent her from being murdered?

content:
According to information received from the region, the areas around the villages of Henarşîxan and Gagal, near Marivan (Merîwan), have been subjected to heavy weapons fire and artillery shelling since early this morning.

title: Murder of Vesile Akın leaves five children without their mother
content:
On 9 November, Vesile Akın, 35, was attacked with a knife on Bismarck Street in Düren, in Germany’s North Rhine-Westphalia state, by her 39-year-old husband, Ferhat Akın. The couple had been living separately due to severe marital problems. Vesile Akın, a mother of five originally from Mardin (Mêrdîn), died in hospital from her severe injuries. Ferhat Akın, who fled the scene, was subsequently caught by police.




She had previously requested protection




It was reported that Vesile Akın had contacted the police and requested protection because she had been threatened by her husband. Reports indicate that police had previously taken action against him due to their marital problems and his threats, and that restraining measures had been imposed. However, the woman reportedly continued to be harassed.




Despite her previous complaints and the protective measures reportedly put in place, Vesile Akın was murdered. Her death has raised serious questions about the effectiveness of security measures and mechanisms designed to protect women from violence.

title: Fuel crisis in Kobanê takes heavy toll on residents
content:
The increase in fuel prices across Syria has deepened the economic crisis in Kobanê. Following the rise in fuel costs, prices for food, transport and other essential goods have also increased. In the city, where the cost of many products has doubled or tripled, people's purchasing power continues to decline, while concerns over heating are growing ahead of the winter months.




Rising fuel prices are particularly affecting traders and small business owners involved in commerce and production. Higher transportation and production costs are being passed on to consumers through increased prices. Meanwhile, difficulties in obtaining diesel have forced residents to turn to electric heaters for warmth, placing additional pressure on the electricity network.




Speaking to ANF, residents and shopkeepers in Kobanê said they would face numerous difficulties this winter. They stated that although the amount of fuel being distributed had not changed, the prices of almost every product they purchased had increased.




The cost of transporting a truckload of goods has doubled




Kamıran Baz, a business owner in Kobanê, said there had been serious difficulties in obtaining fuel this year. He explained that residents struggling to find diesel had begun purchasing electric heaters, which was also having a negative impact on the electricity network.

title: YRK Commander pays tribute to the martyrs: We will ensure that their goals are achieved
content:
On 5 November, the Press Center of the People’s Defense Forces (HPG) announced the identities of nine guerrilla fighters from Rojhilat who lost their lives between 2006 and 2022 in various regions of Kurdistan.




On 9 November, the HPG Press Center announced the identities of 15 guerrilla fighters from the Maku city of East Kurdistan who joined the Kurdish freedom movement and lost their lives at different times and in various locations between 2007 and 2024.




Speaking to ANF, Şiyar Şevger, a member of the Command Council of the East Kurdistan Units (Yekîneyên Rojhilatê Kurdistan, YRK), made the following remarks in memory of the martyrs:










https://video.anf-news2.com/live/firat/2ff679a0_20261111095750_2026-11-11-habermerkezi-siyar-sevger-yrk-komutanligi-uyesi-nirxandin-1.mp4










“I dedicate this process that has been initiated to all our martyrs. I commemorate all our martyrs across the four parts of Kurdistan and bow respectfully before their memory.




Recently, the names of martyrs from East Kurdistan (Rojhilat), as well as followers of Apo from Rojhilat who fell in North Kurdistan (Bakur), have been announced. These martyrs have fostered a spirit of unity among Kurds. The martyrs have consolidated the paradigm put forward by Leader Apo [Abdullah Öcalan] to defend the Kurdish people. The martyrs are leading the way for humanity in the Middle East. The paradigm they have championed is intended to serve all humanity and the unity of the Kurdish people.




In fact, the martyrs have enabled us to understand ourselves and our history. More importantly, they have helped us recognize our enemies who have carried out massacres against our people. It is thanks to Leader Apo’s ideas and philosophy, together with the sacrifices of the martyrs, that we have reached this point today. Their goals will undoubtedly be achieved, and the struggle they waged will not have been in vain.




As the people of Rojhilat, we must honor and stand by the martyrs with great pride. Regardless of which city or village they come from, all our people, families and patriots must rally around the families of the martyrs, come together and show solidarity with them. They must not be left alone. The pain of every family is the pain of all Kurds. Our families have paid a heavy price and sacrificed their loved ones. Their grief is immense. Therefore, no one should leave them alone. We owe to the martyrs who gave their lives to defend our honor.




There are many martyrs from Sine in particular. There are martyrs from our other cities as well, but Sine is a city of resistance and revolution. All our people in Sine must unite around these families and stand by them. We have nothing to fear.




The role of our mothers in this revolution is particularly important. Everyone must stand by the mothers who raised their children and entrusted them to this movement. Mothers are the hope of the Kurdish people and the peoples of the Middle East. As long as our mothers are alive, Kurdistan will undoubtedly achieve success.




To the martyrs whose names have been announced so far, particularly those from Rojhilat and the other parts of Kurdistan, and to all the martyrs whose names will be announced in the future, we make this pledge: We will certainly uphold their struggle and ensure that their goals are achieved.




Recently, some reports have appeared in the media questioning why the names of our martyrs have been announced so late. I believe all our people know that we are a movement engaged in struggle in the mountains of Kurdistan. The Apoist Movement has fought against the occupiers of our homeland everywhere, including in the mountains. It has carried out this struggle in the face of all kinds of technology, weapons and chemical weapons.




Amid such intense warfare, there was no opportunity to announce the deaths of our comrades in a timely manner. A peace process began following Leader Apo’s call. This peace process also marks a transition to a new phase of struggle. This transition has created an opportunity to announce the names of the martyrs. The names of martyrs from Bakur, Rojava and Bashur had been announced previously. In recent days, the names of the martyrs from Rojhilat have also been announced. This is the reason for the delay in announcing their deaths.




Our people must understand that all other speculation is part of a special warfare strategy. They should not give credence to such speculation. The Apoist Movement is not that kind of movement; everything it does is transparent. We are a people’s movement. The aim of special warfare is to divide the Kurdish people.




Young people and intellectuals should respond to these claims on various platforms. Our people’s struggle will surely succeed.”

title: The importance of Kurdish democracy
content:
While the Kurdish people and their friends everywhere have been eagerly anticipating “national unity,” news that even the existing administration in Southern Kurdistan has split into two has, frankly, caused considerable astonishment. Moreover, it has provoked significant anger and backlash. At the same time, it has prompted everyone to reassess their expectations and views and question the reasons behind this situation.




Yet the call made in recent months by Kurdish People’s Leader Abdullah Öcalan for the establishment of a “Democratic Unity Government” had generated considerable hope and expectations among the public. National unity was also the most widely discussed issue in the Kurdish press and public discourse. Although everyone expressed it from their own perspective, the need for national unity was the issue on which there was the greatest consensus. Both political awareness and collective sentiment reflected this need.




Admittedly, the persistent fragmentation among Kurdish principalities throughout history left those who contemplated and advocated national unity with little hope or confidence. This situation has been a constant source of criticism and frustration. The experience of Southern Kurdistan offered little reason for optimism in this regard.




Although the Kurdistan National Congress (KNK) was established a quarter of a century ago, it has been unable to fulfill its role or function effectively because certain parties have refused to participate and have obstructed its work. Despite nearly two years having passed since the elections in Southern Kurdistan, parliament had not convened, and a new government had not been formed.




Undoubtedly, all of this led to disappointment among Kurdish society and its supporters, weakening their faith in the prospect of national unity. Nevertheless, the Kurdish people remained determined and steadfast in their pursuit of unity, aware of the immense importance of Kurdish national unity for the Kurds, the Middle East and humanity as a whole. Considerable knowledge and understanding have been developed on this issue, accompanied by an increasingly strong sense of its significance. Accordingly, the Kurdish people never abandoned their demand for unity, while continuously questioning the factors obstructing it and seeking ways to overcome them.




The stance and efforts of the Kurdish Freedom Movement on this issue have always been positive. In fact, the movement has consistently devoted a substantial proportion of its resources to efforts aimed at achieving national unity. Abdullah Öcalan’s creative approach and extensive efforts, in particular, have always been worthy of recognition.




Indeed, it was Öcalan who carried out all the preparations for the establishment of the Kurdistan National Congress. Had he not been subjected to an international conspiracy, his aim was to organize the national congress under favorable conditions and through effective methods, assume its leadership and ensure that all activities were coordinated at the highest level through this institution. This was also the primary reason he chose to travel to Europe when confronted with a conspiratorial campaign against him.




This leadership project was thwarted by the October 9 and February 15 attacks of the international conspiracy. Although the KNK was subsequently established on the basis of those preparations and has continued its activities for a quarter of a century, its achievements have fallen far short of realizing Öcalan’s vision.




Why, then, has Kurdish national unity not been achieved despite so much discussion and demand, and why has the KNK not been made effective? In fact, this is one of the most important questions facing the Kurds today, perhaps even the most important, and one that must be answered accurately and adequately. The current developments in Southern Kurdistan provide an opportunity to raise this question courageously and seek answers. The discussions conducted in this context are marked by a considerable lack of courage and an overly superficial approach. Moreover, the rhetorical grandstanding of nationalist perspectives prevents these discussions from becoming comprehensive and in-depth.




According to the nationalist perspective, such discussions are essentially unnecessary because the national leadership of the Kurds is embodied by the Barzanî family! From this standpoint, national unity means rallying around the Barzanî family! Furthermore, Kurds are supposedly a homogeneous society, meaning that different classes and social groups do not exist within Kurdish society! Consequently, there can be no leaders or organizations representing such groups, and seeking them out is considered both wrong and dangerous!




It is abundantly clear that this mentality is the primary obstacle that blocks discussions and efforts toward national unity from the very outset. This understanding is fundamentally flawed and has failed to produce solutions for decades. It is neither democratic nor pluralistic. On closer examination, it is a monolithic and anti-democratic approach. It is also rooted in family and dynastic rule, leaves the door open to religious fundamentalism, and is sexist and based on male domination.




We can therefore identify the insufficient development of Kurdish democracy and the prevalence of anti-democratic attitudes and approaches in Kurdish politics as the primary reasons why Kurdish national unity has not been achieved despite widespread demands and extensive discussion. These attitudes and approaches give rise to monolithic, domination-oriented and authoritarian politics. They obstruct the development of democratic principles and forms of governance, allowing a system based on family and party interests to prevail. They also promote a monolithic and centralized approach to governance, leaving little room for the development and effective functioning of local administrations, which are among the key measures of democracy. The influence of this mentality and governing style, prevalent in Southern Kurdistan, is not confined to that region alone but extends across all of Kurdistan.




It is clear that achieving national unity and advancing democratization are as inseparable as flesh and nail. Therefore, those who genuinely seek national unity must also demand democracy, and indeed, they must prioritize it. Only a system of governance based on strong local administrations, women’s freedom and ecological living can truly foster unity.




Notably, such an approach to local governance does not exist in Southern Kurdistan, or administrations themselves become factors contributing to division. Yet establishing strong, democratically elected local and regional administrations in every city would both democratize the overall system of governance and facilitate its functioning. The geographical and social structure of Southern Kurdistan is particularly well suited to such a model of governance.




Therefore, those who criticize the division that has emerged in Southern Kurdistan and call for unity must, if they are to remain consistent and achieve practical solutions, first and foremost demand genuine democratization and actively struggle for it. There is no other way to achieve national unity. Historical realities clearly demonstrate this. It is evident that demanding national unity without also demanding democracy and engaging in the struggle for democratization will only serve nationalism and ultimately fail. This, in turn, is the fundamental source of the persistent lack of solutions.




It is abundantly clear that a freedom-based solution to the Kurdish question can only be achieved through Kurdish unity, which in turn depends on the development of a highly advanced, functioning Kurdish democracy that serves as a model for others. The development and effective functioning of Kurdish democracy would not only provide the foundation for Kurdish national unity but also form the backbone of democratization in the Middle East by paving the way for and realizing a freedom-based and democratic solution to the Kurdish question.




It is clear that a Democratic Union of the Middle East can only be achieved through Kurdish democratization and unity. This would also represent a major contribution to the advancement of democracy on a global scale.




Therefore, genuine and effective Kurdish democratization is not only indispensable for the Kurds themselves but also of vital importance to the peoples of the region and the world through its contribution to broader democratization. Accordingly, nothing can be more meaningful or important than working and struggling to develop such a democracy. The creation of such a Kurdish democracy is the key to resolving all these issues. This means that, for the Kurds, the central challenge and the most meaningful fight is the struggle for genuine democracy.




Source: Yeni Özgür Politika

title: Families of fallen guerrilla fighters demand access to their graves
content:
Nearly three decades after the deaths of their loved ones, families of fallen Kurdish guerrilla fighters gathered for a two-day commemoration. Organized by MEBYA-DER (Association for Solidarity, Assistance, Unity and Culture of Families Who Lost Relatives in the Cradle of Civilizations), the event honored 19 people who lost their lives in the Kurdish freedom struggle during the 1990s. For many families, it was the first opportunity in years to mourn their children and siblings together. Their most important demand remains unfulfilled: they want to know where the remains of their loved ones are located and to be able to visit their graves.













The families linked their commemoration to the hope of an end to the decades-long war. They emphasized that the ongoing Peace and Democratic Society Process must produce concrete results. They said they did not want other families to suffer the same loss or spend decades living without certainty about the fate of their loved ones.










https://video.anf-news2.com/live/firat/6a4204e4_20261110234226_2026-11-11-amed-filiz-bayram_mehmet-emin-kilic_seniha-yolay-sehit-aileleri-sehit-anma_1.mp4










“As a mother, this is my only demand”




Seniha Yolay is among the mothers who still do not know where their children are buried. Her son Şahabettin Yolay, who went by the name Siyabend in the guerrilla movement, joined the PKK in 1994 and fell in 1998. She had not seen him since he left home. It was only years later that the family learned of his death, without ever receiving further information about his whereabouts.




“My son left the house saying he was going to school. He never came back. In 1998, we learned that he had lost his life. Since then, we have heard nothing more about him. I kept asking questions, but no one could tell me anything. Today, after 30 years, we held a memorial service for him. I want to know where my son’s grave is. As a mother, this is my only demand,” Yolay said.













Yolay stated that being able to mourn her son alongside other families now held great significance for her. For many years, she added, the families had been left alone with their grief and uncertainty.




“Being able to mourn them, even after all these years, is very important to us. The fighting has continued for decades. This peace process must achieve its goal, and no more bodies should be brought home. We families want peace. We do not want anyone else to suffer or lose their life.”




Yolay emphasized that the families had never forgotten their loved ones, despite the many years that had passed.




“This bloodshed has continued for 50 years. It must stop. From now on, people should no longer have to live in fear of receiving another news of death.”













“We want them to have a grave”




Filiz Bayram also attended the commemoration. Her brother Meki Bayram, known by the name Çiya Dilbirîn, joined the PKK in 1992 and was martyred in 1994. The passing decades have done nothing to diminish the family’s memories of him or their grief.




“My brother is gone. I hope that from now on, no one else will lose their life. The peace process must finally be realized through concrete steps. No one should have to suffer anymore. Enough is enough,” Bayram said.




She noted that the collective memorial service had brought back memories that remained as vivid as ever for the families, despite the passage of time.













“After 33 years, we are mourning here and shedding tears once again. To us, everything feels as though it happened yesterday. No mother, no sister ever forgets their fallen loved ones or those days. We have forgotten neither the suffering we endured nor the people we lost.”




Bayram called for an end to the armed conflict and a peace process that would go beyond political statements.













“The war must finally end, and the sounds of tanks and artillery must fall silent. We have endured everything imaginable over the years. Now, peace must finally come to this country. Genuine peace.”




Above all, however, she said she wanted to have a place where she could commemorate her brother.




“We want them to have graves. And if there are no graves, we at least want to know where their remains are. We want to be able to stand at their graves, even if only once. This is not just our demand, but the demand of every family in the same situation.”













Many families have still been unable to say goodbye




Mehmet Emin Kılıç, a board member of MEBYA-DER, emphasized the particular significance of such commemorations for families who have been denied the opportunity to say goodbye for decades. He noted that numerous families lost their children during the war without subsequently receiving confirmation of their deaths or information about the whereabouts of their remains.













“These families lost their children 30 years ago and heard nothing more about them for years. Even today, there are relatives who have been unable to mourn their children,” Kılıç explained.




Even though memorial services can now be held, the central question remains unanswered for many families; they still do not know where their loved ones are buried, Kılıç said.













“The families still cannot find peace because they continue to seek answers about the whereabouts of their children’s remains and graves. Today, we organized a commemoration, but the relatives have repeatedly raised their demand to know where the graves are.”




Kılıç pointed out that decades of uncertainty have made it difficult for many families to come to terms with and process the deaths of their children and siblings. They must therefore be given the opportunity to locate and visit their loved ones’ graves, he added.




“The families’ primary demand is to be able to visit their children’s graves. Even if only a single bone remains, we want to go there and see it. Families must be given the opportunity to locate and visit the graves,” Kılıç concluded.

title: Freedom for Abdullah Öcalan vigil in Strasbourg enters its 750th week
content:
The freedom for Abdullah Öcalan vigil, held in Strasbourg, France, since June 25, 2012, has entered its 750th week. Through the protest, which has continued for more than 14 years, participants are demanding the physical freedom of the Kurdish leader who has been incarcerated in İmralı Island Prison since 1999.




During the new week of action, Tori Orak, Kurbet Dağ and Adalet Rojhilat from the Liège region of Belgium have taken over the vigil.




In a joint statement, the activists commemorated the fallen members of the Kurdish freedom movement whose deaths have been announced in recent months. They reaffirmed their remembrance with the slogan “Şehîd namirin” (Martyrs are immortal).




Call for support for the peace process




The activists called on the families of the martyrs and the entire Kurdish population to support the Peace and Democratic Society Process initiated by Abdullah Öcalan. They emphasized that they wanted to see Öcalan free and once again among the people.




The group said they had taken responsibility for the vigil this week as representatives of the Kurdish community in Liège.




“We hope that the entire Kurdish people will embrace this process, organize themselves and prepare for the developments ahead,” the activists said.

author: Unknown
title: Nine Kurds, including seven political activists, remain forcibly disappeared in Iran
content:
Nine Kurdish citizens, including seven political activists, remain forcibly disappeared months or years after their arrests by the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) Intelligence Organisation and the Ministry of Intelligence of the Islamic Republic of Iran.




They are Osman Mameh, Arman Khalegh-Panah, Edris Feqhi, Mohsen Ghaderi, Sara Rashidi Kachalanlou, Zahra Pir-Dehghan, Parvin (Akhtar) Rasegh Ghezelbash, Khaled Barzanji and Sirwan Habibi.




Seven are members of the Kurdistan Free Life Party (PJAK) or the Free Women’s Society of Eastern Kurdistan (KJAR). Their arbitrary arrests took place in Bukan, Saqqez, Baneh, Orumiyeh, Paveh and Kamyaran from August 2021 onwards, without minimum legal safeguards.




The Kurdistan Human Rights Network (KHRN) has established that security and judicial authorities verbally informed the families of Ghaderi and Khalegh-Panah that the two men had been killed.




Neither family has received official documentation or a death certificate substantiating the claim, and neither man’s body has been returned.




The other families have also received no clear answers about the fate or whereabouts of their loved ones, despite repeatedly approaching security and judicial authorities. The authorities concerned have denied knowing about the arrests.




All nine have been denied access to independent lawyers of their own choosing and all contact and visits with their families since their arrests.




In light of the evidence and circumstances of each case, KHRN considers the authorities’ refusal to acknowledge the arrests or disclose the individuals’ fate and whereabouts to constitute the crime of enforced disappearance.




These continuing violations affect both the disappeared individuals and their families, who are denied the right to know the truth about what has happened to their loved ones and where they are held.




Given the continuing nature of enforced disappearance and the international obligations of the Islamic Republic of Iran, KHRN calls on the international community to pursue these cases urgently and exert effective, meaningful pressure on the authorities to disclose the disappeared individuals’ fate and whereabouts and ensure accountability.




This appeal is directed particularly to the UN Human Rights Council, the UN Special Rapporteur on the situation of human rights in the Islamic Republic of Iran, the UN Special Rapporteur on torture and other cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment or punishment, and the UN Working Group on Enforced or Involuntary Disappearances.




KHRN calls for:




– Increased international pressure on the responsible authorities

: Use official communications, public statements and diplomatic and human rights mechanisms to require the authorities of the Islamic Republic of Iran to acknowledge responsibility for the arrests, disclose the disappeared individuals’ fate and end their enforced disappearance.




– Guarantees for the liberty, safety and rights of the disappeared individuals:

Demand an immediate end to secret detention, disclosure of places of detention, access to independent lawyers of the individuals’ own choosing and their families, and judicial and independent oversight.




– Independent and effective investigations:

 Demand prompt, independent, impartial and effective investigations into the arrests, transfers and secret detention, including the roles of IRGC Intelligence Organisation and Ministry of Intelligence forces and contradictory claims that some individuals may have been killed.




– Support for families and their right to the truth:

 Require documented and transparent information about the disappeared individuals’ fate, an end to threats, intimidation and pressure against families, and guarantees of their right to seek the truth and access justice.




– Accountability and an end to impunity:

 Identify and hold accountable everyone who ordered, carried out or bears official responsibility for these continuing enforced disappearances, through investigations and prosecutions consistent with fair-trial standards.




Names and details of the disappeared individuals:




Edris Feqhi




Edris Feqhi, a Kurdish political activist from Sanandaj and a PJAK member, was arrested on 24 July 2021 after being wounded in an IRGC ambush in the mountains around Bukan.




KHRN’s investigations indicate that IRGC forces shot him in the leg. He initially managed to hide, but forces from the IRGC’s Hamzeh Seyyed al-Shohada Headquarters arrested him while he was still wounded following a large deployment to the area.




He was taken first to the IRGC-run Arefian Hospital in Orumiyeh and then to the IRGC Intelligence Organisation’s detention facility in the city.




On 27 July 2021, the state-affiliated Tasnim news agency, citing the Hamzeh Seyyed al-Shohada Headquarters, reported that two members of a “Kurdish party” had been killed and a wounded member arrested.




PJAK initially announced on 6 August 2021 that Feqhi and fellow member Mohsen Ghaderi had been killed in an armed clash with IRGC forces near Bukan. It later issued another statement saying that Ghaderi was alive and Feqhi had been arrested after being wounded.




At least two people held at the IRGC Intelligence Organisation’s detention facility in Orumiyeh in autumn 2021 previously told KHRN that they had seen Feqhi in its infirmary.




Despite this evidence, no reliable information about his fate or whereabouts has emerged since.




Osman Mameh




Osman Mameh, a Kurdish man from Bukan, was arrested by “security” forces near the city’s Welfare Organisation office on 18 November 2022 while returning home during the “Women, Life, Freedom” uprising.




His fate and whereabouts remain unknown despite his family’s repeated enquiries with security and judicial authorities in Bukan and Orumiyeh over the intervening years.




The Ministry of Intelligence office in Bukan has repeatedly summoned members of his family, interrogating and threatening them over their efforts to publicise his disappearance.




Although Ministry of Intelligence forces claimed to know nothing about his fate, they referred during these interrogations to photographs and videos on his mobile phone and to “attempts to discover and sell antiquities”.




The pressure forced Mameh’s wife and child to leave Iran.




KHRN submitted his case to the UN Working Group on Enforced or Involuntary Disappearances. After examining it, the Working Group transmitted the case to the government of the Islamic Republic of Iran on 14 November 2024, seeking clarification of his fate and whereabouts.




His family has still received no information regarding Mameh’s fate or condition.




Mohsen Ghaderi




Mohsen Ghaderi, a political activist from Bukan and a PJAK member, was arrested by IRGC Intelligence Organisation forces in the Hangeh-ye Zhal border area of Baneh County on 22 June 2025.




During summer 2025, the organisation summoned his family twice and told them that he had been killed in a military clash in the same area in late June that year. It also prohibited the family from holding any memorial ceremony.




However, a kolbar arrested alongside Ghaderi gave the family a different account after being provisionally released on bail following three months of arbitrary detention.




He said no military clash had occurred and that IRGC Intelligence Organisation forces had arrested them together and taken them first to an IRGC detention facility in Baneh and, a few hours later, to the organisation’s Shahramfar detention facility in Sanandaj.




The kolbar was provisionally released on bail after three months of interrogation, once it had been established that he had no connection to Ghaderi.




The family’s enquiries in Baneh also indicated that no military clash had taken place in Hangeh-ye Zhal on the date given by the IRGC Intelligence Organisation. Several local residents confirmed that security forces had arrested two people at that location on that date.




Ghaderi was last seen at the Shahramfar detention facility in September 2025. No reliable information about his condition or whereabouts has emerged since, although some unofficial sources have suggested that he may have been transferred to an IRGC Intelligence Organisation detention facility in Orumiyeh.




Security authorities had previously told his family that he had been killed in August 2021, following a clash in the mountains around the village of Alamabad in Bukan.




During that incident, Ghaderi and Edris Feqhi had been caught in an ambush by forces of the IRGC’s Hamzeh Seyyed al-Shohada Headquarters.




PJAK initially reported that both had been killed, but later announced that Ghaderi was alive and Feqhi had been arrested after being wounded.




A video subsequently emerged in which Ghaderi confirmed that he was alive.




Despite the authorities’ renewed verbal claim of his death in 2025, his family has received no official evidence substantiating it, and his fate remains unknown.




Sara Rashidi Kachalanlou




Sara Rashidi Kachalanlou, a 33-year-old Kurdish political activist from Maku and a KJAR member, was arrested near Paveh by IRGC Intelligence Organisation forces on 11 January 2026, during the protests.




She was travelling in a passenger car from Kermanshah to Paveh when “security” forces arrested her without a warrant.




She was taken to the IRGC Intelligence Organisation’s Nabi Akram detention facility in Kermanshah’s Naft Square. No clear, reliable information about her fate or whereabouts has emerged since.




Her family has repeatedly approached security and judicial authorities in Kermanshah over the past several months, but has received no clear answer about her arrest or fate.




Arman Khalegh-Panah




Arman Khalegh-Panah, a 35-year-old Kurdish man from Saqqez, was arrested at the entrance to the city on 8 March 2026 after IRGC forces shot and wounded him.




He was travelling in a private car with Sheikh Zahed Shahabi when security forces surrounded the vehicle and opened fire without warning. Two bullets struck Khalegh-Panah below the waist.




His family has repeatedly approached judicial and security authorities in Saqqez, Sanandaj and Tehran, but has received no clear or satisfactory answer about his condition or whereabouts.




During one of these visits, the Saqqez prosecutor reportedly told the family verbally that Khalegh-Panah had been killed. However, the family has received neither a death certificate nor a forensic report, and his body has not been returned.




An enquiry with the Civil Registration Organisation on 3 October 2026 showed that he remained registered as “alive”.




No official evidence substantiating reports of his death has been provided, and his fate and whereabouts remain unknown.




Khaled Barzanji




Khaled Barzanji, a Kurdish political activist from Sanandaj and a PJAK member, was arrested by IRGC forces on 10 July 2026 at a house on an orchard property in the village of Vash Tappeh (Uch Tappeh) in Bukan County.




Two other people, reportedly owners of the orchard, were arrested alongside him. Their identities remain unknown, but available information indicates that one was provisionally released on bail after a period in detention.




Barzanji has been denied access to an independent lawyer of his own choosing, telephone contact and family visits since his arrest.




Despite his family’s repeated enquiries with judicial and security authorities in Bukan and Orumiyeh, officials have denied any knowledge of his arrest, whereabouts or health.




PJAK confirmed his arrest in a statement on 22 October 2026, saying that no information about his fate had been obtained.




Zahra Pir-Dehghan




Zahra Pir-Dehghan, a 32-year-old Kurdish activist from Chaldoran and a KJAR member, was arrested by IRGC Intelligence Organisation forces in Orumiyeh on 25 June 2026.




KHRN’s findings indicate that, following her arbitrary arrest, she was held for a period at an IRGC Intelligence Organisation detention facility in Tabriz before being transferred to a secret detention facility run by the organisation in Orumiyeh.




In a statement issued in October 2026, KJAR identified her as a member and said she had been in Orumiyeh to carry out political activities relating to women.




Her family has repeatedly approached judicial authorities, the Ministry of Intelligence office and the IRGC Intelligence Organisation in Orumiyeh over the past several months to seek information about her situation and whereabouts, but has received no answer about her fate.




Parvin (Akhtar) Rasegh Ghezelbash




Parvin (Akhtar) Rasegh Ghezelbash, a 33-year-old Kurdish woman from Maku and a KJAR member, was arrested by IRGC Intelligence Organisation forces in Orumiyeh on 28 June 2026.




KJAR identified her as a member in a statement issued in October 2026, saying she had been in Orumiyeh to carry out political activities relating to women.




Her family has repeatedly approached judicial authorities, the Ministry of Intelligence office and the IRGC Intelligence Organisation in Orumiyeh over the past several months.




Security and judicial authorities have refused to provide an explanation of her fate or whereabouts.




Sirwan Habibi




Sirwan Habibi, a Kurdish political activist from Sanandaj and a PJAK member known within the party as “Aram Sine”, was arrested by Ministry of Intelligence forces in Kamyaran’s Besat neighbourhood on 9 September 2026.




Eyewitnesses said dozens of unmarked Ministry of Intelligence vehicles with tinted windows had surrounded several streets in the neighbourhood on the evening of 8 September.




At around 1.00 am local time, security forces pursued Habibi as he rode a motorcycle. Witnesses said one of their vehicles struck the motorcycle at high speed, seriously injuring him.




After the motorcycle overturned, the forces violently arrested him.




Several bystanders called the police emergency number, 110, and approached to help, but plainclothes forces dispersed them by firing into the air.




One witness said a police patrol vehicle also arrived, apparently unaware of what was happening. Security forces blocked its path and forced the officers to leave, describing the matter as “security”-related.




Witnesses said Habibi resisted arrest, but the forces beat him, covered his face with a cloth and took him away in a Samand car.




His family has repeatedly approached the Ministry of Intelligence’s office and judicial authorities in Kamyaran and Sanandaj, but these institutions have denied knowing about his arrest.




Enquiries have also indicated that no identifiable judicial case has been registered for him in either city’s courts.




In a statement on 14 September 2026, PJAK said Habibi had been arrested while carrying out a party assignment and had been unarmed.




Despite eyewitness testimony, no security or judicial institution has acknowledged responsibility for his detention.




His whereabouts and physical condition remain unknown, raising particular concern given the serious injuries he sustained when the Ministry of Intelligence vehicle struck his motorcycle.

title: Protests in several cities: Guarantee the right to life of ill prisoners
content:
Human rights organizations and political initiatives have protested in several cities across Turkey and Northern Kurdistan against ongoing human rights violations in Turkish prisons. The demonstrations highlighted demands for medical care for prisoners with health conditions, the release of seriously ill inmates and an investigation into the death of Tuncer Sağlam, who died at Sincan Prison in Ankara on November 7. Protests demanding the release of ill prisoners had already taken place in several cities the previous day.




The organizations also called for an end to the obstruction of medical treatment and the implementation of legal measures adopted as part of the Peace and Democratic Society Process.




Izmir: Criticism of delayed releases




Outside the courthouse in the Bayraklı district of Izmir, Ayfer Yıldırım, Co-Chair of EGE TUHAYDER (Association for Solidarity and Cooperation with Families of Prisoners and Convicts in the Aegean Region), stated that Tuncer Sağlam had not received adequate medical treatment despite suspected pancreatic cancer. Because no definitive diagnosis was established, he was not released, Yıldırım said and called for an investigation into the responsibility of the prison administration, judicial authorities and healthcare institutions involved.

title: Kurdish political prisoner sentenced to 15 years in prison and fined in Iran
content:
Branch 26 of the Islamic Revolutionary Court in Tehran has sentenced Kurdish political prisoner Ahmad Tamouei to a total of 15 years in prison and a fine of 12.5 billion rials on charges of “assembly and collusion against national security” and “carrying and possessing weapons,” the Kurdistan Human Rights Network (KHRN) has reported.




The court issued the sentences in recent months against Tamouei, who is held in Greater Tehran Central Penitentiary.




Under Article 134 of the Islamic Penal Code, which governs sentencing for multiple offences, only the most severe punishment, 10 years’ imprisonment and the fine, will be enforceable.




Tamouei, a political activist from Salmas, had previously spent 14 years in Orumiyeh Central Prison before his release in 2021.




He then moved to Tehran, where he worked as a driver for the ride-hailing service Snapp.




In the early hours of 23 February 2026, Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) forces violently arrested him without a warrant at a checkpoint on Kargar-e Jonoubi Street in Tehran and took him to a security detention facility.




IRGC forces subjected him to severe physical and psychological torture for one day before transferring him to Ward 2A of Evin Prison on 24 February.




Following the outbreak of war, Tamouei and several other detainees were moved from the ward to a secret security detention facility in easte

author: Unknown
title: Çiğdem Doğu: AKP's delaying tactics pose serious risks
content:
Kurdistan Women's Communities (KJK) Executive Council member Çiğdem Doğu appeared on a special program broadcast by Medya Haber television, where she discussed the Peace and Democratic Society Process initiated by Leader Apo (Abdullah Öcalan) and violence against women.




Çiğdem Doğu emphasized that the Peace and Democratic Society Process cannot be reduced to disarmament alone, arguing that a democratic solution to the Kurdish question and the democratization of Turkey must be addressed together. She stressed the importance of recognizing Leader Apo's role as coordinator of peace and political participation, saying that transparency, mutual dialogue and concrete steps are essential for building social support for peace.




Çiğdem Doğu also called on women to take action ahead of November 25, the International Day for the Elimination of Violence against Women. She emphasized that violence against women cannot be explained as a series of isolated incidents but is produced by the male-dominated system. She stressed that women must go beyond resisting violence by building free lives, organizing themselves and developing self-defense mechanisms. Çiğdem Doğu said that women must establish control over their lives in economic, social, cultural and physical spheres, calling for November to be dedicated to the struggle for women's freedom under the slogan, "Now is the time for women, now is the time for women's self-defense."




Çiğdem Doğu also discussed the youth movements emerging in different countries, describing them as expressions of significant social opposition to the existing political system. Citing the student movement in Serbia, she said that young people no longer accept the capitalist way of life or the existing order and have the potential to bring about profound change by joining forces with society.




Abdullah Öcalan took a step by initiating the Peace and Democratic Society Process and assumed full responsibility. However, the Turkish state has yet to take any concrete steps in response. There has been discussion in certain circles, but nothing tangible has emerged. Let me also mention that reports suggest Öcalan has been moved to a new location. Yet the Turkish state has made no official announcement concerning Öcalan's coordinating role. Could you provide some information about this?




Before answering, I would like to mention that we have entered November, and the anniversary of November 27 is approaching. On this occasion, I congratulate President Apo on the anniversary of November 27 and extend my congratulations to our people. Throughout our history of struggle, we have lost thousands of martyrs and martyred comrades. Each of these martyrs played an enormously significant role in affirming the existence of the Kurdish people and opening the path toward freedom and a free life. They opened this path for us and showed us the way. On the occasion of November 27, I commemorate all our martyrs with love, respect and gratitude.




November 25 is also approaching. From the Mirabal sisters to Rosa Luxemburg, our comrades Sakine Cansız (Sara) and Evîn Goyî, and all the women comrades who were martyred throughout the years of war, these deaths and massacres resulted from attacks produced by the male-dominated system. There are also women murdered in social life as a result of this murderous, hierarchical system and the violent masculinity it produces. Hundreds of thousands, even millions of women have been killed. The struggle against this violence and the creation of a life in which women can live freely constitute a fundamental responsibility and obligation for our women's struggle. I therefore commemorate all women who have been murdered.




Turning to your question, there is certainly a process underway, and it is being widely discussed. Some say that everything is progressing smoothly. We also assess the situation. In reality, the process is largely standing still. It is not progressing as smoothly as some claim. There are difficulties and steps that have not been taken. We can therefore speak of an existing process, but how effectively and healthily it is advancing remains highly questionable. From our movement's perspective, it is a process that is not functioning or moving forward. It has not collapsed, but neither is it actively progressing.




Are they deliberately dragging out the process?




Yes, the process is being prolonged. But this delay poses a very serious danger. You asked about reports that Leader Apo has been moved to a new location. As far as we know, this is true. However, special warfare is also being conducted around this development. Ümit Özdağ recently made a statement claiming that Leader Apo had actually been freed but that the Justice and Development Party (AKP) government was having difficulty announcing it. Of course, this is not the case. There is a new location, but it remains a continuation of imprisonment. It is not a situation in which Leader Apo has been freed and can move around freely. Leader Apo must be free within the framework of this process, able to work freely and live freely.




This is essential for the process to advance and reach a healthy conclusion. As a movement, this is our fundamental position. A process in which Leader Apo is not free, cannot work and cannot participate more actively and effectively has no conditions for progress. The objective conditions for advancement cannot be established under such circumstances. The political significance of moving to a new location must therefore be understood in this context. A committee has been established. Its formation was officially announced, although its name was changed and it was described as a disarmament committee. Leader Apo called it the Peace and Political Participation Committee. The central issue under discussion is Leader Apo's role as the Coordinator of Peace and Political Participation within this committee.




The new location can only have meaning in this context, because Leader Apo fundamentally needs to be free. Its significance can only lie in enabling Leader Apo to work and participate actively as the committee's coordinator. There is talk of the "law of fraternity" in this peace process. For the process to advance in a healthy manner, it is extremely important that Leader Apo be able to assume an official, publicly recognized and effective role within this committee. Leader Apo must be able to meet journalists, academics, politicians and other individuals who can contribute to the Peace and Democratic Society Process. There must be opportunities for discussion and dialogue. An environment must be created in which Leader Apo's ideas, views, approach and strategy can reach the broadest possible sections of society and become widely understood. Yet none of these steps have been taken.




Would it not be better for Turkish society if Abdullah Öcalan could meet journalists, answer their questions and explain the paradigm of fraternity, allowing the democratic nation paradigm to become a reality for the peoples of Turkey and Kurdistan? Should the Turkish state not take more open and concrete steps?




Of course, it would be much better. As Leader Apo has repeatedly emphasized, we have experienced 50 years of struggle and a very difficult period of war. Naturally, mutual prejudices and fears have developed. This applies to both sides, to the Kurdish people and to the peoples of Turkey. There is therefore an urgent need to transform this atmosphere. How can that happen? We believe that the government's and state's approach must become much more visible and concrete. Creating such an atmosphere is important for building social support for peace. Fears must be overcome, we must get to know one another better, and relations must become more transparent. How much can the two sides communicate with each other? How effectively can they explain their concerns and circumstances? What is our strategy? What, for example, does a democratic republic strategy mean?




I sincerely believe that Leader Apo should be able to meet journalists and representatives of different sections of society. Leader Apo's views should be freely and openly communicated throughout society. Leader Apo must be able to address the Turkish public. I believe that the peoples of Turkey will understand the Kurdish People's Leader. They will understand what Leader Apo means and what a democratic republic represents. When we speak of a democratic nation, we are not seeking to divide Turkey. We do not want to partition this country. Yet this accusation has been attached to us. The definition of terrorism has largely been framed around allegations of separatism.




What harm could a democratic nation, a democratic republic or a democratic society cause anyone? What harm could they cause the peoples of Turkey, a woman, a man, a family or a young person living in Afyon, Edirne, Sinop, Antalya or any village or city in Turkey?




'Peace will harm no one'




Not only would these ideas cause no harm, but they would also create an environment in which shared life, democratic coexistence and living together would strengthen Turkey and its peoples. Mutual prejudices and fears would gradually disappear, and the distance between communities would diminish. We believe this. That is why the move to a new location must be accompanied by these steps as a matter of urgency. There is no reason to fear democracy. Why should anyone fear peace? It is something worth seriously considering. Why would anyone be afraid of peace? There was a situation of conflict, and a period of war emerged from those circumstances. The Kurds were denied recognition. The struggle arose as a necessity to overcome that denial.




Leader Apo has explained this repeatedly and continues to do so. Yes, there was a war, and we have reached this point. Now is the time for peace. Now is the time for fraternity. Yet we continue to see approaches that resist this perspective, particularly in the media and among certain politicians. There is also fear within the ruling AKP government. The answer to why the process is not advancing must largely be sought here. There is fear. What would be lost if peace were achieved? What could the Turkish state possibly lose through peace? On the contrary, it would gain much more. There would be significant gains for the state economically and politically, as well as opportunities to develop a more democratic culture of coexistence and political life among the peoples.




For example, there is frequent talk of a "regional ownership strategy" or the "Turkey Century" vision. These are objectives that the AKP government has presented as part of its political vision. But how can a Turkish state that has not resolved the most fundamental problem within its own country develop a regional strategy? Is it possible to pursue a regional strategy based solely on security concerns and particular interests? To use their terminology, there is a "terrorism" problem, and the approach is simply to disarm those involved and consider the matter settled. This is an extremely superficial, narrow and dangerous approach. If you do not resolve a problem, it will continue to reappear, grow and eventually produce different consequences.




Are the contradictions within the AKP not also contributing to the growth of this problem? The AKP has been unable to resolve its own internal contradictions, and there has been a major financial scandal within the party.




There are certainly very serious problems produced by the war, both inside and outside the AKP. Under the banners of nationalism, patriotism and declarations of love for the homeland, countless massacres have been committed. That is one dimension. Another dimension is the creation of enormous opportunities for profiteering. We see companies operating within the state, the government and political structures. The alliances and relationships between political actors and companies have created extensive opportunities for profit. How did this happen? If there had been genuine peace, healthy state administration and effective oversight mechanisms, would such enormous opportunities for profiteering have emerged? A political environment has developed in which even the little bread remaining in the hands of the people is taken away and stolen. We cannot consider this independently of the war. Of course, this is also a characteristic of the capitalist system itself. But the system has become even more corrupt as capital has used the war to expand its opportunities for profit.




There is no oversight within the state or government institutions. Nobody supervises anybody else. Such oversight does not serve their interests, and nobody holds them accountable. The institutions responsible for oversight should be investigating these matters. But the judiciary and many other state institutions have become paralyzed, producing serious consequences. The situation within the AKP reflects this reality. Similar consequences are emerging in different sectors. If there were peace, if the Kurdish people and the peoples of Turkey could come together within a democratic political environment, and if this atmosphere of hostility and the politics built upon it disappeared, corruption, profiteering and moral decay could certainly be prevented.




Why am I saying all this? Because we are currently in such a process, and problems are erupting. Imagine a person with an infected wound. You say, "I will heal this wound." You open it, but you neither operate on it nor treat it. The wound remains open, becomes exposed to more germs and grows increasingly infected. 




That is the situation we face. There are unhealthy approaches within the opposition, and there are problems emerging within the AKP. Rather than adopting the superficial approach of disarmament, we must carry out a proper, radical operation by democratizing the system and identifying the problem for what it is. This is the Kurdish question. It is a question of democratization, of Turkey's democratization. We must name it and undertake this operation together. The result would be a healthier and more democratic Turkey. Leader Apo has a historic role to play here. Nobody should portray Leader Apo as an enemy. Nobody should approach Leader Apo through special warfare or hostile characterizations. The Kurdish question does not concern Turkey alone. It is a multilayered issue.




'Democracy will benefit everyone'




The Kurdish question concerns Rojava and Syria. It concerns Başûr (Southern Kurdistan) and Iraq. It directly concerns Rojhilat (Eastern Kurdistan) and Iran. It has a very broad sphere of influence and involves multiple dimensions. The continued refusal to recognize Leader Apo's role and mission in resolving such a complex, multilayered question, attempts to trivialize that role or even portray Leader Apo as an enemy, are profoundly misguided. Such an approach carries the danger of losing a historic opportunity. Everyone must therefore recognize Leader Apo's role as Coordinator of Peace and Political Participation. This role must be acknowledged as an open, official and legitimate reality. Such recognition would also contribute to genuine normalization. I believe that everyone who understands and becomes familiar with Leader Apo's views will agree with this. It is therefore important to open the way for the process in this manner. Steps must be accelerated. The healthiest approach is not simply to say that the process is progressing well, but to advance it through concrete action.




Democracy will benefit everyone. Peace will benefit everyone. There should be no fear of democracy, peace or a solution. If a new republic is to emerge, it will be through overcoming our fears. The opposition should not fear this. Neither should ordinary people, workers or laborers. It is possible to develop such a process together. But as I have said, we can achieve this only by overcoming our fears and expanding the areas in which we come together. Leader Apo's role is extremely important in this respect.




We hope the state overcomes its fears. I do not believe that workers or Turkish society are afraid.




Special warfare creates precisely that perception!

title: ISIG: At Least 193 workers killed in workplace incidents in October
content:
The report published by the Workers’ Health and Safety Observatory (ISIG) said that at least 193 workers died in workplace fatalities during October and provided data on the causes of these deaths.




According to the report, 22 percent of workplace fatalities were caused by crushing and building collapses, 18 percent by traffic accidents, and 16 percent by falls from height.




The report states that 15 of the workers who lost their lives in October were women and 178 were men. It also records the deaths of nine child workers and 25 refugee and migrant workers in workplace fatalities.




In its September Workplace Fatality Report, ISIG stated that at least 226 workers had lost their lives in workplace fatalities across Turkey. The same figure of at least 226 worker deaths was also reported in its August report.




Meanwhile, ISIG's Child Workplace Fatality Report, covering the period from September 2025 to August 2026, recorded the deaths of 95 children in workplace fatalities.

title: Spring named after Martyr Zinar
content:
A spring flowing down the slopes of the Pirîz region in the mountains of Kurdistan not only brings life to its surroundings but also preserves the memory of the friendship between local villagers and guerrilla Zinar. Used by local residents as a source of drinking water and by travellers as a place to rest, the spring became known as “Kanîya Şehîd Zinar” (Martyr Zinar’s Spring) following Zinar’s death as a martyr. He had devoted considerable effort to protecting and maintaining it.




With their natural caves, steep cliffs and cold-water springs, every corner of the mountains of Kurdistan holds its own story. Among the hidden natural wonders high in the mountains, springs play an important role in sustaining the lives of both people and other living creatures.







 







Various species of plants grow around Martyr Zinar’s Spring. As the water nourishes the surrounding vegetation, greenery spreads throughout the valley, turning the area into a resting place for travellers as well. Those crossing the mountain roads stop by the spring to catch their breath and cool off with a bowl of cold water.
