title: Climate change can be prevented through the struggle against capitalism
content:
The 31st United Nations Climate Change Conference (COP31) is being held in Turkey to discuss ecological destruction and climate change. Environmental movements are organizing an alternative gathering and protest demonstrations in response.




Turkey currently ranks among the countries causing the greatest destruction of nature worldwide. Almost no city or district has been spared from environmental destruction. Nature is being deliberately devastated, particularly in Kurdistan. The Turkish state has built dozens of dams to separate guerrilla areas from one another and destroyed forests in areas where guerrillas operate. It has eliminated the living spaces of villages under the pretext of mineral exploration. The areas where dams have been constructed are among humanity's earliest settlements. This has also been another dimension of the cultural genocide carried out against the Kurdish people.




Policies of ecological destruction are also being implemented throughout Turkey. Streams that provide essential water supplies to villages in the Black Sea region have been destroyed. Forests have been devastated, and water sources poisoned in many places, particularly in the Kaz Mountains. The Justice and Development Party (AKP) government has launched unprecedented attacks on nature to enrich companies close to it. The AKP, which describes itself as Islamist, has turned hostility toward nature into a political policy to generate profits for its supporters. Money has become the AKP's only religion. Those benefiting most from profiteering in Turkey today are AKP members. The AKP can boast of making its supporters wealthy. Almost all those involved in investment fund fraud are AKP supporters, while many of the victims are also AKP members. Such a government thinks of nothing other than money and profit. AKP members have become people who swallow everything whole. In short, the AKP, which claimed to have come to power to fight corruption, has established an entirely corrupt system.




Marx said that capitalists would cut down a tree if they could not sell its shade. This is precisely the mentality of the AKP government. There is virtually nothing left in Turkey that the AKP has not sold. Finance Minister Mehmet Şimşek's greatest talent is his constant search for new sources of revenue. With such a mentality, even the air will eventually be sold.




Now this government, which is so hostile to nature, is organizing COP31. It has even enlisted Tarkan in an attempt to deceive the world. The AKP has become skilled at deceiving both its own people and the international community. The reality of the AKP is that it blames others for the wrongs it commits. Erdoğan, in particular, has become an expert at this. He can tell all kinds of lies without the slightest embarrassment. Through COP31, he will explain how much Turkey supposedly cares about nature. He will probably point to the few public gardens he has had built as evidence of his environmental credentials. Perhaps he will even boast about how environmentally conscious his wife is.




The AKP government's assault on nature is a clear example of an authoritarian state's practices. It acts as though it can say, "I am the state, and I can turn nature upside down wherever I want." Yet nature is humanity's living environment. Settlements were established in particular places because those areas were suitable for human life. Settlements that have existed for thousands of years are being forcibly destroyed by an authoritarian state. No power has the right to make decisions concerning nature without the consent of the people. Yet this authoritarian state destroys people's living environments without their consent. From this perspective, holding COP31 in Turkey is deeply ironic.




Capitalist modernist forces around the world are hostile to nature. Industrialism, which is inherently destructive to nature, is being legitimized. Capitalist modernist forces attack nature from the air, land and sea, only to shed crocodile tears afterward. They conceal their true nature by organizing conferences on eliminating the factors that damage the climate. Capitalist powers destroy nature while competing with one another, then hold meetings to discuss how to prevent air pollution. This is the extent of the hypocrisy and dishonesty of capitalists.




Once everything becomes permissible in the pursuit of wealth and profit, nature is polluted and the climate is altered to a degree that threatens humanity's future. The mentality that considers the destruction of nature acceptable for profit and production must therefore be eliminated. Capitalist modernist forces will not do this. The destruction of nature can only be stopped by mobilizing all sections of society outside these capitalist modernist forces.




All humanity is currently under threat. Capitalism creates this threat in multiple dimensions. Neither air pollution nor climate change can be prevented without opposing capitalism.




Turkey is hosting COP31 to conceal its hostility toward nature. The conference serves no other purpose for Turkey. Perhaps those speaking there are delivering their speeches while standing on one leg! Nothing could be more hypocritical than those who destroy nature presenting themselves as its defenders.




Source: Yeni Yaşam newspaper

title: Incekara: Determination of young people proves that resistance is possible
content:
Protests launched by high school students in Paris against poor educational conditions have had a domino effect, spreading across France and to other countries. What began as a protest over education has developed into broader opposition to the system, encompassing the rising cost of living, declining wages and the housing crisis. These developments have also drawn attention to Turkey, where exploitation and inequality are even more deeply entrenched. University students took to the streets in Istanbul on the anniversary of the establishment of the Council of Higher Education (YÖK), an institution created in the aftermath of the fascist military coup of September 12, 1980. Students protested against the government's increasingly repressive measures. Demonstrations in Beyazıt Square and Beşiktaş were particularly marked by anger over a directive issued by the Ministry of Interior concerning universities in September. Istanbul University student Yasin Incekara spoke to ANF and said, "The determination shown by young people during the March 19 protests demonstrated that it is possible to resist the repressive regime being established in Turkey and showed how these blockades can be broken."




'Young people face similar forms of repression worldwide'




Yasin Incekara, a second-year sociology student at Istanbul University, said that young people taking to the streets across Europe and other parts of the world reflected the problems they share. Incekara emphasized that although Europe is often portrayed as a prosperous society, young people there also struggle with poverty and the problems created by the capitalist system. He said, "Over the past few months, we have seen young people taking to the streets against poverty, the lack of a future and repressive policies, not only in the Middle East but also in Europe, which is presented as prosperous. The youth uprising that has emerged particularly in France shows that young people face similar forms of repression not only in Turkey but in many parts of the world."




'March 19 showed young people's determination to seek freedom'




Incekara said that although resistance in Turkey has been weaker than in other countries, the March 19 protests demonstrated how young people could break through the restrictions being imposed on them. He described the March 19 protests and subsequent developments as evidence of young people's determination to pursue freedom in the face of oppression. Incekara said, "Through their determination to demand freedom against oppression, young people demonstrated during the March 19 protests that it is possible to resist the repressive regime being established in Turkey and showed how these blockades can be broken."




'Repressive directives seek to label revolutionary students as terrorists'




Incekara said that the authorities had intensified repression through various mechanisms in response to the determination shown by young people in their struggle. He pointed to the 17-article directive sent to universities by the Ministry of Interior in September, which he described as fascist, as the latest example. He argued that the directive sought to label students involved in progressive and revolutionary activities at universities as "terrorists." Incekara said: "The directive explicitly refers to providing private security personnel at universities with training similar to that given to police officers, as well as intensifying efforts to recruit informants and pressure students into becoming collaborators. It also opens the way for officers from the Anti-Terrorism Branch to set up information stands at universities under the pretext of awareness-raising and preventive activities, allowing them to conduct intelligence operations. Through these stands, the police aim to criminalize students involved in political struggle in the eyes of newly enrolled students, portraying them as marginal groups associated with terrorism and manipulating newcomers with warnings to 'stay away from them.' Of course, this does not reflect reality. If there is any group seeking to spread terror today, it is the capitalist state and the police themselves."




'Families are also pressured to inform on their children'




Incekara continued: "Just recently, a comrade from the Federation of Socialist Youth Associations was unlawfully abducted by police in Ankara. Our comrades from the Revolutionary Youth Union have also been receiving threatening phone calls from police officers. The police do not stop there. They directly contact our comrades' families. They call our families and attempt to portray our activities as being connected to terrorism. At the same time, they pressure families to act as informants by asking questions such as, 'Who are your children meeting? What are they doing?' These methods impose a profound humiliation on both families and revolutionary young people. We recently held a press conference at the Taksim branch of the Human Rights Association (IHD) to expose these practices, including summonses to the Vatan Police Headquarters. Our comrades have been forcibly summoned for questioning, subjected to pressure to become informants and faced numerous similar practices. Over the past three weeks, police have called eight of our comrades as well as their families. They particularly target families because they know that one of the first obstacles a revolutionary young person may encounter when deciding to struggle is opposition from their own family. The state is aware of this and attempts to exert pressure through family members. Last year, the family of our fellow student Ilayda Zorlu, who was studying at Karadeniz Technical University, was contacted by police because she had participated in International Working Women's Day activities on March 8. She subsequently lost her life under suspicious circumstances after being shot with a bullet from her father's service weapon. Her father was a police officer. That same year, our comrades who protested Ilayda's suspicious death outside the Süreyya Opera House in Kadıköy were detained and subjected to torture. I was also detained and tortured for delivering a political speech at my university protesting the loss of Ilayda Zorlu's life at such a young age. I am now facing trial and a possible five-year prison sentence."




'State student grants effectively tell us to die'




Incekara also drew attention to the economic difficulties facing university students, emphasizing that grants provided by the Credit and Dormitories Institution (KYK) fall far short of covering their basic needs. He said that he was forced to take on casual jobs to support himself. Incekara also said: "The little over 4,000 Turkish lira provided by the state today is essentially the capitalist state's way of telling young people: 'You might as well die. We do not care that you are condemned to misery, poverty and a future without prospects. Do whatever you want.' Young people are being driven to suicide because they cannot sustain their lives at university and are struggling with poverty. People living in state-run student dormitories, or struggling in their everyday lives, are reaching a point where they see no way out other than death. It is hardly surprising that the system promotes such profound hopelessness at a time when people, particularly young people, are being condemned to poverty and deprived of a future. But there are certainly things we can do against this. We must strengthen the struggle for freedom and a future. We must expand organized resistance. As young people, we must come together on campuses and wherever struggles are taking place. We must strengthen solidarity. We must demonstrate that liberation lies in a revolutionary way of life and in organized struggle. Without solidarity among ourselves, the capitalist system can easily condemn us to poverty and throw us into prison. We face various forms of repression precisely because we struggle for education in our mother tongue, against poverty and deprivation, and for our rights to free, quality education, housing and adequate nutrition. Our universities are being placed under siege through government-appointed trustees, fascist directives and the constant presence of police officers. Meanwhile, children forced to work in Vocational Education Centers (MESEM) are being killed in workplace accidents. When we speak out against this, we face further repression from the capitalist state."




'There has been a setback, but it can be overcome'




Incekara said that the recent decline in the youth movement and broader social opposition could not be explained solely by their own shortcomings. He argued that imperialist capitalist states around the world were attempting to create an atmosphere of fear and intimidation. He recalled that the fascist military coup of September 12, 1980, had sought to suppress social opposition and the progressive revolutionary movement. He said that the establishment of the Council of Higher Education following the coup was part of the same policies. Incekara described the Council of Higher Education as a project designed by the military junta to suppress the revolutionary democratic movements and progressive revolutionary youth whose influence had been growing both inside and outside universities.




Incekara said: Of course, there has been a setback. We are talking about the generation of Sinan, Mahir, Ibrahim and Deniz, who drove the US Sixth Fleet into the sea, carried out punitive actions against American imperialism and Zionists, and set fire to the official car of Komer, who was known as the 'Butcher of Vietnam.' Of course, compared with that period, there has been a decline. But this is not something that cannot be overcome. It certainly will be overcome. As I said at the beginning, we saw this during the March 19 protests. We witnessed people who have never known any government other than the Justice and Development Party (AKP) throughout their lives standing up against this ever-increasing oppression. We saw people pouring into the streets, resisting police barricades and fighting back against torture. This is undoubtedly valuable, and we must repeatedly examine what these developments mean for our struggle today."




'We need a movement that goes beyond the limits of the system'




Incekara recalled that the protests launched by young people living in the suburbs of Paris, demanding better educational conditions, more teachers and smaller class sizes, had gradually expanded with the participation of workers and other laboring sections of society. He emphasized the importance of connecting the youth movement with the demands of different social groups and argued that a similar approach was needed in Turkey. Incekara said: "Today, revolutionary leadership must be capable of guiding young people and working-class masses. There must be a political center. The issue is not simply the removal of the AKP government. Developments in Serbia demonstrate something important. The system is capable of skillfully exploiting such situations. Young people struggling for their rights in Serbia are once again being directed toward elections and attempts are being made to channel their movement into the ballot box. The situation in Turkey is not very different. The attitude of the Republican People's Party (CHP) during the March 19 protests, when it sought to neutralize the actions of young people, was clear for everyone to see. We need a mass movement capable of going beyond the limits of the existing system and uniting around the goal of revolution against that system. We need a generation of young people whose demands go much further and who are capable of building a life worthy of human dignity. Of course, this does not mean that we should disregard present conditions or abandon organizing around immediate demands. It is certainly important for a young person to organize around the problems they experience at university or in a state-run student dormitory and to ignite the spirit of resistance through those demands. However, our responsibility as progressive and revolutionary people is to take these demands further and enable people to struggle collectively against capitalism, imperialism, capital and neoliberal policies."

title: Women’s vigil in Amed commemorates 14 victims of femicide and unexplained deaths
content:
Women gathered outside the courthouse in Amed (Turkish: Diyarbakır) on Tuesday for the sixth time to protest against femicide, gender-based violence and the failure to adequately investigate suspicious deaths. The vigil, organized by the Network Against Violence, focused this week on the names and life stories of 14 women who were murdered between November 2 and 10. Numerous women joined the demonstration alongside representatives of political parties and civil society organizations.




Under a banner reading “Women Stand Vigil for Justice and Memory,” participants carried photographs of women who had been killed. Chants such as “Jin, Jiyan, Azadî” (Woman, Life, Freedom), “Femicide is political” and “Bijî tekoşîna jinan” (Long live women’s struggle) echoed throughout the gathering. With the slogan “Do not protect, do not whitewash, prosecute,” they denounced impunity for violence against women.




Remembering 14 women and their life stories




Speaking on behalf of the network, Irem Ilhan of the Association for Solidarity from a Women’s Perspective (DAKAHDER) stated that women refused to allow the victims’ fates to be forgotten. She emphasized the need to insist on thorough investigations in a society where women’s deaths are frequently classified as suicides, accidents or unexplained incidents. She described the systematic threat to women’s lives as femicide.




The participants then read aloud the stories of 14 women, explicitly distinguishing between confirmed homicides and deaths whose causes have yet to be determined.




Among the victims was 33-year-old Şefika Yeşildağ, who was stabbed to death by her former husband, Osman Oruç, in Aksaray on November 2. The couple had been divorced for six years. According to her mother, the man had continued to harass Şefika. Nazmiye Özer, 56, was also killed by her former husband on November 7, six years after their divorce. Women’s organizations called for an investigation into possible previous threats and failures by state authorities responsible for providing protection.




Latife Mengüç, 50, was shot dead on November 5 by a man from whom she wanted to separate. The perpetrator subsequently took his own life.




Domestic violence




Particularly distressing was the case of Huriye Çiçek and her daughter Zeynep Demircan. The 50-year-old mother and her 25-year-old daughter were killed in an armed attack in early November, carried out by Huriye’s son, who was also Zeynep’s brother. An eleven-year-old girl was seriously injured in the attack.




Hülya Aktaş, 73, was stabbed to death by her son on November 6. Another of her sons was also killed in the same attack.




Citing these cases, women’s organizations emphasized that family ties offered no guarantee of protection against patriarchal violence and that violence within the family must not be treated as a private matter.




Other victims included 31-year-old Hilal Mete and 46-year-old Ayşe Sena Demir. Both were shot dead inside a vehicle on November 5. A suspect was arrested. Satı Aydoğmuş, 68, was also killed in an armed attack that claimed the life of another person.




Unexplained deaths must be investigated




In several of the cases presented, it has yet to be established whether the women were victims of violent crimes. Participants therefore demanded comprehensive forensic examinations and transparent investigations.




These cases include the death of 18-year-old Havva Büşra Kural, who was found dead alongside her father in an apartment on November 2. The circumstances surrounding the deaths of 44-year-old Melek Altun, Olessya Shudrina, also 44, and Melek Kaval, who were found dead in their apartments in early November, also remain unclear.




The vigil also commemorated an unidentified woman whose body was discovered on November 4 off the coast of Izmir, in the Bayraklı district. Women’s organizations called for her identity to be established and the cause of her death to be determined.




The vigil thus also drew attention to women whose deaths have not yet been confirmed as homicides but whose fates could remain unresolved without effective investigations.




“Justice is needed for all women”




After the names were read aloud, Irem Ilhan emphasized the responsibility of state institutions to protect women, saying: “When a woman is killed despite having reported violence, applied for protection or already been granted protective measures, not only the perpetrators but also any public officials who may bear responsibility must be held accountable.”




She continued: “Justice is needed not only after a woman has been murdered, but for all women who are alive,” Ilhan declared. “Women’s lives are not bargaining chips. Violence is not destiny. Impunity is unacceptable. Forgetting is not an option.”




Irem Ilhan noted that the women gathered not merely to document the number of deaths, but to change the social conditions that enabled such acts. She said their struggle was about defending women’s lives, rights and voices.




Attack on the Kabaiş family condemned




Another focus of the vigil was the still-unresolved death of Kurdish student Rojin Kabaiş. Irem Ilhan criticized shortcomings in the investigation and stated that the family’s search for the truth was now being accompanied by threats and attempts at intimidation.




Speaking on behalf of the “Justice for Rojin” initiative, Dilan Ergül addressed the recent attack on Rojin’s uncle, Ahmet Kabaiş. She said the family had repeatedly received threats because they continued to demand answers. “Although the threats were known to the authorities, adequate protection was not provided. The threats have now escalated into physical attacks,” she added.




Ergül described the attack on Ahmet Kabaiş as an attack on the entire struggle for justice in the Rojin Kabaiş case. She emphasized that the initiative would not abandon its demands for a thorough investigation.




“We are not afraid. We are fighting for Rojin and for all women whose deaths remain unexplained, and we are fighting for one another. In the face of all these attacks, we will continue our collective struggle. We will achieve real justice for Rojin Kabaiş,” Ergül declared.




The vigil concluded with a minute of silence, after which participants applauded and once again chanted their slogans.

content:
Students in several cities across the Cizîrê region of Rojava demonstrated against restrictions on Kurdish-language education imposed by the Syrian transitional government. title: YPG internationalist Konstantin Gedig remembered in Kiel
content:
This Saturday, the seventh annual commemoration of Konstantin Gedig – Şehîd Andok Cotkar was held in Kiel. Andok was martyred on October 16, 2019, in an attack by the Turkish Air Force on the western Kurdish border city of Serêkaniyê (Ras al-Ain), in violation of international law. Since 2016, he had fought against the Islamic State (ISIS) as a member of the People’s Protection Units (YPG). To this day, Andok’s killing has had no political consequences for Turkey, a NATO member, and there is still no information about the whereabouts of Konstantin’s body.




Shortly after 3 p.m., the Kurdish Community Center in Kiel was filled to capacity. More than 100 friends, comrades and family members gathered in the hall, lovingly decorated with flowers, flags and photographs, to commemorate Konstantin Gedig – Şehîd Andok Cotkar and remember his struggle. They came to remember Konstantin, the humorous and lively person, the son, the friend, the brother, the farmer, the student of Kurdish, the medic and the fighter for justice. They also came to remember the struggle for freedom waged against ISIS and Turkey’s war of aggression. In this struggle, Andok and 11,000 other fighters lost their lives, while 19,000 were wounded, in an effort to protect the lives of countless others.













“When you lose your child, every memory is sacred”




In a moving speech, Konstantin’s mother, Ute Ruß, once again described how the family had experienced his journey to Rojava. On September 1, 2019, Konstantin contacted his family to say that he was on his way to Sulaymaniyah to join the fight against ISIS. From that moment on, time took on a different meaning for the family: researching the political situation in North and East Syria, searching for photographs of Andok and hoping for signs that he was alive.




Since his killing seven years ago, their daily lives have been shaped by efforts to reconstruct Andok’s final moments, the search for his body and the struggle for justice. Even today, new information about Andok, a fighter and frontline medic, continues to emerge: small mementos handed over to the family, stories shared by fellow fighters and photographs brought to them. This year’s invitation to the commemoration, for example, features a photograph of Andok taken in the summer of 2017, which filmmaker Pedro Brito da Fonseca gave to the family.













The struggle for justice is directed against what the family describes as deliberate attempts by the Turkish and German governments to erase the memory of Andok. Ute Ruß spoke in harrowing terms: “Nothing terrible is impossible. The Turkish state’s treatment of fallen enemies is profoundly degrading. Graves and bodies are desecrated on an unimaginable scale. Families have to beg for the return of their loved ones’ remains. A dead person is no longer treated as a human being; they are degraded, regarded as dirt in the eyes of the Turkish state.”




The search for Andok’s body has been made more difficult, according to the family, by the German government’s lack of interest and its unwillingness to confront Erdoğan. As a result, even seven years after Andok’s death, there is still no grave where his family can mourn him with dignity.




A special form of remembrance is the Konstantin Andok Literature Prize. Awarded since 2023, the prize is supported by Konstantin’s parents and was initiated by the Soli-Netz solidarity network, with contributors including Dario Azzellini, Yossi Bartal, Christian Baron, Jörn Boewe and Kerem Schamberger. Nearly 500 entries were submitted for the third edition of the competition, held under the motto “Speak. Write. Break the silence.”




During the commemoration, an excerpt was also shown from a laudatory speech delivered by Christian Baron at the most recent award ceremony. Baron emphasized that, under capitalism, literature and art must always take a stand against the existing order, exploitation, oppression and NATO wars waged in the name of Germany’s 

raison d’état

.













The flower of Heval Andok




Musical performances accompanied the commemoration. As has almost become a tradition at these gatherings, 

Zana û Andok

 was sung, a tragic song about comrades Zana and Andok, who symbolize the pain and resistance of the Kurdish resistance movement. Following performances of 

Ez Nisêbin Tu Qamişlo

 and 

Çû

, everyone joined together to sing 

Bella Ciao

, including a verse rewritten in honor of Heval Andok.




Thus ended a deeply emotional, yet beautiful and defiant Saturday afternoon dedicated to the memory of Konstantin Gedig – Andok Cotkar. It was an afternoon that left participants strengthened and carrying a clear message: Remembrance is resistance against state-imposed forgetting. Resistance for Konstantin-Andok, for Rojava, for life.

title: Turkey steel factory explosion kills at least 16 people
content:
A fire broke out following an explosion at the HABAŞ Iron and Steel Factory in the Bozköy neighbourhood of Aliağa, Izmir. The death toll among workers has risen to 16, while 15 injured workers, four of whom are in critical condition, continue to receive treatment in hospital.




It was announced that search and rescue operations are continuing to reach four workers trapped beneath the rubble. According to initial assessments, the explosion is believed to have occurred when an overhead crane broke loose during the pouring of molten steel and fell into an electric arc furnace.




As part of the investigation launched into the incident, four public prosecutors have been assigned to the case, and five people have been taken into custody.

title: Muratakan: Lack of concrete steps undermines public trust in the process
content:
Yunus Muratakan, Co-Chair of the Peoples' Equality and Democracy Party (DEM Party) in Diyarbakır (Amed), spoke about the resolution of the Kurdish question and the ongoing peace process, drawing attention to its historical background, legal guarantees, participation in democratic politics and the importance of social reckoning. Muratakan said that the Kurdish question could not be addressed solely through security-oriented policies, emphasizing that a lasting solution would only be possible through the recognition of democratic rights and the establishment of constitutional guarantees.







 







Muratakan discussed the historical development of the Kurdish question, saying that the centralized and uniform approach to governance that emerged with the founding of the Republic restricted the rights of different identities, languages and cultures. He stated that this approach, institutionalized through the 1924 Constitution, paved the way for policies of denial and repression targeting Kurdish identity and cultural rights. Muratakan added that restrictions on democratic expression, organization and political participation contributed to the emergence of the armed conflict.




'A process without a legal framework cannot become permanent'




Muratakan said that the period of armed conflict had imposed heavy human, economic and social costs on Turkey, recalling that tens of thousands of people had lost their lives, villages had been burned and evacuated, and forced displacement and serious human rights violations had occurred.




Muratakan also discussed peace and dialogue initiatives that emerged from the 1990s onwards, noting that the peace process launched in 2013 had received significant public support. He described the work of the Wise Persons Committee, the participation of political parties in discussions and public support as important achievements of the process. Muratakan said that Turkey had entered another period of intense conflict following the collapse of the process in 2015.




Muratakan stressed that past experiences offered important lessons, saying, "A process may begin through political will, but it cannot become permanent without legal guarantees. Any process that lacks a legal framework remains vulnerable to provocations and political interference."




'The process must move towards building positive peace'




Muratakan described the developments following the 27 February call as the beginning of a new era, saying that the declaration of a ceasefire, the decision to dissolve the organization and steps towards disarmament were significant. He also noted that the legal regulation introduced in Parliament represented an important beginning but contained shortcomings in its scope and content.




Muratakan said, "At this point, attention must be drawn to the DDR mechanism used in international conflict resolution experiences. Disarmament, demobilization and reintegration must be addressed as an integrated process. It is crucial to establish legal and institutional arrangements that enable people who have participated in armed struggle to reintegrate into social life and democratic politics. Negative peace means the end of armed conflict. Positive peace, however, requires addressing the structural problems that caused the conflict, guaranteeing rights and freedoms, and establishing a democratic social order. What we need today is a process that does not remain limited to negative peace but also builds positive peace."




Muratakan also criticized the scope of the legal regulation introduced in Parliament, saying that a step, albeit limited, had been taken towards seeking a solution through legal means with an organization that had waged an armed struggle against the government in Turkey's history.




Muratakan drew attention to shortcomings in the regulation's scope, saying, "For the first time in the history of the Republic of Turkey, a very small step has been taken towards recognizing through law an organization that has engaged in armed struggle, an insurgent organization, and resolving the rebellion through legal means. The fact that the law covers only a particular group involved in armed struggle, while excluding intentional homicide and related offenses, as well as people who were investigated before 2005, is a serious shortcoming. This process is also not entirely consistent with the conventional DDR processes implemented around the world."




Muratakan stressed that a legal regulation aimed solely at ending armed struggle was insufficient and that democratic rights and the political sphere needed to be expanded to resolve a serious, historical and deeply rooted issue such as the Kurdish question. He said that they frequently encountered these concerns during visits to shopkeepers and public meetings organized by the party:




"Just yesterday, during a visit to a district, people asked us, 'We do not trust the process. What guarantees do you have? All right, disarmament has taken place. But what rights will we have following disarmament?' Everyone is asking us these questions. They are also wondering what administrative and judicial measures will be in place in the future to protect the rights of those who have laid down their arms.




What we are saying is this: When Mr. Öcalan initiated this process, he sought to establish it not merely because of negative peace, meaning a state of non-conflict, but also with the aim of building positive peace. He said that political and legal guarantees were necessary for the process to succeed. In this respect, the fundamental rights and freedoms of Kurds as individuals, as well as their collective rights as a people, must be constitutionally guaranteed. These are matters that require a process."




'Rights must be legally guaranteed'




Muratakan said that obstacles to fundamental rights and freedoms under Turkey's current Constitution must be removed through legal reforms and called for the rights of all citizens to be guaranteed. He emphasized that freedom of expression, the right to self-government and the freedom of peoples must be among the fundamental elements of these changes. 




Muratakan said: "When we consider all these issues together, this state of non-conflict must certainly have legal guarantees and be legally enforceable. Secondly, the right of those who have disarmed to participate in democratic politics must be legally guaranteed, and the relevant mechanisms must be established. A third issue that consistently comes up in our discussions with the public and in their demands is what will happen to political prisoners. We are repeatedly asked why our former co-chairs, Figen Yüksekdağ and Selahattin Demirtaş, have not been released."




'

Transitional justice and social reckoning are necessary'




Muratakan also drew attention to the importance of transitional justice and social reckoning, saying that equal citizenship and cultural rights must be guaranteed by law and the Constitution. He referred to the burning of villages, torture and unsolved murders in the past, emphasizing that confronting the past was essential for building lasting peace. He said, "We need transitional justice and social reckoning after these 40 years of conflict. People are demanding the right to learn about the past, access the truth and see those responsible brought to justice. For Turkey to emerge from this process successfully and for it to develop into positive peace, constitutional guarantees must be established and the democratic rule of law must be rebuilt."




'Steps must be reciprocal'




Yunus Muratakan emphasized that the peace process must advance through reciprocal steps, saying that unilateral measures would not be sufficient to establish lasting peace. He stressed that no side would benefit from war and referred to international experiences of conflict resolution, adding: "One of Mr. Öcalan's statements is particularly important to us: 'A journey of a thousand kilometers begins with a single step.' However, this step must be reciprocal. None of us has anything to gain from war. We must return to a win-win approach.




Examples from around the world clearly demonstrate that processes of non-conflict can never become permanent unless they open the way for democratic politics, are secured by legal and constitutional guarantees, and restore rights that have been taken away. This applies to the Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia (FARC), the Irish Republican Army (IRA), as well as earlier examples such as Bosnia and Herzegovina and South Africa."




Muratakan said that they regarded the process as the "Democratic Society and Peace Process" and emphasized that the people's fundamental guarantee lay in organized struggle. He said, "We consider this process extremely important and valuable. The fundamental guarantee for our people within this process is ourselves and our organized struggle."

title: IOM: 3,834 displaced people return home in Iraq
content:
Pascal Reyntjens, Chief of Mission of the International Organization for Migration (IOM) in Iraq, issued a statement on the return of displaced people to their homes in Iraq.




Reyntjens said that the organization continues to coordinate with the Iraqi government on closing displacement camps and facilitating the integration of displaced people, with the participation of government institutions, United Nations (UN) agencies and relevant organizations.




Reyntjens stated that the Iraqi government remains determined to consolidate the Behirkê and Dîbegê camps in Erbil (Hewlêr), along with three camps east of Mosul, into a single camp.




He added that the IOM, the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR) and the Iraqi government continue to engage with camp residents to discuss possible solutions.




The IOM Chief of Mission in Iraq reported that 639 families, comprising 3,834 people, have returned to their homes or been relocated to other areas as part of integration efforts under the facilitated voluntary return program since the beginning of 2026. title: Çite: Mining, geothermal and solar projects accelerate in Kurdistan
content:
As the Peace and Democratic Society Process is being discussed, the mountains, pastures and waters of Northern Kurdistan have once again fallen under the shadow of excavators, axes and drilling machines over the past year. Developments stretching from Gabar, Cudi and Besta to the valleys of Dersim covered by mining licenses, from the geothermal fields of Varto (Gimgim) and Karlıova (Kanîreş) to the pastures of Kervanpınar (Arzoxlî), are not isolated incidents. Records from the past year reveal a series of interconnected acts of environmental destruction.




Tree felling, which has continued almost uninterrupted for seven years in Cudi, Gabar and Besta, showed no signs of slowing over the past year. In just one week, 1,950 tons of trees, equivalent to approximately 3,000 stacked cubic meters of timber, were cut down in Besta and Gabar. The logging spread to the slopes of Mount Gabar overlooking the Eruh (Dêh) district of Siirt (Sêrt). The felled trees were stacked along roadsides.




Şırnak and Siirt: The axe of 'security' in Besta




Hundreds of trees were cut down in October in the Çemê Tahlo area of Besta by village guards brought from Hosyan village in Siirt's Pervari district, under military supervision. Footage published in late September showed tons of trees that had been felled in February and left to dry being transported out of the area in trucks bearing Ankara registration plates, covered with tarpaulins, and passing through military checkpoints.




The Şırnak and Siirt bar associations filed criminal complaints with public prosecutors on 29 October against those responsible for the logging and relevant public officials, citing allegations of unauthorized tree felling and illegal transportation of forest products. The bar associations also demanded the disclosure of logging permits and Environmental Impact Assessment (EIA) decisions. Media reports also indicated that some of the felled trees had been transported to military bases.




Forest cover in Şırnak recently declined from 44 percent to 36 percent. Although authorities announced last year that logging had been halted, new footage subsequently emerged.




Muş and Bingöl: More than 185 days of protest in Varto




Two geothermal power plant (GPP) exploration projects by a US-based company, covering 16 villages in Varto, Muş (Mûş), and six villages in Karlıova, Bingöl (Çewlîg), have sparked widespread opposition. A protest vigil that began in early May in Çalıdere village in Varto reached its 185th day on 4 November. Villagers have taken legal action against plans to open their pastureland to company operations. An administrative court ordered an on-site inspection of the project area on 8 October. The arrival of construction machinery in Kaynarpınar village under gendarmerie escort in August caused tensions between villagers and security forces.




Residents of Varto continuing their resistance had issued a new call for action on 2 November. The protesters and the Varto Ecology Platform called for mass participation in a crucial court-appointed expert inspection as part of the lawsuit seeking cancellation of the project, urging people to gather at the drilling site.




Diyarbakır: Pastures threatened by solar projects, heritage by excavators




A protest led by village women began in October in Kervanpınar (Arzoxlî), a village in the Sur district of Diyarbakır (Amed), against plans to build a solar energy plant (SEP) on communal pastureland. The company reportedly entered the site accompanied by security forces before the legal process had been completed. A stone believed to contain a coral fossil was discovered during excavation work. Concerns were also raised that the project area overlapped with an archaeological site.




Villagers from Ağaçlı (Cixse) in the Kulp (Pasûr) district, who had maintained a protest vigil against a solar power project for more than two months, joined the resistance. They were accompanied by villagers from Lice (Licê), who had succeeded in stopping similar projects. Representatives of the city's local administration also participated in a march at the site. In central Diyarbakır, attempts to cut down or relocate trees aged between 25 and 30 years as part of the Fırat Boulevard project also drew criticism.




Dersim: Munzur on the mining license map




Mining activities have intensified in Dersim over the past decade, with more than 150 mining operations currently underway in the province. Plans seek to bring 26 percent of Ovacık (Pulur), 22 percent of the Munzur Mountains, 56 percent of Dersim's pastureland and 42 percent of its nature parks under mining licenses. An area equivalent to 5,040 football pitches in Pülümür (Pîlemûriye) and Mazgirt (Mêzgir) was put out to tender for Group IV mining operations. A mining project planned for the Sekasur area between Hozat and Pertek was prevented through public resistance in August. Fires that broke out the same month in the Venk area of Munzur Valley National Park and along the Yolkonak–Beydamı route affected a limited area.




The figures reveal the scale of destruction




A total of 2,207 Environmental Impact Assessment applications have been submitted across 24 cities and 192 districts in Kurdistan. Decisions stating that an EIA was not required were issued for 625 of these applications. Across Turkey, approximately 24,000 hectares of forest burned in 2026. Official records show that 81,473 hectares were affected by fires in 2025. These wildfire figures refer to Turkey as a whole, rather than specifically to Kurdistan.




Leyla Çite: Not isolated incidents, but a form of colonial policy




According to Amed Ecology Assembly activist Leyla Çite, these developments reflect the way global capitalism implements colonial policies in colonized countries. Çite said that the conflict and warfare that have continued in Northern Kurdistan for the past 50 years led to the depopulation of rural areas and forced migration under the pretext of "security." She added that some residents returned to their lands through return projects introduced in the early 2000s.




Çite said: "Since the beginning of the Peace and Democratic Society Process, we have seen capital freely enter areas previously considered inaccessible, particularly in Diyarbakır, Dersim and Şırnak. We have witnessed some business circles openly expressing this at official economic conferences. These groups have effectively declared that they want the peace process to move forward not because they want deaths to stop and an honorable peace to be achieved, but because they want to fill their pockets."




'Security forces act as private guards for companies'




Leyla Çite listed the forest areas devastated by coal and mining operations in Şırnak, geothermal projects around Muş and Bingöl, exploration for rare elements and minerals in Dersim, Diyarbakır and Mardin (Mêrdîn), cyanide-based mining operations, oil exploration, hydroelectric power plants (HPPs) and solar energy projects.




Çite said: "Blasting operations at quarries cause damage to many residential areas and irreversible destruction of local ecosystems. We know that a catalogue containing a map of Kurdistan's underground and aboveground resources has been created on the website of the Ministry of Environment, Urbanization and Climate Change. We see domestic and foreign capital being invited into these areas, while security forces on the ground are positioned as though they were the companies' private security personnel.




We can say that the expiration of the relevant provisions of the Treaty of Lausanne has opened control over underground resources to capital accumulation by foreign companies. We also see that some businesspeople from Northern Kurdistan who claim to be 'patriots' have become partners in this policy, acting as local collaborators of global and 'domestic and national' companies."




'

Ecocide also targets the social fabric'




Leyla Çite said that dam and hydroelectric power projects were carried out under the pretext of "security" during the 1980s, 1990s and 2000s, while over the past decade they have been justified through concepts such as "development," "energy needs" and "clean energy." She argued that these terms serve to conceal the real objectives.




Çite emphasized that development means the development of capital, while energy needs refer not to the needs of the people but to those of the market and, consequently, capital, which depends on producing goods for consumption. She said, "Ecocide targets not only nature but also the social fabric. People who are forced to leave their villages because of mining activities have no choice but to work as cheap labor when they migrate to cities."




'There can be no genuine peace without ecological peace'




Leyla Çite also addressed the peace process, saying: "We cannot speak of genuine peace without ecological peace. We have seen that, for capital, the economic value of peace lies in restricted areas, forests, lands and mineral resources that were inaccessible for years on security grounds. If forms of domination continue, democratic spaces for collective social life are not established, and the power to make decisions about life remains in the hands of the authorities and capital, war will continue, even if it takes different forms.




The peace process must enable Kurdish cities to have a say in their own local democratic administrations, economies and ways of life. City and village assemblies can provide a lasting foundation for this."




'

Institutions side with companies, not the people'




Leyla Çite pointed out that responsibility for these developments does not lie with a single institution or actor.




Çite said: "The plunder of nature is planned centrally from Ankara through a comprehensive mapping of mining resources. We know that Environmental Impact Assessment procedures are carried out through the Ministry of Environment, Urbanization and Climate Change and the Ministry of Energy and Natural Resources. Public participation meetings are merely symbolic exercises introduced to secure access to European funding. Positive EIA decisions are issued despite objections from local communities.




The solar power project in Kervanpınar demonstrates that all institutions, from the governor's office to the military, have sided with the company rather than the people. The Ministry of Agriculture and Forestry should have opposed the project because the area is pastureland. Likewise, the Ministry of Culture and Tourism should have objected because the site contains coral fossils dating back millions of years and could qualify as an archaeological area. Instead, we have seen these institutions side with capital."




'We are planning mass vigils and protests'




Leyla Çite said that the Ecology Assembly's legal department had submitted reports to all relevant ministries and provincial directorates and had also filed a criminal complaint against the Diyarbakır Cultural Heritage unit for failing to fulfill its duties. Çite said, "We are planning mass vigils and protests outside the governor's office and relevant institutions that are complicit in unlawful practices, if necessary, to ensure that the law is enforced. Energy policies must be transformed so that they serve the interests of society and its right to have a say, rather than the profits of capital."

title: Duygu Özbay: Centralized exams deepen educational inequalities
content:
The Common Written Examination System introduced by the Ministry of National Education has drawn criticism from education workers. Teachers warn that centralizing examination procedures will diminish their decisive role in teaching and assessment, while disregarding differences in the physical, economic and social conditions of schools.




Teachers emphasize that the system is far from ensuring equal educational opportunities. They warn that a standardized approach to assessment, which fails to consider students' different learning conditions and needs, will further deepen existing inequalities in education.




Duygu Özbay, co-chair of Branch No. 2 of the Education and Science Workers' Union (Eğitim Sen) in Diyarbakır (Amed), spoke to ANF about the Common Written Examination System.




'Centralized exams make teachers passive'




Duygu Özbay said that the common examination system increases centralization in education and weakens teachers' decisive role in teaching and assessment.




Özbay said: "We have previously stated that the common examination system is highly centralized. The education system has become even more centralized with the introduction of the Turkey Century Education Model (Maarif Model), the Ministry of National Education's new national curriculum framework. We regard the common examination system as one of the methods used to implement this model. In a sense, the Ministry is trying to make the model appear more comprehensive and successful. However, making assessment and evaluation so centralized places teachers in a very passive position in the classroom.




When preparing examination questions, we take into account our students' readiness to learn, their living conditions, their specific needs, the physical conditions of the school and how prepared each child is to absorb particular knowledge. Every student's learning process is different. Educational policies must therefore take these differences into account. However, the centralized examination system operates without considering children's individual circumstances. It also removes teachers' decisive role in the classroom and establishes an even more centralized structure."




'

Children do not start from equal positions'




Duygu Özbay said that students do not begin their education under equal conditions. She emphasized that poverty, the denial of mother-tongue education, overcrowded classrooms and difficulties accessing education directly affect learning processes.




Özbay also said: "It is particularly important to recognize that children have different starting points. The learning conditions of a child studying in an overcrowded classroom are very different from those of a child studying in what we consider an ideal classroom of twenty students. There are also children who cannot receive education in their mother tongue. There are children living in poverty and others who cannot access educational opportunities. The education system must therefore recognize these different starting points and, above all, address the inequalities between them.




The right to education in one's mother tongue is one of the most important dimensions of these inequalities. Poverty is another. We are still confronted with the reality of children who have not been able to enter the education system. Our assessments in Diyarbakır show that there are still children who cannot attend school. Months have passed, yet many children remain excluded from education because school transportation services have not started and tenders for these services have not been completed. Subjecting these children to a common examination system before they have even gained access to education is itself a form of inequality.




We therefore believe that the problems within the education system must be resolved before children are subjected to this examination system. Children must enter the education system with equal opportunities. However, simply attending a classroom does not mean that a child benefits from equal educational opportunities. If schools and the education system continue to reproduce existing inequalities, that structure must first be changed. Children must be able to receive education in their mother tongue, develop their reading and comprehension skills, and participate in education according to their individual needs."




'

Students' learning conditions are being ignored'




Duygu Özbay said that both students and education workers had reported that questions in the common examinations were excessively difficult and beyond students' levels.




Özbay continued: "Mathematics, biology and science examinations have been held so far. Feedback from students and education workers indicates that the questions were very difficult. It is extremely important that examinations be prepared by education workers and conducted under teachers' supervision. We know our students' individual circumstances, their levels and how proficient they are in different subjects. Sometimes we simplify the curriculum according to students' needs because we are dealing with an extremely demanding curriculum.




However, when examinations are prepared centrally by the Ministry alone, teachers are forced to deliver the entire curriculum in all its intensity. Yet a child may not be ready to absorb that knowledge. Some of our students have learning gaps from previous years. Children's education was seriously disrupted during the pandemic and the earthquakes. The learning losses that emerged during those periods have not been addressed. We regard these as learning gaps.




Can centrally prepared examination questions genuinely take all these problems into account? There are serious doubts about this. Essentially, a centralized system means subjecting all students to the same assessment and evaluation conditions. Yet children's circumstances are not equal. Every centralized method implemented without equalizing those conditions reproduces failure and inequality.




We do not evaluate children solely through quantitative data. We cannot understand a child's learning process by looking at a single examination result. We also see that process-oriented assessment is being undermined. Process-oriented assessment means preparing examinations appropriate to a child's circumstances and needs, taking into account what the child can do and the stage they have reached. Students must be evaluated not only on what they cannot do, but also on their development and learning process. However, the current examination system eliminates this approach. As a result, an unequal learning environment is created for children."




'

Teachers are being reduced to data entry clerks'




Duygu Özbay said that centralized examinations negatively affect not only students' learning processes but also teachers' professional roles.




Özbay said: "We see that the teacher's role as an active participant in the pedagogical process is being eliminated. The fact that teachers are disregarded as active participants, with the Ministry deciding even which questions they can ask, represents a critical problem for the education system. Our role as teachers in shaping the pedagogical process is being undermined. Teachers who know their students, understand their needs and follow their learning processes are now being reduced to people responsible for implementing decisions made centrally.




The education system has perhaps never been this centralized. We also criticized previous education systems for being centralized. However, each new system makes us long for the previous one. Every new measure brings us face to face with an even more centralized structure. Today, this practice places serious pressure on both education workers and students.




Recent policies have virtually reduced teachers to clerks whose only responsibility is entering data. Examples include preparing and completing development reports, centralizing the examination system, restricting teachers' authority to prepare questions, leaving only two questions to teachers' discretion, and requiring examination scores to be entered into the system separately for each question. Education workers spend almost all their time entering data."




'The minister must see the real conditions in schools'




Duygu Özbay emphasized that the Minister of National Education should visit schools that reflect the actual conditions of education in Diyarbakır. She stressed the importance of visiting schools in poor neighborhoods and villages, as well as those with inadequate facilities.




Özbay said: "The Minister of National Education will visit Diyarbakır. Which schools he chooses to visit is very important. Will he visit schools where everything has been arranged in advance, where conditions differ from those of other schools, and which have been specifically selected by the Ministry? Or will he visit schools where he can genuinely encounter the educational realities of the city? That is what matters most to us.




He should be able to visit a school in Bağlar, a school in Sur (Sûr), or a village school. Today, we are told that the Maarif Model has been designed around sustainable technology. However, we need to ask which schools actually have the technological infrastructure required by this model. Do schools have interactive whiteboards? Are their internet connections adequate? Can students stay warm in their classrooms? Do schools have cleaning staff? These are all fundamental problems.




The physical conditions of schools have still not been improved. Teacher appointments have not been made, and the need for teachers in schools and among students remains unmet. Overcrowded classrooms are a major problem, and the situation is getting worse. Education workers are also facing problems such as being declared surplus staff. Therefore, we cannot claim that the education system is successful simply by looking at how a school appears from the outside."

title: Following in Şaristan's footsteps...
content:
Some people come into this world merely to breathe; others are born as the embodiment of an ideal. Martyr Şaristan represented a determined will that refused to surrender to the comfort of an ordinary life, even from her first breath, and carried storms within her soul. Her story is not simply the account of one person's life, but an epic tale of a land's suffering, a people's resistance and a woman's unwavering rebellion against the system.




Her childhood unfolded in a land where there was nothing ordinary about life. There was no room for being "ordinary" in the environment in which she grew up; one either stood tall or bowed down. Şaristan felt this reality deep within herself from a very young age. Even as a child, she was driven by a burning desire to stand on her own feet.




She was a child who possessed the courage to forge her own path rather than follow those laid out by others. The dignity she displayed when she took on her family's burdens and supported them despite financial hardship was the first sign of her iron will. The injustices she encountered at an early age and her confrontation with the true face of the enemy planted a seed of rebellion within her. Over time, that seed would grow into a mighty tree of resistance.




Her struggle did not begin in the present. It had started years earlier as a great battle for existence, through which a woman sought to prove that she would not be crushed by the machinery of the system. Standing against the system with such courage and determination required more than physical strength; it demanded extraordinary character and unwavering conviction. Şaristan had developed that strength of character.




She rejected the role of the "silent woman" imposed on her by the system and chose instead to become the architect of her own freedom.




The years she spent in prison were not a breaking point for her. Rather, they became a fortress in which her spirit matured. She paid the price for her honorable resistance against the enemy's oppression behind the cold walls of prison, where she developed herself, remained faithful to her ideals and forged her spirit into steel armor.




By 2012, the hunger strikes had left deep marks on her body, but they had also strengthened her unwavering determination. That hunger strike was not merely a protest; it was a battle for existence against the darkness that had descended upon her people and their struggle. She continued her resistance without regard for the damage to her body, the pain or the exhaustion, demonstrating the unshakable strength of her character. Time did not simply pass behind those walls. Şaristan emerged from prison as a pioneer.




Then the mountains of freedom called to her. By the time she was released from prison at the end of 2012, Şaristan was no longer the person she had once been. She was a fighter who had come to understand the impossibility of living within the system and knew the price of freedom. She entered the mountains not as a new student, but as an experienced pioneer who could guide others and whose every step was deliberate. Her character was so strong that she earned a special place in the hearts and minds of her comrades as someone sincere, pure-hearted and inspiring.




She knew not only how to fight, but also how to complement her comrades, clear the way for them and fill every gap through self-sacrifice. She understood that helping a comrade meant fulfilling one's own struggle. Overcoming an obstacle in a comrade's path was, for her, one of the greatest steps she could take along her own.




Today, when we remember her, we recall not only her smiling face but also her upright stance, unwavering courage and the heart with which she filled every void with a spirit of comradeship. When I watched the last footage of her recorded in the war tunnels, I saw more than an "end." In her eyes, I saw the radiance of victory, the light of freedom and an unmistakable message: "Either we will live through resistance, or, if death is inevitable, it must be an honorable death."




Those words are not a cry that calms the storm within me, but one that transforms it into an even greater ideal. Our martyrs have only one wish: to live freely or die with honor. The history of our struggle is built upon this unshakable truth.




We are not the true owners of this path. We are merely those entrusted with the path they left behind. The martyrs are the true owners of this struggle, and by walking this path, they transformed it into their own truth. Our responsibility is more than simply fulfilling a duty. It is to honor that path, keep their memories alive and rebuild their legacy every day.




Şaristan is no longer by my side, but her courage runs through my veins and her ideals remain my compass. As I travel to Yüksekova (Gever), I am not simply heading to a geographical place. I am going to continue her unfinished story and carry the honorable path she left behind even further. Today, I make the light of victory I saw in her eyes the torch that guides my own path.

title: Dilan Kunt Ayan: Abdullah Öcalan is the coordinator of the process
content:
Budget discussions began amid protests as Justice Minister Akın Gürlek arrived at the parliamentary commission. title: PUK and New Generation file a lawsuit challenging parliamentary session in Hewlêr
content:
The dispute over the political leadership of the Kurdistan Region of Iraq (KRI) has now reached Iraq’s Federal Supreme Court. The Patriotic Union of Kurdistan (PUK) and the New Generation Movement (Tevgera Nifşê Nû) have jointly filed a lawsuit challenging the parliamentary session held on November 4 in Hewlêr (Erbil). They are seeking to have the session and all decisions adopted during it declared invalid. At the center of the dispute is the election of the parliamentary leadership, which the Kurdistan Democratic Party (KDP) pushed through without reaching an agreement with the other major political forces.




According to Hemdad Şahin, spokesperson for the New Generation Movement, who spoke to Shafaq News on Tuesday, the lawsuit has been officially registered with the Federal Supreme Court. The two parties argue that the session was held in violation of the prescribed procedures for convening parliament and therefore lacked a lawful basis. A court ruling is still pending.




Disputed majority in the election of the parliamentary leadership




The legal dispute stems from the November 4 session, through which the KDP sought to resume parliamentary proceedings that had remained largely paralyzed since the 2024 regional elections. A total of 52 out of 100 MPs attended the session. This meant that the quorum required for parliamentary business was narrowly met, although several major parliamentary groups did not participate.




The Patriotic Union of Kurdistan, the New Generation Movement and other opposition parties had boycotted the session because no agreement had been reached beforehand on how parliamentary proceedings should move forward. Nevertheless, the KDP succeeded in holding the election of the parliamentary leadership. Vala Farid was elected Speaker of Parliament, Rami Nouri Deputy Speaker and Muna Qahveci Secretary. Several MPs affiliated with the boycotting parties attended the session in defiance of their parties’ decisions, helping to secure the narrow majority.




These circumstances lie at the heart of the dispute. While the KDP defends the election by pointing to the quorum achieved and the parliamentary rules of procedure, the parties filing the lawsuit dispute whether the session was lawfully convened in the first place. Iraq’s Federal Supreme Court will now be tasked with determining whether a numerically sufficient majority also met the legal requirements for a valid election of the parliamentary leadership.




Parliamentary deadlock since the 2024 elections




The fact that the dispute has now reached the courts reflects a political crisis extending far beyond the appointment of the parliamentary leadership. Since the regional elections on October 20, 2024, the major parties have failed to reach an agreement on forming a new government. The KDP won 39 seats in the elections, the PUK secured 23 and the New Generation Movement obtained 15. Consequently, no single party holds a parliamentary majority.




In particular, disagreements over the allocation of key government positions and the future balance of power between the KDP and PUK have repeatedly stalled negotiations. Although the new parliament held its inaugural session in December 2024, no government has been formed. The KDP’s decision to proceed with the election of the parliamentary leadership in early November without a broader political agreement further intensified the conflict.




The PUK responded by announcing that it would not recognize the session or its outcomes. On November 6, party leader Bafel Talabanî announced his party’s withdrawal from the existing regional government. The dispute over parliamentary procedures thus escalated into an open confrontation over the future cooperation of the two parties that had previously governed together.




Court ruling could force new negotiations




While political divisions remain entrenched, efforts are also underway to resume dialogue. KDP leader Masoud Barzani called on the PUK on Monday to engage in fresh talks. However, no agreement is yet in sight. By filing a joint lawsuit, the PUK and the New Generation Movement have made clear that they are unwilling to accept the parliamentary decisions imposed by the KDP as the basis for further negotiations.




The consequences of the legal proceedings will now depend on the Federal Supreme Court’s ruling. If the court declares the November 4 session and the election of the parliamentary leadership invalid, the parliamentary leadership will have to be elected again. Until then, the legality of the appointments pushed through by the KDP remains the subject of legal dispute.

title: Iraqi Martyrs Foundation: 85 mass graves have been opened in Shengal
content:
More than twelve years after the genocide committed by the so-called Islamic State (ISIS) against the Yazidi population of Shengal, efforts to exhume and identify the victims continue. According to Iraq’s Martyrs Foundation, 90 mass graves have been discovered so far. Of these, 85 have been fully excavated, with the recovery of human remains and documentation completed. In total, the remains of around 700 people have been recovered.




Abdulilah Naili, head of the foundation, told the Iraqi daily newspaper Al-Sabah that 300 victims had been identified and their remains returned to their families. Identification was carried out through forensic DNA analysis. Genetic samples obtained from the mass graves were compared with blood samples collected from relatives during regular search and identification campaigns.




More mass graves may be discovered




According to Naili, work on the five remaining burial sites is expected to be completed within the coming months. This will mark the conclusion of investigations into the mass graves currently documented by the foundation. However, he said, it would not mean that the crimes had been fully investigated. Previously unknown burial sites could still be discovered during construction and reconstruction work in Shengal.

title: Kurdish organizations in Switzerland deny any links to criminal groups
content:
The Democratic Kurdish Council of Switzerland (CDK-S) and the Association of Kurdish Women in Switzerland (YJK-S) have firmly denied any links to criminal groups that publicly portray themselves as part of the Kurdish freedom movement. Their statement follows an investigation published on November 4 by Swiss public broadcaster SRF into alleged mafia-style networks with links to Basel and international operations. Subsequent media coverage repeatedly associated the groups in question with the Kurdish freedom movement and organizations affiliated with it.




In a joint statement on Tuesday, the two Kurdish umbrella organizations criticized the media for sometimes accepting the self-portrayals of criminal groups without sufficiently verifying their actual organizational ties. CDK-S and YJK-S specifically rejected allegations of cooperation with the group known as “Tolhildan” and other similar structures.




“No institutional ties whatsoever”




“We state unequivocally: We have no institutional ties whatsoever to Tolhildan or any other gang structures. These groups’ claims of affiliation with the Kurdish freedom movement cannot be regarded as evidence of any relationship with our organizations. We reject the misuse of our institutions’ names and symbols, or the values of our people’s struggle for freedom, to lend legitimacy to such groups.”

title: Hatimoğulları: This is not the first workplace killing at HABAŞ
content:
Tülay Hatimoğulları, Co-Chair of the Peoples’ Equality and Democracy Party (DEM Party), leveled serious accusations against the company and the relevant state authorities following the devastating explosion at the HABAŞ steel plant in Aliağa. The explosion at the iron and steel plant, located approximately 60 kilometers north of Izmir, killed 18 workers and injured another 18. Hatimoğulları described the disaster as a “workplace killing” and blamed years of failures in occupational safety measures.




After visiting the injured workers in hospital, Hatimoğulları traveled to the plant on Tuesday with a delegation. Speaking outside the factory, she stated that this was by no means the first fatal incident at HABAŞ. She recalled that eleven workers had lost their lives at the plant over the past ten years alone. She said there were serious indications that essential safety measures had not been implemented for a long time.










https://video.anf-news2.com/live/firat/0a66ee8f_20261110152022_2026-11-10-izmir-tulay-hatimogullari-dem-parti-es-genel-baskani-habas-is-cinayeti-aciklama-1.mp4










Two fatal incidents within just a few weeks




The explosion occurred on Monday morning while the plant was in operation. According to initial information from the Izmir Governor’s Office, an overhead crane broke loose during a casting operation and fell into an industrial furnace. The resulting explosion triggered a fire, sending thick clouds of smoke rising above the plant.




It was the third fatal incident within just a few weeks. In October, temporary worker Hakan Doğan fell from a height of approximately eight meters and lost his life. On November 5, 20-year-old temporary worker Eyüp Eğinli died when an explosion occurred while a tire on a piece of industrial machinery was being inflated. Including the victims of the latest disaster, a total of 20 workers have lost their lives at HABAŞ within a short period.




Hatimoğulları stressed that these deaths demonstrated the need for a comprehensive investigation into working conditions and the responsibility of the company’s management. She recalled previous court proceedings in which HABAŞ had been found to bear 70 percent of the responsibility for fatal workplace accidents. Those responsible had been sentenced to two years and six months in prison but had nevertheless been able to continue working at the company.




Call for the resignation of ministers and regulatory officials




The DEM Party Co-Chair therefore directed her criticism not only at the company’s management but also at the state authorities responsible for overseeing occupational health and safety. Despite repeated fatalities, she said, sufficient action was apparently not taken.




“The Minister of Labor and Social Security, the Director General of Occupational Health and Safety, the Minister of Industry and Technology, and the head of the supervisory and inspection authority, all of whom bear responsibility, must resign immediately. They must not remain in office for a single day longer,” Hatimoğulları declared.




The public prosecutor’s office has since launched an investigation into the explosion. According to Turkish Deputy Justice Minister Can Tuncay, arrest warrants have been issued for eleven individuals, including HABAŞ Chairman Mehmet Rüştü Başaran. Investigators are examining whether technical defects, inadequate maintenance or violations of safety regulations contributed to the disaster.




Criticism of continued production after the explosion




Meral Danış Beştaş, Co-Spokesperson of the Peoples’ Democratic Congress (HDK), also criticized the treatment of workers. She noted that while the search for victims was still underway at the plant, workers in another section of the factory were required to continue working. Beştaş described this as reflecting an attitude in which economic interests took precedence over the protection of human life, even in the face of numerous fatalities.




Beştaş called for a nationwide period of mourning to draw attention to the scale of the disaster and the continuing loss of life in workplace accidents. Hatimoğulları and Beştaş extended their condolences to the families of the workers who lost their lives and wished the injured a speedy recovery.




HABAŞ exports steel to Israel




The HABAŞ Group has also faced criticism over its trade relations with Israel. According to available information, the company has continued exporting high-quality steel to Israel since 2024. These business relations have become politically controversial, particularly in light of Israel’s war in the Gaza Strip and the Turkish government’s announced suspension of trade with Israel.
