content:
At the start of the 31st United Nations Climate Change Conference (COP31) in Antalya, the Ecology Commission of the Peoples’ Equality and Democracy Party (DEM Party) called for a fundamental transformation of international climate and energy policies. The commission argued that the climate crisis could not be overcome through market-based mechanisms but instead required a democratic and socially just restructuring of society’s systems of production and ways of life.




In a statement on Tuesday, the commission blamed the capitalist model of production and consumption for the ongoing destruction of the environment.




“Policies focused on unlimited economic growth, the exploitation of natural resources, deforestation and dependence on fossil fuels are exacerbating the crisis. Existing international climate agreements have failed to bring about binding changes. Instead, official climate negotiations have been reduced to market mechanisms and emissions trading.”




Criticism of Turkey’s energy policies




The DEM Party sees a fundamental contradiction between Turkey’s role as host of COP31 and its actual energy policies. title: PEN conference in Amed calls for recognition of the Kurdish identity, language and culture
content:
The international “Language and Peace” conference, held on November 6 and 7 in Amed (Turkish: Diyarbakır), has published its final declaration. Participants called for constitutional and legal guarantees of linguistic and cultural rights, recognition of Kurdish identity and the release of political prisoners. They also emphasized the responsibility of writers and intellectuals to stand up for truth, justice and lasting democratic peace.




Organized by PEN International, the Kurdish PEN Center and the municipal administrations of Amed, Sur, Yenişehir, Bağlar and Kayapınar, the conference was held under the theme “The Role of Literature, Language and Intellectuals in Processes of Dialogue, Peace and Equality.” The two days of discussions focused on the conditions necessary for social coexistence based on equal rights and recognition of different identities.




'Peace must not be reduced to disarmament'




In their final declaration, participants welcomed the ongoing efforts to achieve a peaceful resolution of the Kurdish question. They described calls for peace and corresponding political steps as necessary and positive developments. However, they emphasized that such efforts could only lead to lasting results if accompanied by legal guarantees and social change.




“For peace to be built on strong and lasting foundations, cultural and linguistic rights must be recognized, and conditions that enable freedom must be established,” the declaration stated.




The final declaration stressed that peace must not be defined solely in terms of laying down arms. Rather, it must encompass social equality and recognition of the political, social, economic, cultural and human rights of all people. According to the participants, coexistence within a common state and constitutional framework must also be based on equal rights, equal opportunities and free dialogue within society.




Call for recognition of Kurdish as a language of education and official use




One of the conference’s central demands concerns the legal status of the Kurdish language. Participants called for recognition of Kurdish identity, language and culture, as well as the establishment of the necessary conditions for their free development. This includes legal provisions guaranteeing the right to education in one’s mother tongue and ensuring the official use of Kurdish.




Linguistic equality must not be limited to symbolic recognition but must be reflected in the education system and public life, said the final declaration, which also rejected all forms of forced assimilation. In a society based on equality, it said, no one should be compelled to abandon their cultural identity or conform to another identity.




'Freedom for writers and political prisoners'




Alongside linguistic rights, the conference emphasized freedom of opinion and expression as a fundamental prerequisite for democratic peace. Particular significance was attached to the symbol of the “empty chair,” which PEN uses to draw attention to writers who are imprisoned, persecuted or prevented from freely expressing their views.




The empty chair serves as a painful reminder of the ongoing attacks on freedom of thought and human freedom, the declaration stated. PEN International and the Kurdish PEN Center therefore called for the immediate and unconditional release of all imprisoned writers, journalists and political prisoners.




“As long as critical thinkers and writers remain behind bars, no peace initiative can attain moral or democratic legitimacy,” the organizations declared.




'Literature becomes the voice of those who have been silenced'




The final declaration also emphasized the particular social responsibility of literature and culture. “Where political institutions reach their limits, literature can connect directly with people, bring experiences to light and foster mutual understanding. Literature becomes the voice of those who remain silent or whose voices have been forcibly silenced,” the declaration stated.




Participants reaffirmed their conviction that literature and culture are not merely secondary elements of political peace efforts but among their fundamental prerequisites.




“As writers and PEN representatives, we wholeheartedly believe that literature and culture are essential components of peacebuilding. We pledge never to place our pens in the service of conflict, hatred or chauvinism. Instead, we will use them with unwavering determination in the service of truth, justice and the universal recognition of our shared humanity.”




In conclusion, the conference called on the state and political decision-makers to initiate a sincere and comprehensive dialogue based on equality and constitutional guarantees. It also urged civil society initiatives to participate with courage and foresight in efforts to achieve genuine, constitutionally guaranteed and lasting peace.

title: Tons of oak trees cut down on Mount Gabar
content:
Tree felling continues on the Mişarê Plain of Mount Gabar in Şırnak countryside. Logging activities, which have intensified in the region recently, have reportedly accelerated with the approach of winter on the mountain slopes facing the Eruh (Dihê) district of Siirt (Sêrt).

Footage recorded on the Mişarê Plain in Eruh showed tons of oak trees felled on different dates lined up along the roadside for transportation. The logs, stacked on top of one another, were seen stretching for hundreds of meters.

Meanwhile, the Şırnak and Siirt bar associations had previously filed criminal complaints with the chief public prosecutors’ offices, demanding an end to the tree felling in the region.

title: Saki: Turkish citizens top the list of deportations from Europe
content:
Deportations across Europe have accelerated following the implementation of the new Pact on Migration and Asylum. These measures have begun to affect not only undocumented migrants but also asylum seekers and political refugees who have been granted asylum.




The adoption of the pact has been followed by an increase in deportation orders targeting Kurdish refugees in particular. Numerous Kurdish political refugees have begun to be returned to Turkey from the European countries where they reside. Refugees, including politicians, poets and writers, face trials carrying potential prison sentences of several decades under cases brought against them after their return to Turkey.




Peoples' Equality and Democracy Party (DEM Party) MP Özgül Saki spoke to ANF about recent developments affecting migrants in Europe and the growing number of deportation orders.




'The price of the crisis is poverty, massacres and displacement'




Özgül Saki said that pressure on refugees had intensified following the implementation of the new Pact on Migration and Asylum on 12 June 2026. She added said: "Following its entry into force on 12 June, the Council of the European Union (EU) formally adopted a new regulation known as the Return Regulation on 1 October 2026, aimed at accelerating the deportation and return of irregular migrants who have no legal right to remain.




We must first recognize that since 2013, we have been witnessing mass migration on a scale unprecedented in previous periods. The period of conflict that began with ISIS attacks in Syria and Iraq, Israel's genocidal policies against Palestine, the escalation of tensions between Ukraine and Russia into a prolonged war, the Taliban's return to power in Afghanistan and US attacks on Iran have displaced millions of people. In my view, the underlying cause is the imperialist capitalist system's continued reliance on war as a regional strategy to resolve its own crises. The price of this crisis continues to be paid by the peoples of the region through poverty, massacres and displacement.




We are witnessing the re-emergence of colonial reflexes. Efforts to remain protected within Europe's own borders are proceeding alongside expansionist ambitions beyond them. Concepts described as 'European values,' such as human rights, democracy and equality, have lost their meaning. We are confronted with a Europe dominated by governments that regard everything as permissible in the name of 'security' and 'defense,' are turning toward fascism and envision a white Europe.




There is a widespread expectation that migration statistics will increasingly be used as a political tool, particularly amid the rise of the far right in Germany, the Netherlands and France. The prominence of 'returns,' 'border security' and 'irregular migration' in election campaigns indicates that this right-wing and fascistic trajectory will continue. As a result, a deliberate anti-migrant political agenda is being implemented through new, multilayered mechanisms of pressure on refugees."




'Restrictions begin at the border'




Özgül Saki said that, according to the Council of the European Union, the regulation adopted on 1 October expands member states' powers to carry out deportations.




Saki continued: "We have already begun to see the serious consequences of the new legislation in recent months. The coming period will bring highly unfavorable conditions both for migrants already living in European countries and for those seeking to apply for asylum.




The Council of the European Union stated that the new rules adopted on 1 October will complement the Pact on Migration and Asylum and contribute to its implementation. The regulation gives member states greater scope to carry out returns and allows for the establishment of 'return hubs' in countries outside the EU. This means that people who have been issued return decisions and are deemed to have no right to remain in the EU may be transferred to these centers under agreements or arrangements concluded with the relevant non-EU countries




Eurostat figures and recent EU data show that asylum applications across the EU have declined by approximately 24 percent. However, this decline has been achieved by deliberately making the application requirements more complicated from the outset. The aim of what the pact calls the 'accelerated asylum procedure' is to process applications at the border within a very short period. People fleeing war, poverty and violence are required to undergo identity, health and security checks within just five to seven days before they can even submit their applications. In other words, the restrictions begin at the very first stage, at the border."




'87 percent of asylum applications from Turkey are rejected'




Özgül Saki also assessed the situation regarding Turkey. Saki said: "The situation regarding Turkey is equally clear. Recent reports indicate a 40 percent decline in asylum applications from Turkey. Strict regulations and the rejection of 87 percent of applications from Turkey have played a major role in this decline. Under this 'accelerated procedure,' migrants whose applications are rejected by one country will be unable to apply to any other EU country, effectively trapping them behind both legal and physical barriers. The aim is to keep migrants outside Europe's borders. This will make migration routes more dangerous, force people to take longer journeys and increase mass deaths.




Data from the United Nations International Organization for Migration (IOM) show that the number of irregular migrants attempting to reach Europe by sea fell by 39 percent in the first nine months of 2026 compared with the previous year. However, deaths along migration routes have increased. By mid-September, at least 2,292 migrants had died or gone missing along Mediterranean and Atlantic routes, compared with 1,999 during the same period last year. Although the number of arrivals along the route covering crossings to Italy and Malta fell by approximately 55 percent, the number of deaths rose from 844 to 996.




Meanwhile, the EU is selectively recruiting the skilled labor it needs while deporting asylum seekers it regards as a 'burden.' Through the establishment of 'talent pools,' migrants will be categorized as 'skilled' or 'unskilled,' and those selected will be brought to Europe under restrictive contractual conditions. Moreover, Frontex, the EU's border enforcement agency, is being granted powers so extensive that it will be able to intervene in the internal affairs of countries where asylum seekers are held.




Last week, we visited Uzbekistan with the Migration Subcommittee of the Parliamentary Assembly of the Organization for Security and Co-operation in Europe (OSCE PA). Uzbekistan is presented as a positive example in terms of migration policies. The Uzbek government, which has signed migration agreements with Austria and Germany, is implementing a program that could be described as a migration exchange. Training centers provide vocational education for machinists, mechanics, nurses and cooks. Those who complete their training will be employed in Germany and Austria for specified periods, according to the number of workers requested. In exchange, Uzbekistan will accept an equivalent number of migrants returned from those countries.




These agreements, which effectively risk normalizing human trafficking by bringing it within a legal framework, are becoming increasingly widespread among Balkan, Asian and European countries. The countries entering into these agreements are also signing extensive cooperation protocols with Frontex."




'Turkish citizens top the list of deportations'




Özgül Saki said that Turkish citizens ranked first among those deported from EU countries and drew attention to the fact that nationals of other countries were also being sent to Turkey.




Saki said: "According to Eurostat data, a total of 132,600 people were refused entry into the Schengen Area at the EU's external borders throughout 2025. Human rights organizations have long argued that arbitrary detention and the return of vulnerable people to dangerous countries reflect policies focused more on deterrence and pushbacks than on protecting people from persecution.




Turkish citizens rank first among those deported from EU countries and returned to third countries, with 13,405 people. An important distinction must be made here. The category 'refused entry' covers people who are denied permission to enter the EU at border crossings or airports. The category 'returned,' on the other hand, refers to people who have already crossed the border and entered the EU but are subsequently removed through an administrative decision.




Turkey ranks first not in refusals of entry at border crossings, but in actual deportations from the EU. One of the main reasons is that the EU regards Turkey as a 'safe third country.' The justification is that countries that are candidates for EU membership are automatically considered safe countries. The establishment of return hubs has also been facilitated by the removal of the requirement that migrants be sent to their country of origin or to a country with which they have a direct connection."




'Racist attacks are increasing'




Özgül Saki drew attention to the rise in racist attacks against refugees in Europe and said that anti-migrant rhetoric was becoming increasingly widespread among governments.




Saki said: "Migrants and refugees face discrimination in almost every European country. They are forced to live under the constant threat of violence and hatred in the streets, at work and in their homes. Attempts at lynching and attacks that sometimes escalate into pogroms occur in many countries, including Turkey. However, the most dangerous development in recent years is that anti-migrant sentiment has become part of official discourse, with governments adopting successive regulations that legitimize this approach.




In Turkey, operations to apprehend and deport irregular migrants have reached their highest level over the past six months, including through measures such as Mobile Migration Points. These operations, officially described as an 'all-out war against irregular migration and smuggling networks,' are being carried out under the coordination of the Ministry of Interior. However, there are serious legal problems with these operations. Monitoring reports published by Mülteci-Der in August 2026 indicate that lawyers' access to their migrant clients in removal centers has been restricted through administrative practices whose legal basis remains unclear."




'Most asylum seekers from Turkey are Kurdish'




Özgül Saki also addressed the deportation of Kurdish political refugees to Turkey, pointing to the EU's classification of Turkey as a 'safe country' as a contributing factor.




Saki said: "The safe third country designation has had a major impact. Turkey is also regarded by the EU as a safe third country. In Germany, Turkey ranks third among asylum seekers' countries of origin, after Syria and Afghanistan. The protection recognition rate for applicants from Turkey is below 10 percent. According to Pro Asyl, an independent Germany-based human rights organization defending the rights of refugees and asylum seekers forced to flee their countries, most asylum seekers from Turkey are Kurdish.




One report stated that 84 percent of Turkish citizens who applied for asylum in Germany in 2023 identified themselves as being of Kurdish origin. The German Ministry of Interior reported that the number of Turkish citizens required to leave the country had exceeded 15,000. According to data from the Federal Office for Migration and Refugees (BAMF), 22,560 Turkish citizens were awaiting deportation at the end of September 2025. Turkey ranked first in this category.




As for the reasons, German authorities generally argue that there is no individually substantiated evidence of political persecution and that Kurdish identity alone is insufficient. Claims of political repression are often rejected on the grounds that they are 'not sufficiently credible or documented.' Discrimination based on Kurdish identity alone is considered insufficient to qualify for international protection.




In Norway, according to Hengaw, Sirwan Aminpour, who sought asylum in the country after participating in the Green Movement protests in 2009, was detained in January 2026 and transferred to the Trandum detention center. He faces the risk of deportation to Iran. In another case, Kurdish asylum seeker Nourzad Alimoradi, who had been waiting for eight years, was sent from Norway to Turkey and attempted suicide at Istanbul Airport. His deportation to Iran was temporarily suspended.




In the Netherlands, approximately 5,900 first-time asylum applications were submitted in the third quarter of 2026, representing a 13 percent decline compared with the previous year. Parliament approved the implementation of the EU Pact on Migration and Asylum in May 2026. The measures envisage faster and more restrictive procedures, border screening and quicker return decisions. It was also reported that the Netherlands and four other European countries were planning to send asylum seekers who had exhausted all legal remedies to a 'third country' outside the EU by the end of 2027. The Dutch Immigration and Naturalisation Service (IND) excluded applicants from Turkey from its pilot written hearing procedure on the grounds that their cases were too complex.




The situation facing Iranian Kurds is even more severe and has deteriorated significantly in recent months. Iran's ambassador to Iraq announced that Baghdad had agreed to expel members of Iranian Kurdish opposition groups from Iraqi Kurdistan or hand them over to Iran. Iran describes these groups as 'terrorists' and organizations acting on behalf of the United States and Israel. The war and tensions involving Iran in the region have further intensified this pressure. Tehran has also reportedly requested the extradition of 36 Kurdish opposition figures and activists from Iraq and European countries, including Germany, France, Belgium and Sweden.




Organizations such as Hengaw and Hana frequently report that Iranian Kurdish activists whose asylum applications have been rejected in Turkey face the risk of deportation to Iran. For example, the asylum application of Kurdish activist Rezgar Sheikh Jegari, who has lived in Turkey for 11 years, and his family was rejected by the United Nations Refugee Agency. Turkish migration authorities subsequently issued a second negative decision. Journalist Zanyar Aziznezhad said that he had been held in a removal center for approximately a year, beaten by guards and pressured to sign deportation documents. According to Aziznezhad, Turkey is seeking to increase deportation numbers in order to maintain EU funding.




The process of the Kurdistan Workers' Party (PKK) laying down its arms has strengthened the argument in some countries that the 'risk has decreased.' However, courts do not always accept this argument. Deportation decisions are based on two main grounds: the rejection of asylum applications due to insufficient documentation, and the classification of Turkey or Iran as 'safe' countries or countries where the level of risk has declined.




The security dimension, particularly allegations of links to the PKK and intelligence assessments by agencies such as Säpo, is especially prominent in cases involving Sweden. We witnessed a similar case in Estonia. Kurdish poet Tekin Ağacık's asylum application was rejected, and he was sent to Turkey, where he was detained at Istanbul Airport over terrorism allegations.




In cases involving Iran, the official grounds generally include rejection of asylum applications, irregular entry or residence, and concerns relating to 'public order and security.' Human rights organizations argue that such decisions violate the principle of non-refoulement, which prohibits returning people to countries where they face serious risks. These individuals face the risk of politically motivated arrest and torture in Iran."

title: Kurdish political prisoner in Iran denied urgent treatment
content:
The Tehran Prosecutor’s Office continues to block Kurdish political prisoner Motalleb Ahmadian’s transfer outside Evin Prison for urgent medical treatment, despite repeated medical warnings over his deteriorating health and serious complications from a cancerous tumour.




Ahmadian, from Baneh, Kurdistan Province, is in his 17th year of imprisonment and suffers from multiple illnesses.




An informed source told the Kurdistan Human Rights Network (KHRN): “The Legal Medicine Organisation has repeatedly informed the judge overseeing the prison and the Tehran Prosecutor’s Office that, given the deterioration in Motalleb Ahmadian’s health, he must be transferred outside prison as soon as possible so that he can receive treatment for his multiple illnesses, undergo the necessary medical procedures and recover in suitable conditions.”




The source said the prosecutor’s office had nevertheless refused to approve the transfer, heightening concerns about irreversible harm to Ahmadian’s health and the risk to his life.




Ahmadian has undergone several operations to treat complications caused by the cancerous tumour. During these procedures, his gallbladder was completely emptied, and surgeons also operated on parts of his liver and intestines, the source said.

content:

title: Four Kurdish citizens remain detained in Iran, whereabouts unknown
content:
Four Kurdish citizens arrested by security forces in Bukan, Miandoab and Piranshahr in West Azerbaijan Province between 2 and 4 November remain detained with their exact whereabouts and condition unknown.




The detainees – Diyar Abroun, Jamileh (Mina) Mohammadamin-Azar, Saadi Karimi, and Mahmoud Pileh – have been denied access to legal counsel and family visits since their arrests.




The Kurdistan Human Rights Network (KHRN) has learned that security forces violently arrested Abroun, from Piranshahr, on 2 November.




On 3 November, Ministry of Intelligence forces raided Mohammadamin-Azar’s family home in Bukan and arrested her and her husband, Khoshnaw Azizpour, without a warrant.




Azizpour was released after several hours of interrogation, while Mohammadamin-Azar was reportedly transferred to a security detention facility in Orumiyeh, the provincial capital, with her exact place of detention remaining unknown.




Security forces also arrested Karimi, another citizen from Bukan, on the same day.




On 4 November, security forces arrested Pileh, from the village of Gug Jalu in Miandoab County.

title: Yıldız Çakar’s poetry wins international award in the US
content:
The poem “Mohra Reş” (The Dark Seal) by Kurdish poet and novelist Yıldız Çakar has won the Special International Honorable Mention at the Julia Vive Feminist Poetry Festival, held in Philadelphia, USA. The award, presented in the category of “Poetry, Memory and Resistance,” recognizes Çakar’s distinctive literary treatment of women’s struggle, collective memory and resistance.




Organized by the Madre Tierra Women’s Center (CIMMT), the Julia Vive Feminist Poetry Festival will take place on November 13 at the Taller Puertorriqueño Cultural Center in Philadelphia. Bringing together 100 poets from different parts of the world, the festival selected Yıldız Çakar’s poem “Mohra Reş” (The Dark Seal) for the Special International Honorable Mention in the “Poetry, Memory and Resistance” category.




The award committee informed Yıldız Çakar of its decision in a special letter. Highlighting the poet’s literary strength, the letter noted that she explores themes including violence against women, femicide, collective memory, land, loss and women’s resistance through a distinctive Kurdish perspective.




The letter also emphasized that Çakar’s poem expands the festival’s literary horizons beyond Latin America and the Caribbean, giving it a global dimension. It highlighted the work’s powerful connection to women’s struggles for freedom and dignity.

title: Koma Berxwedan: Release Nûdem Durak and ill prisoners
content:
Members of Koma Berxwedan and other artists issued a statement to draw attention to the situation of Kurdish artist Nûdem Durak, who has been in prison for 11.5 years and is reportedly battling serious illnesses.




Reacting to the 19-year-and-6-month prison sentence handed down to Nûdem Durak, the artists said that her health had deteriorated and that her life was in danger. They called for the release of all sick prisoners, particularly Nûdem Durak.




Criticising the continued imprisonment of sick prisoners at a time when the Peace and Democratic Society Process is being discussed, the artists called on human rights organisations, intellectuals, politicians and the public to intensify their efforts and raise their voices.







 







Freedom of ill prisoners must be our top priority




Speaking on behalf of Koma Berxwedan, Hekim Sefkan said that, at a time when hopes for peace were growing, decisions continued to be made that contradicted human rights and the spirit of the process. Reacting to the prison sentence imposed on Nûdem Durak, Sefkan said it was unacceptable that the artist was being kept behind bars despite her serious health problems.




Sefkan said: “At a time when hopes for peace are growing, decisions and actions that contradict human rights and the spirit of the process are also continuing. One such decision is the 19.5-year prison sentence imposed on artist Nûdem Durak. She has been in prison for 11.5 years. She is ill. Keeping her in prison for another 19.5 years at such a time goes against both the spirit of the process and human rights.




We call on all intellectuals, artists, human rights defenders and our people to raise their voices against this injustice. We want people to take a stand against this unlawful treatment, to speak out for all sick prisoners, and to make this our number one priority. All ill prisoners, beginning with our artist Nûdem Durak, must be released as soon as possible so that they can continue their treatment in humane conditions. On this issue, we call on everyone, particularly human rights organisations, to increase pressure on the state institutions responsible for these decisions. All relevant institutions must intensify their struggle against these decisions, which disregard human rights.”




The peace process is, above all, a test of sincerity




Artist Seyda Perinçek also criticised the prison sentence imposed on Nûdem Durak, drawing attention to the increasingly serious health conditions of sick prisoners. Stating that the release of sick prisoners would be an important step in the Peace and Democratic Society Process, Perinçek emphasised that the state must take concrete action on this matter.




Perinçek said: “The condition of sick prisoners is becoming increasingly serious. One of them is artist Nûdem Durak who has been in prison for 11.5 years because of her work for Kurdish art and Kurdish culture. She is trying to survive under extremely difficult conditions while battling illness.




We must struggle for all sick prisoners, with Nûdem as a particular example. We must take a stand against this torture and this inhumane situation, because our friends are being left to die in prison. The peace process is, above all, a test of sincerity. Addressing the situation of sick prisoners must be the starting point for demonstrating good faith. In particular, our friends who are ill and have been imprisoned for many years must be released.”




Nûdem is in prison for her dedication to Kurdish culture and art




Bermal Çem, speaking on behalf of Hünera Mizgîn, said that Nûdem Durak had been punished for her contributions to Kurdish culture and art. Çem said that Durak had been held in prison for years and was struggling with serious health problems. She added that her illness was progressing and that she was at risk of losing her voice. Emphasising that the situation of sick prisoners is not merely a concern for their families and loved ones, but a matter for society as a whole, Çem appealed to intellectuals, human rights defenders and politicians.




Çem added: “Nûdem was arrested despite being innocent and has been held in prison for years. Her only ‘crime’ was contributing to Kurdish culture and art and keeping them alive. Today, she is fighting for her life in prison while suffering from cancer. Despite this serious illness, she was sentenced to 19.5 years in prison. Her condition is deteriorating, and she could even lose her voice.




We must struggle for all ill prisoners held in prisons, with Nûdem as a particular example. Intellectuals, human rights defenders, politicians and our people in particular must make the struggle for these people's freedom their top priority. At a time when the peace process, democratic society and democratisation are being discussed, it is a great disgrace that the efforts of these people, particularly Kurdish women, to preserve culture and art are being obstructed through prison sentences. The punishment of a young woman with such a severe sentence should be a concern not only for the Kurdish people but for all humanity. Everyone must stand up and struggle against this.”

title: A border built with water: Six dams in succession
content:
There are six dams along a stretch of just 45–50 kilometers on the Ortasu (Rubozik) Stream, located on the border between Northern Kurdistan (Bakur) and Southern Kurdistan (Başur). Under normal circumstances, dams should either not be built because of the damage they cause to the ecological balance, or should only be constructed following an Environmental Impact Assessment for irrigation, flood prevention and electricity generation. However, these six dams serve a somewhat different purpose. The 2007 activity report of the State Hydraulic Works (DSI) states that their function is entirely security-related. This represents an unprecedented category worldwide, a new type of dam.




A look at the map reveals that all six dams have been built along a single stream. Each has its own tender, dam structure and reservoir. Yet for those living in the valley, they are all part of the same story: villages whose roads have been cut off, whose pastures and farmland have been lost, and whose residents face the winter fearing landslides and floods.




The fundamental question that needs to be asked is: Why does the Turkish state use dams so extensively as a security instrument in Kurdistan?




'Security dams': A new category




A report published in the newspaper Hürriyet on 26 October 2011 clearly revealed why these six dams were being constructed. The report emphasized that the dams were intended to "solve the problem" by flooding caves used by guerrillas and people engaged in cross-border trade. The deep valleys of Aynatepe, Gürbül Mountain, Bezenik Mountain and Düğün Mountain, which form the border stretching from the Qilaban (Uludere) district of Şırnak (Şirnex) to the Çelê (Çukurca) district of Hakkari (Colemêrg), contained strategic locations. Guerrilla transit routes also passed through these valleys.




A project tendered in 2008 and prepared by the DSI for "energy storage" along the borders with Iraq and Iran included a total of 11 dams. Seven were located in Şırnak (Silopi, Şırnak, Uludere, Ballı, Kavşaktepe, Musatepe and Çetintepe), while four were in Hakkari (Gölgeliyamaç, Çocuktepe, Beyyurdu and Aslandağ).




Reports based on a DSI map obtained by the press in July 2009 stated that the reservoirs would flood hundreds of caves and crossing points used by the Kurdistan Workers' Party (PKK), cut off logistical support and prevent infiltration and smuggling.




The military and strategic function of the dams




The primary rationale behind the construction of these dams was a strategy of territorial control. The deep valleys along the border formed natural corridors for the PKK's logistical and shelter networks. By filling these valleys, the reservoirs physically block transit routes while also restricting military movement in the region.




This represents a concrete shift from the tactics of the 1990s, characterized by "burn the villages, dry up the water," toward an approach based on "transforming the terrain to prevent operations." The dams reinforce the border with a natural barrier while simultaneously reshaping the region's socioeconomic structure. However, the long-term ecological and social costs of this strategy have not been adequately discussed in public.




Reshaping geography in the name of 'securitization'




Rather than resolving the Kurdish question through peaceful means, the state sees no problem with reshaping the region's geography and ecosystem and displacing its inhabitants through securitization policies. Dams built in succession are turning artificial borders into natural barriers.




The term "security dam" appeared in the DSI's 2007 report, although officials later stated that these dams were being constructed for irrigation and energy production. While official discourse presents them as "energy and irrigation investments," the experiences of villagers in the region do not correspond to this narrative.




It has been reported that the canals and distribution networks required for irrigation have largely not been constructed, while electricity generation remains limited to a total installed capacity of 15 megawatts. This capacity reportedly represents just 0.044 percent of the total installed capacity of hydroelectric power plants in Turkey.




Meanwhile, the risks of landslides, water leakage and flooding caused by the dams pose serious dangers to local communities. This situation reinforces criticism that the dams' primary function is not "development" but "keeping the region under control."




Mapping the chain: Six dams, one valley




The Ortasu Stream is a tributary of the Hezil River. Coordinates available in open sources show that the Çetintepe, Musatepe, Kavşaktepe, Ballı and Uludere dams are arranged from east to west, stretching from Ortasu village toward İnceler. The Şırnak Dam forms the link in the chain closest to the city center.




The six dams have the following characteristics:




Çetintepe Dam: 

Located at the uppermost end of the chain, near Ortasu village and the Gülvazı area. It stands 60.5 meters high and has a reservoir capacity of 44.33 million cubic meters. It is officially listed in the records of the State Hydraulic Works among completed and commissioned projects, with a planned hydroelectric power plant (HPP) capacity of 2 MW.




Musatepe Dam:

 Located near Ortabağ village, the dam stands 34.5 meters high and has a reservoir capacity of 12.29 million cubic meters. Construction work, including a 1.5-kilometer security road, has been completed, and the project has entered the reservoir-filling stage.




Kavşaktepe Dam: 

Situated in the Işıkveren and Taşdelen valleys, the dam stands 66 meters high and has a reservoir capacity of 19.05 million cubic meters. Construction has been completed, and the facility is listed in the DSI inventory as a completed project intended for security and energy purposes.




Ballı Dam:

 Located near Ballı village, a few kilometers downstream from Taşdelen, the dam stands 49 meters high and has a reservoir capacity of 7.09 million cubic meters. Construction of the dam structure and infrastructure has been completed, and the facility has entered operation and reservoir filling.




Uludere Dam:

 Located in the İnceler area, the dam stands 55.5 meters high, has a reservoir capacity of 20.1 million cubic meters and a crest length of 431 meters. The project is listed among the dams completed under DSI investments.




Şırnak Dam:

 Located approximately 25 kilometers southeast of Şırnak city center, the dam stands 56.8 meters high and has a catchment area of 398.3 square kilometers. Reportedly the first dam in the chain to be completed and begin storing water, it became operational in 2011–2012. The dam remains operational, together with its three-kilometer embankment road.




Excluding Şırnak Dam, the other five dams have a combined storage capacity of approximately 102.9 million cubic meters. The largest reservoir in the chain belongs to Çetintepe Dam, located at the uppermost end of the route, with a capacity of 44.33 million cubic meters.




Data available from open sources indicate that the total cost of the six dams was approximately $166 million (259.5 million Turkish lira). However, according to information published by Energy Atlas, the hydroelectric power plants planned along the Ortasu Stream have a combined installed capacity of just 15 MW. This reportedly represents approximately 0.044 percent of Turkey's total installed hydroelectric capacity.




The imbalance in the cost-benefit analysis




Despite public expenditure of $166 million, the dams contribute only 15 MW of installed capacity to the region's energy production. This represents less than one-thousandth of Turkey's total installed hydroelectric capacity. The same amount could instead be allocated to agriculture, livestock farming, cross-border trade and infrastructure, potentially generating far greater socioeconomic benefits for the region.




This suggests that the dam investments have been shaped more by political and military priorities than by economic considerations. Moreover, given the potential cascading effects of these dams, where the collapse or overflow of one dam could affect those downstream, the absence of a publicly available emergency response and risk management plan creates a serious safety vulnerability for the region.




Cross-border water policies and geopolitical risks




The dams in Ortasu are no longer merely a domestic issue for Turkey. They are also part of broader cross-border water policies. The fact that the Hezil River flows toward Iraq means that these dams also affect water flows in Iraq. Iraqi villagers reported experiencing these effects as early as 2011, when water began to be stored in Silopi Dam and they observed a reduction in the flow of the Hezil River. This situation should also be assessed in terms of regional water security as an extension of Turkey's water policies in the Euphrates and Tigris basins. The long-term impact of the dams on agricultural land and drinking water resources in Iraq and Syria has yet to be comprehensively investigated.




Lives, livelihoods, nature and memory




Public safety is one of the most important concerns. The Ministry denied allegations of cracks in the dams in February 2023 but acknowledged that water leakage had occurred.




Livelihoods and the border represent another dimension of the problem. Limited agricultural land has been submerged, while livestock farming has either disappeared entirely or reached the brink of collapse because of restrictions on access to pastures and military operations. The suspension of cross-border trade following the Roboskî Massacre has also left people in the area facing hunger. Villagers from Taşdelen and Işıkveren said in 2022 that they wanted to return to their former villages, but the routes back were caught between dam reservoirs and areas at risk of landslides.




Dams have lasting effects on the ecosystems of the areas where they are built, creating environmental and water-related problems in the region. Humidity increases, snowfall decreases, and the sediment carried by rivers accumulates in reservoirs. As a result, plains and agricultural land throughout the river basin become increasingly barren.




Ali Şengali, a villager from Southern Kurdistan, said in 2011 that the flow of the Hezil River had decreased after water began to be stored in Silopi Dam, leaving villagers unable to fish. He also warned that the dams still under construction at the time would affect their orchards once completed. The effects of the dams were therefore already being felt.




Independent measurements of river flows that could verify these claims are not publicly available. As a result, the impact of the dams remains a matter of unquantified changes in water flows. Cemeteries in villages submerged by the reservoirs have also been affected by these policies. Burial grounds, which are essential elements of individual and collective memory, were flooded following the construction of the dams.




The link between ecosystems and the climate crisis




The ecological effects of dams are not confined to the local environment; they also contribute to the climate crisis. Reservoirs can increase humidity in the region and alter precipitation patterns, negatively affecting agriculture and livestock farming. Furthermore, the accumulation of river sediment in reservoirs reduces the fertility of agricultural land downstream, increasing the risk of desertification.




Changes to water flows in the Euphrates and Tigris basins caused by dams could also lead to water shortages in neighboring countries such as Iraq and Syria, potentially triggering regional migration. The dams in Ortasu are therefore not merely a security or energy issue, but also a matter of climate justice.




Roboskî: A massacre in the shadow of the dams




The dams are located in the same region as Roboskî, where Turkish military aircraft carried out an airstrike on 28 December 2011, killing 34 civilians, including 17 children, and 59 mules. Despite years of struggle for justice, the state has remained silent in the face of the continuing demands for justice from the families of the young people killed. Meanwhile, it spent $166 million on six dams located approximately half an hour away.




The peace process and the dams




The construction of six dams in the region continues even as the peace process is underway. Rather than directing its resources toward resolving the Kurdish question, the state continues to spend them on projects that will have potentially irreversible sociological and ecological consequences for the region. Moreover, these practices do not merely harm local communities and the environment. They could also have consequences for countries in the Euphrates and Tigris basins, including Syria, Iraq and Iran, making it more difficult for their populations to access safe food and clean water.




The issue of the six dams is therefore not simply a matter of security or cost. It is a regional problem directly connected to water resources, ecological destruction and the climate crisis.

title: Akın: Policies destroying nature and society must end for ecological peace
content:
The Conference of the Parties (COP), held annually under the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC) to combat climate change, brings together countries from around the world. The 31st conference (COP31), which will address critical issues such as climate finance, reducing greenhouse gas emissions and the energy transition, will take place in Antalya from 9 to 20 November 2026.




However, the deepening ecological crisis despite nearly 30 years of conferences has reignited debate over the role of these summits in combating climate change. Ecologists are questioning whether these meetings offer genuine solutions for protecting nature and the climate.




Ibrahim Akın, Co-Deputy Chair of the Peoples' Equality and Democracy Party (DEM Party) responsible for Ecology and Agriculture, spoke about the importance of ecological peace in the context of the Peace and Democratic Society Process, the background of the summit and the People's Climate Summit, which has emerged as an alternative gathering ahead of COP31.




'Ecological destruction impoverishes and displaces peoples'




Ibrahim Akın defined ecological peace as restoring balance in the relationship between humanity and nature and freeing nature and living environments from exploitation. He drew attention to the impact of ecological destruction on peoples and said: "Under capitalism, nature has been transformed into a source of capital accumulation. Our land, water and air have been turned into commodities. The exploitation of nature has been added to the exploitation of labor. Peoples who resist this plunder have often been confronted by state security forces, the judiciary and mechanisms of repression. Therefore, attacks on nature do not merely cause ecological destruction. They also impoverish peoples, displace them and sever their ties with their history and culture. In this respect, ecological destruction is part of the war being waged against the people."




'

Ecocide is also a devastating attack on the future of societies'




Akın said that ecological peace carries a meaning beyond the silencing of weapons in the context of the Peace and Democratic Society Process, emphasizing that it requires an end to policies that destroy nature and society. He continued: "Social peace cannot be achieved without guaranteeing peoples' right to have a say and make decisions over their lands, waters and living environments. To achieve this, the commodification of nature must end, the will of local communities must be recognized and acts of ecocide must be stopped. Ecocide is a devastating attack not only on nature but also on the future of societies that live in harmony with it. A system that continues to wage war against nature cannot promise genuine peace to humanity.




Ecological peace means taking steps to heal nature wounded by war and enabling humanity and nature to establish an egalitarian, free and sustainable relationship."




'The deepening ecological destruction despite more than 30 years of summits is no coincidence'




Ibrahim Akın said that the deepening ecological destruction, despite more than 30 years of summits, signed agreements and announced targets, was no coincidence. He explained the reasons as follows: "This is because the climate crisis is the product of a capitalist system of production and consumption that regards nature as an unlimited reservoir of raw materials, labor as a cheap input for production and every aspect of life as a source of profit. We cannot overcome this crisis by relying solely on technological solutions, carbon markets and international commitments without questioning capital's need for unlimited growth or confronting the interests of fossil fuel companies and major monopolies.




This does not, of course, mean that international cooperation or COP summits are unimportant. However, we must also acknowledge the limitations of these platforms, whose interests they serve and what their decisions actually change in real life. Nevertheless, I see COP summits as platforms that make it possible to bring the climate crisis onto the international agenda."




Turkey's insincere and contradictory approach




Akın drew attention to what he described as Turkey's insincere approach to preparations for COP31, saying that the summit was being treated as an international promotional event rather than an opportunity to confront the root causes of the climate crisis. 




Akın said: "Instead of confronting the causes of the climate crisis, the country's fossil fuel policies, mining activities, the destruction of forests and agricultural land, and profit-driven urbanization, we see that the summit is being treated as a kind of international trade fair and promotional event. Efforts to turn environmental policies into a showcase for campaigns promoting certain individuals and circles, particularly the Zero Waste campaign, are especially striking."




Policies of ecological destruction from the Northern Aegean to Kurdistan




Akın also pointed to the contradiction between Turkey's hosting of COP31 and the continuation of policies of ecological destruction across the country. He said, "This is actually the fundamental problem with the government's approach to nature and society. While messages of environmental and climate awareness are being conveyed to the international community, forests, pastures, water basins and living environments are being opened up to capital for the sake of corporate profits."




Akın emphasized that these policies were incompatible with the spirit of the Peace and Democratic Society Process and continued: "These policies, ranging from offshore wind energy projects in the Northern Aegean to mining and energy investments in Kurdistan, turn ecological destruction into a matter of dispossession and domination. Moreover, instead of using the ongoing period of non-conflict as an opportunity for democratic and social transformation that would strengthen the hopes for peace among the peoples of the region, the government is making considerable efforts to pave the way for companies to plunder the region. Exploiting society's hopes for peace in the interests of capital is incompatible with the true meaning of peace.




For us, genuine peace means not only the silencing of weapons but also ensuring that peoples have a say over their own living environments, lands, waters and futures. The social foundations of peace are being weakened as nature continues to be handed over to companies in Kurdistan and other regions of Turkey, the will of local communities is disregarded, and those engaged in ecological struggles continue to face repression."




Akın defined peace as a political and social transformation that prioritizes the shared future of peoples rather than the interests of companies. He said: "Ecological justice cannot be achieved through policies that plunder nature, nor can lasting peace be established through practices that disregard the will of peoples. What we need is a political and social transformation that does not use the environment as a promotional showcase, but places nature and life above the profits of capital and makes peace a guarantee of the shared future of peoples rather than the interests of companies."




An alternative to COP31: The People's Climate Summit




Akın called for participation in the People's Climate Summit, which will be held alongside COP31 in Antalya in November 2026. He said that the People's Climate Summit would be an alternative gathering centered on the needs of peoples and climate justice: "The People's Climate Summit does not regard the climate crisis merely as a technical issue to be negotiated by states and corporations. Beyond that, the summit will be a gathering that addresses the crisis as a political and social issue directly affecting peoples' lives, labor, relationship with nature and future.




I would also like to take this opportunity to invite all citizens, workers, ecological movements, women, young people and people's organizations to participate in the People's Climate Summit gatherings, which will take place from 14 to 18 November, and to bring together our experiences, struggles and proposals for solutions."




Akın outlined the fundamental differences between COP31 and the People's Climate Summit as follows: "While governments and business interests negotiate their own interests at COP31, the fundamental importance of the People's Climate Summit lies in bringing together the voices and experiences of peoples, workers, local communities, women, young people and ecological movements struggling against ecological destruction. This is because those who bear the heaviest burden of the climate crisis are the very people who have contributed the least to creating it. Yet the boundaries of possible solutions are often determined by the interests of capital and the political calculations of states.




The People's Climate Summit provides an important platform for amplifying the voices of peoples against the climate crisis, bringing ecological justice together with social justice and contributing to the organization of genuine transformation from below."




Ibrahim Akın said that wars and militarism deepen ecological destruction and stressed the need to oppose the use of periods of non-conflict by companies to open up new areas for exploitation. He emphasized the importance of the People's Climate Summit, addressing opposition to war, the transition away from fossil fuels, the rights of nature, food sovereignty, labor struggles and peoples' right to determine their own futures as interconnected issues.




Summarizing the purpose of the People's Climate Summit, Akın said, "Beyond the official agenda of COP31, the People's Climate Summit aims to provide a platform for struggle that questions the economic and political relations behind ecological destruction and considers peace together with nature, society and the freedom of peoples."




Ibrahim Akın also explained their approach to COP31, stressing that the international struggle against climate change should not be rejected entirely. He said, "Our approach to COP31 is neither to regard the summit as a solution in itself nor to reject the international climate struggle altogether."




Akın emphasized that their main objective was to transform this process into a platform for struggle defending climate justice, historical responsibilities, a genuine transition away from fossil fuels, workers' rights and the living environments of local communities.




Call to join the rally in Antalya on 14 November




Ibrahim Akın also called for participation in the rally to be held in Antalya on 14 November as part of the Global Day of Action, at the invitation of the Labor and Democracy Forces. 




Akın concluded: "Finally, I would like to draw attention to the rally that will take place in Antalya on 14 November, the Global Day of Action. We will come together at an international rally bringing peoples together on 14 November, at the invitation of the Labor and Democracy Forces, to strengthen our collective struggle. We call on all citizens who want to raise their voices and objections against ecological destruction, war, plunder and exploitation to participate in this gathering.




I invite everyone to the 14 November rally in Antalya to strengthen solidarity among peoples, reinforce our collective struggle and unite our voices for a future based on nature, labor and peace."

title: DEM Party: Workplace deaths are consequence of a system of impunity that protects capital
content:
In a written statement, the Labour Commission recalled that on 8 November 2025, a fire broke out at a perfume-filling factory belonging to Ravive Kozmetik in the Dilovası district of Kocaeli. Seven workers, three of them children, lost their lives and six others were injured. “A year has passed. Yet, just as the pain of the families of the seven workers we lost has not subsided, their search for justice has still not yielded results,” the statement said.




The statement continued: “What happened in Dilovası was not a workplace accident, but the result of a model of production that disregards workers’ health and their right to life, of a lack of inspections, and of the capital’s insatiable pursuit of profit. title: Apoist prisoners: Fulfil the requirements of the process
content:
Apoist prisoners said in a statement: “Do not leave the Peace and Democratic Society Process at the level of rhetoric; fulfil its requirements! The physical freedom of our Leadership, along with the immediate release of all sick prisoners, is an issue on the agenda of this process that cannot be postponed.”




The statement added: “We, as political prisoners who have been held behind bars for years because of our ideas, our political identity and our commitment to our people's struggle for freedom, address our people and the public today.




The Peace and Democratic Society Process, initiated by our Leadership, represents a strategic shift and transformation aimed at rebuilding social life, political relations and approaches to struggle on democratic foundations. The transition from a strategy of armed struggle to one of democratic society and democratic politics places historical responsibilities on all social and political actors, above all the state and those in power. Concrete steps in keeping with the spirit of this process must be taken, the conflict-ridden conditions of the past must be overcome, and the way must be opened for a democratic solution.”




The statement continued: “However, the failure to take the democratic and legal steps required by the process, together with the government's delaying tactics and its tendency to drag things out, is having severe and potentially irreversible consequences, particularly for political prisoners behind bars. While there is talk of making peace part of social life and opening the way for democratic politics, prisons continue to be treated as places of isolation, punishment, the imposition of repentance and the breaking of prisoners' will. This is in clear contradiction with the very essence of the process.




Today, hundreds of our comrades are facing serious health problems, progressive illnesses and conditions that threaten their lives. Delays in hospital transfers, the obstruction of medical treatment and the failure to provide humane conditions appropriate to their health needs are unacceptable. When the right to life and the right to health are at stake, no political, administrative or security-related justification can absolve the authorities of their responsibility. Continuing to hold seriously ill prisoners in prison means openly putting their lives at risk.”




Condolences to the family of Tuncer Sağlam




The statement recalled that “most recently, the death of our comrade 

Tuncer Sağlam

, who had been battling advanced cancer and who, despite all the conditions of imprisonment, never wavered in his commitment to the struggle for freedom and a democratic society, is a painful expression of this reality. His death has once again demonstrated that the right of sick prisoners to healthcare and medical treatment is an urgent matter of the right to life that cannot be postponed.




We remember our comrade Tuncer Sağlam for his commitment to the free Kurdish will, his people and the struggle for a democratic society. In his person, we also remember with respect and gratitude all our comrades who have fallen as martyrs in prison. We extend our condolences to our patriotic people, particularly his family and loved ones, and reaffirm our pledge to keep his struggle and memory alive through the construction of a democratic society and a free life. The Peace and Democratic Society Process requires that the issue of political prisoners currently held in prisons be addressed from the perspective of a democratic solution. For peace to take root in social life, concrete steps must be taken in those areas where the most serious human rights violations occur.”




The statement underlined that “the arbitrary implementation of sentence enforcement provisions established within the existing legal framework, and the continued deprivation of freedom of political prisoners who have completed their sentences on various administrative pretexts, are unacceptable. Allowing political considerations to determine release procedures, imposing demands for expressions of repentance and pursuing policies of pressure intended to break prisoners' will are incompatible with any claim to democratisation. No one should be imprisoned because of their ideas, political identity or stance in the struggle for democracy.




In this regard, seriously ill prisoners must be released immediately and granted unconditional access to medical treatment and healthcare services. Our comrades who have completed their sentences but remain imprisoned must be freed, and unlawful practices in prisons must come to an end. While continuing to speak of peace and a democratic solution on the one hand, the government's failure to fulfil its responsibilities in the face of this grave reality in prisons is undermining public confidence in the process. Peace develops not through rhetoric alone, but through concrete legal and political steps that guarantee fundamental rights and freedoms.”




Fulfil the requirements of the process




The statement added: “We address the government and state authorities directly: Do not leave the Peace and Democratic Society Process at the level of rhetoric; fulfil its requirements! Address the issue of political prisoners in prisons from the perspective of a democratic solution. Immediately carry out the medical treatment and release procedures for seriously ill prisoners. Do not obstruct the freedom of prisoners who have completed their sentences through arbitrary sentence enforcement practices. Put an end to the imposition of repentance, policies of isolation and unlawful practices. Take concrete legal and political steps without delay towards emptying the prisons!




We reiterate that the success of the Peace and Democratic Society Process is possible only if democratisation is made a concrete reality in every sphere of life, rather than remaining a matter of words. The physical freedom of our Leadership, along with the release of all sick prisoners, is an urgent item on the agenda of this process that cannot be postponed. On this basis, we, as Apoist prisoners, will continue to intensify our struggle, with unwavering belief and determination in our commitment to freedom, peace and a democratic society, so that our people's aspirations for peace, equality and freedom may be realised.”

author: Unknown
title: Whereabouts of KJAR members detained in Urmia unknown since June
content:
The Kurdistan Free Women’s Community (KJAR) announced that it has been unable to obtain any information about two of its members detained by Iranian security forces in Urmia.




In its statement on Sunday, KJAR reported that its member Zahra Pirdehghan (32) was detained by Iranian state forces on June 25, while another member, Parvin Rasegh Qizilbash (33), was detained on June 28. The organization described the detentions as a clear violation of human rights.




According to the statement, the families reported that despite the considerable time that had passed since the two women activists were detained, they had received no information about where they were being held, their health conditions, or their fate. Neither the security authorities nor judicial institutions provided any information regarding their situation.




KJAR warned that depriving its members of their rights to legal representation, regular communication, and contact with their families, as well as subjecting them to enforced disappearance, constituted violations of international law.




The organization demanded that the fate of its members be disclosed immediately and called for their fundamental rights, including access to medical examinations and communication, to be guaranteed.

title: ‘We cannot envision peace independently of any people or culture’
content:
As the Peace and Democratic Society Process continues, women came together to discuss the process and share their experiences of peacebuilding. Hundreds of women gathered at the “Women Side by Side, Discussing the Future” conference to address cultural, political, and social issues. Attended by women from various cities across Kurdistan and Turkey, the conference in Ankara explored women’s roles in peace processes and their ongoing efforts, as well as issues related to ecology and mother-tongue rights.




Painter Neşe Toprak, who attended the conference as a representative of the cultural sector, reflected on its atmosphere and outcomes. Emphasizing that efforts to embed peace in society must encompass all peoples and social groups, Toprak highlighted the importance of women, culture, ecology, and the struggle for mother-tongue rights in the process.




Toprak explained that the conference was organized to give concrete expression to women’s role as active participants in the process. Following nearly two months of preparation, it was held under the leadership of 82 organizing groups. The conference brought together participants from numerous cities across Turkey and from Europe, including women working to ensure that peoples can freely preserve and express their own languages, cultures, and civilizations.










https://video.anf-news2.com/live/firat/21711330_20261107194045_2026-11-08-amed-nese-toprak-barisin-toplumsallasmasi-kadinlarin-ortak-mucadelesiyle-mumkun_1.mp4










‘Peace must encompass all peoples’




Describing the conference as a highly attended event with an exciting atmosphere, Neşe Toprak said that hopes for an end to the policies of assimilation and war that the Kurdish people had faced for years generated optimism about the new process. Highlighting the significance of discussions resuming after an interruption of nearly ten years, Toprak said that extensive assessments had been made on what it means to embed peace in society, what kinds of initiatives could be undertaken in different areas, and how peace could be brought into everyday social life.




Toprak noted that the conference featured sessions and panels attended by women politicians, where participants discussed how political peace could be built and reflected in society. Women from different areas of struggle shared their experiences, emphasizing that culture and ecology were also fundamental components of efforts to embed peace in society.




Stating that ecology was another major topic on the conference agenda, Toprak said discussions had taken place within the framework of the democratic, ecological, and women’s liberation paradigm. Drawing attention to the exploitation of nature and ecological destruction in Kurdistan, Toprak said:




“We cannot consider ecology separately from social peace. What we mean by bringing peace into society encompasses every aspect of life. Culture, ecology, and women’s freedom are all integral parts of life. We depend on the land we live on, so we must take responsibility for it and protect nature.




At the conference, we focused particularly on the exploitation of nature in Kurdistan, ecological problems, and how to combat them. We discussed how to build a better life, protect nature, and develop an ecological way of living.”




‘Every people should have the right to education in their mother tongue’




Emphasizing the important role of culture in embedding peace in society, Neşe Toprak said that mother-tongue rights and the right to education in one’s mother tongue were among the key issues discussed at the conference.




Noting that they were working in the field of Kurdish culture and art, Neşe Toprak said, “We see ourselves not merely as artists but, more importantly, as people working to preserve and promote culture. For this reason, we cannot consider culture separately from peace and its integration into society. There was extensive discussion, particularly about mother-tongue rights and the right to education in one’s mother tongue. We emphasized that every people should be able to receive education in their own mother tongue.”




Stressing that the Kurdish people’s struggle could not be viewed separately from the struggles of other peoples for their languages and cultures, Toprak concluded: “We are not struggling solely for the Kurdish people. We attach importance to the struggles of all peoples whose languages, cultures, and very existence have been denied and who have been subjected to assimilation. The demands of a friend who is working to preserve the Hemşin language were also important to us. As Kurds, Kurdish politicians, and cultural workers, we expressed our commitment to standing in solidarity with them and supporting their efforts.”

title: Culture and arts festival in Rome commemorates Nagihan Akarsel
content:
The 'Voce Arcaica' (Ancient Voice) Art and Culture Festival, organised annually in Italy by the Jineolojî Academy, was held in memory of Nagihan Akarsel, a member of the Jineolojî Research Centre, writer and journalist who was assassinated in an armed attack outside her home in Sulaymaniyah (Silêmanî) on 4 October 2022.




The festival took place on November 7 at the Teatro Biblioteca Quarticciolo in Rome. The morning program featured performances and sound and rhythm workshops focusing on the ancient voices of women. The activities, attended by Italian, Kurdish, and migrant women, explored women’s experiences of transforming sorrow, grief, and emotions into artistic expression.
