author: Unknown
title: Karacabey: Kurdish theatre is banned based on political risks
content:
Art in Turkey has faced censorship and repressive policies since the early years of the Republic. Theatre has also been subjected to the repression and censorship seen across many fields of artistic expression.




The struggle to produce political theatre continues in Turkey despite numerous obstacles, with political plays being banned and Kurdish-language productions unable to find stages. Meanwhile, Kurds and other communities living in Turkey who are regarded as the "other" are often represented on stage through negative characters.




ANF spoke to Associate Professor Süreyya Karacabey, an academic known for her work on theatre theory, playwriting and art criticism in Turkey, who was dismissed from her position by a statutory decree (KHK) in 2017. We discussed the state of theatre in Turkey, her assessments of the latest peace process and the role of art in the struggle for peace.




‘The desire to connect with society has a political dimension’




Süreyya Karacabey stated that theatre has a political dimension in a broader sense and pointed out that the struggle to establish a connection with society continues. She emphasised that political, social and economic conditions play a decisive role in shaping the theatrical environment.




Karacabey continued: ‘‘Throughout history, discussions about theatre have examined the ways in which publicly funded theatres, private theatres and independent theatres exist within the broader theatrical environment. Attempts are made to identify patterns and trends through the nature of productions and the choices being made. Most of these developments, however, are not simply the result of freely changing aesthetic preferences. They belong to a field shaped by multiple factors at the intersection of politics, society and economics. When theatre was regarded as a public service, reaching the majority of society was a primary objective. Once that approach was abandoned, the introduction of sponsorship systems led to the emergence of a different theatrical landscape.




The history of this transformation is long. However, in a structure lacking the arrangements necessary for theatre to sustain its own autonomous system, the resulting picture would inevitably reflect a struggle between unequal actors. And that is precisely what happened. The desire to establish a connection with society, setting aside the tautology that theatre is always directed towards society, is a desire with political implications. The desire to connect with one's own audience has now become more pronounced. Who constitutes society? What are its dynamics? Does performing before large crowds necessarily mean establishing a connection with society? These are all questions that need to be discussed. If connection always involves interaction, learning from one another and mutual influence, and if it is related to a broader objective, it becomes difficult to speak of such a connection within a world of micro-level relationships.’’




‘The forces shaping theatre have changed’




Karacabey stated that theatre is not free and offered the following assessment of its current situation: ‘‘Is anything free in this country for theatre to be free? Every distortion of a terrible economic system can be seen in the theatrical field. There are theatres dominated by capital, publicly funded theatres receiving state support, private theatres forced to operate as companies, and independent stages. Large-scale productions are now monopolised by theatres financed either by capital or by the state. What we are witnessing goes beyond the traditional sponsorship system.




The forces shaping theatre have changed: the celebrity-focused editorial policies of ticketing platforms, award systems structured to promote high-budget productions, the space that arts and culture media devote to sponsored projects, and large-scale stages established inside shopping centres. The entry of capital into the field has institutionalised the argument that 'this is what audiences want', spread the pressure to produce 'plays that will sell' and increasingly shaped repertoire choices according to market signals. On the one hand, there is a system that brings renowned directors and designers from Britain. On the other, the same system takes populist steps, filling auditoriums with thousands of seats with productions barely more sophisticated than school performances. The production system transfers decisions about which play will be staged, who will be involved and where it will be performed from artists to producers and investors.




Above all, this means the elimination of creative freedom. You cannot choose the play you want or work with the people you want. The freedom of theatres excluded from the unequal distribution of resources to express what they wish is curtailed by the deprivation of their very right to exist. Freedom of expression, already severely restricted by political pressure, has become intertwined with creative freedom rendered impossible by economic pressures. To speak of the freedom of theatres dependent on capital, the state or local authorities would require an apology to the very word 'freedom'.’’




‘The path has been blocked for independent theatres’




Süreyya Karacabey stated that the system has left independent theatres without a way forward and that theatres struggling to survive without financial support face structural problems. Sharing the findings of a study on independent stages in Istanbul, Karacabey said: ‘‘The system is already pushing independent theatres into an undefined space. The path forward has been blocked for them. Theatres trying to survive without support are being turned into the pariahs of this system. Let me share the findings of another study: 'According to interviews we conducted with 68 independent stages in Istanbul, 88.2 per cent receive no sponsorship or donations whatsoever. Those that do receive support have to make do with very small amounts. Some 73.5 per cent either employ no full-time staff or operate with just one person. We are talking about functioning theatre venues, yet they do not even have essential staff such as lighting technicians, sound technicians, ushers or box-office attendants. These operations depend on daily-paid or volunteer workers. Most of the time, artists from the companies renting the stages take on these responsibilities themselves. Some 75 per cent of independent stages say they lack an institutional communication strategy, while 82.4 per cent have a member of their team handling communications as an additional responsibility. These are theatre venues that cannot provide regular employment, establish professional teams or invest in promotional infrastructure. The phrase "we are improvising our way through it", which we heard repeatedly throughout the research, does not describe a stylistic preference. It has become the everyday expression of structural deprivation.'




Consider the explosion in one-person productions and plays with very small casts across the country. Of course, there have always been cases where this was an aesthetic choice. But today, it is no longer an aesthetic preference. It is the result of economic necessity.’’




Karacabey also addressed the situation of political theatre in Turkey, stressing that political theatre cannot be understood solely through political slogans and propaganda. She said: ‘‘Let me try to answer both of your questions together. The relationship between politics and theatre has a long history. We can also read older texts politically. Consider contemporary interpretations of Antigone or Shakespeare's plays. When political theatre emerged as a form of theatre involved in class struggle, combining political arguments with theatrical expression and therefore pursuing a particular mission, it was closely connected to the understanding of politics prevailing at the time. There was a world that needed to be changed and a conception of the artist whose work served that transformation.




It was a form of theatre that questioned its role in social and historical change and sometimes brought the objectives of contemporary politics onto the stage or into the streets. Some forms chose to become direct instruments of action, appearing in the middle of strikes, in factories, at rallies and in working-class neighbourhoods. Others adopted more artistic approaches on stage, seeking to transform their audiences. It was a way of bringing art and politics together in an era of mass mobilisation. There were also examples that advocated art's direct participation in action, going beyond its contribution to social benefit.




In Turkey, this approach emerged during the 1960s through playwrights' discussions of social criticism, cultural imperialism and national theatre. It gained momentum through various applications of the theatrical approaches of Piscator and Brecht. By the 1970s, one of the most politically active periods in the country's history, its objective had shifted from raising political awareness among the masses to becoming integrated with them.’’




Karacabey also said: “Political theatre's connection with class and its desire for change, which it also advanced through its own organisation, corresponded to the demands of that period. The groups you mentioned in your question, which prioritised political slogans and propaganda, multiplied during those years. We can speak here of a structure that entirely placed its autonomous existence at the service of politics. Most criticism was directed precisely at this point. But political theatre was never merely propaganda theatre. Like every theatrical form, it encompassed groups pursuing different approaches and generated debates about the function of theatre. Creative examples produced more lasting results by involving themselves in genuine structural transformation, through collective writing, the nature of their relationship with the masses, mutual interaction and other practices.




As changes around the world transformed the meaning attributed to politics, political theatre was inevitably going to change as well. The difficulties facing political theatre today must be understood in this context. Of course, examples of political theatre still exist. But in a period when politics has been stifled and obscured, political theatre needs to abandon certain established assumptions in order to redefine its function. Many things that were relevant to the world of the 1970s are no longer relevant today. Repeating them merely evokes a memory of political theatre that has lost its impact. Alternatively, when you adopt the slogan 'everything is political', you risk overlooking politics' relationship with the public and its objective of collective emancipation.




The world has changed, but exploitation has not disappeared. Neither have inequalities nor the deprivation of freedoms. What has disappeared is the political framework that once guided political theatre. Under these circumstances, perhaps theatre itself will have to assume responsibility. For me, theatre that simply expresses politically correct positions is not political theatre. Theatre becomes political when it produces solutions to collective concerns.’’




‘The representation of the other has always been problematic in Turkey’




Süreyya Karacabey stated that the representation of the "other" has been problematic throughout Turkey's history and offered the following assessment of theatre's approach to different identities: ‘‘The representation of the other in Turkey has always been problematic, as we all know, even if we set aside the efforts of individual voices without forgetting their contributions. Clearly, answering this question properly would require the findings of substantial research. However, I can speak about some general impressions. On the one hand, we are living in a period when more plays dealing with identities are being staged. Yet the affirmation of these identities has to be rendered harmless because it is surrounded by the threat of greater discrimination.




We may still encounter the direct humiliation and parody of an identity by a dominant identity, as happened in the past, but this is no longer particularly widespread. That is because a section of society capable of reacting against such representations has emerged, although it is undoubtedly small. There is actually a strange situation here: As long as these identities are presented as harmless subjects of cultural pluralism, without criticising state policies, there is no problem. Classical racism has changed, and we can now speak sentimentally about the contributions of multiculturalism, provided it poses no threat.




Theatre has found a more subtle approach. But when you look at television series, where representations are genuinely aimed at appealing to mainstream culture, the 'others' are still associated with the darker side of the story.’’




‘Kurdish-language theatre is considered a political risk’




Süreyya Karacabey also assessed theatre's approach to the Kurdish question in Turkey, pointing out that even plays addressing the issue indirectly have often been forced to use coded and metaphorical language.




Karacabey said: ‘‘We are talking about a prohibited area. Although few in number, plays addressing the Kurdish question indirectly have certainly been written. But unless they adopted an indirect language and a metaphorical structure, it was impossible for them to be staged. In the world of the 1970s, when the underdeveloped East, injustices in the land ownership system and the institution of landlordism were criticised, the issue was not so much Kurdish identity as a region of the country that had been left behind. I do not know of any play that directly discussed the Kurdish question as a struggle for political identity. How can anyone exercise freedom of thought under such circumstances? To discuss issues independently, you must first be free or be prepared to take certain risks. Those who are prepared to take those risks are already unable to practise theatre."




Karacabey stated that producing Kurdish-language theatre is regarded as objectionable and said: "Language is undoubtedly a constitutive element of collective memory. The mother tongue is a right, and I feel embarrassed that we even have to discuss this in this day and age. Defending a people's right to think, speak and create art in the language into which they were born is not a privilege. It is a fundamental right. However, because the current approach is concerned not with recognising this natural right but with denying it, the right is prohibited according to assessments of political risk.’’




‘Politics must not turn the means into an end’




Süreyya Karacabey also addressed the Peace and Democratic Society Process, emphasising that pragmatic methods must not turn the means into an end.




Karacabey said: ‘‘Examples from around the world show that peace processes extend over very long periods and that, even after various stages and considerable efforts, peace can still only be built on fragile foundations. What makes these foundations fragile are the changing conditions of negotiations and the obstacles to genuinely establishing a new structure.




This is a matter for politics. I believe pragmatic methods must not turn the means into an end. After all, for someone who has always insisted on peace, what could be better than the goal of a society whose members no longer fight one another? Where do Turks and other peoples stand in the negotiations between the Kurds and the state? If they are automatically regarded as standing behind the state, that is deeply troubling. If they are not, where are they?




This is a long road. It must become rooted in society, establish more unifying conditions for the common good, and this concern must become a concern shared by all of us. I hope the way forward will open up.’’




‘Art engages with the impossible’




Süreyya Karacabey stated that artists who feel responsible for society and the world share a common path of struggle. She highlighted the role of art in the struggle for peace: ‘‘I think these questions actually lead us to the relationship between society and art. For artists who feel responsible for the collective and the world, the path of struggle is shared. Because the kind of country they live in matters to them, they do not hesitate to take responsibility.




They find a way through their own artistic language and do not hesitate to become part of the struggle. That is because prohibitions imposed on one section of society, and the denial of rights and justice, are directed against everyone. They know they must establish a connection with the whole. Once they think in this way, they become part of that responsibility, and their dreams take on a collective character.




Under these circumstances, there is no need to assign them a task. That is because the reason for our collective existence will be to build a country where we can all live together in freedom. But we must not forget what someone once said: 'Politics is the art of the possible, whereas art engages with the impossible.'’’

title: Constitutional Court orders retrial of Mazlum İçli after ten years in prison
content:
Mazlum İçli has already spent more than ten years of his life in prison. He was accused of involvement, at the age of 14, in the killing of four people during the Kobanê protests in Amed (Turkish: Diyarbakır) in October 2014. He was sentenced to a total of 124 years and eight months in prison. However, evidence that could exonerate him was not adequately considered during the trial. Turkey’s Constitutional Court has now confirmed serious deficiencies in the reasoning behind the verdict and ordered a retrial. İçli’s defense team intends to seek his immediate release.




The ruling, issued on September 16, 2026, could mark a decisive turning point in a case that has been fraught with contradictions for years. At the heart of the case is the question of why İçli was convicted despite several witnesses confirming that he was attending a wedding in the district of Kulp, approximately 140 kilometers away, at the time of the alleged crime. Video footage and an expert report also support his alibi.




The Constitutional Court particularly criticized the criminal court’s failure to provide a reasoned assessment of conflicting expert reports. While one examination suggested that İçli might be identifiable in footage from the crime scene, another report by the same expert confirmed with a high degree of probability that he was present at the wedding. title: Women organize symposium on social memory and trauma in Amed
content:
A symposium titled “Speaking Out: Social Memory, Testimony and Trauma” began at the Ali Emiri Conference Hall in cooperation with Amed Metropolitan Municipality, the Trauma Studies Association, and the Forum for Social Peace and Freedom.




Speaking during a session titled “Waiting at Ground Zero: Trauma, Unresolved Grief and the Power of Testimony in Enforced Disappearances,” moderated by social worker İrfan Ekinci, Sebla Arcan, a member of the Human Rights Association’s (İHD) Commission on Disappearances in Custody, said, “A person experiencing trauma due to the disappearance of a loved one can neither move forward nor go back. They remain trapped in that moment.”




Highlighting the trauma caused by enforced disappearances, Arcan said, “The effects continue for two or three generations after an enforced disappearance. But other things are also passed down through generations in connection with enforced disappearances. A sense of justice, the determination to struggle, and the spirit of resistance are also transmitted. What is passed down from generation to generation is not only trauma and grief but also political consciousness.”

title: Seriously ill prisoner Tuncer Sağlam dies in Ankara
content:
Seriously ill political prisoner Tuncer Sağlam died in Ankara on Saturday morning. Sağlam was arrested and imprisoned in 2024 in the province of Van on charges of “propaganda for a terrorist organization.” Due to his critical health condition, he had most recently been receiving treatment at Etlik Hospital in Ankara, where he died after 25 days of treatment.




Sağlam was initially held at Van High-Security Prison. After his health deteriorated significantly, he was transferred to Sincan Prison No. 2 in the Turkish capital, Ankara, on October 9. His condition continued to worsen during his subsequent hospitalization, and he eventually had to be intubated and placed on mechanical ventilation.




Following the completion of the autopsy, Tuncer Sağlam’s body is expected to be transferred to his hometown of Van, where he will be laid to rest.

title: Mihemed: Women’s participation in decision making is a fundamental guarantee for future Syria

title: Final declaration of the Conference on the Social Institutionalization of Women’s Policies
content:
Women’s policies in Kurdish municipalities are no longer to be limited to individual institutions or social services but are intended to shape every aspect of municipal self-governance. This was one of the key outcomes of the Conference on the Social Institutionalization of Women’s Policies, held on November 2 and 3 in Amed (Turkish: Diyarbakır). In a final declaration published following the event, participants outlined a comprehensive program to rebuild municipal women’s structures, promote women’s economic self-determination, and ensure their organized participation in political decision-making.




Organized by the Women’s Council of Democratic Local Administrations and hosted by Amed Metropolitan Municipality, the conference was held under the slogan “Through Production and Organizing, We Embed Our Women’s Struggle in Society.” Through a total of 21 resolutions, the participating women’s organizations aim to establish a new organizational, financial, and social foundation for municipal women’s policies.




This approach is also shaped by years of state intervention in Kurdish municipal politics. The appointment of government trustees led to the closure of numerous women’s institutions, the abolition of independent municipal programs for women, and the dismantling of structures built up over many years. The conference therefore views the rebuilding of these institutions not merely as an administrative task but as part of the struggle for democratic self-governance and social transformation.




Rebuilding after years of state-imposed trusteeship




Over the decades, the Kurdish women’s movement has developed an approach to municipal governance that regards women’s liberation as a prerequisite for a democratic society. This includes autonomous women’s councils, solidarity-based economic models, institutions providing protection against violence, and women’s participation in political decision-making processes. With the removal of elected municipal administrations and the appointment of government trustees, these structures were systematically undermined in many cities across North Kurdistan. The final declaration describes the consequences as profound damage to both municipal institutions and their roots in society.




The participants therefore see themselves as facing a dual task: rights and institutions secured through years of struggle must be restored, while new structures must be so firmly rooted in society that women’s policies no longer depend solely on the political composition of a particular municipal administration.




“Overcoming the damage caused by state-imposed trusteeship, strengthening the achievements of women once again, and ensuring their permanent institutionalization are among our fundamental tasks for the period ahead,” the declaration stated.




The conference links this objective to a fundamental transformation of municipal decision-making processes. In the future, women’s policies are no longer to be the exclusive responsibility of dedicated women’s departments. Instead, all municipal departments are to be required to incorporate women’s needs, rights, and perspectives into their planning, budgets, and services.




Women’s policies to shape all municipal decisions




One of the most far-reaching resolutions concerns the institutional status of women’s policies. The conference called for principles of women’s liberation to be formally incorporated into the regulations, responsibilities, and working procedures of all municipal institutions.




This applies not only to social services and protection against violence but also to urban planning, economic development, education, culture, transportation, and the allocation of public funds.




Gender-responsive budgeting is particularly important in this regard. Municipal budgets are to be more closely aligned with the realities of women’s lives and their needs. At the same time, financial resources allocated to women’s policies are to be secured, and women’s organizations are to be involved in the preparation, implementation, and oversight of municipal budgets.




The conference also called for women’s departments to be strengthened in terms of staffing and technical resources. Existing shortcomings in premises, equipment, and organizational responsibilities are to be systematically identified and addressed through binding action plans.




Cooperation between women’s economic initiatives, educational programs, and protection against violence is also to be improved. Rather than operating as separate projects, these areas are to be brought together through joint planning and evaluation structures that coordinate different measures.




Protection against violence: From shelter to long-term self-determination




Another key focus of the conference was the fight against violence against women. Participants called for the expansion of women’s shelters and counseling centers in line with actual needs.




The aim is not merely to increase the number of facilities. Their safety, accessibility, and professional resources are equally important. New facilities should only open once sufficient qualified personnel and the necessary technical infrastructure are in place.




In rural areas, additional women’s life centers are to be established to serve several neighboring villages.




The resolutions go beyond providing immediate assistance to women experiencing violence. Survivors of violence are to have long-term access to safe housing, financial support, childcare, legal counseling, and social assistance. The aim is to prevent economic dependence or a lack of childcare options from forcing women to return to abusive living conditions. Staff working in women’s shelters and counseling centers are also to receive regular professional guidance, supervision, and peer support to help reduce their workload and emotional strain.




To improve legal assistance, existing cooperation agreements with bar associations are to be renewed and expanded. The plans include more binding procedures for handling requests for assistance and closer cooperation between the institutions involved.




At the same time, responsibility for preventing and addressing violence is to be shared more broadly across municipal administrations. A binding policy framework for dealing with violence is to be implemented in all municipal departments and regularly reviewed.




Women’s communes as a new form of social organization




The conference’s broader vision for social transformation is particularly evident in its plans to establish women’s solidarity communes. These are initially to be established in selected neighborhoods or near existing women’s counseling and women’s life centers. Unlike conventional counseling centers, these communes are intended not only to provide professional support services but also to enable women themselves to establish and sustain solidarity-based structures. Mutual support, collective organizing, and protection against violence are to become more firmly rooted in women’s immediate living environments.




In doing so, the conference builds on the Kurdish women’s movement’s approach to communal organization. Women’s councils, neighborhood assemblies, and local women’s initiatives are not merely to serve as points of contact for municipal administrations but are expected to independently articulate social needs and help shape political decisions. Closer cooperation is planned with the Free Women’s Movement (TJA), provincial women’s councils, and other women’s organizations.




Municipal work is thus intended to move increasingly beyond administrative buildings and into neighborhoods, villages, and everyday life. The participants emphasized that simply raising awareness of municipal services was not enough. Instead, women’s own capacity for organized collective action must be strengthened.




Economic independence through collective production




Women’s economic circumstances feature prominently in the conference resolutions. Poverty, precarious employment, unpaid care work, and economic dependence are identified as major obstacles to social self-determination.




As an alternative, the conference advocates a municipal, solidarity-based women’s economy. Collective forms of production are to be expanded and more closely aligned with local needs. To this end, each municipality is first expected to assess the products, economic skills, and production opportunities available locally. Based on these assessments, independent economic models are to be developed rather than implementing identical projects everywhere.




Another initiative focuses on marketing and distribution. Central sales outlets and permanent marketing and distribution networks are to be established for products made by women’s cooperatives and through collective production. Cooperation between municipalities is also to be improved, enabling women to sell their products beyond their immediate local markets.




The participants link these economic measures to a redistribution of care responsibilities within society. A lack of childcare, caregiving obligations, and inadequate transportation connections often make it difficult for women to access employment, education, and political organizing. For this reason, daycare centers, childcare services, and accessible transportation options are to be expanded. The long-term objective is to ensure that care work is no longer borne predominantly by individual women and families but is organized as a collective social responsibility.




Education as a means of social transformation




The conference places fundamental importance on education. Planned programs are intended to go beyond vocational training to challenge gender relations and patriarchal patterns of thinking. The proposed topics include the ideology of women’s liberation, self-defense, egalitarian relationships, democratic family structures, and overcoming male dominance. Corresponding workshops are also to be offered for men. Educational programs are to be conducted by individuals familiar with the pedagogical and political foundations of the women’s movement. Their content and methods are to be regularly reviewed and further developed.




At the same time, municipal educational institutions are to become more closely involved in social science research and the development of their own projects. Regular studies in neighborhoods and villages are intended to help identify social needs more accurately and translate the findings into concrete political measures.




Particular emphasis is placed on young women. Their experiences and demands are to be more fully incorporated into political, cultural, and social programs. Young women are also to develop their own forms of organization and participate directly in municipal decision-making processes.




Multilingualism and the participation of marginalized women




The final declaration explicitly links women’s policies to the right to language, cultural identity, and social participation. Multilingual municipal administration and the use of mother tongues are to be strengthened in education, culture, the arts, sports, and social institutions. This gives language rights a distinct significance within women’s policies. Women should not only be able to access municipal services in a language prescribed by the state but also contribute their own languages and cultural experiences to shaping public life.




Special measures are planned for women facing multiple forms of discrimination, particularly women with disabilities and refugee women. The conference called for their needs to be addressed beyond the framework of general social programs. Instead, their autonomous organizing and participation in political decision-making are to be actively promoted. At the same time, ableist, discriminatory, and exclusionary social structures must be challenged.




Women-centered cities and ecological living spaces




Beyond the immediate scope of municipal administration, the conference outlined a long-term vision for shaping cities and living environments. Under the concept of the “women-centered city,” ecological, democratic, and communal forms of coexistence are to be developed. Municipal action plans are envisaged for this purpose, to be implemented and regularly reviewed across all participating local administrations.




This approach links the design of public spaces to issues of safety, mobility, economic independence, and democratic participation. Women are not merely to be regarded as users of urban services but are to participate in planning and transforming their living environments. In addition, autonomous living spaces are to be created where women can live free from violence, economic dependence, social exclusion, and precarious living conditions.




Women’s organizing as a prerequisite for lasting change




The conference resolutions also reflect a process of political reflection and consensus-building within the Kurdish women’s movement. The participants emphasized that institutional achievements alone cannot provide lasting protection against political setbacks. Problems within their own organizational and working structures must also be openly addressed, and patriarchal patterns of behavior must be overcome.




The declaration identifies solidarity among women, collective responsibility, and a willingness to engage in criticism and self-criticism as essential foundations for this process. Women’s liberation is not understood as a political goal that can be achieved once and for all, but as an ongoing social process requiring continuous organizing and practical change.




“We regard women’s freedom as the foundation of social freedom and the organized will of women as a driving force in shaping democratic life,” the final declaration stated.




Through the 21 resolutions, the participating women’s organizations committed themselves to combining the rebuilding of municipal institutions with stronger grassroots organizing. The conference summarized its political objectives in its concluding appeal:




“Through the strength of our organizing, we will produce, organize, embed our struggle in society, and build a free life together. Now is the time for women, now is the time to strengthen the organized struggle and create a free life together.”

title: Martyrs of Kurdistan’s Freedom Struggle commemorated in Sine
content:
Following the HPG’s announcement of the identities of nine guerrillas from Rojhilatê Kurdistan who fell as martyrs in the freedom struggle in previous years, a memorial event was held in the city of Sanandaj (Sine).







During the commemoration, the Martyrs’ Families Committee and Peace Mothers carried photographs of the fallen guerrillas and repeatedly chanted the slogan “Şehîd namirin” (Martyrs never die).







 







At the event, organised by the Martyrs’ Families Committee and the Peace Mothers, it was stated that the martyrs had become symbols of unity among all parts of Kurdistan.







It was also emphasised that the martyrs of the freedom struggle, from Kobanê, Shengal, Amed, Qamishlo and Hewraman to Sine, had set an example of defending humanity against ISIS.




At the end of the ceremony, the Martyrs’ Families Committee of Rojhilatê Kurdistan extended its condolences to the people of Sine and the patriotic people of Kurdistan. The committee also reiterated that the martyrs of Rojhilatê Kurdistan are martyrs of the entire Kurdish people.

title: Laura Quagliuolo: Öcalan's freedom is key to lasting peace
content:
The Call for Peace and a Democratic Society issued by Abdullah Öcalan on 27 February 2025 brought discussions on a democratic solution to the Kurdish question into a new phase. International calls for Öcalan's freedom and the implementation of the European Court of Human Rights (ECtHR) ruling on the "right to hope" also continue. Demands for Turkey to fulfill its obligations under the supervision of the Council of Europe's Committee of Ministers are increasingly coming to the fore.




Italian feminist activist, writer and member of the Rete Jin women's solidarity network Laura Quagliuolo spoke to ANF about the Peace and Democratic Society Process, the importance of Öcalan's freedom for a democratic solution, the failure to implement ECtHR rulings and the role of women in building peace.




Efforts to find a democratic solution to the Kurdish question have continued since the call issued by Abdullah Öcalan on 27 February 2025. How do you assess the process at its current stage? What do you think are the fundamental conditions that must be met to achieve lasting peace?




I think the Peace and Democratic Society Process in Turkey has not yet been realized. We have not reached that point yet, primarily because Abdullah Öcalan is not free. I believe Öcalan's freedom is a very important condition for the Kurdish people to achieve freedom and for their existence to be recognized. The Kurdish people can no longer be ignored. As you know, Abdullah Öcalan's call was extremely clear and powerful. The guerrillas came down from the mountains and laid down their weapons. Their weapons were burned in a ceremony. This was an enormously significant step toward peace.




However, the Kurdish people must also be recognized. Their language, traditions, culture and way of life must be recognized. They can no longer be subjected to oppression, as the Turkish state has done in the past and continues to do today. Therefore, the most important issue, first and foremost, is the freedom of Abdullah Öcalan and the many other comrades who remain imprisoned under various circumstances.




Abdullah Öcalan's situation is particularly serious and troubling. Because after nearly 28 years of imprisonment, they must acknowledge that he has always been someone who has taken steps toward peace in the Middle East. Another condition is recognizing that the Kurdish people, and not only the Kurds but other peoples as well, are working and living according to the principles that emerge from Abdullah Öcalan's paradigm. This must be recognized because it represents hope not only for Turkey but for the entire Middle East and, if I may say so, for the whole world.




As you mentioned, despite the ongoing process, there has been no fundamental change in the legal status or prison conditions of Kurdish People's Leader Abdullah Öcalan. This remains one of the Kurdish side's most fundamental demands. Do you believe lasting peace can genuinely be built without securing the conditions necessary for Öcalan's freedom and participation in the process?




As I said before, Öcalan's freedom must be guaranteed. He must have the freedom to speak to the people, to his own people. It is not only a matter of allowing him to participate in meetings. Conditions must also be established in which he can express his views and be heard by everyone. Because, in my opinion, he is a man of peace. He is also someone who can help guide this peace process in the right direction. But they cannot continue to keep him imprisoned like this. They need to take steps, and serious ones at that.




The ECtHR ruled against Turkey in 2014 over the aggravated life sentence imposed on Kurdish People's Leader Abdullah Öcalan without the possibility of release. However, more than 12 years later, the ruling has still not been fully implemented. How should this position be interpreted? What concrete steps do you expect from the Council of Europe's Committee of Ministers at its meeting in December?




You know, Europe constantly talks about peace and many other things. But in reality, Europe is not genuinely committed to achieving peace, whether in the Middle East, in the war between Russia and Ukraine, or anywhere else. They talk, but they have done nothing in the face of the genocide in Palestine. That is the situation in Europe. They speak and then fall silent. What remains after their speeches is silence. That is exactly what happened 12 years ago. You know, the court, all those rulings and everything else... The court ruled against the Turkish state over this imprisonment. But afterward, they were not consistent in ensuring that their own decisions were respected. They are doing nothing to secure the implementation of their rulings or to compel Turkey to comply with them.




They simply left the matter there. They announced their decisions and then allowed Turkey to do whatever it wanted. Throughout all these years, the Turkish state has clearly demonstrated its intentions and what it really wants to do: stop the peace process, obstruct it, oppress the Kurdish people and seize control of their municipalities. You know, they have done everything they could to silence all of this. Europe, meanwhile, has done very little. Neither Europe as a whole, nor the Commission or other institutions, nor individual states have taken meaningful action. They have remained truly silent. Therefore, this silence sends a message to the Turkish state, to Erdoğan and to others: You can do whatever you want.




Democratic confederalism offers hope for the whole world




I think what they need to understand is this: If they want peace not only in Turkey and Syria but throughout the Middle East, they must support the work being carried out by the Kurdish people in every part of Kurdistan. They must support the building of a different society, the inclusion of women in social life and all these efforts.




Yes, I am talking about democratic confederalism. This model is being implemented almost everywhere, although at different levels. Particularly in Syria, and even in Turkey. Because when I visited Bakur, or Northern Kurdistan, about ten years ago, I saw with my own eyes that democratic confederalism was already being practiced in some form in areas where Kurdish mayors had been elected. That is how I see it.




You recently joined hundreds of individuals and organizations in signing an international appeal demanding the implementation of the right to hope for Kurdish People's Leader Abdullah Öcalan. What significance do you think this international solidarity and mobilization has for a democratic solution to the Kurdish question?




Yes, as I said earlier, I believe that the struggle for Abdullah Öcalan's freedom is extremely important for the situation in that region. Moreover, as I have already mentioned, its significance extends far beyond that region. Because Abdullah Öcalan addresses everyone in his writings, not only the people living in that region. Therefore, the presence of someone like him is extremely important.




He does not really want to be a leader in the conventional sense. He wants to be a guide. Having such a guide, being able to speak with him and ensuring that he can participate in important decision-making discussions would be truly significant. And, unless I am mistaken, I believe the Kurdish people want the same thing. I think this is one of the conditions the Kurdish people want to see fulfilled so that they can genuinely achieve peace and work together with the national institutions of Turkey, Syria or other countries.




Kurdish women have played an important role in the struggle for peace, democracy and women's rights for many years. As a feminist activist who has been involved in this struggle for decades, how do you assess women's role in the current peace process? Why is their participation so important for building genuine and lasting peace?




This is one of the fundamental issues facing the entire world. You know, women have always been a driving force for peace, and a very powerful one. They have always played a very important role in holding society together, speaking about peace and preserving social cohesion. This is extremely important. We have also seen how important women's role in society is in North and East Syria. Women played, and continue to play, an extremely important role in maintaining peace, preventing violence, stopping violence and attacks against women, and keeping society together.




Therefore, this is very important not only there but everywhere. It is their concern, but it is also the concern of those of us living in Europe and of people throughout the world. Women are struggling for this as well.




Finally, what role should the European Union and the international community play in supporting this peace process? What message would you like to convey to the European public regarding the freedom of Kurdish People's Leader Abdullah Öcalan and a solution to the Kurdish question?




My message is that they should listen to what Abdullah Öcalan says, read what he writes and understand what he expects from the international community. I think the current Pope has also understood this. I mean, if you read his latest encyclical, it almost seems as though he has read Öcalan too. You can see this in what he says about peace, society, women, young people and many other issues.




Therefore, I believe the international community, particularly those who have a say in decision-making, need to read and listen. Because today, throughout the world, we are talking much more about war than peace. This is truly devastating. All the promises made after the Second World War have, in a sense, been swept aside. Human rights, peace, dialogue and all those values have been abandoned.




And for what? For the militarization of society, the struggle to control resources, attempts to dominate territories and conflicts between opposing sides. It is society that suffers the consequences of all this.




That is why they must first listen, read and then make their assessments. Once they have done so, they must also be prepared to take steps to secure Abdullah Öcalan's freedom and put peace processes into practice.

title: KJK: The time for self-defence is now!
content:
The Coordination of the Kurdistan Women’s Community (KJK) issued a written statement ahead of 25 November, the International Day for the Elimination of Violence against Women. Emphasising the importance of strengthening women's organisation and unity against male-dominated violence, the KJK stated that the Peace and Democratic Society Process would create new opportunities for women's free participation and their struggle for freedom.




The statement said: "Violence against women has never before been carried out with such depth and systematic intensity. Male-dominated violence, which has reached horrific levels and permeates every month, every day and every moment of the year, has made it imperative to say ‘enough is enough’. In this regard, effective results can only be achieved if we, as women, unite in organised struggle against femicide, the destruction of life, society and nature perpetrated by capitalist modernity — the representative of our era's murderous system of domination — and its derivatives, which inject these forms of destruction into every cell of life.




Against a culture of violence embedded in every aspect of social life, we, as women, need plans and projects that establish a multidimensional perspective of struggle, ranging from transforming the organisation of everyday life and relationships to building alternative structures for a free life. At a time when violence has become a culture and a way of life, the process of democratic integration initiated by Rêber Apo [Abdullah Öcalan] brings all peoples and oppressed groups together within a framework of interconnectedness, while opening up new horizons of struggle for all the oppressed, particularly women."




The statement added: "With the development of the Peace and Democracy Process, our women's liberation perspective and the seeds of an alternative life will grow much stronger. One of the fundamental objectives of the Peace and Democratic Society Process is to pave the way for women's democratic and free participation. Through this process, the ground will also be created for a more comprehensive and profound struggle against violence targeting women, as well as all attitudes that marginalise and objectify women in every sphere of life. The Democracy and Peace Process will therefore also be a process through which women's freedom, their understanding of liberation and their fundamental human rights can be advanced in every sphere of life.




This year, we approach the International Day for the Elimination of Violence against Women on 25 November with a new, comprehensive and profound perspective. We respond by strengthening women's unity in Kurdistan, the Middle East and across the world, and by advancing their collective struggle. Let us transform 25 November, the International Day for the Elimination of Violence against Women, into an even stronger expression of women's solidarity, unity and struggle than in previous years."




The statement continued: "The reality of 25 November places upon women's movements, above all, the duty and responsibility to organise through women's own collective wisdom and to democratise society under women's leadership. For this reason, everyone — particularly women comrades — must strengthen and expand their organisation with every step they take, successfully carrying this march towards freedom into cities, villages, streets, neighbourhoods, factories, schools, homes and the lives of individuals. The male-dominated system, which is the gravedigger of society and women, operates strategically and politically at global, regional and local levels. If it implements its agenda multidimensionally at every moment of life, then we, as women's movements, must also wage a multidimensional struggle everywhere and at all times, based on a strategy and politics of women's liberation.




We can develop our existence by expanding our world of meaning through struggle, organisation and the power of self-defence. On this basis, we can change and transform society and men, and create a world in which it is possible to breathe freely. In this way, the tradition of 25 November, the International Day for the Elimination of Violence against Women, whose roots go back to the Mirabal sisters and extend to Sakine Cansız, will open the doors to a world free from violence.




Let us strengthen our organised, collective women's struggle under the slogan 'through women's organization against violence, the time for self-defence is now!' to overcome violence and lay the foundations of a new life alongside women struggling for freedom, equality and justice. Let us speak with one voice and one heart on 25 November, the International Day for the Elimination of Violence against Women, and make the 21st century an era of women's liberation."

title: KNK warns of division in South Kurdistan and calls on KDP and PUK to engage in dialogue
content:
The Kurdistan National Congress (KNK) has warned of further divisions among Kurdish institutions amid the escalating government crisis in South Kurdistan. Following the Patriotic Union of Kurdistan’s (PUK) announcement that it would withdraw from the regional government and its threat to establish parallel administrative structures in Sulaymaniyah, the KNK called on the two dominant parties in the Kurdistan Region of Iraq (KRI), the KDP and PUK, to resume negotiations without delay. It stressed that political power struggles must no longer be conducted at the expense of the population and the region’s constitutionally guaranteed autonomy.




The latest escalation was triggered by Wednesday’s election of a new parliamentary leadership in Hewlêr (Erbil). After nearly two years of political deadlock, the Kurdistan Democratic Party (KDP), together with smaller parties and minority representatives, pushed ahead with the parliamentary session. The PUK and several opposition parties boycotted the vote because no agreement had been reached on the future distribution of power. With 52 of the 100 members of parliament participating, the session barely secured the required majority. KDP politician Vala Fareed was elected speaker of parliament.

title: Dismissed by decree and imprisoned, Engin Cengiz returns to music at MKM
content:
More than 125,000 public employees were dismissed from their positions through emergency decrees issued under the state of emergency declared after the attempted coup on 15 July 2016. While the government defended these measures as actions targeting those involved in the coup attempt, the process also paved the way for the dismissal of public employees opposed to the government.




Ten years have passed since the emergency decrees were issued. Many of those dismissed were imprisoned, some were forced into exile, while others remained unemployed for long periods. Some were forced to work in construction to make a living, and some lost their lives in workplace accidents.




Engin Cengiz, who now works as a music teacher at the Mesopotamia Cultural Center (MKM), was among those affected during this period, when 125,678 public employees were dismissed according to official figures.




Cengiz was dismissed from his position as a music teacher by an emergency decree in 2016 and was subsequently imprisoned for a period. He spoke to ANF about his experiences during the emergency decree period, the difficulties he faced after his dismissal and how he became involved with the Mesopotamia Cultural Center.







 







‘The turning point came after a two-day strike during the Kobane protests’




Cengiz described the circumstances surrounding his dismissal under an emergency decree, explaining that he had been a music teacher for 15 years. 




Cengiz said: “By that time, I had approximately 15 years of teaching experience. I was a music teacher and had worked in Malatya for a long time. Before that, I was active in trade union organizing and the labor movement. Although the labor movement has a class dimension, we also took a stand on social issues in Turkey, the Middle East and around the world, on the problems faced by oppressed people and on our own existence as a community.




There was a civil war and a massive offensive in Rojava, Syria.




That was actually where the rupture occurred. There was a two-day strike in December over the events in Kobanê. Because we participated, many of us became direct targets. From the state's perspective, however, I was already a prominent figure in the area where I worked because of my activities. Subsequently, after the attempted coup, I was dismissed from my position through an emergency decree.”




Dismissed on the anniversary of the founding of the republic




Cengiz said that he was dismissed on the anniversary of the founding of the republic, stressing that losing his job on 29 October, at a time when they were demanding a democratic republic, held particular significance for him. 




Cengiz said: “The day I was dismissed was perhaps the day when all the coincidences and disasters I could experience in a lifetime came together. The fact that it was 29 October was significant in itself. Because experiencing something like this on the anniversary of the proclamation of the republic, while demanding a democratic republic, gave the whole situation an entirely different meaning.




My brother had been living in exile in Southern Kurdistan for nearly 10 years because of his sentence. He had met someone there, and they were planning to get married. The other family was from Hakkari (Colemêrg), and they came to visit us. We are originally from Oltu in Erzurum. The wedding took place, but neither the bride nor the groom was there. We finished the wedding ceremony with a sense of sadness, and just as everyone was about to return home, a message arrived informing me that I had been dismissed. It was actually something I had expected.




Interestingly, one of my former students from middle school was also at the wedding that day, and we were both dismissed on the same day. We experienced the tragicomic side of the process. I had prepared myself in my own way. Given everything that was happening in Turkey and the Middle East, it would not have been very ethical to question what had happened to me. I did not feel any particular sadness. I simply thought that we were experiencing another repetition of something terrible and that we would have to rebuild our lives from that point onward.”




Detained in Malatya and imprisoned for 10 months




Cengiz, who was arrested shortly after his dismissal under an emergency decree, said, “After I was dismissed on 29 October, I spent a few months exploring different possibilities. I even came to Istanbul for a few weeks. I wanted to travel a little, shake off the mindset of being a civil servant and discuss with musician friends what we could do. Then I returned to Malatya, where my home was. About four or five months later, on 17 January, I was detained in Malatya, and a period of imprisonment lasting 10 months began.”




Cengiz said that the reason for his imprisonment was his reconnection with his Kurdish identity. He also said: “There were the apparent reasons and the reasons they fabricated. The real reason was standing by my people and my community and taking part in political activities. The most significant factor was defending my Kurdish identity and standing behind the struggle. The traditional structure of the state has a habit of criminalizing Kurdish identity and associating it with terrorism. The main aim was to subject me to this process because I was an assimilated person who had reconnected with his Kurdish identity.”




Worked in a laundry and a hotel




Cengiz said that he could no longer remain in Malatya after his release from prison and moved to Istanbul. He described his experiences during that period: “After I was released from prison, there were hardly any conditions that would allow me to stay in Malatya. It was a small, close-knit social environment, and things had reached a point where people could barely even greet us. We had years of experience there and valuable friends who stood by us. However, some sections of society had become frightened because of the accusations against us.




I came to Istanbul towards the end of 2017. Friends from my high school years helped me. I worked in a laundry for a while. During that time, I felt as though I were among the characters described in old Russian novels, people at the very bottom of society working in precarious jobs. This was a reality of life, but an unjust one. I also worked in a hotel for a period. Then, gradually, as I became involved with the Mesopotamia Cultural Center, music began to play a more active role in my life again.”




‘Even if I face starvation, I will never accept this approach’




Cengiz said that he became involved with the Mesopotamia Cultural Center after working in other jobs and resumed his musical activities there. He described how he came to join the Mesopotamia Cultural Center : “Unfortunately, I received no support in that regard. Istanbul's art scene has its own particular way of operating. For example, after I was released from prison, a well-known artist asked for permission to perform one of my compositions. Even though I told him that I had just been released from prison and was in a difficult situation, he said to me, ‘Someone like me is performing a composition by someone like you. I'll make you famous. What more could you want?’




Saying something like that to someone who had suffered so much was a reflection of the degeneration that had taken place. I refused to give him my composition, telling him that even if I faced starvation, I would never accept such an approach. As a result, it did not bring me any significant financial benefit.




During the time I worked in Istanbul, I felt like a screw fitted into one of the gears of capitalism, and the feeling of becoming a refugee weighed heavily on my spirit. Having come to this city against my wishes, I found myself almost inevitably coming together with refugees. As a musician and someone who was part of the community, I turned to MKM, which I already knew. After working at the hotel, I realized that this way of life was not for me and that I needed to continue my life as a musician, so I joined MKM.”




‘At MKM, I saw that the sacrifices made had created a sense of belonging and meaning’




Cengiz stressed that the first thing he noticed at MKM was how the sacrifices made had acquired meaning. He said: “I was welcomed with great solidarity at MKM. I clearly saw that the sacrifices made had created a sense of community, emotion and meaning. My friends and the institution provided tremendous support in helping me overcome my shortcomings and find meaning in life again. In this brutal age of capitalism, this relationship of comradeship was extremely valuable.




MKM was an institution dedicated to Kurdish music and political music. I am here because I chose a life without great material expectations, one in which I would not have to depend on anyone. This was the most appropriate place to serve our culture and community and share my knowledge and experience with young people.”




‘The ongoing process shows that what was done back then was unjust’




Engin Cengiz also addressed the Peace and Democratic Society Process, saying that it demonstrated the injustice he had experienced in the past. Cengiz said: “Victimizing people for exercising their legitimate civil and social rights on the anniversary of the proclamation of the republic reflects a failure to find a solution. The fact that the Peace and Democratic Society Process initiated by Mr. Öcalan is now continuing through talks also shows that what was done back then was unjust. The Kurdish question and discriminatory policies cannot be resolved without dialogue and negotiations. Established assumptions must be challenged.




Both the Kurdish people and the other peoples of Turkey must embrace this process. Peace is essential for societies exhausted by war. I have experienced serious hardships over the past 10 years, but if peace is achieved, I am willing to forgive what I have endured on that condition alone.




Turkey and the Middle East need peace, and Mr. Öcalan is the key interlocutor for achieving it. If this process moves forward without arrogance, a more democratic life can be built.”

title: Halide Türkoğlu: Concrete steps are essential for the process
content:
Peoples' Equality and Democracy Party (DEM Party) Women's Council Spokesperson Halide Türkoğlu held a press conference at the party's headquarters ahead of the Women's Council meeting.




Türkoğlu began her speech by commemorating former Women's Council member Nesrin Aslan with respect and longing. She said that the women's conference would produce a powerful document for the success of the process. She stated: "Every gathering, action and event organized by women around the demand for a dignified peace as part of the Peace and Democratic Society Process has strengthened this spirit. Women have demonstrated with strong determination that they are present in resistance, in struggle and at the negotiating table, and that no process can be shaped without women."




Türkoğlu once again welcomed the "Women Stand Together, Discussing the Future" conference, held in Ankara on 31 October and 1 November, saying that it had been organized "in this spirit." She added: "We wholeheartedly believe that the outcomes of this conference will constitute a powerful document for the success of the Peace and Democratic Society Process. Women already have their roadmap for peace and are ready to build their present and future."




Support for the Peace Mothers' demands




Türkoğlu also expressed support for the demands of the Peace Mothers, saying: "If peace requires courage, it is the Peace Mothers who have demonstrated this courage most clearly for years. Despite harsh winter conditions and all kinds of health problems, they raised their demands from the vigil they held in tents in the heart of Ankara, calling for the success of the Peace and Democratic Society Process, for other mothers to be spared the same suffering and for genuine peace."




'The way must be opened for Mr. Öcalan'




Türkoğlu continued: "They once again raised their voices in the strongest possible terms, demanding that Mr. Öcalan be allowed to continue his work under free and equal conditions and that political prisoners be released. On behalf of our DEM Party Women's Council, I once again salute the determination demonstrated by the Peace Mothers. Their demands are our demands."




Concrete steps must be taken




Halide Türkoğlu called for an end to further delays in establishing the conditions necessary for meetings with Abdullah Öcalan. She said: "The conditions of Mr. Öcalan, the chief negotiator of the process, must not be addressed solely in terms of relocation. The establishment of conditions that would allow journalists, academics, human rights organizations, women and all sections of society to meet with Mr. Öcalan must not be delayed any longer. Regulations must be introduced to complement the legislation referred to as the Framework Law. The Peace and Political Participation Council and all other councils must begin their work. The proposals for democratization contained in parliament's joint report must be enacted into law. These concrete steps are essential for the process to succeed. One of the most important areas requiring concrete action is the prisons. Enemy law must not be applied in prisons while peace is being discussed outside. Political prisoners and ill prisoners must be released."




Impunity is killing women




Türkoğlu also drew attention to violence against women, stating that at least 20 women had been killed in October alone. Türkoğlu said, "Policies of impunity protect men by covering up crimes committed against children. We will continue to pursue accountability for these crimes of sexual abuse against children." She added: "It is not only men who kill women. It is the policies of impunity that embolden these men. It is the protective measures that remain on paper, the restraining orders that are violated and the protection orders that are never implemented."




Türkoğlu then addressed the inheritance controversy surrounding Jülide Kural, saying that it could not be separated from patriarchal thinking. She said: "On behalf of our Women's Council, I express my solidarity with her and declare that Jülide Kural is not alone."




Everyone who enabled and financed the fund must face trial




Türkoğlu demanded that everyone who financed and facilitated the fund be brought to justice. She said: "The fact that such large-scale fraud can be carried out so easily demonstrates how this country is governed through criminal networks. Everyone who has supported and enabled this fund-related criminal network must face trial. We will not give up our struggle until those who have stolen the rights and labor of the people, women and the poor are held accountable."




Türkoğlu also criticized the budget, describing it as "a concrete manifestation of a mentality that seeks to shape women's existence and will through family policies." She continued: "Those who make decisions on behalf of women have once again excluded women from decision-making processes. Of course, these are not policies we are unfamiliar with or encountering for the first time. The mentality behind this budget also knows us women very well. It knows why women will object to this budget, what demands they will raise and what inequalities they will expose. This is because women have been struggling for years against the invisibility of their labor, poverty, violence, inequality and the restriction of their living spaces."




The budget must fund women's liberation, not weapons




Türkoğlu stressed that they would mount the strongest possible opposition to the budget, from the parliamentary committee stage through to the General Assembly debates. She said: "We will not merely reject this budget. We will also demonstrate what kind of budget the Peace and Democratic Society Process requires. Because a budget for peace must allocate resources to life rather than weapons, to justice rather than inequality, and to women's liberation rather than policies that confine women to their homes."




Türkoğlu said that women demanded adequate resources to combat violence and outlined their demands: "Women want measures to combat women's poverty, secure employment and conditions that enable them to achieve economic independence. They want sufficient resources allocated to combating violence against women and the expansion of shelters and support mechanisms. Unless these demands are met, women will never give their approval to this budget."




Türkoğlu also condemned attacks on the co-chair system. Türkoğlu said: "You cannot criminalize this achievement, which we have secured through immense effort and sacrifice, with your patriarchal mentality. It is true that our co-chair system disrupts your hierarchical structure and your entire way of thinking. It challenges your patriarchal order. Have no doubt that it will continue to do so. Co-chairship is our purple line."




Call for solidarity on 8 November




Türkoğlu recalled that the trial concerning the Dilovası workers' massacre had recently been held. She said: "On Sunday, 8 November, the anniversary of the Dilovası massacre, we will gather in the women's contingent in front of the Dilovası Central Mosque at 2:30 pm for a commemoration and march."




Türkoğlu also called on all women to unite around the struggle for justice in support of the DEM Party Women's Council's demand that 8 November be declared the International Day of Struggle Against the Killing of Women Workers.

title: KCDP: 20 women murdered in October
content:
The We Will Stop Femicide Platform (KCDP) has published its October 2026 report on femicides, stating that at least 20 women were murdered, and 39 others lost their lives under suspicious circumstances.




Of the 20 women murdered, five were killed by their husbands, four by their current partners, one by someone they knew, one by their father, four by their former husbands and two by their former partners. The relationship between the perpetrators and the remaining three women could not be established. The report noted that 25 percent of the women were murdered by their husbands.




Nine women were murdered in their homes, three in the street, two in cars, two at their workplaces and one in a recreational area. The location of the murders of three women could not be determined. According to the report, 45 percent of the women murdered in October were killed in their homes.
