title: Tuğba Hezer: Women must have a direct say in negotiations
content:
Kurdish politician Tuğba Hezer spoke about the social dimension of the Peace and Democratic Society Process, the role of women in the process and the struggle for women's rights. Hezer drew attention to the exclusion of women from decision-making mechanisms in previous peace processes and Kurdish women's struggle for their identity and language. She said that women must have a direct say and decision-making power in negotiations.




Hezer highlighted the devastation caused by war and social inequalities in women's lives, the denial of women's identity and their exclusion from peace processes.




Hezer said: "Women bear the heaviest consequences of war, conflict and social inequalities. Yet throughout history, decisions in peace processes have largely been made without women. The denial of women's identity in Turkey, particularly Kurdish women's struggle to exist with their own mother tongue, identity and as women, cannot be separated from the devastation caused by war. Women experience the destruction of war while also facing patriarchal state violence. We struggle against these inequalities in every sphere, from politics and education to public and social life.




A different approach is needed in this process. We cannot accept women being treated merely as people whose demands are heard and on whose behalf decisions are made. If we are going to call it a negotiating table, then a table without women means that half of society is absent. Women must not simply have others speak or make decisions on their behalf. They must participate directly as active subjects.




Peace is not merely the silencing of weapons or the end of conflicts. Questions of identity, women's ability to live freely, equal citizenship, mother tongue, education, labor and public life are also part of peace. We cannot speak of genuine peace where women's right to life is not guaranteed, their identities are not recognized and they cannot live freely. Women's freedom must not be treated as an issue to be addressed after peace has been achieved. It must be one of the fundamental objectives of the process from the outset.




Turkey faces serious obstacles that must be overcome in democracy, rights and freedoms, the rule of law, freedom of expression and justice. We have a long struggle ahead of us, from guaranteeing mother tongue rights and equal citizenship to women's freedom and social freedoms. We must pursue this struggle together with all democratic sections of society, particularly women. A democratic solution to the Kurdish question, women's freedom and Turkey's democratization are inseparable."




'

The past two years have been marked by waiting'




Tuğba Hezer pointed to the differences between the state's approach and the expectations of women, Kurds and democratic circles over the two years of the process. She said that the perspective of a democratic society had not been sufficiently established throughout society.




Hezer assessed the work carried out during this period and the shortcomings that had emerged: "When we look at what we have done over the past two years, I see that we have experienced something of a period of waiting. This does not mean that nothing has been done. There have been tremendous efforts and valuable contributions. Very important conferences, meetings and gatherings have taken place. However, two years is a long time to build something, move it forward and reach broader sections of society.




Looking at the approach of the state and the government, we see that they view the process primarily in terms of disarmament and dissolution. The expectations of Kurds, women, leftist, socialist and democratic circles, however, concern a democratic solution to the Kurdish question, democratization and the construction of a democratic society. It is clear that the state and the government have demonstrated no political will for democratic transformation and have taken no concrete steps in that direction. No steps are being taken even to ensure that peace takes root in society. Problems concerning democracy, fundamental rights and freedoms, justice and freedom of expression continue in Turkey.




There are many steps that could be taken without waiting for the Framework Law to enter into force, yet the state continues to adopt a position of persistent inaction. The language of a century of denial policies is still being reproduced in the media and political discourse, and the Kurdish question continues to be defined as a matter of terrorism.




We criticize the government's approach, but we have also failed to create a broad enough platform to bring our own perspective onto the agenda and establish it within society. We need to bring the democratic society perspective to wider sections of society, develop our own agenda and organize around it at the grassroots level. To achieve this, we must strengthen a common democratic platform that allows us to work with different sections of society, rather than remaining confined to our own areas of struggle."




'The state's will for democratic transformation is important'




Hezer emphasized that concrete steps were now needed in the state's approach to the process, stressing that a solution could not be limited to disarmament.




Hezer said: "It is difficult to say that the state and the government have yet demonstrated a genuine will to pursue a democratic solution to the Kurdish question. What brought the state to this process was not so much a desire to resolve the issue as the necessity of doing so. There is a difference between wanting to resolve something and being compelled to resolve it because of the circumstances. We can see this in practice.




A commitment to a democratic solution requires steps toward democratization, guarantees for rights and freedoms, and genuine transformation. Yet the process is persistently being reduced to disarmament alone. This creates uncertainty.




We must not confine our entire discussion to whether the state is sincere or trustworthy. Throughout history, Kurds have moved forward by relying on their own will, organized strength and the values they have created. Today, too, we must strengthen our own power, organization and social foundations. We can move forward not by waiting to see what the state will do, but by strengthening our own struggle and determination and creating common grounds for struggle with different sections of society."




'The negotiating table draws its strength from social struggle'




Hezer highlighted the social groups represented in the negotiations taking place on Imrali and the importance of social organization in strengthening that representation.




Hezer said: "There is a negotiating table on Imrali. The state sits on one side, while the will of the Kurdish people, represented by Kurdish People's Leader Abdullah Öcalan, sits on the other. But that table consists of more than just two sides. The Kurdish people are there, as are Alevis, different peoples and faiths, women, workers and the ecological movement. We can achieve results to the extent that we strengthen that table.




To do this, we must create the social foundations for peace and democratic society wherever we live, throughout Turkey and beyond, without waiting for others. This also means creating a space where different sections of society can express their own demands and shared expectations, and where democratic politics can grow stronger.




The strength of the negotiating table does not come solely from the talks taking place there. The more organized and powerful the social forces behind that table are, the stronger their representation will be."




'

Violence against women continues during the peace process'




Tuğba Hezer pointed to the contradiction of speaking about peace and democratic society while attacks on women's right to life continued. She described patriarchal state violence as one of the most significant obstacles to women's struggle for freedom.




Hezer said: "How can we speak of peace and democratic society while the war against women's freedom continues? The basic conditions for peace do not exist in a society where even women's right to life is not guaranteed. Peace and democratic society are being discussed on the one hand, while violence against women, patriarchal state violence and interference in women's lives continue on the other. State violence sustains itself through different mechanisms. Attacks against the opposition and the press continue, while women face systematic violence. For this reason, we women need a stronger, broader and more organized struggle. Women's freedom is one of the fundamental conditions for the democratization of society. We must therefore strengthen the foundations of common struggle with women's organizations, democratic institutions and all sections of society."




'28 women were killed in September'




Hezer drew attention to the continuing killings of women, the invisibility of women's labor and the violence women experience under the pretext of protecting the family. She said that 28 women had been killed in September.




Hezer also said: "Every month, we are confronted with another wave of femicides. Twenty-eight women were killed in September alone. Women's labor is disregarded. Under the rhetoric of protecting the family, women are subjected to domestic violence and prevented from having a say over their own lives. Decisions made through the judiciary, the state, the government and public institutions continue to perpetuate a mentality that disregards women.




Patriarchal state violence is increasing every day. Under these circumstances, we must intensify our struggle to defend women's right to life, labor and identity. This struggle is also part of the common struggle to build a democratic society. We cannot speak of a democratic society without women's freedom."




'Women's freedom is a fundamental area of struggle'




Tuğba Hezer said that the struggle for a democratic solution to the Kurdish question, Turkey's democratization and women's freedom could not be postponed at a time when wars and conflicts continued around the world.




Hezer continued: "We are struggling for peace, freedom and democracy amid wars across the world, at a time when these wars are expected to deepen even further. Although this may seem contradictory, it is precisely at such a time, when humanity stands on the brink of such immense destruction, that our struggle will be decisive. We have a long and difficult struggle ahead of us. We must walk this path together with all democratic sections of society, particularly women, and expand the spaces for common struggle. Changing the current situation must become our shared responsibility.




Women have borne, and continue to bear, the heaviest burden of a century of denial policies and fifty years of conflict. Now one chapter is closing, and we are continuing our journey to open a new one. Yet the pain, sorrow and anger of the past still weigh on our shoulders. The Peace Mothers in Kurdistan carry the deepest of these wounds in their hearts. While we owe them peace, they went to Ankara and sought to break the silence. The question we must ask ourselves is not only how the state will respond to their call, but also how much their action will break our own silence.




Because if the Peace Mothers, despite all their suffering and everything they have experienced, are setting out with the last of their strength, traveling hundreds of kilometers to make the voice of peace heard, then we no longer have the luxury of waiting, standing aside merely to criticize or losing faith. We must strengthen the will for peace they carry and collectively assume responsibility for this effort."

title: Lawyer Newroz Uysal Aslan: Real change will come when Mr. Öcalan can engage with the outside world
content:
The relocation of Kurdish People's Leader Abdullah Öcalan within Imrali F-Type High Security Prison has brought discussions about his status back into focus. Presidential adviser Mehmet Uçum's tendency to reduce the status of Abdullah Öcalan, the chief negotiator in the Peace and Democratic Society Process, solely to "disarmament" has drawn widespread criticism. The disagreement over Öcalan's status, one of the most important aspects of the process, came to the fore once again after Peoples' Equality and Democracy Party (DEM Party) MP Ömer Öcalan, who recently visited his uncle on Imrali, reported that Öcalan opposed this restrictive approach and criticized attempts to address the process solely in terms of disarmament. DEM Party MP Newroz Uysal Aslan spoke to ANF and recalled that Abdullah Öcalan's status was that of chief negotiator. Uysal said: "The change in Mr. Öcalan's conditions must go beyond discussions about relocation and place him in a position where he can genuinely engage with society and guide the process."




'Relocation does not mean Mr. Öcalan's conditions are adequate'




Newroz Uysal Aslan said that Abdullah Öcalan's relocation within Imrali Prison was significant but insufficient to meet the needs of the process. Uysal stressed that the relocation should have taken place at the beginning of the process and had therefore been delayed. Uysal said: "We cannot say that defining the change solely in terms of relocation is sufficient either for his legal status or for the position of chief negotiator that would enable him to guide this process. Many individuals and groups have made statements on this issue. Some have approached it sensationally, while others have treated it as a matter of tabloid interest. However, beyond all this, Kurdish People's Leader Abdullah Öcalan holds the position of chief negotiator.




The conditions required for this position have not been fulfilled for more than two years. Relocation alone does not mean that these conditions have been made adequate. Therefore, what really matters is ensuring the means of communication with the outside world required by the Coordination for Peace and Political Participation, including communication with the movement, political actors, the press and academia. Because moving from one location to another within a prison does not create a fundamental or effective change in the process. The real change will become evident through the contacts Mr. Öcalan establishes with the outside world. Mr. Öcalan himself has approached the issue of relocation from the very beginning in terms of facilitating his relations with the outside world and the work of the coordinator. Otherwise, it is unethical to discuss his transfer to another location within the prison where he has been held for 27 years in such a sensationalist and tabloid manner.




The questions that need to be asked are these: Will his coordination role function alongside this relocation? Has the necessary legal status been established? Will the structures and cooperation required for this coordination be established with others who will work with Mr. Öcalan, including political institutions, different political movements outside the prison and representatives within the state? And when will we, as the public and as society, be able to see and discuss these developments? These are the real questions, and they have still not been fully answered. The relocation is important, but it does not, on its own, meet the needs of the process."




'The approach to Öcalan's status must be clarified'




Newroz Uysal Aslan criticized presidential adviser Mehmet Uçum for defining Abdullah Öcalan's status solely in terms of disarmament. Uysal said that Uçum had viewed the process from the outset through the lens of regional war, Turkey's growing power in the region and the concept of a "strong state," while attempting to confine the Kurdish people to a narrow and restricted political space. She stressed that Uçum's approach did not necessarily mean that the state or government would conduct the process accordingly, or that Öcalan, the Kurdish movement and Kurdish political actors would accept such an approach.




Uysal said: "Many groups have already repeatedly stated that such approaches, particularly the language being used, poison the process and are incompatible with its objectives. This approach is precisely one of the reasons why we want Mr. Öcalan's relocation to be assessed together with his working conditions and the relationships he will establish with the outside world. Disarmament and the cessation of conflict are part of this process, but they are not its only components. The state persistently wants other issues to be discussed only after disarmament has been completed. Mr. Öcalan, the Kurdish movement and those in Turkey who support democracy and the process, however, argue that these issues must advance simultaneously or be addressed together. There is clearly a difference in approach here, but we do not consider either the designation 'Disarmament Coordination' or the position adopted by Mehmet Uçum acceptable. Our position on this matter is clear. We have consistently stated that the approach to Öcalan's status must be clarified, and we reiterate the need for statements to be made in this regard."




'The opposition must firmly defend peace to prevent political exploitation'




Newroz Uysal Aslan also commented on Abdullah Öcalan's warning to his nephew, DEM Party MP Ömer Öcalan, that the process must not be used for electoral purposes. Uysal emphasized the importance of this warning at a time when discussions about early and snap elections were intensifying. She recalled that the Justice and Development Party (AKP)'s failure to secure a parliamentary majority on its own had played a role in the collapse of the resolution process in 2015. Uysal also said: "Turkey has a political memory shaped by past experiences in this regard. But in response to this approach, I would like to recall Mr. Öcalan's message from December 2024. In that message, which consisted of several points, Mr. Öcalan emphasized that the ongoing process must not be used for short-term political interests.




He repeatedly stated that the issue should not be viewed as a political party's instrument or through whether a particular party remains in power, but rather as a matter concerning the future of a people and a commitment to peace in the face of war in the region. Political parties may seek to exploit the process for their own political calculations. Particularly given the AKP's negative record in this regard, the concerns that have emerged are, frankly, realistic. To prevent this, the process must genuinely accelerate, be discussed on appropriate grounds and, most importantly, be supported by all political actors, parliament and the opposition. They must act not by treating this process as a government project, but by recognizing that peace is a fundamental demand of the people. If this happens, the process will cease to be merely an instrument of the AKP's political calculations."




'The Peace Mothers' demands are also our demands'




Newroz Uysal Aslan stressed that Abdullah Öcalan must be provided with conditions in which he can live and work freely. She described the Peace Mothers' vigil in Ankara, held to demand these conditions, as highly valuable and meaningful. Uysal said, "The demands put forward by the Peace Mothers are also our demands," and outlining the steps she considered necessary for the process to advance on the right basis: "The most important step that must now be taken to advance the process is to move beyond discussions about the relocation of Kurdish People's Leader Abdullah Öcalan, the chief negotiator, and establish conditions in which he can genuinely engage with society and guide the process.




The implementation of the European Court of Human Rights (ECtHR) rulings, the release of ill prisoners and similar matters that are already required by law must not be turned into subjects of political bargaining. These steps must be taken without making them dependent on the Framework Law, using a decision by the National Security Council as a pretext, or waiting for administrative decisions. Most importantly, the principle of the right to hope, which Turkey has evaded implementing for 12 years, must be put into effect. We must not forget that by openly indicating that it would not take steps regarding the right to hope, Turkey effectively announced that it would not fulfill its international obligations. Frankly, we can regard this as a first both for the Council of Europe and in Turkey's history. It is still impossible to accept the continued failure to implement the right to hope or its presentation as a legal obstacle to Mr. Öcalan's freedom. This is a legal obligation, and fulfilling it is also one of the most fundamental political needs of the process."

title: Bafel Talabani: We are withdrawing from this government
content:
The Patriotic Union of Kurdistan (PUK) Executive Council convened with the participation of its President, Bafel Talabani. Following the meeting, Talabani released a video statement in which he commented on political developments in the Kurdistan Region and the process of forming a government.




Talabani stated that they had held several meetings with officials in Erbil (Hewlêr), but despite progress in the discussions, no agreement had been reached and parliament had been unable to convene. “On every occasion, progress was made in the discussions, but no results were achieved, and parliament could not convene. It has been demonstrated that the KDP does not know how to govern. We had previously warned that such a situation would arise. We do not recognise this session,” Talabani said.




‘We are withdrawing from this government’




Stating that the PUK Executive Council had authorised him to make the decision, Talabani announced the party's withdrawal from the government in the following terms: “Today, the PUK Executive Council authorised me, and we declare that we do not recognise this session. This government has failed. Therefore, our decision is to withdraw from this government. We are prepared to make any sacrifice. We are concerned with resolving the Rojava issue, the peace process, and our brothers and sisters in Rojhilat.”

title: Bulut: Concerns grow as the peace process drags on
content:
Elif Bulut, a member of the Central Executive Board (MYK) of the Peoples' Equality and Democracy Party (DEM Party) and Co-Spokesperson of its Central Organizing Commission, answered ANF's questions about the scope of organizing in the new period and the importance of recent public meetings.




What new methods has your party developed, or does it plan to develop, for engaging with people locally and organizing at the grassroots level during this period of efforts to strengthen democratic politics?




Since the process began moving forward on 1 October, our most important priority has been to explain it both to our own support base and to everyone in our wider circles, whether close to us or not. Continuously renewing our existing organizational structures and adapting them to current developments has always been one of our most important responsibilities. Traditional models of organization can no longer meet the needs of contemporary politics.




The process may bring many developments, both positive and negative. Taking both possibilities into account, we plan to develop a political cadre and an approach capable of responding to the new period, while advancing the process through collective discussion and participation with our entire support base. At the same time, we aim to prepare for the coming period by engaging in discussions with all leftist and socialist organizations, labor and democracy forces, and all those with whom we conduct a common struggle. We seek to strengthen local organization, develop horizontal organizational models and use all our past experiences to restructure our organization for the future.




You continue to meet with people through the Budget Campaign for Bread, Peace and Justice. As politicians, what do you learn from the people during these meetings?




As politicians who work among the people and alongside them, we are using this campaign to reveal what the real issues are. Our aim is to ensure that Parliament recognizes the people's actual concerns. Look at the budget prepared by a government that has closed its eyes and ears to the country's problems and seeks to strengthen the oppressors rather than the oppressed. We are trying to shape the 2027 budget in favor of the people by saying, "This is what the people's budget should look like. These are the issues, these are the problems, this is the poverty people face, and these are their expectations."




We explain to people that a decent standard of living is possible through a fair distribution of the budget, while also listening directly to the problems they experience. We listen not only to individual problems but also to the concerns of every section of society and their proposals for solutions.




The struggle to earn a living and the struggle for peace are not two separate issues. We explain how the enormous resources allocated to the defense industry over the years because of the unresolved Kurdish question have contributed to the deepening of poverty. We know that democratization becomes more possible in a peaceful environment and that all institutions can become fairer through democracy. Our experiences show us how necessary it is to discuss this reality together with the people.




For this reason, the importance of peace becomes even more apparent throughout the campaign. We try to explain that people's poverty is not simply the result of failing to find jobs that provide sufficient income, but rather a problem rooted in the system as a whole.




We explain to workers that there is no longer any justification for allocating budget resources to weapons and war, and that these resources should instead be redirected to the public budget. This would make it possible to provide wages and pensions that ensure decent living conditions, from the minimum wage to retirement benefits.




Is the concept of "communal organization" sufficiently understood, or will it become clearer through struggle and practical experience?




The concept of the commune is not entirely new to us, but because it has not been widely used as a practical tool, there is still a great need to explain it. Practical experiences are essential for it to take root in society. To explain what establishing a commune in a particular area can change in our lives and what purpose it serves, it must be experienced in practice. Only then can people fully understand what a commune is and begin to adopt it as a form of organization. There are currently extensive discussions, ideas for communes are being developed, and efforts are underway to create practical examples. Progress can be made gradually in this way.




You place the women's liberation paradigm and youth organization at the center of your politics. Are your current practices in these areas sufficient?




As the DEM Party, our greatest distinction is that we conduct politics along a women's liberation-oriented line. Of course, we cannot claim that we have overcome every shortcoming within our autonomous women's organization. We are struggling for both democratization and women's freedom in a world where patriarchal structures are deeply entrenched. This alone makes our work difficult. The responsibilities imposed on women by traditional gender roles make it harder for them to participate actively in politics. Working in both autonomous women's politics and mixed political structures, while also carrying responsibility for care work, means effectively working three times as much. Naturally, this creates an enormous workload.




No transformation can be truly egalitarian unless women are an effective force within it. For this reason, we are working to expand our organization and strengthen the collective women's struggle so that women become more empowered in every sphere.




Our youth organization has always been among the structures most heavily subjected to state repression. This makes organizing even more difficult. Constant pressure, detentions, arrests and attempts to obstruct young people's political participation create serious difficulties, but new ways are always found. The Youth Assembly is currently carrying out important organizational work once again. It is seeking to expand its structures, engage with young people from different backgrounds and place greater emphasis on organizing university students.




If the party cannot renew itself through younger generations, its entire structure will inevitably fall behind. If you fail to keep pace with the demands of the times, you lose your future. We are also working to create more opportunities for women and young people in politics and expand their influence.




How has the Peace and Democratic Society Process been received during public meetings?




There was curiosity and excitement when the process first began. Some people were waiting with enthusiasm, while others were deeply concerned and distrustful. As the process has dragged on, excitement has gradually given way to anxiety. One of the people's foremost demands is the release of prisoners. So many people are being held in prison unjustly and unlawfully that almost everyone's life has been affected. Beyond those in prison, there are just as many people facing criminal proceedings. The Court of Cassation is full of cases in which convictions could be upheld at any moment.




The Kurdistan Workers' Party (PKK) has dissolved itself, but the situation of the guerrillas, particularly Abdullah Öcalan, remains uncertain. Freedom and the possibility of return are awaited. People want to see concrete steps on issues ranging from those living in exile abroad to the government-appointed trustees. The Framework Law was passed before Parliament adjourned, but its requirements have still not been implemented. Everyone is waiting to see when the law will be put into practice.




Most questions and concerns revolve around whether the Justice and Development Party (AKP) will derail the process. There is a previous experience, and the events that followed the 2013–2015 process remain painfully fresh in people's memories. Since the current process began, manipulative statements from some circles, such as "The AKP cannot be trusted; they will deceive you," have inevitably begun to influence people.




Nevertheless, people have not lost hope in the process, and there is tremendous trust in Mr. Öcalan, its principal actor. Although progress appears slow, there is also a growing understanding that, despite all the concerns, there can be no turning back.




There have been claims that the process has slowed down. Do you expect it to accelerate following the Kurdish People's Leader's relocation to a new facility?




Mr. Öcalan's relocation was a development that had been awaited for a long time. Mr. Öcalan had made it very clear that this move would not take place without clarification of his status. Although the relocation is a positive development, it has come very late and remains insufficient.




Initially, we expected a development that would clarify his status and pave the way for the relevant commission to begin its work. However, the relocation took place before this happened. A leader conducting such an important process must be provided with conditions that allow him to work freely. This is also what the Kurdish people expect.




What are the most critical priorities for ensuring that the process takes root in society?




The DEM Party has never been a party that defends the rights of only one section of society. We conduct our political struggle with the understanding that everyone's liberation is interconnected. Peace and democratization can take root in society by building alliances with the broadest possible sections of society and strengthening the common struggle.




Guided by this understanding, our party prioritizes reaching out to every section of society repeatedly, explaining our position, listening to people and providing a common ground for struggle for all peoples and marginalized groups. We act in this direction in all our activities, seeking to expand our reach, strengthen our organization, address our shortcomings and prepare for the politics of the new period.

content:

title: Osman: Over 238 children killed or injured in military attacks in Bashur over the past 30 years
content:
Kameran Osman, a member of the Community Peacemaker Teams (CPT), spoke at a panel titled “Being a Victim of War, Crisis and Displacement During Childhood”, held as part of the International Scientific Conference on Children and Youth at the University of Sulaymaniyah (Silêmani).




Speaking about the impact of war on children, Osman shared new data. He said that more than 238 children have been killed or injured in military attacks by the Turkish and Iranian armies in the Kurdistan Region over the past 30 years. He emphasised that the effects of war on children are not limited to physical casualties.




He noted that children displaced by war often lose or see their ties weakened with the countries, communities and lands where they live. Osman also highlighted how war deeply affects children's mental health, identity, education, language and dignity.




People in border villages still wake up to the sound of bombs




Osman recalled that schools and educational institutions in villages have also been targeted in military attacks by the Turkish army and Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC), stating that children's safety has been disregarded.

title: Gülten Kaya: Art requires the courage to engage with life
content:
Gülten Kaya has always been at the heart of music, poetry and stories of her homeland, both through her own personal journey and as Ahmet Kaya's life partner and Yusuf Hayaloğlu's sister.




Gülten Kaya, with whom we discussed the transformation of the music world, said that digital platforms also generated ethical and moral problems of their own. She identified creating works in one's mother tongue as one of the most important pillars of collective memory.




Gülten Kaya said of Ahmet Kaya's music: "It is socially conscious, it bears witness, it is authentic, literary, recent history, poetry, emotion and sacrifice. His music reflects both recent history and all the suffering experienced by society." She also criticized the reduction of art to an apolitical industry: "All creative fields, from painting to literature, cinema to music, require the courage to engage with life. Art is one of the fields in which the greatest courage is needed to bear witness to life, particularly in countries like ours."




ANF spoke to lyricist and music producer Gülten Kaya about the transformation of the music world and the impact of digitalization on music production and consumption habits.




The music industry has evolved toward a digitalized, algorithm-driven market model in recent years. How is this transforming music's role in creating collective memory and fostering social empathy?




Digital environments and platforms also generate ethical and moral problems of their own. We can consider these problems from both human-centered and system-centered perspectives, and the two are not independent of each other. Technology undoubtedly has a significant impact on how people perceive the world and is increasingly determining that perception. Although we cannot yet speak of a fully developed music industry in Turkey, looking at the global music industry, we can say that its participation in this new process, which could be described as a digital revolution, has begun, albeit belatedly. The music industry is an important stakeholder in cultural heritage. Competition and the necessity of participating in this transformation seem to be unfolding simultaneously.




For me, one of the most important pillars of collective memory is creating works in one's own mother tongue. As for fostering empathy, that is achieved through good, high-quality creative work rather than through the digital process itself.




Does the culture of singles that are rapidly consumed and forgotten negatively affect the soul of music?




I do not think such a generalization would be particularly sound, because this format alone is not what affects the soul of music. Focusing on anything that is quickly consumed and forgotten, including singles, diverts our attention from the multilayered nature of the problem. The fundamental issue here is the quality of creative work. An artist may produce hundreds of works or just one. Therefore, the lasting value of a work cannot be explained by its format.




The disposable culture introduced into our lives by popular culture, the trap of speed in our era, the emphasis on quantity rather than quality in production, the failure to establish an emotional connection with listeners, simplistic and unliterary lyrics written over nearly identical musical arrangements, and the way such works circulate despite cultural and musical ignorance, only to disappear just as quickly... There are dozens of factors we could mention.




As in every field, concepts such as "good" and "right" are, of course, relative in art. But anything that connects with and touches your inherited cultural identity deserves a unique place in your personal repertoire of experiences.




Does the use of artificial intelligence to generate voices and music concern you? What consequences could it have?




Frankly, it worries me considerably. Replicas of art, design and all creative fields have already been circulating for quite some time, in a way that has almost begun to gain legitimacy. Life seems to be moving toward a time when even human beings may be cloned. This process, which is advancing while creating its own market and economy, is beginning to take the place of authenticity in every field. Once again, what we most need to hold on to is ethics and conscience. We need the intellectual capacity, education and cultural knowledge to recognize the difference in value between what is genuine and what is artificial, and to appreciate that difference.




Of course, alongside the measures and legal regulations that every country must introduce in response to this new artificial age, respect for art and labor, and recognition of their value, must also become part of the education system.




Artificial intelligence carries extraordinary risks within itself. From art to politics, it could eventually become impossible to control, and that is undoubtedly frightening.




Ahmet Kaya's music has become part of the collective memory of suffering and resistance in this region. What does the continued appreciation of his music mean, despite all the changes in the music world?




Ahmet Kaya's music is not the kind of "disposable music" we discussed earlier. It is socially conscious, it bears witness, it is authentic, literary, recent history, poetry, emotion and sacrifice. His music reflects both recent history and all the suffering experienced by society. When you weave your own historical experiences, your observations of the streets where you live and the realities of everyday life into the fundamental themes of art, your work does not become outdated.




What exactly are artists being tested by at a time when music is being reduced to an apolitical entertainment industry?




Life does not seem to forgive apolitical attitudes in music, just as it does not in any other field of art. I am genuinely surprised by the astonishment of those who adopt such positions. I think these individuals are being tested by their own blindness and ignorance. We live in a region where contradictions stand before us like mountains. If these contradictions do not lead to development, art and creative production, then there is both artistic and social blindness, although we must not overlook the climate of seemingly endless fear.




All creative fields, from painting to literature, cinema to music, require the courage to engage with life. Art is one of the fields in which the greatest courage is needed to bear witness to life, particularly in countries like ours.




Concert bans, which still continue, and the era of confiscating cassette tapes have increasingly given way to new forms of censorship. Are algorithms establishing a new system of "acceptable art," and how can this new form of control be challenged?




Concerts belong to the streets; they are encounters with the people. No matter how much systems seek to impose their own version of "acceptable art," good art finds its way to the hearts it seeks to reach in today's digital and globalized world, regardless of the algorithms involved. Since the 1980s, despite the censorship laws we have struggled against, every creative work that authorities tried to lock away in drawers eventually reached its audience. This is a fact. Even when concert permits are denied, artists are prosecuted for their work, or obstacles are placed before them in every possible way, good art finds its own path. I believe this.




What do you see as the greatest opportunities and dangers that the relationship between music and artificial intelligence will present for musicians in the coming years?




Although artificial intelligence may offer creative artists some limited technical conveniences, I believe the dangers it poses will be far greater. The possibility that all those artificial, synthetic voices could replace real ones is truly frightening. This represents a major risk that could lead to exploitation, affecting politicians and ordinary people alike.




Furthermore, it is undeniable that the shortcuts and overwhelming volume of artificial content generated by AI will create barriers for new voices, emerging talents and undiscovered musicians. Digital technologies are producing music at unprecedented speed and scale, while genuine and artificial emotions are constantly being substituted for one another.




Artificial intelligence models are trained by processing the works of numerous artists. How should the reduction of creative labor and lived experience to datasets be addressed in terms of copyright and justice?




The global music industry is still at the beginning of this revolutionary period. Present and future music technologies will develop entirely new tools and capabilities that we cannot yet imagine, and competition will evolve into a completely new economic system. Of course, artists must be protected by the copyright frameworks of international digital platforms. However, achieving justice within these systems seems unlikely in an environment of fierce competition. As always and everywhere, musicians need to be organized, at least through professional associations, to ensure a fair distribution of revenues within the profit-driven strategies of the giant companies that provide this infrastructure and bring their music to audiences around the world.




What responsibilities do musicians and listeners have in this transformation?




I would place the responsibility not on listeners but on musicians. They must avoid taking shortcuts, stay as far away from the artificial world as possible and never abandon high-quality creative production. The digital world no longer involves the distribution costs that existed in the past. Musicians can also keep production costs as low as possible by working in acoustic formats and secure intellectual property rights in the global market.




I have tried to provide brief answers to questions concerning a complex, multilayered field and its problems. But I would like to conclude with this: Art has a much longer life than an artist.

title: Nurcan Değirmenci: As women, we must stand together
content:

Nurcan Değirmenci said that she began her artistic career at the Mesopotamia Cultural Center in 1995 and had struggled shoulder to shoulder with women for many years, both as a musician and as a Kurdish woman. title: DEM Party: Abolish the Council of Higher Education, a vestige of the 1980 military coup
content:
In a written statement, the DEM Party’s Education Policies Commission called for the abolition of the Council of Higher Education (YÖK), a vestige of the 12 September 1980 military coup.




The statement said: “Established on 6 November 1981, in the aftermath of the 12 September military coup, the Council of Higher Education (YÖK) has continued for 45 years to be one of the principal institutions through which a centralised and tutelary system of governance is imposed on universities.”




The statement noted that, particularly under AKP rule, this structure had become one of the instruments through which the political authorities intervened in university affairs, and added: “It is unacceptable that young people are pushed out of politics, that their freedoms of association and expression are restricted, and that universities are transformed into institutions that produce obedient individuals. Young people are not merely the social and political actors of the future; they are actors in society and politics today.”




The DEM Commission outlined the kind of university it envisions as follows:

title: Nilüfer Koç: Council of Europe must consider the new process
content:
A total of 845 signatures from 50 countries have been collected as part of the "Freedom for Abdullah Öcalan, a Political Solution to the Kurdish Question" campaign. International support, including that of 109 Nobel Prize laureates, has been brought to the Council of Europe. Most recently, 620 signatories from 29 countries sent a letter to the Council of Europe's Committee of Ministers.




ANF spoke to Nilüfer Koç, Co-Spokesperson for Foreign Relations of the Kurdistan National Congress (KNK), about the results of the international campaign, diplomatic initiatives to be pursued at the Council of Europe, steps toward implementing the right to hope, and upcoming efforts aimed at securing Abdullah Öcalan's physical freedom.




Nilüfer Koç commented on reports that Abdullah Öcalan had been moved to a new building on Imrali Island, stating that his transfer to a larger space did not constitute a fundamental change in his conditions. She emphasized that the arrangement amounted only to an expansion of his physical surroundings and that access to Imrali Island and visits remained under state control.




Koç pointed out that the island was surrounded by the sea and that the state decided who could travel to and from it. She said, "The state will take you there whenever it wants and will either allow or deny permission to those wishing to visit. This is a situation entirely under state control. That alone is a problem. Changing the size of a cell on the island is not a particularly decisive factor either. In my view, this amounts to little more than a delaying tactic."




Koç emphasized the importance of Abdullah Öcalan's political struggle reaching society and the political sphere, stating that the existing conditions prevented this from happening. She noted that Abdullah Öcalan had taken considerable risks to build democracy and peace in Turkey and had been engaged in political struggle for many years. She stressed that changing his physical surroundings would not be sufficient to enable this struggle to reach society.




Koç also stated that the isolation conditions on Imrali prevented the idea of peace from taking root in society and becoming an effective part of the political agenda. She emphasized that meaningful change would only be possible if Abdullah Öcalan were allowed to establish contact with the outside world.




Koç said, "His relocation is also a cosmetic measure in this respect. It does not change the course of the process. Establishing connections with the outside world, as Abdullah Öcalan himself has requested, would genuinely contribute to the process. Such a development could further strengthen the Kurdish people's confidence in the process."




Koç reiterated that the changes to Abdullah Öcalan's physical conditions had not altered his imprisonment or isolation. She said, "Abdullah Öcalan remains a prisoner on Imrali Island. The conditions of his captivity have not changed. He has simply been transferred from one cell to another. We should not be misled by this."




'Abdullah Öcalan's status must be clarified for the process to advance'




Nilüfer Koç pointed out that the steps taken by the Kurdish side in the Peace and Democratic Society Process were clear, while the state had maintained a slow and uncertain approach to taking concrete measures. She emphasized that Abdullah Öcalan's status needed to be clarified for the process to move forward, recalling that numerous proposals had been presented since 27 February to advance the process.




Koç stated that Abdullah Öcalan had put forward calls and proposals on major issues, including the establishment of commissions, legislative arrangements, the burning of weapons and the dissolution of the Kurdistan Workers' Party (PKK). She said that he had addressed the entire political spectrum in Turkey in his efforts toward peace. Koç emphasized that clarifying his status was essential for these efforts to continue and for him to maintain the role he had undertaken in the process.




Koç said that the state had not yet made a definitive political decision on resolving the Kurdish question and that the prevailing uncertainty and repeated delays stemmed from this indecision. She pointed to growing contradictions within the state, referring to debates surrounding corruption allegations and the fund crisis, and argued that the state under the Justice and Development Party (AKP) government was experiencing serious internal decay.




Koç described Abdullah Öcalan's proposals as an approach that extended beyond the Kurdish question and also sought to democratize the state structure in Turkey. She said, "Abdullah Öcalan's proposals constitute a project to cleanse state institutions tainted by corruption through democracy. The overwhelming majority of society would benefit from this solution."




'Relying on external power balances is a short-term policy'




Nilüfer Koç said that rather than resolving the Kurdish question, the state was relying on shifting power balances and regional agreements in the Middle East. She argued that Turkey was attempting to buy time through developments in foreign policy. Koç stated that the state was calculating that it could maintain the existing situation through external alliances without resolving the Kurdish question but emphasized that this approach would not provide a lasting solution.




Koç said: "The resolution of the Kurdish question is also a very important factor in external power balances. We need to look at Iran, Iraq and Syria, Turkey's neighbors. Eastern Kurdistan (Rojhilat), Southern Kurdistan (Başur) and Rojava Kurdistan are also asserting the Kurdish people's right to self-determination through struggle. The Kurdish question is therefore not merely an issue of Turkey's domestic politics, but also of its foreign policy. Wherever the Turkish state turns, it will encounter the Kurdish question. Everyone in the region is currently seeking power balances in which they can invest. The strength of the Kurds is also a force capable of significantly changing these balances."




Koç pointed out that a new regional order was taking shape in the Middle East and that strategic changes were underway. She said that the alliances and political balances established today could change tomorrow. Koç argued that Turkey was acting according to day-to-day developments rather than developing a long-term policy.




Koç continued: "Power balances change, new actors emerge, and alliances between actors shift. I believe Turkey has been driven into an impasse in this respect. Turkey is trying to prolong its position through diplomacy by taking advantage of certain openings created by the chaos in the region. The presence of multiple centers of power and the multipolar nature of regional politics mean that political developments take the form of conflict and compromise. As a result, conflict and compromise frequently alternate. Even the United States, which claims hegemony, is struggling to manage this political situation. How, then, can a state like Turkey, which is experiencing serious internal decay, manage it? Domestically, the Kurdish freedom struggle, particularly Abdullah Öcalan's Peace and Democratic Society strategy, has brought Turkey to a point where it must decide its future. The choice is between democracy and deepening decay. The Kurds are a highly dynamic people who are aware of their own strength."




Koç stated that Turkey's domestic problems were also making this policy unsustainable. She said that, alongside debates over corruption, practices aimed at silencing the opposition and the arrest of journalists were continuing to intensify. Koç emphasized that the state could not move forward by relying on foreign policy developments without resolving its internal problems, arguing that the way forward lay in implementing the Peace and Democratic Society Project.




Koç said: "The region is undergoing restructuring based on new agreements rather than old ones. The Turkish state cannot save itself from these global pressures through day-to-day diplomacy and political maneuvers. The Turkish state is experiencing a crisis as a result of the changes being imposed around it. It is becoming clear that the state faces a structural problem. The Republic established in 1923 has now become outdated. Unless Turkey undertakes democratic restructuring as proposed by Abdullah Öcalan, it will become increasingly dependent on external powers."




Koç said that global and regional powers acted according to their own interests and that their calculations might not always align with Turkey's expectations. She emphasized that foreign policy agreements and compromises would not eliminate the Kurdish question. Koç stated that Turkey would sooner or later have to confront its domestic problems, the need to resolve the Kurdish question and the necessity of democratization. She also said, "Turkey needs democracy."




'Abdullah Öcalan's freedom is not solely a matter of the process'




Nilüfer Koç emphasized that the question of Abdullah Öcalan's freedom should not be considered solely in relation to the Peace and Democratic Society Process. She said that the process had created a new political opportunity and argument in this regard, but that the issue had much broader legal and political dimensions.




Koç said: "If there were no process, should Abdullah Öcalan not be free? In my view, there is an issue here that goes beyond the process itself. His abduction and the fact that he has been held unjustly on Imrali for 27 years are problems in themselves. Holding the leader of people, a person who seeks nothing other than democracy and freedom, under such conditions is an injustice in itself."




Koç drew attention to the legal dimension of this injustice, recalling the 2014 judgment of the European Court of Human Rights (ECtHR). She stated that the Court had ruled that aggravated life imprisonment was incompatible with Article 3 of the European Convention on Human Rights in relation to the right to hope and said that Turkey needed to bring its legislation into line with the Convention.




Koç noted that the judgment had still not been implemented despite the years that had passed, describing this as a political stance. She pointed to the responsibility of the Council of Europe's Committee of Ministers, which oversees the execution of judgments, and emphasized that the Council of Europe must enforce its own legal framework and ensure that Turkey fulfills the requirements of the judgment.




'The Council of Europe's position is being tested by the peace process'




Nilüfer Koç stated that the Council of Europe's position on Abdullah Öcalan reflected a continuation of its longstanding political approach to the Kurdish question. She said that the Peace and Democratic Society Process had made the contradictions in this approach more visible.




Koç argued that the Committee of Ministers, the Council of Europe's political and executive body, was still operating on the assumption that the period of conflict between Turkey and the Kurds was continuing. She emphasized that the institution's perception of Turkey as an ally or partner also contributed to its reluctance to fulfill its legal responsibilities.




Koç recalled that a new peace process was underway and that Abdullah Öcalan had issued calls for peace and a democratic society. She said that the Council of Europe needed to take these new circumstances into account and reconsider its position.




Koç said, "The Council of Europe, as far as we can see, continues to insist on its old policy toward the Kurds." She criticized the Committee of Ministers for continuing to act like a third party benefiting from the conflict at a time when Kurds and Turks were no longer engaged in war. She asked, "There was a century-old equation surrounding the Kurdish question: When two sides fight, a third party benefits. The Council of Europe seems to be continuing to play the role of that third party. Yet in Turkey, Kurds and Turks are no longer engaged in an actual military conflict. Why does the third party still adopt a position as though the two sides were at war?"




Koç emphasized that the Council of Europe's relationship with Turkey as a member state, ally and partner should not take precedence over its human rights obligations. She stated that the Peace and Democratic Society Process required the institution to reassess its approach. Koç also pointed out that support for the international signature campaign was not limited to those who shared Abdullah Öcalan's ideas. She noted that the signatories included both people who ideologically supported his views and those who opposed what they regarded as a legal and political injustice. She emphasized that the failure to implement a judgment issued by the ECtHR had prompted objections from different sections of society.




Koç recalled that the Council of Europe and the ECtHR had dealt with numerous cases involving human rights violations in Turkey over the past 40 years. She noted that these mechanisms had been used not only by Kurds but also by opposition groups in Turkey. Koç said that the current opportunity for peace also placed responsibilities on the Council of Europe. She emphasized that the Committee of Ministers should adopt a position supportive of peace and ensure the implementation of the ECtHR judgment concerning Abdullah Öcalan.




'Pressure must increase ahead of the 1–3 December meeting'




Koç stated that the international signature campaign needed to enter a new phase. She drew attention to the meeting of the Council of Europe's Committee of Ministers scheduled for 1–3 December, saying that Abdullah Öcalan's situation and the case concerning implementation of the ECtHR judgment would be on the agenda.




Koç emphasized that the case before the Committee of Ministers was important for ensuring that Turkey introduced the necessary legislative amendments in accordance with ECtHR judgments. She stressed that international campaigns needed to continue. However, Koç also pointed out that international signatures and campaigns alone were insufficient, emphasizing the importance of different sections of society across all parts of Kurdistan taking ownership of the process.




Koç warned that developments in Northern Kurdistan and Rojava in particular posed serious regional dangers. She said that developing a common position among people in different parts of Kurdistan would be important both for Abdullah Öcalan's freedom and for the Peace and Democratic Society Process.




Koç stated that the Peoples' Equality and Democracy Party (DEM Party), which has representation at the Council of Europe, needed to assume a more active role in turning the international campaign into diplomatic and political results. She recalled that the DEM Party was directly involved in the negotiation process through its Imrali delegation, emphasizing that the party's activities in Strasbourg would strengthen rather than weaken the negotiations.




'The DEM Party must take a more proactive approach in Strasbourg'




Nilüfer Koç pointed out that the DEM Party could assume a more effective diplomatic role at the Council of Europe. She emphasized that the party needed to move beyond a passive approach to diplomacy and pursue more proactive initiatives.




Koç recalled that the DEM Party was demanding the democratization of Turkey's laws as part of the negotiation process. She said that initiatives undertaken in Strasbourg, at the Council of Europe, were also part of this struggle. Koç emphasized that these efforts would strengthen the negotiation process in favor of democracy rather than undermine it. She said, "The DEM Party is effectively acting as a mediator. It has an Imrali delegation and is directly involved in this negotiation process. Therefore, one dimension of the struggle to facilitate negotiations and advance democracy consists of activities carried out in Strasbourg, at the Council of Europe."




Koç stated that the DEM Party and other opposition parties had opportunities to contribute to increasing political and diplomatic pressure on the Council of Europe's Committee of Ministers. She emphasized the importance of making more effective use of these opportunities.




Call to all sections of society, from the Kurdish Women's Movement to students




Nilüfer Koç said that not only political parties but all sections of society needed to take action ahead of the December meeting of the Council of Europe's Committee of Ministers. She called on the Kurdish Women's Movement, the Kurdish Students' Union and various social organizations to become involved. Koç emphasized the need to send letters and emails to the Committee of Ministers and continue digital media campaigns. She stressed that these initiatives went beyond continuing the signature campaign and represented society's collective support for Abdullah Öcalan's determination and struggle for peace.




Koç said, "I believe these efforts will be important in demonstrating our commitment to the path toward peace outlined by Abdullah Öcalan."




Koç stated that the Council of Europe's credibility would be seriously questioned if the Committee of Ministers failed to adopt a concrete decision at its December meeting. She described the meeting as a turning point for the institution. Koç recalled that the Council of Europe's fundamental responsibility was to ensure that member states complied with the European Convention on Human Rights and to take the necessary measures to secure their compliance. She criticized the lack of a consistent and comprehensive approach to democratization throughout Turkey's membership of the Council of Europe, arguing that political, economic and military interests had influenced the institution's position.




Koç said that Abdullah Öcalan was currently assuming the role that the Council of Europe's Committee of Ministers should be fulfilling, taking considerable risks to ensure the success of the Peace and Democratic Society Process. She emphasized that the Council of Europe needed to respond to these efforts and assume responsibility for improving Abdullah Öcalan's conditions.




'Non-Kurdish groups are also speaking out against this injustice'




Nilüfer Koç stated that numerous non-Kurdish groups had also supported the international signature campaign, emphasizing that its demands should not be regarded as a concern exclusively for Kurds. She said that appeals and signatures from civil society organizations demonstrated that legal and political objections concerning Abdullah Öcalan's situation had gained international support.




Koç noted that although the signature campaign had concluded, its demands remained on the agenda. She emphasized the importance of continued appeals to the Council of Europe's Committee of Ministers by the international community and civil society.




Koç stressed that Kurds needed to raise their voices more strongly and called on all sections of society in Turkey, Rojava, Eastern Kurdistan and Southern Kurdistan to participate in these efforts.




Koç pointed out that demands to improve Abdullah Öcalan's conditions, implement the right to hope and secure his freedom were not merely matters concerning conditions on Imrali Island, but could also have significant consequences for the future of the region. She said, "Because the only democratic project currently being proposed in the region is the one presented by Abdullah Öcalan. While all regional and global powers are attempting to resolve problems through violence, the Kurdish side is presenting peace as an alternative. This is a truly historic development." 




'Abdullah Öcalan's freedom will create new hope in the region'




Nilüfer Koç stated that enabling Abdullah Öcalan to communicate directly and freely with the outside world, implementing the right to hope and securing his freedom would create new hope across the region. She said that such developments would also have an impact on different countries in the Middle East.




Koç emphasized that this would affect Eastern Kurdistan and Iran, Southern Kurdistan and Iraq, as well as Rojava and Syria. She said that Abdullah Öcalan's freedom would create new political opportunities at the regional level and that the Council of Europe could play an important role in this process.




Koç stated that the Council of Europe's Committee of Ministers possessed mechanisms it could use to encourage Turkey to move toward peace. She emphasized that the institution could employ not only diplomatic means but also its economic and political instruments.

title: Executions and prison sentences continue in Iran
content:
The Kurdistan Human Rights Organisation has published a report on Iran’s repression of Rojhilatê Kurdistan (Eastern Kurdistan) and Iranian citizens.




The report states that courts in Tehran and Mashhad have sentenced five protesters, Alireza Rezai, Vahid Kehermani, Mehdi Jalali, Metin Şebani and Emir Dilşad, to death. All five were arrested during the January 2026 protests.




According to the report, all five were convicted of “collaborating with enemy states”. Two female prisoners tried in the same case, whose identities have yet to be established, were each sentenced to 30 years in prison.




Mehdi Jalali, who previously served as an imam, was reportedly sentenced to death by the Special Court for Clerics on charges of apostasy.




Meanwhile, 19 religious scholars held in Urmia Central Prison (Yakup Muradi, Ibrahim Jiyani, Areş Agahi, Esed Muhammediyan, Awine Kaytarani, Çiya Nasrullahi, Resul Yusuf, Siyamend Alipur, Hemin Ahmedi, Emin Dilnişin, Şehriyar Hızır, Cafer, Vezir Zersaw, Rahim Asare, Afşin, Areş Kulizade, Mihran Nirumendi, Kamyar Şeyhi and Mevlud Ateşbar, as well as Saadet Taşke) have reportedly been sentenced to prison terms ranging from six to ten months.




The report also states that the prisoners have been denied leave, limited freedoms and the right to receive medical treatment outside the prison.

title: MKG: Repression against women journalists continued in October
content:
According to the October 2026 report on rights violations published by the Mesopotamia Women Journalists Association (MKG), one woman journalist was arrested and imprisoned, two women journalists were detained, and another journalist’s home was raided in Turkey last month. In addition, one woman journalist was subjected to ill-treatment, and one incident of obstruction of news coverage was documented.




The report stated that an investigation was launched against one woman journalist, another was sentenced to 18 months in prison, and nine women journalists continued to face trial in nine separate cases. It emphasized that prosecuting journalists for reporting on violence and rights violations against women constituted an infringement of the public’s right to information.




Digital censorship and dismissals




Highlighting the continued digital censorship targeting the free press, the report documented the blocking of two websites and restrictions on access to 20 news articles. It stated that these measures made it more difficult for information about rights violations against women to reach the public.




The report noted that 162 journalists lost their jobs. However, it was not possible to determine how many of them were women. MKG drew attention to the precarious working conditions and discrimination faced by women journalists.
