title: Karayılan: Our martyrs are our greatest values
content:
Following the announcement of the identities of nine guerrilla fighters from East Kurdistan (Rojhilat) who lost their lives at different times during the Kurdish freedom struggle, Murat Karayılan issued a statement addressing their families and the public. The commander of the central headquarters of the People’s Defense Forces (HPG) paid tribute to the fallen fighters’ contributions to the Kurdish freedom movement and recalled the historical significance of the participation of people from Rojhilat in the collective liberation struggle across all parts of Kurdistan.




Karayılan also addressed the current political situation in East Kurdistan and Iran. In light of regional developments, he called on the people to place their trust in their own collective strength, build structures of solidarity, and organize independently of external powers. He also described the Peace and Democratic Society Process initiated by Abdullah Öcalan as a development whose significance extended far beyond North Kurdistan.










https://video.anf-news2.com/live/firat/302bdf04_20261105151543_2026-11-06-behdinan-murat-karayilan-jibo-biranine-sehiden-rojhilat-mesaj-farsi-1.mp4










Murat Karayılan’s statement reads as follows:




“First of all, I would like to extend my greetings and respect to our people in Rojhilat in particular. Among those who have fallen in recent times, some of whose names have already been announced while others have not yet been made public, are several of our comrades from Rojhilat. On behalf of the leadership of our movement and our central headquarters, we extend our condolences to the families of the martyrs whose names we are now announcing. Our sympathies also go out to the entire population of Rojhilat.




On behalf of all our fallen comrades, we remember Heval (Comrade) Artêş (Muhammed Fevzi) and Heval Sila (Zehra Ismaili) with respect, admiration, and gratitude. We bow before their memory and renew our promise to them, the promise we made together as comrades. We will remain faithful to that promise. We will fight to the end to realize their hopes and dreams and bring their cause to success. We will carry their struggle to victory and, in doing so, immortalize their memory.




They gave their lives for their homeland




Dear comrades, esteemed families,




All those whose names we are announcing at this time resisted under extraordinary circumstances and fell in that struggle. As we have already emphasized, this holds particular significance. I would like to express my appreciation to all the families who raised such courageous individuals. We extend our greetings and respect to the mothers and fathers of the martyrs.




The fact that young people from Rojhilat joined the struggle throughout Kurdistan, particularly in Bakur (North Kurdistan), and demonstrated such great willingness to make sacrifices reflects an honorable stance. They did not act out of personal interest. They gave their lives for their homeland. That is why these comrades are especially precious to us, and we bow before their memory. Through their deaths, they have also left us a message that we must put into practice.




As I have explained before, people from Rojhilat began joining our movement in 1989. However, a decisive development took place during the international conspiracy against Rêber Apo [Leader Abdullah Öcalan]. Although our movement had not yet established its own organizational structures in Rojhilat at the time, the people rose up. Protests and uprisings broke out across East Kurdistan, marked by great determination and willingness to make sacrifices.




This stance deserves the highest recognition. At that time, our comrades and our entire people felt that we had support and that Rojhilat stood by our side. The people of Rojhilat understand the significance of political leaders and their historical responsibilities. They had already gained this experience during the time of Qazî Mihemed and Abdurrahman Qasimlo. That is why they also understood the capture of Rêber Apo as a historic turning point and rose up against it.




Rojhilat’s contribution to the collective liberation struggle




Following this period, the participation of young people from Rojhilat in the guerrilla movement continued to increase. We must not forget comrades such as Doctor Afat and Dilxwaz, who fought and fell in East Kurdistan. We also remember Heval Şivan Gever and his many years of work in the region.




Young people from Rojhilat quickly found their place within the guerrilla movement and continued to develop their capabilities. Many assumed important duties and responsibilities within a short period, even under extremely difficult conditions.




Our people know, for example, Heval Simko, who went as far as the Black Sea region and assumed leadership responsibilities there. His determination and courage made this possible.




Another example is Heval Rêzan Cawîd, who joined in 2003. He was an educated, knowledgeable, exceptionally dedicated, and courageous individual. Thanks to his abilities, he soon took on greater responsibilities and became co-chair of KODAR-PJAK.




When young people from Rojhilat become familiar with Rêber Apo’s thoughts and ideas and engage with them, they often develop a strong connection to these principles within a short period. On this basis, they are able to rapidly develop their abilities and political work.




Heval Hîwa Sine fought in Botan and Erzurum, where he assumed command responsibilities, and later participated in the resistance in Kobanê. He served as a regional commander and fell there. He made significant contributions over many years.




Heval Rênas Seqiz was also active in the Erzurum region for a long time. He subsequently returned to Rojhilat and continued his work there before moving to Rojava. Through his dedication, he also assumed responsibility as a regional commander there and became a target of the enemy.




We have known numerous comrades from Rojhilat who took on responsibilities in this way. Heval Mizgîn Ronahî was a member of the special forces and served as a commander in Zap. She fell after putting up determined resistance.




Heval Egîd Rojhilat came from Îlam and was also a member of the special forces. He carried out numerous important duties within our movement. In South Kurdistan, particularly in Kirkuk, he played a significant role in the fight against ISIS. He later assumed regional command responsibilities in Metîna, where he fell.




Once again, I would also like to remember Ronahî, Şîrîn Elemhulî, Ferzad, Ferhat, and Soran. Even in the face of execution, they refused to bow down and continued to resist.




The people from Rojhilat who joined our movement earned their place through their dedication, courage, willingness to make sacrifices, and resistance. They assumed significant responsibilities in our struggle. A land and a people capable of producing such individuals also possess the strength to achieve their freedom.




I have mentioned only a few names here. It would be impossible to list them all. Many other comrades from Rojhilat, as committed followers of Rêber Apo’s ideas, have taken on important responsibilities. We remember them all with respect, admiration, and gratitude.




Families can be proud of their children




Those whose identities we are now announcing also belong to this tradition. The vast majority of them fell within the past ten years. As we have already explained, the war during this period differed fundamentally from its earlier phases. Perhaps there had never before been a war of such intensity.




Under these extraordinarily difficult conditions, our comrades put up historic resistance. Every mother and father who raised such individuals can be proud of them. Their families raised them and instilled values in them. Later, fully aware of their responsibilities, they freely chose their own path.




They fought in Bakur, Bashur, and Rojava, where they lost their lives. Their life journeys demonstrate the determination and courage they possessed. Their families can look back on them with pride.




Dear comrades, esteemed families, dear people,




Our entire region is currently engulfed in war. Iran and Rojhilat, in particular, are going through an extremely sensitive and significant period. We are aware of the needs and demands in Rojhilat. At the same time, we know that a society capable of producing such individuals and leaders also possesses the strength to overcome great difficulties.




What matters is not becoming dependent on other powers, but taking Rêber Apo’s Third Way as a foundation and relying on your own strength. This applies to all parts of Kurdistan, but particularly to Rojhilat.




You have your own experiences. The uprising under the slogan “Jin, Jiyan, Azadî” [Woman, Life, Freedom] was neither an ordinary nor an insignificant experience. The stance demonstrated at that time was also extraordinary. We are convinced that, on this basis, you can achieve a great deal if you take action and organize yourselves.




An organized society is everything




One thing must never be forgotten: An organized society is everything; an unorganized society is nothing. That is why you must organize within your communities and strengthen your unity. Every village, every neighborhood, and every region must act in solidarity, cooperate, and support one another.




At present, economic difficulties and financial hardships are severe. Those who have the means must support those in need. You must stand by one another, demonstrate solidarity, help each other, and, above all, organize yourselves.




Through organization, people develop a will of their own. An organized society can become an extraordinarily powerful force.




That is why, particularly at this crucial stage, our people must take responsibility for themselves and develop their own collective strength. As we have already said, this is possible only through organization.




Social unity as the foundation of political agency




No one can deter a society in which tens of thousands of people are organized from pursuing its goals. That is why we must follow the path of our martyrs everywhere, develop comprehensive social organization, and continue the struggle. We believe in a promising future for the people of Rojhilat. Our people have begun taking their affairs into their own hands and are increasingly aware of where and how they need to act.




There are also revolutionary institutions. If these institutions fulfill their duties in a timely manner and live up to their responsibilities, many problems can be resolved and new developments made possible. However, what remains decisive is that the people themselves take action, organize, and develop an unwavering collective will. This is possible and by no means beyond reach.




Who is truly powerless? Those who are fragmented, lack organization, and have no social alliances. A society that develops its own alliances and relationships of solidarity, on the other hand, can find solutions even under the most difficult circumstances. This is precisely what is expected of our Kurdish people today.




The democratic resolution process concerns all of Kurdistan




As you know, the democratic resolution process is currently on the agenda in Bakur. Rêber Apo developed and initiated this process to bring our struggle to success and achieve our goals. Although there are currently difficulties in its implementation, we are convinced that this new strategy will pave the way for significant developments. This issue does not concern the north alone. It is of great importance to all Kurds and to Kurdistan as a whole.




Rêber Apo says: “I want to create a space where Kurds can live.”




Today, we Kurds need a space in the Middle East where we can live freely. We need the opportunity to lead free lives on our own land, on the basis of equality with neighboring peoples. Such a space is essential. All efforts are directed toward achieving this.




That is why the work Rêber Apo is currently undertaking is, by its very nature, of national significance. We are convinced that all our people are following these developments closely.




Our martyrs are our greatest values




In this context, we must protect and preserve our values even more strongly. Our greatest values are our martyrs. They embody our present, our future, and the source of our strength. We must unite around their memory and strengthen our unity on the basis of their political legacy. In this way, we will immortalize their memory. To honor them, we must continue their struggle.




To our esteemed families, I would like to say: The families of our martyrs are also our families. They must recognize the value that their loved ones represent. At the same time, it is important to continue the path taken by the martyrs through their own work and commitment and to assume responsibility within society. With this hope and this goal, I once again extend my condolences to all the families of our martyrs and wish them strength and success.




We will follow the path of our martyrs and achieve our goal. Let no one doubt that. The struggle of these individuals shows us the way. It will lead us to success and victory.




In this spirit, we say once again: Şehîd Namirin! Şehîd Namirin! Şehîd Namirin!”




Identities of nine fallen guerrilla fighters from Rojhilat




The Press Center of the People’s Defense Forces (HPG) on Thursday announced the identities of nine guerrilla fighters from Rojhilat who lost their lives between 2006 and 2022 in various regions of Kurdistan.








The HPG obituary said:




“Our comrades Artêş, Sıla, Zana, Welat, Fedakar, Rêbûwar, Bêkes, Bahoz, and Nebes, the courageous sons and daughters of East Kurdistan, waged a tireless and continuous struggle and fully fulfilled their revolutionary duties. Through their determined participation, their unwavering commitment to the political line of our leader Abdullah Öcalan, and their selfless fighting spirit, they have joined the ranks of the immortals.




Our comrades, who fought to realize Abdullah Öcalan’s philosophy and felt a profound sense of responsibility in the face of our leader’s imprisonment, undertook historic duties under the most difficult conditions. Through their deaths, they became tangible examples for those of us continuing their struggle of the qualities that a militant committed to our leader’s political line must embody.




We declare that we will carry the banner of resistance passed down to us by our fallen comrades until victory. In this spirit, we extend our condolences to our patriotic people in East Kurdistan and to the families of our fallen comrades.”

title: Ciwan İbrahim is Rojava
content:
“I am a child of Serêkaniyê. My mother’s name is Enisa, and my father’s name is Abdurrahim. Who are you? Where do you come from?” These were the words Ciwan İbrahim addressed to the militants of Jabhat al-Nusra. It was 2012, and the battle for Serêkaniyê was underway. Despite being wounded in the hand, Ciwan refused even to have his injury bandaged and would not abandon his fighters. “If I withdraw, my comrades will be affected. I am putting all my strength into this battle,” he said, as he considered how to continue directing the fighting with his other hand.




Ciwan İbrahim’s 18-year journey, stretching from Serêkaniyê to Lebanon, from Garê to the resistance tunnels of Zap and the Rojava Revolution, was marked by this determination. Throughout this journey, he distinguished himself at different times as an accomplished journalist, a commander, and one of the leading figures among the people.




Some of us came to know him when he announced the establishment of the People’s Defense Units (YPG), others as a commander of the Asayish (Internal Security Forces), and still others as he rode his motorcycle through the streets of Qamişlo.




Today, Rojava mourns the loss of this legendary commander.




From Lebanon to the mountains of Kurdistan




Ciwan İbrahim (Nosican İbrahim) was born on October 3, 1983, in Serêkaniyê. He had two sisters, Lorîn and Şirîncan, and a brother named Dilciwan. As the eldest child, he was the apple of his family’s eye. Both his mother and father were teachers, and he received his primary and secondary education from them.




From an early age, he became familiar with the Ba’ath regime’s policies that denied the existence of the Kurdish people. Through the activities carried out by Kurdish leader Abdullah Öcalan in Rojava and his efforts to raise political awareness among the population, Ciwan became acquainted with the Kurdish Freedom Movement. In 2001, two years after the international conspiracy against Öcalan, he returned to Kurdistan from Lebanon.




After spending a considerable period in the Garê region, he moved to Zap. In 2010, he joined the Special Forces (Hêzên Taybet), where he underwent profound ideological and military development in accordance with the principles of self-sacrificing militancy.




In 2011, as the Rojava Revolution began to take shape, he once again turned toward his homeland, Rojava, to take a leading role in revolutionary activities. This return marked the beginning of a new chapter in his life.













The early days of preparations for the revolution




That year, meetings were being held across Rojava, young people were brought together, and efforts were underway to organize the population. The institutions of the revolution had not yet been established. Much of the work was carried out through clandestine meetings and training sessions. The home of Ciwan’s father, Abdurrahim İbrahim, was among the places where these meetings took place.




Ferhad Şamî, former press spokesperson for the Syrian Democratic Forces (SDF), first met Ciwan during this period. Recalling those days in an interview with ANF, Şamî said, “I met him during the first meetings in 2011. We were attending training sessions with Mazloum Abdi, Martyr Hisen Çavuş, and Henife Hisen. At the time, the Ba’ath regime wanted to launch attacks, but we were taking precautions.”




He contributed to every field




Ciwan’s activities during those years extended across the fields of media, youth organizing, and self-defense. Programs were developed to provide young people with media training, and training sessions were organized in various cities across Rojava.




Şamî also joined these efforts at Ciwan’s request. He continued:




“We prepared a program and began the training sessions. We provided media training to young people in Serêkaniyê, Dirbesiyê, and Til Temir. We then traveled to Hesekê and Qamişlo, eventually reaching Dêrik.”




While media training continued, organizing communities in the cities and developing self-defense initiatives were also of great importance. As part of these efforts, youth groups were formed during the process of removing regime soldiers from the cities. Ciwan, Martyr Hemze Tolhildan, Martyr Serhed, Martyr Seydo, Martyr Goran, and Martyr Lewend took on this responsibility.













For all of Kurdistan




Journalist Dîlan Osman also recalls that they were still young at the time and eager to take part in preparations for the revolution. She describes the arrival of Ciwan and his comrades in Rojava as part of a broader vision of struggle encompassing all of Kurdistan:




“Heval (Comrade) Ciwan was one of the figures who played a major role in the Rojava Revolution. He was among those who returned to their homeland to prepare for the revolution. At the time, we were young and enthusiastic, and we had aspirations. We wanted to stand alongside them and take on responsibilities. Heval Ciwan and his comrades were thinking not only of Rojava, the smallest part of Kurdistan, but of all parts of Kurdistan.”




Ciwan went from house to house to prepare the population for the revolution, explaining the developments ahead and discussing with people what kind of life they could build.




As the crisis in Syria deepened, it was essential for the population to be prepared and for the social foundations of the revolution to be established. For this reason, organizing efforts extended into every aspect of life.




Dîlan Osman recalls these efforts as follows:




“Today, everyone knows him as a commander of the Asayish, but he had already made significant contributions long before that. You know what is called the ‘Revolutionary People’s War’? Heval Ciwan was one of its pioneers. He was among those who answered the questions of why a revolution was necessary and how it could be carried out through their actions.




They went from house to house, explaining these ideas to everyone, from children to the elderly. The establishment of people’s councils was also an important stage in this organizing process. Heval Ciwan worked to establish councils so that people could govern their own lives. This was followed by the beginning of the transition to the Autonomous Administration system.”













He did not surrender Serêkaniyê to the armed groups




Today, whenever we ask people about Ciwan İbrahim, the battle for Serêkaniyê is the first event they recall. The battle, which took place in November 2012, holds an important place both in his life and in the course of the struggle in Rojava.




Ferhad Şamî, who witnessed the fighting at the time, recounts what happened:




“Jabhat al-Nusra launched an attack with 73 battalions and more than 10,000 militants, using heavy weapons. Alongside Heval Ciwan, Martyr Jiyan Tolhildan, Martyr Dozdar Hemo, Martyr Seydo Rojhilat, Martyr Serhed, Martyr Lewend, Martyr Goran, and Cemşid also took part in defending the city. Serêkaniyê was his hometown, and it was saved thanks to these comrades.”




One of the incidents that remains particularly vivid in Şamî’s memory is the encirclement of the area where Martyr Goran was positioned.




“More than a hundred militants surrounded the area where Martyr Goran was located. There was a vocational school opposite the encircled position. Our comrades had only hand grenades. Heval Ciwan went in with hand grenades and rescued his comrade. That was how courageous he was,” Şamî recalls.




The resistance gave the YPG its identity




The struggle in Serêkaniyê also contributed to the development of the YPG’s military identity. At a time when armed groups were advancing in many areas, the resistance they encountered in Serêkaniyê provided an important experience in terms of the YPG’s positioning and its relationship with the population.




Şamî emphasizes the significance of those days:




“The armed groups were gaining ground everywhere, but they suffered a setback in Serêkaniyê. After Sheikh Maqsoud, the people rallied around the YPG thanks to these comrades.”




He protected Christians and Arabs




Following the defense of Serêkaniyê, developing security mechanisms and protecting cities became major responsibilities in Rojava. Ciwan brought his military experience into the field of security. With the establishment of the Asayish in 2013, he worked to develop security systems in the cities.




Ciwan’s approach to security also encompassed the protection of cities where different communities lived together. He attached great importance to enabling Arab, Syriac, Armenian, and Circassian communities to establish their own security mechanisms.




This approach also changed Dîlan’s perspective:




“He placed great importance on cities inhabited by multiple communities. We used to say, ‘We are patriots, the Kurds always come first, and we have a cause.’ But Heval Ciwan did not see it that way. He would say, ‘If you want to protect and defend yourselves, you must also organize the other communities.’ This brought about a change in our thinking.”




During the years when ISIS attacks intensified, this approach found practical expression in the work of the Asayish. Protecting neighborhoods inhabited by Christians and Arabs was among Ciwan’s priorities.




Ferhad Şamî emphasizes the relationship Ciwan established with the Christian community in Qamişlo:




“Christians and Arabs loved him very much, too. He was the one who did the most to protect Christians from ISIS. In 2014, 2015, and 2016, the Asayish protected their neighborhoods. He would say, ‘We must protect Christians and Arabs,’ and he established a battalion for Christians in Qamişlo.”




Şamî says he last saw Ciwan in Hol in 2016. He recalls that Ciwan continued his work even when armed groups were searching for him.




He became a star in Garê




Following his duties in Rojava, Ciwan İbrahim once again turned toward the mountains of freedom. In 2019, while carrying out his revolutionary duties in the Garê region, he lost his life in an attack by the Turkish state.




After the deaths of Ciwan and 28 guerrillas were announced on November 2, condolence gatherings were held across Rojava. Hundreds of people from Zirgan, Til Temir, Qamişlo, Amûdê, Tirbespiyê, Çilaxa, Rimêlan, Girkê Legê, and Dêrik attended the commemoration held in Hesekê.













‘I am proud of Ciwan’




Following the condolence gathering, we also spoke with his mother, Enîse Topal Hemo, to tell the story of Ciwan’s life.




Originally from Afrin, Enîse Topal Hemo belongs to the Şikakî tribe. After hearing from the comrades who had worked alongside Ciwan, we listened as his mother shared her memories of her son’s life and character.




As she begins to speak about her fallen son, she says, “Ez qurbana xorta bim” (“I would sacrifice myself for my son”).




“Ciwan left an ache in my heart, but he also placed a golden crown upon my head. I am proud to be his mother. I hold my head high because of my son. Ciwan İbrahim is Simko Şikakî.”




As Mother Enîse speaks about what her son did for his people, she also recalls what he was like at home:




“He did the most wonderful things for his people. He was very intelligent, and he never once gave me any trouble. He had a pure heart and was a good person. He helped me with the housework. He loved me, his neighbors, and his friends very much. I never saw any shortcomings in him.”




She expresses her longing for her son through the bond he established with his people:




“Ciwan İbrahim is the patience of Rojava. Rojava is Ciwan İbrahim. I will rename Serêkaniyê after Ciwan İbrahim.”




He was the father of the poor




Ciwan İbrahim’s connection with the people was not limited to his revolutionary activities and responsibilities in the field of security. Those who knew him also emphasize his concern for people in need and his close involvement in the problems faced by the community.




Dîlan Osman describes how people remembered Ciwan during condolence visits:




“Everyone who visits the family says, ‘Heval Ciwan was the father of the poor.’ He looked after everyone and was truly a man of the revolution. For example, whenever he saw someone living in poverty, he would find a way to help them. Before we knew it, we would hear that he had somehow managed to help them. Even when people fell ill, they would ask, ‘Where is Heval Ciwan?’ He was present in every city across Rojava, particularly in the Cizîr region. He was the people’s first general.”




A memory left behind by a camera




Ciwan İbrahim was also a media worker who provided Dîlan Osman with journalism training in 2013. One of Dîlan’s most cherished memories of him involves his camera. One day, Ciwan gave Dîlan the camera he had received as a gift and always carried with him.




Dîlan recalls that moment:




“Before leaving Rojava, he gave me his camera as a gift. He said, ‘It’s yours now, but always take pictures of people smiling.’ I told him, ‘You should keep it. You loved this camera so much, and you took the most beautiful photographs with it.’ But he said, ‘No, I want you to have it now.’ Perhaps you don’t realize it at the time, but that was the last gift he ever gave me. I still have that camera.”

title: Veysi Aktaş: A struggle disconnected from society cannot succeed
content:
What role can literature, language, and intellectuals play in shaping a democratic peace? This question is at the heart of an international conference that began on Friday in Amed (Turkish: Diyarbakır). Under the title “The Role of Literature, Language and intelligentsia in Processes of Dialogue, Reconciliation, Peace and Equality,” writers, academics, and representatives of civil society organizations and political parties have come together. Discussions focus on the social responsibility of cultural figures, the freedom of the Kurdish language, and the prospects of the Peace and Democratic Society Process.




The event, held at the Ali Emiri Conference Hall, is organized by the international writers’ association PEN, the Kurdish PEN Center (PENa Kurd), Amed Metropolitan Municipality, and the district municipalities of Sur, Yenişehir, Bağlar, and Kayapınar. It began with a moment of silence.







Peace requires linguistic and cultural freedom




At the opening, Ömer Fidan, a writer and chair of PENa Kurd, stated that literary figures must take responsibility for building a dignified peace. He said the conference aimed to strengthen the social and cultural dimensions of the peace process.




Mürüvet Demir of the Peace Mothers’ Council recalled the decades-long suppression of the Kurdish language and said: “People were subjected to repression and violence simply for speaking Kurdish. The opportunities available today to use and develop the language publicly are the result of a long struggle by society.”




Writer Mizgin Ronak drew attention to the situation of imprisoned literary figures. She said numerous writers remained in Turkish prisons and that their works must be made accessible to the public. She emphasized that Kurdish literature has a rich historical and cultural heritage whose development must continue even under repressive conditions.







Writer Ilhan Sami Çomak, who himself spent many years in prison, described freedom to use one’s mother tongue and the release of political prisoners as essential prerequisites for a successful peace process. He particularly highlighted the situation of people who have been imprisoned for decades, as well as seriously ill prisoners.




Serra Bucak, co-mayor of Amed Metropolitan Municipality, also stressed that peace would not be possible without linguistic equality. She said everyone must have the freedom to speak, sing, and create literature in their mother tongue.




Literature as a means of fostering social understanding




The panel titled “Literature, Language and Universal Rights in Peace Processes,” moderated by Diba Keskin, then began. Burhan Sönmez, president of PEN International, spoke about the responsibility of writers in overcoming social conflicts. “Writers from different countries can help develop a common language of peace and support processes of mutual understanding across national and cultural boundaries,” he emphasized.




Author Bêrîvan Doskî highlighted the importance of the mother tongue for identity, culture, and the future of society. She said that despite decades of attacks, the Kurdish language had continued to develop. To strengthen this development, she called for joint cultural and arts festivals, greater literary engagement with social struggles, and exchanges with writers from other communities.







Aktaş: Intellectuals must not distance themselves from society




In his speech, Kurdish politician Veysi Aktaş critically examined the role of intellectuals in the current peace process. He warned against separating cultural and academic work from social struggles.




“The peace process is of great importance to all peoples. Intellectuals have an important role to play in its success. Their responsibility is to open up new paths for society and provide guidance. However, if they lose touch with social realities, they develop an elitist attitude that distances them from the people.”




Aktaş, who was imprisoned for several years alongside Kurdish leader Abdullah Öcalan on the Turkish prison island of Imrali, called for a more comprehensive examination of the social conditions necessary for peace, freedom, and coexistence based on equality.




In his assessment, the contributions made by intellectuals so far have been insufficient. Although efforts are underway, he said, they needed to be deepened and more closely linked to grassroots organizing.




“Intellectuals have not yet reached a level at which they can fully fulfill their responsibilities. Politics is not merely about struggling against those in power. It also encompasses struggles in the fields of culture, art, and language. When intellectuals distance themselves from politics, they become detached from reality and retreat into a purely intellectual understanding of themselves.”







‘There is a deadlock in the transition to the second phase’




Referring to the Peace and Democratic Society Process, Aktaş described the current period as a critical transitional stage. He said the process consisted of three phases and was currently moving toward the second, but obstacles had emerged.




“Our struggle to ensure that the necessary legal steps are taken is of great importance. This process consists of three phases. We are in the transition to the second phase, but there is a deadlock at this point.”




Aktaş pointed out that grassroots organizing is particularly important under these circumstances. He warned against viewing the peace process solely as a matter of political negotiations.




“The process has reached a stage where those who are best organized will succeed. Therefore, we must strengthen our organizing efforts together with the people. A struggle disconnected from society can never succeed.”




He stressed that this applied not only to political issues but also to women’s liberation, ecology, and cultural rights. Intellectuals, in particular, need to take responsibility in these areas and expand their cooperation with social movements, he added.




“For peace to succeed, intellectuals must become aware of their role and responsibilities and actively engage in the process. We need intellectuals who appeal to the conscience of society and act using the right methods.”




In his contribution, writer German Rojas addressed the connection between literature, culture, and social life. He emphasized that intellectuals needed to strengthen their ability to persuade and their collective organizational structures in order to effectively contribute to social change.

title: IHD documents hundreds of human rights violations in Turkish prisons
content:
The Human Rights Association (IHD) documented a total of 899 human rights violations in Turkish prisons between July and September 2026. The most frequently reported violations concerned access to food and drinking water, protection against ill-treatment, and the right to communication. The organization warned of a further deterioration in prison conditions and accused the Turkish government of allowing problems to persist even when they could be easily resolved.




The report on the human rights situation in prisons across the Marmara region was presented at a press conference held at the IHD branch office in Istanbul’s Beyoğlu district. Gülseren Yoleri, a member of the IHD Central Executive Board, Meral Nergis Şahin, co-spokesperson for the Prison Commission, and commission member Sevilay Yılmaz Birgin took part in the presentation.




The investigation was based on complaints and submissions from prisoners and their relatives, as well as publicly available information. The report noted that prisons were operating beyond their designated capacities.




Ill-treatment and inadequate living conditions




Most of the documented rights violations concerned prisoners’ basic living conditions. In 293 cases, the IHD recorded inadequate access to food and clean drinking water, as well as deficiencies in hygiene and personal care. Another 258 violations involved physical assaults, ill-treatment, degrading treatment, and torture.




Restrictions on fundamental rights also accounted for a significant proportion of the violations. The organization documented 136 violations of the right to communication, including cases of isolation. In 117 cases, the right to healthcare was violated. These were accompanied by 39 violations involving unlawful detention and unequal treatment in the enforcement of sentences, as well as 28 cases in which prisoners’ access to justice was obstructed or denied.




In addition, the IHD recorded six violations related to hunger strikes and three violations of the right to life. Another 15 rights violations were identified through an analysis of publicly available online sources. The individually listed categories add up to 895 cases. However, the IHD reported a total of 899 rights violations. The discrepancy of four cases is not explained in the available summary.




Political causes of prison abuses




In its assessment, the Human Rights Association linked increasing prison overcrowding to the deterioration of detention conditions. According to the organization, both the prison population and the number of documented rights violations are rising. The IHD particularly criticized the fact that even problems that could be resolved through relatively simple measures remained unaddressed.




“This demonstrates that the underlying cause lies in the persistent continuation of government policies that give rise to human rights violations in general and violations of prisoners’ rights in particular,” the report stated.




The IHD therefore considers strengthening social mobilization and human rights advocacy against these violations a key prerequisite for bringing about change.




‘We want to give prisoners a voice’




The Prison Commission emphasized that its reports were not intended merely to compile statistics.




“We prepare these reports not simply to provide information. Our primary goal is to give those behind prison walls a voice, at least to some extent, to make their pressing problems visible, raise awareness, and help prevent rights violations.”




At the same time, the IHD acknowledged the limited scope of its investigation. It said the documented cases were based on a relatively small number of complaints and submissions from the prisons examined. The actual number of rights violations could therefore be significantly higher.




According to the organization, the investigation covered 16 prisons. These included the Marmara/Silivri, Bakırköy, Kandıra, Edirne, Tekirdağ, Ümraniye, Metris, and Maltepe prison complexes. The published list also included facilities outside the Marmara region, including those in Izmir and Bolu.




In conclusion, the Prison Commission stressed that the struggle to secure humane prison conditions must not be left to prisoners alone: “Human rights violations in prisons cannot be prevented solely through the struggle of prisoners themselves. This also requires support through struggles outside prison walls. This report is also our call for solidarity with prisoners and their families in the face of problems that have now reached an enormous scale.”

title: Court overturns fine imposed on Syriac Orthodox church in İdil
content:
The Syriac Orthodox Church of the Virgin Mary in İdil district of Şırnak province has secured a preliminary legal victory against the AKP-run municipality. The Şırnak Administrative Court has suspended the enforcement of a fine of approximately 1.17 million Turkish lira (around 20,800 euros), which had been imposed on the church foundation over a guesthouse allegedly built without a permit. The main proceedings are still ongoing.




In June, the municipality imposed an administrative fine of 1,170,743.24 lira on the foundation of the historic Syriac Orthodox Church of the Virgin Mary and sealed the guesthouse in October. The foundation subsequently challenged the measure in court.




In its ruling, the Administrative Court found that the municipality had failed to adequately investigate who had actually constructed the building in question. According to the court, the mere fact that the building lacked a construction permit was not sufficient to hold the church foundation responsible.




The court criticized the incomplete examination of the facts and ordered the suspension of the fine without requiring a security deposit. As a result, it concluded, the penalty cannot be enforced until further notice. A final decision on its legality has yet to be made.

title: Journalist Haşim Abak detained in Mardin
content:
Kurdish journalist Haşim Abak, a reporter for the Mezopotamya News Agency (MA), was detained on Tuesday night in the district of Nusaybin in Mardin province. Abak was traveling in a vehicle when he was stopped by police.




Necla Özgezer and a 16-year-old identified by the initials H. T. were also taken into custody alongside him. On Wednesday morning, the three were transferred to the Mardin Police Headquarters and handed over to the Counterterrorism Department (TEM).




They are expected to be questioned later in the day. No information has yet been provided regarding the reasons for their detention.

title: Study reveals 86.7% of Kurds in Munich report discrimination
content:
The Kurdish population living in Germany is estimated at approximately 1.5 million. An expert report published by Mediendienst Integration on 15 October 2026, titled Kurds in Germany: Between Asylum, Social Participation and Anti-Kurdish Racism, examines the demographic situation of Kurds in the country, asylum procedures, social participation and experiences of discrimination.




The expert study underpinning the report was prepared by Professor Çinur Ghaderi of the Protestant University of Applied Sciences Bochum (EvH Bochum). The study was supported by the Robert Bosch Foundation.




The Munich component of the research examined the living conditions of Kurds and their experiences of racism in detail. The study, prepared by Professor Çinur Ghaderi, Monique Kaulertz and Mary Lam, was conducted at the request of the Democracy Unit (Fachstelle für Demokratie) of the City of Munich.




183 out of 210 respondents reported experiencing discrimination




The Munich study, conducted in 2025 and published in January 2026, revealed the extent of discrimination faced by Kurds in the city. The research included a quantitative survey involving 210 participants, alongside 23 individual expert interviews and nine focus group discussions. Approximately 65 people participated in the focus group discussions.




Of the 210 survey respondents, 183 reported experiencing discrimination at least once in Munich during the previous 12 months. This represented 86.7 percent of participants.




Among respondents, 66.4 percent reported experiencing humiliating behaviour, while 64.4 percent encountered disrespectful or condescending attitudes. Half of the participants said they had experienced exclusion, 44.2 percent reported verbal abuse or insults, and 11.8 percent said they had been physically assaulted.




Among those who reported discrimination, 57.4 percent identified their Kurdish identity as a reason, while 56.8 percent cited their origin. The study noted that discrimination based on Kurdish identity could also occur in connection with other identities and affiliations.




The researchers emphasised that the findings reflected only the experiences of participants in Munich and should not be regarded as a nationwide survey representative of the entire Kurdish population in Germany.




Discrimination does not occur only on the streets




According to the research, Kurds experience various forms of discrimination in public spaces, within the education system, in workplaces and in their interactions with public institutions. The findings show that discrimination is not limited to overt insults and physical attacks but also manifests through condescending behaviour, exclusion and institutional barriers.




The report highlights that security-focused approaches towards Kurdish political and civil organisations can reinforce social mistrust and prejudice. It also notes that people with insecure residence status and stateless Kurds are in a more vulnerable position because of legal uncertainties and barriers to accessing social resources.




The researchers also emphasise that the Kurdish community should not be viewed solely through its experiences of discrimination. The report states that Kurds contribute to Munich's cultural, social and political life and engage in activities that strengthen social solidarity and support democratic participation.




The exact Kurdish population in Germany remains unknown




According to data published by Mediendienst Integration on 22 October 2026, approximately 1.5 million Kurds live in Germany. However, the country does not maintain official population statistics based on Kurdish ethnic identity.




One of the main reasons is that population records in Germany are based on criteria such as citizenship and country of birth rather than ethnic identity. Kurds may hold German, Turkish, Syrian, Iraqi or Iranian citizenship, while some are stateless.




According to data obtained by Mediendienst Integration from the German Federal Office for Migration and Refugees (BAMF), the number of asylum applications submitted by Kurds between 2010 and June 2026 reached 656,245. Of these, 607,896 were registered as initial applications. During the same period, 378,316 people were granted protection status.




However, these figures do not directly indicate the total Kurdish population living in Germany. Estimates of the Kurdish population must also take into account other forms of migration, family reunification, naturalisation and different residence statuses, alongside asylum applications.




Asylum policies and security concerns




The nationwide expert report examines the processes through which Kurds from different countries have arrived in Germany and the consequences of asylum policies. Asylum applications, protection decisions and the risks of deportation facing Kurds from Syria and Turkey are among the report's main subjects.




The study also assesses Kurdish social and political participation, existing research on anti-Kurdish racism and the structural barriers faced by the Kurdish community.




The Munich study notes that associating Kurdish identity with discussions of security and terrorism has caused some participants to feel that they are viewed with suspicion and excluded. According to the research, this has also led some Kurds to feel constantly obliged to explain themselves and their identity.




Researchers make recommendations to municipalities and policymakers




The Munich study includes recommendations for local authorities, public institutions and civil society organisations on combating discrimination. The researchers recommend developing support mechanisms that take the needs of Kurds into account, preventing institutional discrimination and strengthening social participation.




Considered together, the general estimates of the Kurdish population in Germany and the research examining experiences of discrimination in Munich highlight the social visibility of Kurds, their access to equal rights and the need to combat discrimination.




Sources:

 

City of Munich Democracy Unit, Protestant University of Applied Sciences Bochum, Mediendienst Integration, Robert Bosch Foundation and the German Federal Office for Migration and Refugees (BAMF).

title: Özdal: Ruling elites openly robbed large sections of society
content:
The economic and political repercussions of the financial developments that erupted in Turkey in September and became known publicly as the "fund crisis" continue to be debated. Allegations have emerged that numerous individuals, including figures affiliated with the Justice and Development Party (AKP), obtained illicit profits through investment funds.




Some figures released in connection with the crisis suggest that losses may have reached as much as 2.7 trillion Turkish liras. Investigations involving the names of AKP figures and state officials have intensified public debate, while criticism of the government's handling of the crisis has also grown. President Tayyip Erdoğan's latest remarks on the fund crisis have been interpreted as an indication of growing discontent over the developments even among AKP supporters.




Journalist Hakkı Özdal spoke to ANF about the causes of the fund crisis, the relationship between political authorities and financial circles, the role of international capital and the crisis's potential impact on society.




'The bubble economists and journalists had warned about has burst'




Hakkı Özdal said that numerous warnings had previously been issued about the developments known as the fund crisis. He emphasized that the crisis had not emerged suddenly, but was the result of a financial system that had operated for years before being pushed into crisis by international intervention. Özdal added that international financial institutions had intensified their warnings to Turkish authorities and that the crisis erupted following regulations introduced by the Capital Markets Board (SPK) concerning money market funds and hedge funds.




Özdal said: "The chain of events described as the fund crisis actually emerged when a form of fraud that had been going on for years, and about which certain journalists and financial market commentators had long been issuing warnings, was triggered by international intervention and then inevitably exploded. As you know, international financial institutions began intensifying their warnings to Turkish authorities at the beginning of the summer. The Capital Markets Board subsequently introduced significant restrictions and tighter regulations on money market funds and hedge funds, which came into effect on 28 August. The fund crisis then struck like a tsunami. A bubble that international financial institutions, as well as economists and even journalists in our country, had already identified finally burst."




'Ruling elites openly robbed large sections of society'




Özdal argued that the high returns generated through money market funds primarily benefited political and economic elites. However, he noted that small savers, wage earners, industrialists and tradespeople had also turned to these funds in an effort to protect their savings. Özdal underlined that persistently high inflation over many years had driven broad sections of society toward alternative investment instruments, adding that mass participation in these funds had paved the way for large-scale financial fraud.




Özdal said: "The beneficiaries of the massive profiteering through high returns on money market funds were the elites of political and economic power. This is now plainly evident. However, in our country, which has been struggling with high inflation for nearly eight years, wage earners in particular turned to these funds to protect their modest savings from the devastating effects of inflation. It also appears that small and medium-sized industrialists and traders, as well as a very large number of small business owners, who have been unable to access credit and affordable financing amid high inflation and high interest rates, invested money in these funds even to address their short-term financing needs. These massive financial fraud schemes were made possible precisely by this widespread participation. In a sense, the ruling elites openly robbed a very large section of society. Yes, there is absolutely nothing wrong with calling it what it was: robbery."




'Those running the regime had no choice but to intervene'




Özdal said that the political leadership had been forced to intervene after the crisis erupted, warning that its consequences would not be confined to financial markets but could also affect production, trade and employment. Özdal pointed to estimates suggesting that the losses exceeded $100 billion, arguing that the crisis would have social and political consequences as well as economic ones.




Özdal continued: "Once the system collapsed, those running the regime in Turkey had no choice but to intervene. You cannot pretend there is no fire when there is one, and this is an enormous fire. Moreover, the scale of the damage, which is now almost universally estimated to exceed $100 billion, shows that the problem will not remain confined to financial markets but will spread to what is called the 'real economy,' affecting production and trade. Bankruptcies, liquidations, layoffs... And, of course, the personal tragedies that will accompany all of this... Beyond the economic cost of this massive fraud, there will also be a social and, consequently, political cost."




'

International financial capital is watching Turkey's response'




Özdal said that President Erdoğan's latest statements were aimed at minimizing the political cost of the crisis. He noted that the involvement of figures associated with the AKP leadership in the investigations had placed the government in a difficult position. Özdal also emphasized that international financial circles were closely monitoring developments in Turkey.




He said: "Erdoğan's latest statements are also aimed at minimizing this cost as much as possible and containing it within a limited sphere. It emerged that one of his own deputy party chairs was directly involved, and that person was made to request to be relieved of their duties. It is clear that numerous people directly connected to the party, including Ertan Aydın, who designed the campaign strategy for Erdoğan's most recent election victory, have been unable to distance themselves from the affair. Indeed, this does not appear to be an internal matter that can simply be covered up. International financial capital is watching what Turkey does. Protecting Fatma and Ertan could prove far more 'costly.' That is why they seem to be trying to establish something resembling a narrative of 'cleansing ourselves.' Erdoğan's remarks show that there is considerable unease over the issue not only among the party's voters but also within its organizational structures."




'A crisis beyond the opposition's capacity to address'




Özdal argued that the fund crisis could not be explained solely through Turkey's domestic politics and that developments needed to be considered within the broader context of international political and economic relations. He said that although the opposition's response to the crisis was important, the developments had an international dimension extending beyond the opposition's ability to intervene.




Özdal said: "I do not want to be misunderstood, but there is an aspect of this crisis that is 'beyond the opposition's capacity to address.' What I mean is that, regardless of what the opposition does, and mistakes have certainly been made, this is not a situation that can be overcome by blaming the Republican People's Party (CHP), foreign powers or others. Clearly, these developments have an international context and cannot be considered separately from the war involving Iran, Israel's actions and policies in the region that have reached the level of genocide, or the tensions in the Black Sea and Eastern Mediterranean. Even the uncompromising position of the 'brotherly country' during the recent Azerbaijan crisis, and its categorical rejection of the relationship of tutelage that Turkey imagines it exercises over Azerbaijan, must be assessed within this context."




'The crisis will negatively affect everyone's daily lives'




Özdal said that the effects of the fund crisis would become more visible in the coming period, warning that problems originating in financial markets could have negative consequences for production, trade and everyday life. He also argued that the crisis could affect electoral policies and force the government to seek new financial resources.




Özdal concluded: "This crisis will undoubtedly have negative consequences, first in financial markets, then in production and trade, and ultimately in everyone's daily life. In a sense, one could say that 'we are only just getting started.' Turkey faces an election that, it appears, will take place in 15 or 16 months. First and foremost, significant damage may have been done to the financial foundations necessary to sustain this regime. Moreover, the resources available for measures commonly referred to as an 'election economy' also appear to be shrinking. New sources of financing will be needed to compensate for these losses, and Gulf and Saudi capital must be seen as one possible option. We maysee agreements resembling the Mecca Alliance, along with certain concessions and reluctant compromises in regional politics."

title: Mehtap Sakinci: Femicide is political
content:
Lawyer Mehtap Sakinci, one of the founders of the 10 October Peace Association, spoke to ANF about peace, justice and the women's struggle on the 11th anniversary of the 10 October Ankara Train Station Massacre.




Sakinci said that femicide was political and criticized Turkey's withdrawal from the Istanbul Convention and the shortcomings in the implementation of Law No. 6284. She stressed that women played an important role in building peace and called on women to stand together and strengthen their struggle ahead of 25 November, the International Day for the Elimination of Violence against Women.







 







'

Women are an important part of the struggle for peace'




Mehtap Sakinci lost her husband, lawyer Uygar Coşgun, in the Ankara Train Station Massacre carried out by the Islamic State of Iraq and Syria (ISIS) on 10 October 2015. She continues to honor the memory of those who lost their lives at the peace rally 11 years ago and to express their longing for peace on every platform.




Sakinci expressed her enthusiasm about attending the conference, where women's role in building peace was being discussed and said: "I was genuinely excited to take part in this event, where women stand together and the importance of women's role in building peace is truly emphasized."




Sakinci said that women coming together reminded them of their collective strength in social struggles. She continued: "By reminding ourselves that being a woman and the strength women demonstrate in this country, in this world and under the circumstances we live in should never be underestimated, we are showing one another just how important a role women play in the struggles for peace, democracy and labor rights in this country."




'Courtrooms stand strong through the power of women'




Mehtap Sakinci said that she had served as president of the 10 October Peace Association for nearly 10 years before handing over the position to her colleagues a year ago. She spoke about the association's establishment and the struggle for justice carried out by women who lost loved ones in the massacre.




Sakinci said that women's voices and solidarity had played a decisive role in the legal struggle following the massacre and added: "I handed over responsibility for the process to my colleagues a year ago. But as a woman, as someone who lost her husband and as a woman who has paid a price in this country, I remain a living witness to just how difficult it is for a woman to carry this struggle forward.




When we established the association as families of those who lost their lives, I embarked on this journey as a woman who had lost her husband, alongside fathers who had lost their children. Throughout this process, I have seen how deeply women's voices, strength, cries and tears have resonated, particularly those of mothers who lost their children.




Today, as the proceedings concerning the 10 October massacre continue, it is once again the strength of women that sustains the courtrooms. They echo with the voices of my fellow women lawyers."




'I have no doubt that peace will come through women'




Mehtap Sakinci emphasized the responsibilities women assumed in building peace and the power of solidarity, stressing that women coming together would strengthen the struggle for peace.




Sakinci said: "I believe it is important to emphasize this: If peace is to come to this country, and if people are to take responsibility for building that peace, I have absolutely no doubt that women will be the ones to make it happen.




Perhaps we also need to remind ourselves of something on platforms like this: People heal one another's pain, and women are a homeland for one another. Women who have suffered, who have paid a price and who have truly stood at the forefront of the struggle for rights in this country need other women beside them. I believe that only when women come together can we bring peace with a louder and stronger voice."




'Turkey withdrew from the Istanbul Convention, and Law No. 6284 remains insufficient'




As 25 November approaches, Mehtap Sakinci recalled Turkey's withdrawal from the Istanbul Convention and criticized the inadequacy of legal provisions and practices intended to protect women from violence.




Sakinci emphasized that femicide was political, saying: "Every day, we are shaken by another femicide, and we know that these killings are ultimately driven by political motives. One of the most significant failures concerning existing legal protections in this country was the rejection of the Istanbul Convention."




Sakinci said that Law No. 6284 on the Protection of the Family and Prevention of Violence against Women was insufficient to protect women, arguing that a patriarchal mentality influenced both the drafting and implementation of legislation.




Sakinci continued: "Law No. 6284 remains insufficient because its scope is too narrowly defined around domestic violence. As a result, men have reached a point where their patriarchal violence is further reinforced.




Unfortunately, we point out today that many laws are inadequate. But particularly when it comes to legislation intended to protect women from violence, we know that no meaningful results can be achieved when those implementing the laws operate within a patriarchal mentality and the legislation itself is formulated according to patriarchal logic.




I believe this issue can only be properly discussed in a forum where the entire approach is reconsidered and placed on a completely different foundation."




Sakinci reiterated that femicide was political and said that she did not believe violence against women could be reduced without a change in the current government.




She said, "The most fundamental guarantee the Constitution should provide us is the protection of our right to life. Unfortunately, this is a country where lives are lost far too easily."




'The system waits for women to become victims'




Mehtap Sakinci said that all state institutions had a responsibility to prevent violence against women, pointing to serious problems in the implementation of existing legislation.




Sakinci stated that women's complaints were not taken seriously enough and said: "The main reason women are not taken sufficiently seriously in many cases where their statements should be taken as the basis is the persistence of certain deeply ingrained, stereotypical attitudes in this country.




We see that no progress has been made in this area, particularly because of government policies aimed at further strengthening men's power.




In practice, a woman files a complaint against a man, but prosecutors and law enforcement authorities do not take it seriously. The system repeatedly seems to wait until the woman becomes a victim. Each time, she may survive by the narrowest of margins or barely manage to escape becoming a victim of that violence."




'Women must stand together on 25 November'




Mehtap Sakinci said that mechanisms such as the Women's Support Application (KADES) were important but insufficient on their own, emphasizing the need to raise social awareness and act collectively in the struggle against violence against women.




Sakinci stressed that women's right to life was constantly under threat. She said, "Today, people consider themselves fortunate if they manage to survive another day. For women, this reality is far more severe. We must therefore see ourselves as part of a collective struggle."




Sakinci emphasized that women needed to stand together in public spaces ahead of 25 November, renewing her call for action and organization: "At this point, we must organize larger and more effective events, demonstrations and actions that will make our voices heard against violence against women.




I want to emphasize that women truly need to stand together this 25 November, raise their voices more strongly and become more politically active. Because femicide is political. Femicide is a political issue."




'We should not have to lose more women'




Lawyer Mehtap Sakinci once again emphasized the importance of solidarity and collective struggle against violence experienced by women, calling on all women to act together.




Sakinci concluded: "Women have no one but one another, and I believe we must do more than simply show empathy. We should not have to lose more women to become aware of what is happening. I call on all women to stand together, close ranks and become more politically active."

title: 12th edition of Serçavan Kurdish Film Days opens in Vienna
content:
The Serçavan Kurdish Film Days, which have been held at different intervals in Vienna since 1999, opened for the 12th time this year.




The festival, taking place at Votivkino, is organised in cooperation with the Assembly of the Kurdish Community in Austria (FEYKOM), the Union of Kurdish Students (YXK), and partner organisations.




The five-day festival, running from 4 to 8 November, features a programme of feature films, documentaries and short films. Addressing Kurdish history, culture, identity, experiences of migration and contemporary social realities, the films present audiences with a variety of perspectives and narratives.







 







The festival opened with the documentary 

To My Sisters

, which tells the stories of Kurdish women fighters and their struggle for freedom. Following the screening, the director took part in an online question-and-answer session and responded to questions from the audience.




Kurds must tell their own stories




Delivering the opening speech, Saya Ahmad, Head of the Alsergrund District, said the festival was important in making the history, culture and lives of the Kurdish community more visible.




Stressing that Serçavan was about more than simply screening films, Saya Ahmad said the festival created a shared space where people could come together, engage in discussions and encounter different perspectives. Ahmad highlighted the importance of representing Kurdish identity, language and culture in the public sphere.




Gule C., from the festival's organising committee, emphasised that Kurdish cinema was directly connected to stories, identities, languages and collective social memory.




Noting that Kurdish lives are often told through the voices of others, Gule C. stressed the importance of the right of Kurds to tell their own stories. She said Kurdish cinema brings a range of experiences to the screen from its own perspective, including love, loss, happiness, pain, resistance, migration and everyday life.




Kurdish women continue their struggle




Speaking at the festival's opening, Green Party MP and lawyer Berivan Aslan said Kurdish filmmakers face repression both in Kurdistan and in Europe.




Drawing attention to the obstacles preventing Kurdish films from being screened in Turkey, Berivan Aslan spoke about the resistance of Kurdish women who fought against ISIS, referring to the opening documentary, 

To My Sisters

.




Emphasising that Kurdish women struggle not only during particular periods but throughout every aspect of their lives, Berivan Aslan highlighted the ongoing nature of women's fight for freedom.




Berivan Aslan also mentioned Selahattin Demirtaş and Figen Yüksekdağ, who remain imprisoned in Turkey, criticising their continued detention despite European Court of Human Rights (ECHR) rulings calling for their release. She called on Europe to assume greater responsibility for securing the freedom of political prisoners.




Following the opening speeches, musician Özlem Bulut performed a selection of kilam and songs for the audience. A fundraising campaign is also being held as part of the festival to support new projects in Kurdish cinema.




On the festival's second day, Azad Altay's documentary 

The Memory of Sur

 (Bîra Sûrê) will examine the destruction of Amed's historic Sur district. Hemo, which explores everyday life and the process of social construction in Rojava, and Kazım Öz's political satire 

Oy'una Geldik

 will also be screened.




On Friday, the films 

Xezîne

, 

Rojava Rûmeta Meye

, 

Habā,

 which address violence against women, and 

Arzela from Amed

, which focuses on the struggle for democracy, will be screened. The day's final screening will be 

Heval Birako,

 which tells the story of two Yazidi siblings escaping captivity under ISIS.




Saturday's programme will feature the short film 

Dengê Kilîtan – Voices and Locks

, 

The Manuscript

, 

Yerli Yurtsu

z (Rootless Resident), which explores Armenian identity and the search for one's roots, and 

Dimilî: Ewro Tirkî Yasax A

, which focuses on preserving the Dimilî language. Following the screenings, there will be a discussion with filmmaker, video journalist and photographer Özgür Rayzan.




At the festival's closing, 

Mugarik Gabe – No Borders

, directed by Boris Guevara, will explore the cultural and musical connections between the Basque Country and Kurdistan. The film features internationally known actress Itziar Ituño and Kurdish singer Mizgin Tahir among others.




The Serçavan Kurdish Film Days will conclude with 

The Legend of the

 

Ugly King

 (Çirkin Kral Efsanesi), a documentary by Hüseyin Tabak about the life, cinema and legacy of Yılmaz Güney.




The festival, which brings together a diverse selection of Kurdish cinema over five days, attracted considerable interest at its opening, with all tickets for the opening screening reported to have sold out.

title: 'Voce Arcaica' Festival in memory of Nagihan Akarsel to take place in Rome on 7 November
content:
The 'Voce Arcaica' (Ancient Voice) Art and Culture Festival, organised annually in Italy by the Jineolojî Academy, is held in memory of Nagihan Akarsel, a member of the Jineolojî Research Centre, writer and journalist who was assassinated in an armed attack outside her home in Sulaymaniyah (Silêmanî) on 4 October 2022.




The festival will take place on 7 November at the Teatro Biblioteca Quarticciolo in Rome, and aims to bring women together through art, culture and collective creation.




In an 

article

, the Jineolojî Academy wrote that the festival was organised to continue the work of Nagihan Akarsel, who made significant contributions to Jineolojî, women's journalism and research on women, and to keep her ideas alive through art.




The article emphasised that art is not merely a form of expression, but also a means of passing on women's collective memory, resistance and experiences of struggle.




Four stops on the festival's journey




As part of this year's third edition, events have been held throughout the year in Rome, Reggio Calabria, Turin, Bologna and the Dutch town of Haelen. At these gatherings, the book 

Voce Arcaica

 (Ancient Voice), a collection of 16 articles by Nagihan Akarsel, was introduced. Participants also took part in a collective embroidery project featuring a portrait of Nagihan Akarsel.
