title: Karasu: The Republic must be democratised according to today's understanding of democracy
content:
Mustafa Karasu, a member of the KCK Executive Council, spoke about current affairs during a special programme broadcast on Medya Haber.




The first part of this interview can be read 

here

.




The AKP government is entering into various alliances, particularly in the region. The benefits and drawbacks of these alliances continue to be debated publicly. Can the AKP secure its own position through such alliances?




After Devlet Bahçeli made his call, what did both Bahçeli and Erdoğan repeatedly say? They said that we needed to strengthen the domestic front. They also described this process as one of strengthening the domestic front. Yes, resolving the Kurdish question means strengthening the domestic front. This is because, from the Ottoman period onward, whenever Turkey has come into conflict with the Kurds, it has lost. Whenever it has maintained positive relations with the Kurds, it has achieved stability and strengthened its position.




Indeed, one of the most important factors in the decline of the Ottoman Empire was its failure to resolve its problems with the Kurds. From the nineteenth century onward, it entered into conflict with them. Once it became hostile to the Kurds, it began to decline rapidly. Had it resolved the Kurdish question and adopted the right approach, the Ottoman Empire might not have disintegrated to the same extent. Now, if the government claims to be pursuing a policy of strengthening the domestic front and repeatedly emphasises this objective, yet then assumes that it can secure its position through alliances formed abroad, I have to say that this is a misconception. No matter what alliances you form abroad, they will not achieve much if you do not first consolidate the domestic front. They may even produce the opposite results. In fact, the anxiety that has led to the formation of so many alliances stems precisely from the failure to strengthen the domestic front. This is preparation for war. The formation of so many alliances in the Middle East, which lies at the centre of ongoing wars, amounts to preparation for such wars—or to taking sides on the various war fronts.




If the domestic front were strong, if Turkey genuinely resolved the Kurdish question and took steps towards democratisation, it would not feel the need—or fall into the misconception—that it could save itself by forming one alliance with this party and another with that one. In this respect, let me be clear: the formation of so many alliances is also taking place under the direction of certain external powers. In his statement, Tom Barrack indirectly indicated that the alliances Turkey is forming are known to us, serve our interests and form part of our policy; they are not separate from it.




Thus, this alliance policy may be an attempt to secure Turkey's position, but it also creates antagonisms. Every alliance is, at the same time, directed against someone else. Of course, a state can form alliances and may need to do so. But because Turkey has failed to consolidate its domestic front, it feels weak. Consequently, it considers entering into various alliances necessary—or, more precisely, it feels compelled to create new enmities.




We do not believe that Turkey can resolve its own problems through alliance policies. The policy of strengthening the domestic front is correct, and this is what the government says it is pursuing. Yet instead of fulfilling the requirements of that policy and strengthening the domestic front, the government prefers to create its own fronts abroad and take sides in existing conflicts. This will not benefit Turkey very much. Turkey will suffer the consequences.




Abdullah Öcalan, the leader of the peoples, has described the process he initiated as one of change and transformation. In this context, efforts to organise a movement for a democratic republic are also on the agenda in the field of political struggle. What would you like to say about these discussions?




A republic was established in Turkey. Yes, a republic is a system of government in which those in power come to office through elections. Of course, a republic does not automatically mean direct democracy. There are many republics in the world that are undemocratic, even dictatorial. Conversely, there are countries without republics, where monarchies still exist, and certain offices are not filled through elections. Sweden, Norway and the Netherlands are examples, yet these countries do have certain democratic institutions, albeit within limits, as well as a democratic outlook.




In this respect, a republic is not inherently a bad thing. Having all institutions filled through elections is a positive development. Indeed, the course of human progress will inevitably move beyond such arrangements one day. There will no longer be kings, queens or similar institutions, nor rulers who inherit their positions from their fathers, through dynasties or family lineages.




In this respect, after the Ottoman Empire, Turkey abandoned that system of government and proclaimed a republic. But it did not become democratic. And because it was not democratic, it could not resolve its problems.




Will Turkey genuinely become democratic? Or will it remain, like many countries in the Middle East, a non-democratic monarchy or authoritarian regime? What will happen to Turkey if it remains that way? Where will it go? Turkey itself needs to consider these questions.




Turkey has its own history and a history of popular struggle. There have been struggles by democratic forces and intellectuals, by working people and by the Kurdish people for freedom. All these struggles make Turkey's democratisation necessary.




Turkey can advance towards its future through democratisation. If it seeks a future, it can secure that future by becoming democratic. Its prospects can then be bright and positive.




For this reason, the Republic must be democratised—but according to today's understanding of democracy. What did democracy mean 200 years ago? It meant little more than elections, with universal and equal suffrage. That understanding has since been surpassed.




We now need a form of democratisation based on an organised society, freedom of thought and organisation, and local democracy. Otherwise, as we see in current debates, people ask what democracy will actually bring. Some still think in terms of the democratic understanding of a hundred years ago, while others speak according to their own particular conceptions of democracy.




That is not what we mean. Today's understanding of democracy—the democratic conception articulated by Leader Apo—is based on freedom of thought and organisation and embraces local democracy.




Democratising the Republic on this basis would resolve all of Turkey's problems. It would resolve not only the Kurdish question but also the Alevi question, the question of women and all the other problems facing society.




Let us make this clear and emphasise it once again: when the Kurdish people, when we, and when Leader Apo speak of democracy, we are not speaking of democracy only for the Kurds. We are speaking of democracy for all of Turkey.




A Republic alone does not guarantee democracy




Some people say that the Kurdish question will be resolved, but ask what will happen to all the other issues. That is not how it works. The Kurdish question cannot be resolved without democratisation in Turkey. And when we speak of democratisation, we mean a process that resolves the Kurdish question, the Alevi question, the question of women and the problems faced by working people. This is what we mean by a democratic republic.




Discussions about a democratic republic have been taking place, with conferences and meetings organised on the subject. These are important because they are helping ideas to mature and take root. Gradually, almost everyone in Turkey who genuinely wants democracy is coming to demand that the Republic be democratised in a meaningful way.




A republic alone does not guarantee democracy. There are certain nationalist circles that think in the rigid terms of the 1920s. They keep talking about the Republic, the Republic, while opposing democracy.




That is not what a republic should be. It is not a defence of the Republic, nor is it genuine republicanism. It is reactionary. It amounts to demanding the continuation of a system founded on hostility towards the Kurds.




Therefore, when we speak of a democratic republic, we mean a republic in which society is organised from the grassroots; freedom of thought and organisation is fully guaranteed; different identities, including Kurdish and Alevi identities, can express themselves freely; and local democracy is established.




We hope these discussions about a democratic republic will help ideas mature throughout society and influence both the state and the government. Turkey has no other path. It must either democratise the Republic or continue to experience the difficulties of the troubled Middle East, facing ever greater risks and dangers.




Attacks on the natural environment in Kurdistan continue unabated. There is some public opposition, but it tends to remain localised. Why is organised resistance to attacks on nature, particularly in Kurdistan, so weak?




Let us make one thing clear. When we speak of nature, we are talking about the very reality that makes human existence possible. Humanity evolved within nature and reached its present state through that process. The evolution of nature gave rise to human beings.




If you disrupt nature, destroy it or eliminate its essential characteristics, you create a danger for all humanity. This threatens all women, all young people, all peoples and all of humanity, regardless of whether they are rich or poor. It is a danger to everyone.




Of course, the wealthy may try to protect themselves from these conditions by promoting environmentalism in their own way, living in pleasant surroundings or using their resources to move away from polluted and damaged areas into more desirable places. That may be their approach. They, too, may talk about environmental protection and seek to live in beautiful natural surroundings. They can use their means to escape degraded environments and settle somewhere better. But the danger remains one that affects all humanity. For this reason, everyone needs to be aware and concerned. Every single person.




Let me put it this way: not everyone possesses a deep level of consciousness. Not everyone can fully understand every issue. Their historical awareness, ideological awareness or other forms of understanding may be limited. But if they are alive, they will defend themselves, as all living beings do. The ecological crisis has now become a matter of self-defence for all living beings. It has become a matter of human self-defence. It is therefore a problem for all humanity. We must make it a priority, bring it to the forefront and keep it constantly on the public agenda.




In Kurdistan, meanwhile, attacks on nature have become part of the genocide against the Kurdish people. The geography of Botan is being devastated. The geography of Dersim is being devastated. Kurdistan is being made almost uninhabitable.




Mesopotamia was described as paradise in the sacred scriptures. Yet today, in the interests of capitalism and as a consequence of the Turkish state's genocidal policies, this paradise is being turned into hell. In this respect, the Kurds must be vigilant. Every Kurd must defend their own village, their water, their streams, their mountains and their forests.




This means honouring their ancestors, who passed these lands down to them. It also means protecting their children and grandchildren, and safeguarding what will be passed on to future generations. There has been some progress in this area, but it is insufficient. Ecologists in Kurdistan must undoubtedly conduct this struggle together with ecologists in Turkey, and the movement must expand across a much broader front.




At present, the efforts are inadequate. Just as the Kurdish people have waged a struggle for freedom for a hundred years—or, more specifically, for fifty years—we need to develop an ecological struggle of comparable determination. This, too, is a form of the Kurdish people's struggle for freedom. It is a struggle for the very existence of the Kurdish people.




For this reason, ecological awareness is extremely important. Ecological organisation is equally important. There must be ecological organisations in every region, every city, every town and even every village. People must defend their natural environment. We see trees being cut down and streams being poisoned. In Amed, villages are defending their land. These are positive developments, but everyone must get involved.




If a particular village is fighting for ecological protection, that struggle must not remain confined to that village. All the surrounding villages should join the struggle alongside it. Every city in Kurdistan must be concerned and involved. It must not be only the people of Botan who take part; all the people of Kurdistan must participate in the ecological struggle. The ecological struggle is not just the struggle of Varto, Dersim or Botan. It is the struggle of Amed and of the entire Kurdish people. In this respect, ecological awareness, organisation and struggle must cease to be the concern of only those places directly under attack. They must become the struggle of the Kurdish people as a whole.




Only then can results be achieved. Otherwise, all our villages will be destroyed, our forests will disappear, and beautiful Botan and Dersim—one of the most beautiful parts of Kurdistan—will be devastated. For this reason, our people must become more conscious of these dangers and intensify their struggle.




An integration agreement has been reached between the Yazidi people in Shengal and the Iraqi state. How do you assess this achievement by the Yazidi people, who have suffered massacres?




We are particularly sensitive when it comes to the Yazidi people. Leader Apo is sensitive to their situation, and so are we, because Yazidism is one of the oldest faiths of the Kurdish people. It is a great cultural and spiritual treasure. Religious beliefs are also part of humanity's accumulated heritage and values. For this reason, preserving the existence of the Êzidî people, ensuring their survival and enabling them to live freely are extremely important. It is especially important that they be able to practise their faith freely.




With the emergence of capitalist modernity, the notion of a single nation gave rise to all kinds of uniformity, and Yazidism was increasingly marginalised. Before capitalism emerged, Yazidism actually had a significant following in the Middle East and Kurdistan. But the homogenising nation-state mentality created by capitalist modernity has subjected all these identities to forms of genocide. This has targeted not only ethnic identities but religious identities as well.




We have always been particularly sensitive to this issue. When ISIS attacked, our movement was among the first to come to the Yazidi people's defence. It was the guerrillas who intervened and saved them from genocide. The ISIS attack was the 74th ferman—the term used for a decree of persecution or massacre against the Yazidis. The guerrillas rescued them from that ferman.




Our movement's role in saving the Yazidis from persecution and genocide was extremely important and decisive. Everyone knows this. Later, our military forces withdrew from the area. Nevertheless, our ideological influence remained. Leader Apo had issued calls in support of the Yazidi people. He stood by them, and because of his support, the Yazidis also listened to his ideas and political approach. In this way, they organised themselves and developed their own self-defence structures.




They have now reached an agreement and are pursuing integration. This has resulted in significant military integration. The YBŞ will remain in its own region as a local component of the Iraqi army. Its members are all Yazidi young people. Had the Yazidis possessed their own self-organised structures and military organisation when ISIS attacked, ISIS would not have been able to enter Shengal. The Yazidis would have resisted, even if it had cost them their lives. But the Iraqi army and the KDP Peshmerga forces withdrew when the attack came. For this reason, the continued presence of a local military force is important.




The Yazidis also have some degree of administrative and political organisation. However, this must be developed into more established legal and political institutions. We hope that progress will also be made in this area. Military integration alone—the integration of the YBŞ into the army—is not enough. The Yazidis also have a distinct religious identity. They need their own administrative and political structures, as well as local democracy. We believe that the organised strength of theYazidi people will enable them to achieve this.




As the youth movement that began in France spreads across Europe, it is also beginning to draw in all sections of society. I would like to ask about the role of left-wing, socialist and democratic forces in ensuring the continuity and effectiveness of these movements. If we turn the critical lens on ourselves as well, what shortcomings have left-wing and socialist movements displayed in these developing mobilisations?




We must acknowledge that capitalist modernity is in crisis. We say that capitalism's crisis is deepening and that the turmoil is intensifying. We argue that capitalism has become an unliveable system and that its end is approaching. This is our assessment as socialists. That assessment is correct. Capitalist modernity has indeed become a system fundamentally at odds with human life, a system that has lost its connection with the way humanity should live.




Yet while we say that the capitalist system is collapsing, that capitalist modernity is profoundly destructive and that it harms all humanity, we must also acknowledge that we, as socialist forces, are ideologically, politically and organisationally unprepared to respond adequately. Our preparations are weak and insufficient. This is clear, and it is a serious problem. Socialism has certain ideological and political shortcomings. As a result, we are unable to provide an adequate response. These shortcomings must be overcome.




Leader Apo has advanced important theses on this question. He has put forward an ideological and theoretical perspective that moves beyond the conventional socialist understanding rooted in a statist mentality. Rather than reproducing that traditional conception of socialism, he proposes a system in which society governs itself democratically without the state, enabling it to overcome capitalism.




It is genuinely only through such an approach that capitalism can be transcended. The crisis of capitalism is profound. Yes, society will overthrow it, but it seems this will no longer happen through extremely violent wars. Once society becomes organised, what use will capitalism be, given that it has already become unnecessary? Organised social forces will overcome capitalism and build democratic socialism in its place. For this reason, democratic socialist forces need to recognise the shortcomings in their ideological and theoretical positions. They must approach the issue critically and engage in self-criticism.




Why are we unable to meet society's needs adequately? Why can we not organise society fully? Why are we failing to respond sufficiently to the needs of young people, women and working people?




We need to ask ourselves these questions. At the same time, we must recognise that these shortcomings have emerged within, and are partly a consequence of, the crisis generated by capitalist modernity. France, meanwhile, has historically been one of the places where revolutions and uprisings have repeatedly begun and erupted, particularly since capitalism entered the historical stage. Consider the French Revolution of 1789. There were also democratic revolutions, often described as bourgeois-democratic revolutions, but the people left their mark on all of them. Popular influence was decisive. The Paris Commune came later, and there were earlier episodes as well. In this respect, French society has historically been inclined towards such uprisings and expressions of resistance.




There is also the crisis of capitalism, the situation of migrants and the hostile attitudes directed towards them. There is the rise of right-wing governments, which societies refuse to accept. These developments, too, provoke resistance. In this context, the uprising of young people in France became an important signal flare, showing what might be possible. Young people in Serbia, for instance, have in a sense made their mark on the country's political leadership. We cannot currently describe Serbia as a democratic socialist country, but the reflection of young people's will in political life is significant. It represents the expression of a democratic will. Similar developments have occurred in Portugal. In fact, this is what will increasingly unfold throughout capitalist countries. They are unable to find solutions.




There are two competing approaches to resolving the crisis. Right-wing governments say that they will come to power, wield the sword and resolve the crisis of capitalist modernity. But whose solution is that? It is not a solution for the people. It is a solution for monopolies and exploiting classes. Social democrats and liberals are also unable to resolve the crisis. They are not genuinely and fully democratic. On the one hand, they appeal to the people; on the other, they protect the interests of the ruling classes. For this reason, social-democratic and liberal policies cannot resolve the crisis of capitalism.




We are therefore passing through a historical period in which genuinely democratic socialist organisations, movements, ideologies and political programmes can offer solutions. If democratic socialists develop the right programme, critically examine the past and formulate a new line of struggle—both ideological and political—they can achieve significant advances under these crisis conditions. In many places, they can establish democratic socialist forms of popular self-government and begin building a new social order. We believe this is possible.

title: Hope lies with young people
content:
Our generation grew up under the influence of the 1968 Youth Revolution. More precisely, we were forged in the fire of that historic revolution. The Revolutionary Youth Movement of 1968 was based primarily on university students. It was the most striking example of conscious, organised youth taking the lead in society as a whole. Through this revolutionary movement, university students proved themselves and passed the test of history.




The 1968 Youth Revolution was the most influential revolutionary wave since the 1917 Soviet Revolution, which emerged during the First World War. It aimed not only to overthrow the system of capitalist modernity, whose crisis was deepening, but also to transcend actually existing socialism, which had moved away from the principles of equality based on freedom and diversity. For various reasons, it undoubtedly failed to overthrow the system of capitalist modernity. However, it played a significant role in the collapse of actually existing socialism, which had proved incapable of correcting or renewing itself. Had actually existing socialism understood the revolution developed by intellectual university youth, and demonstrated the capacity to transform and renew itself on the basis of that revolution's characteristics, perhaps it would not have met the tragic end it did, nor disintegrated in that way.




The 1968 Youth Revolution first developed on the European continent, and its influence gradually spread. From that point onward, Turkish youth, inspired by the forms of organisation and struggle developed by their European peers, reached the peak of their revolutionary activity in 1970–71. The Revolutionary Youth Movement, which also knew how to draw on the Palestinian Resistance in practice, succeeded in leading the democratic revolution that Turkey experienced during the 1970s. New socialist and revolutionary formations in Turkey and Kurdistan also emerged from the fire of this movement. Undoubtedly, the most influential representative of this new wave was the PKK.




Today, under conditions in which the system of capitalist modernity has brought nature and society to the brink of destruction—going beyond even the peak of crisis and chaos—the breakthrough is once again coming from Europe, and once again from the youth. It is the youth who carry hope. This time, however, the spark is being ignited not by university students but by secondary-school students. Scientific and technological advances undoubtedly play an important role in this. It is clear that secondary-school students are using these advances more effectively.




As has so often been the case, the secondary-school youth movement that began in France has, this time too, spread across almost all of Europe in a very short period. It also appears to have succeeded in mobilising different sections of society. In a manner reminiscent of the “sans-culottes” of an earlier era—the so-called “ragged-trousered” masses—the movement of secondary-school students, who were dismissed as “just a few kids”, has already managed to shake the system of capitalist modernity very seriously, and right at its very centre. It is abundantly clear that these “few kids” are achieving extraordinary things and inspiring everyone's admiration. Indeed, the French government has introduced a partial curfew, while it appears that new measures are also being discussed at the European level.




The popular movement led by young people, which continued throughout October and has progressively developed and spread, is undoubtedly extremely intriguing. It demands close attention and a sound assessment. Although its underlying causes are largely understood, it remains difficult to predict how events will unfold, how the movement will progress, and where it will ultimately lead. It is also becoming clear that the movement cannot be easily dismissed or suppressed through simplistic approaches.




One particularly interesting and striking question is why secondary-school students, rather than university students or young people as a whole, are driving this movement. As noted above, secondary-school students appear to be using science and technology more effectively and organising themselves more rapidly. While this is one contributing factor, it cannot, of course, be regarded as the only one. Another possible factor is that a deliberate system of special warfare has been applied to university youth, with the result that this section of the younger generation has, to a considerable extent, been integrated into the system. Just as special warfare policies were implemented against the working class after the 1917 Soviet Revolution, it seems that a similar plan may have been pursued against university students following the 1968 Youth Revolution. If this is the case, university youth can be said to be facing a serious process of criticism and self-criticism.




Clearly, in its current form, this wave of mobilisation appears to be confined to Europe. But that does not mean it cannot spread rapidly. Nor can we claim that precisely the same events of 1968–70 will be repeated. Nevertheless, it is equally impossible to say that the youth-led popular movement in Europe will not spread to Turkey, or that Turkey will remain unaffected. Of course, it will spread to Turkey in one form or another and exert the same influence there. Although nothing definitive can be said about when or how this will happen, it can confidently be stated that such a spread is inevitable. Neither intensified special warfare practices nor the schemes and deceptions developed by the AKP government during what it considers its period of political maturity can prevent this kind of development.




In fact, had the government and the state fulfilled the requirements of the Peace and Democratic Society Process developed by Kurdish people's leader Abdullah Öcalan—that is, had a shift in mentality and politics taken place that would democratise Turkey and resolve the Kurdish question—these developments could have unfolded in a controlled manner, without destructive consequences. The Kurdish side had already defined the process in these terms, describing the Peace and Democratic Society Process as one of change, transformation and restructuring. In order to bring about this change from its own side, both Leader Abdullah Öcalan and the Freedom Movement had undertaken intensive efforts and taken the necessary steps.




A process of change, transformation and restructuring cannot be one-sided; it must involve both sides. Just as the Kurdish side is undergoing the changes in mentality and politics required by the process, the state and the government must also undergo a serious transformation in their outlook and political approach. In other words, they must abandon the mentality and policies that deny the existence of the Kurdish people and subject them to genocide, and instead adopt an approach to democratisation grounded in Kurdish freedom and Turkish-Kurdish fraternity. No such commitment or effort towards change, transformation and restructuring is evident on the Turkish side. There is no talk of legal or political changes to resolve the Kurdish question and democratise Turkey. Indeed, regardless of the purpose behind them, even the statements made by Devlet Bahçeli, leader of the Nationalist Movement Party (MHP), at his parliamentary group meeting, along with the promises he made on that basis, are not being implemented. The necessary work to democratise the Republic is not being carried out.




It is abundantly clear that the AKP is obstructing change. For approximately 25 years, it has governed Turkey under the coup-era constitution imposed after 12 September 1980, and at times it has failed even to implement that constitution. Its entire political strategy is directed towards ensuring Tayyip Erdoğan's re-election within the existing legal system and extending his time in power. It does not hesitate to turn everything into an instrument for achieving this goal. It thinks only of maintaining its own rule, while failing to recognise—or deliberately ignoring—the dangers facing Turkey.




Meanwhile, the dangers surrounding Turkey are growing, and the circle of encirclement is tightening. Some striking and dangerous statements have been made in this regard. Following reactions from the Middle East and Europe, the United States has also strongly criticised Turkey's attempt to develop a maritime territorial-waters policy with Libya, describing the initiative as a provocation. It has also been revealed by an Iranian official who participated in talks during the Mecca Alliance's visit to Iran that a Saudi Arabian minister said, “After Iran, Turkey and Saudi Arabia are next on Israel's list of targets for attack.” Clearly, the AKP's submissive and collaborationist policies are not enough to save Turkey either. It is evident that Turkey's salvation lies in the success of the Peace and Democratic Society Process, which would democratise and strengthen the domestic front. To this end, the Leadership and the Movement, which emerged from the 1968 Youth Revolution and continue to place their hopes in the youth today, must no longer be obstructed. One thing is clear: what does not change will be overcome; whoever stands in the way will be consigned to the dustbin of history.




Source: Yeni Özgür Politika

title: At least 25 people executed in Iran within six days
content:
The “No to Executions on Tuesdays” campaign, which is being organised by political prisoners in 66 prisons across Iran and is now in its 145th week, announced that at least 25 people had been executed across Iran and Rojhilatê Kurdistan (Eastern Kurdistan) over the past six days.




It was reported that Şehab Zuhedi, Omran Amani, Emin Pirdal, Arman Merefeti, Şayan Shekibayi and Metin Farinyan, along with numerous other political prisoners whose names have not yet been made public, have been sentenced to death.




The campaign's statement said: “Neither threats nor death sentences will be able to silence the voices raised against inhumane punishments. We demand the immediate abolition of all death sentences and all forms of killing in Iran.”




Two young protesters executed in Isfahan




Iranian judiciary-affiliated Mizan News Agency has announced the execution of two detained individuals, Amir Hossein Maleki and Amir Hossein.







The report stated that the death sentences handed down to Amir Hossein Maleki and Amir Hossein had been upheld by Iran’s Supreme Court.

title: Ağbayır: Those invoking Dar al-Salam must take responsibility for peace
content:
Muslim feminist Zeynep Duygu Ağbayır, one of the signatories of the "Women Side by Side, Discussing the Future" conference held in Ankara, spoke to ANF about the importance of the conference, what peace means for women and the role of the women's struggle.




Zeynep Duygu Ağbayır, who spoke to ANF on the second day of the conference, expressed her happiness at being among its signatories. She said that the first day had exceeded expectations and that they had placed greater emphasis on forums to enable participants to take a more active role in the discussions.







 







'We have a common aspiration'




Zeynep Duygu Ağbayır said, "We actually have a common aspiration here," and added: "This conference emerged from the question of how we, as women who have been discussing the ongoing process, growing inequality in Turkey, poverty, economic violence and all the problems that come with them separately, can speak with one another despite our different political views, positions and disagreements."




Ağbayır said that the discussions in the forums had demonstrated how useful this approach was, noting that they had come together with many women throughout the day, from Söke in Aydın to Ankara, and from Bodrum to Diyarbakır (Amed).




Ağbayır said that the conference had provided an opportunity to hear about issues they had not known about or previously considered. 




Ağbayır said: "Women are engaged in a political struggle everywhere, from inside their homes to the streets. Sometimes they find themselves confronting the challenges of simply being women, sometimes women's poverty, and sometimes the very reality of child poverty.




That is why we planned today's session around a panel followed by forums, creating a space where we can speak and listen together. What will emerge from this? How can we move forward? We envision a process in which the women here have a say and are the ones speaking today. I hope it will turn out very well."




'We think peace is an issue only certain groups can discuss'




Zeynep Duygu Ağbayır challenged the perception that peace was an issue only certain groups could discuss, emphasizing that peace had not been achieved within society itself. She drew attention to the following problems: "We tend to think that peace is something only a particular group can talk about. But peace does not exist within this society either. We are talking about a society that lacks internal peace. We are talking about a system in which a child can go to school in the morning carrying a pump-action shotgun. We are talking about a world where addiction is increasing and children are left in desperate conditions on the streets because of it. At the same time, we are discussing violence against women. The very existence of male violence often places us under this oppression. The system does not distinguish between Muslim women, secular women or any other women when it does this.




The system does this because it sees you as vulnerable simply because you are a woman. And we really are among the most vulnerable groups. That is another aspect of the issue. Although we are not on the side of the oppressors but among the oppressed, we are women who continue to struggle."




Ağbayır continued: "As a Muslim woman, I believe we live in a society where those who constantly take pride in Islam as a language of peace and repeatedly invoke Dar al-Salam, meaning the abode of peace, should perhaps question why peace does not exist in this society and take responsibility."




She added: "I am still at a point where I cannot call this a peace process. That is something I also want to discuss here. I am among those who believe that peace must be achieved, that we must discuss what kind of peace we want, and that all women must be able to speak freely at that table."




'We will not allow peace to be framed as a story centered on men'




Ağbayır said, "We will not allow peace to be framed as a story centered on men," and emphasized that the issue was not merely about preventing loss of life. She stressed that Muslim women must assume social responsibility in accordance with their faith and help build a peaceful future based on equal citizenship for everyone.




Ağbayır said that faith itself demanded such responsibility: "Faith itself commands this. I say that nothing inhumane can be part of Islam. So where do we stand? What kind of peace do we want? We are the ones who will discuss this. Peace cannot exist where one side is victimized, ignored or subjected to inequality. Democracy cannot exist there, nor can justice be achieved. Peace must also be a process in which we question our own position and what it represents."




'There is no need to debate ECtHR rulings'




Zeynep Duygu Ağbayır criticized the failure to implement the European Court of Human Rights (ECtHR) ruling concerning the "right to hope" of Kurdish People's Leader Abdullah Öcalan. 




Ağbayır said: "Today, Bahçeli uses the term 'founding leader.' If I had used it, I would probably have been imprisoned long ago. We are therefore talking about Öcalan, who has been imprisoned for many years and is regarded as the leader of a people, of a large community. I approach this from the following perspective: Suppose that, as a sociologist, you do not recognize Öcalan as a leader. But when we discuss legal rights and equality, should he be released in light of the ECtHR rulings? We do not need to turn this into a debate. Can he be released from a legal standpoint? Yes, he can.




I say this to those who have reservations: We must address the independence of the judiciary. We see how the right to hope, a concept that has emerged through the experiences of an entire society, relates to everyone's freedom. Therefore, from a position of defending the right to hope, I believe his freedom must be secured on the basis of judicial independence, setting aside everyone's political views and positions."




Zeynep Duygu Ağbayır also criticized the failure to implement the Istanbul Convention and the "My Family Is Safe" operations, saying that she was not seeking justice from those responsible for these practices but was demanding an independent judiciary. 




Ağbayır said: "In a country where even the Istanbul Convention is not effectively implemented, I certainly have no legal demands to make of those who saw the convention as a threat and abolished it, or those who break up other people's families through the 'My Family Is Safe' operations. My demand is directed at the law itself. We live under a system in which the principle of equality requires an independent judiciary. The law does not, and should not, allow impunity."




'We struggle by breaking through these barriers'




Ağbayır said that women would continue to resist attempts to confine them to their homes through religion or other ideological instruments. She continued: "We struggle by breaking through these barriers. That is why we want a legal system that also puts an end to violence. Perhaps some people think: There is already lawlessness and impunity, so what are we even talking about? But we must not stop speaking out. Until something changes, until we make that change happen, we must not abandon our responsibility to raise our voices and do whatever we can, through whatever forms of struggle are available to us.




The system is already trying to render us passive. Look at all those in power today. For example, Muslim women and religious women should be the first to reject the image of a woman confined to her home in the name of religion. Neither a state, nor a religion, nor an ideology can determine the standards by which a woman is considered acceptable."




Ağbayır emphasized that women should define themselves according to their own moral principles and values. She concluded: "That is why we will continue our struggle from a position of responsibility, criticizing the government's policies of impunity and refusing to contribute to the invisibility of violence."

title: The anatomy of special warfare and paths to youth liberation in the Middle East
content:
Special warfare is not an overt military operation carried out with tanks and artillery. It is a system of psychological and social destruction that directly targets society's consciousness, culture and moral values. Within this system, the most strategic targets of dominant and colonial powers are young people and young women. This is because youth is the dynamic driving force of social transformation, while young women are the founding subjects of a free society. The state mentality and dominant powers seek first and foremost to paralyze this revolutionary and pioneering force in order to permanently establish their hegemony over the will of peoples.




As Abdullah Öcalan, whose ideas have become central to the political and philosophical discussions of the Kurdish people, the Middle East and peoples around the world, has strongly emphasized, unless a radical consciousness of "self-defense" is developed against this systematic process of social degradation, society will be completely severed from its historical and moral foundations.




The following sections examine, point by point, the reality into which young people have been pushed, the social destruction caused by the instruments of degradation described as the "three horsemen of the apocalypse," and the paths to liberation, with the aim of providing every young person with a guide to action.




The situation of young people and young women: What has the system reduced them to?




Warmongering and extremist forces originating from capitalist colonial states, which have now become direct instruments of special warfare, have subjected young people to a system of comprehensive control through systematic policies that are "flexible and soft" on one side and "brutal and militaristic" on the other.




Lack of ideology and spiritual emptiness: 

Young people are being subtly distanced from ambitious aspirations, the pursuit of freedom and the consciousness of assuming social responsibility. Life is reduced to the superficial mentality of "live for today and consume," with the aim of preventing young people from reflecting on the future of their countries.




Hopelessness and pessimism:

 Systematic perception management is employed to undermine young people's belief in their own transformative power. A sense of helplessness, expressed through the idea that "We cannot change anything; the system is too powerful," is instilled in young minds, forcing society's leading force towards submission, passivity and escape through migration abroad.




Loss of identity and alienation:

 Through policies of cultural destruction, young people are pushed into a cycle of shame concerning their own languages, historical roots and social values. A generation isolated from its own culture and alienated from its identity becomes the most loyal servant of the deception of capitalist modernity.




The systematic targeting of young women: 

Young women are systematically portrayed by the system as "commodities" or objects of consumption. Through social media illusions and the fashion industry, their minds are diverted from genuine freedom, particularly intellectual and political freedom. Their potential is confined within a cage of "physical appearance and makeup," depriving them of their pioneering roles.




The three horsemen of the apocalypse (instruments of social destruction)




To achieve these objectives, the dominant system deploys three of its most poisonous instruments, directly undermining the moral foundations of society.




Drugs (all physical and psychological stimulants)




Objective:

 To deliberately and systematically facilitate the spread of drug networks in neighborhoods, schools and spaces where young people live.




Consequence:

 The mind of a young person trapped by drugs becomes paralyzed, their will is broken, and they lose the ability to react against injustice. They are transformed from a politically conscious and active subject into a dependent object focused solely on obtaining substances, becoming a heavy burden on their family and society.




Gambling (and digital games of chance)




Objective:

 To create the illusion of "getting rich quickly and easily without working" among young people through online gambling websites, betting applications and digital games.




Consequence:

 The value of labor and production is undermined. Young people who lose everything through gambling are crushed under heavy debts and lose their dignity. In their desperation to obtain money, they become vulnerable to all forms of criminal activity, corruption and even networks of informant recruitment.




Sexual degeneration and the paralysis of will




Objective:

 To separate sexuality from its natural foundations of love, commitment and mutual respect, creating profound social degeneration through the pornography industry and forms of relationships considered immoral.




Consequence:

 This cultural erosion leads young men and women to view one another merely as instruments of physical gratification. The sacred spirit of comradeship and the consciousness of revolutionary loyalty are destroyed. When intellectual productivity comes to a halt, only instincts remain, and animalistic impulses become the sole governing force of life.




What is the way out of this system of oppression?




As clearly articulated from a philosophical perspective, the way to dismantle this oppressive system is not through passive rejection or complaint, but through radical self-organization and the construction of a new way of life. Young people and young women can reclaim their lives and futures through the following steps:




Establishing academies of enlightenment (a campaign for self-education)




Action:

 Young people must stop relying on institutions and establish their own "Self-Education and Reading Groups" as independent academies in every neighborhood, village and street.




Method:

 Philosophy, the history of peoples' resistance, analyses of special warfare and women's science (Jineolojî) must be studied in depth. Young people who develop intellectual competence will not surrender to the lies and traps of the system.




Developing mechanisms of social self-defense




Action:

 Young people and young women must become the moral and physical protectors of their own living environments.




Method:

 Self-defense and social ethics commissions must be established within people's assemblies. Those who introduce drugs into neighborhoods, operate gambling establishments or harass young women must be identified by young people themselves, publicly exposed and socially ostracized. Social isolation is the strongest sanction.




Reconnecting with historical and cultural roots and building a collective economy




Action:

 Mother tongues, indigenous cultures, revolutionary art and historical memory must be preserved against the consumerist frenzy imposed by capitalist modernity.




Method: 

Alternative theater, music, literature and folklore collectives must be established within assemblies. Young people whose inner worlds are enriched by revolutionary art and historical consciousness will not fall into spiritual emptiness. At the same time, agricultural, craft and production cooperatives must be established to revitalize the collective economy and counter the system's economic blackmail.




The joint leadership of young women and youth




Action: 

The patriarchal mentality (baviksalarî) must be radically dismantled within families, assemblies and social spaces.




Method: 

Young women must educate themselves in political and philosophical fields, particularly through Jineology, and raise the banner of rebellion against traditional and modern forms of oppression. The shared and equal roles of women and young people will give the emerging democratic communal system its true spirit and invincible strength.




The reality of Middle Eastern youth, the Leviathan system and a radical way out




Special warfare is a global system that subjugates society not through the force of arms, but by undermining its moral and intellectual foundations. As conceptualized by Abdullah Öcalan, the philosophical genius of our era, this crisis is not confined to a single people but is a systemic plague collectively produced by the centers of global capitalist modernity. This system has effectively become a global Leviathan, a monstrous force threatening to devour humanity.




The policies of dominant systems towards Middle Eastern youth




The capitalist monster and nation-state mechanisms in the region implement different special warfare strategies according to the sociological characteristics of each people.




Kurdish youth: Assimilation, terror and cultural destruction policies




Oppression and distinctive characteristics: 

Because the Kurdish youth's strong passion for freedom and radical activism are well known, the system employs physical destruction, intense political repression and an increasingly severe economic embargo against them.




Instruments of special warfare:

 Policies of linguistic assimilation are implemented to strip young people of their identity, while drugs are deliberately introduced into neighborhoods. Through pressure to become informants and psychological warfare techniques, bonds of comradeship among young people are undermined, and their energy is redirected towards leaving their homeland through migration and refugee routes.




Arab youth: Trapped by unemployment, sectarianism and radicalism




Oppression and distinctive characteristics: 

Following the Arab Spring, global capital and reactionary forces in the region have turned the Arab world into a laboratory of endless civil war and chaos.




Instruments of special warfare: 

Sectarian divisions, particularly Sunni-Shiite tensions, have been artificially inflamed to prevent the enormous energy of Arab youth from developing into democratic transformation. Young people are trapped in a cycle of deep poverty and unemployment, either driven into the killing fields of false radicalism and armed groups such as ISIS and its offshoots, or left to drown in the Mediterranean while pursuing dreams of reaching Europe.




Turkish youth: Blind nationalism, chauvinism and cultural erosion




Oppression and distinctive characteristics:

 The central state mentality in Turkey raises Turkish youth within an ideology of fanatical nationalism, chauvinism and fascism, positioning them as instruments of repression against the freedom demands of other peoples.




Instruments of special warfare:

 To prevent Turkish young people, who are trapped in a severe economic crisis and a lack of prospects for the future, from rebelling against the system, the digital gambling industry, corrupting television programs and sexual degeneration, described as "porno-nationalism," are used as a form of opium. Young people are conditioned to become guardians of the totalitarian state rather than defenders of freedom.




Persian youth: Theocratic repression, hypocrisy and the gallows




Oppression and distinctive characteristics: 

The theocratic regime in Iran, under the guise of religion, surrounds the lives of young people, particularly young women, with the harshest political and social restrictions.




Instruments of special warfare: 

The regime maintains its empire of fear through the execution of young people sentenced to death. On the other side of the coin, however, the system covertly facilitates the spread of drugs and prostitution in the underground world. This structural hypocrisy drives young people into profound existential nihilism, a loss of belief, and confines them to a hopeless and degraded existence behind closed doors.




This remarkable practice of resistance and self-organization is not merely a local patriotic duty. It is freedom itself, the security of today and the guarantee of tomorrow. Middle Eastern youth, rising with this universal and confederal consciousness, will dismantle the capitalist Leviathan and become the founding architects of a new democratic, ecological world based on women's freedom.

title: Iran attacks Komala base in Balîsan
content:
Iran attacked a base belonging to the Komeleya Şoreşgerên Zehmetkêşên Kurdistanê (Association of Revolutionary Toilers of Kurdistan) in Balîsan, southern Kurdistan, this morning. According to the party, the attack took place at around 8:40 a.m. and involved two explosive-laden drones.




Komala stated that no one was injured or killed in the attack northeast of Hewlêr (Erbil). However, the organization reported that the attack caused significant damage to property at the base.




Since the outbreak of the war between Iran, the United States, and Israel, Tehran has repeatedly attacked targets in various parts of southern Kurdistan. More than 30 people have reportedly been killed in these attacks so far.

title: Students demanding education in mother tongue attacked in Hesekê
content:
A demonstration demanding the right to education in the mother tongue was attacked in the northeastern Syrian city of Hesekê. Students had gathered outside the provincial administration building to demand education in their own language. Forces affiliated with the Syrian transitional government intervened against the gathering and fired shots into the air.




According to information obtained by the ANHA news agency, a group believed to be Arab residents from the Xiwêran neighborhood initially attacked the demonstrators with stones. Meanwhile, security forces of the transitional government attempted to disperse the protest and prevent it from continuing, using firearms.




The students condemned the intervention and emphasized the peaceful nature of their demonstration. “What have we done wrong to be prevented from doing this? We took to the streets peacefully and are demanding our right to our own language,” they told ANHA. The protesters also made it clear that the attacks would not deter them from demanding education in their mother tongue.




Since early September, students and their families in Rojava have been protesting against restrictions on Kurdish-language education. The protests were triggered by the Syrian transitional government’s decision to scale back Kurdish-language instruction and limit Kurdish classes to three hours per week. title: Bakırhan visits Figen Yüksekdağ, calls for freedom for political prisoners
content:
Ten years after the wave of arrests targeting the Peoples’ Democratic Party (HDP), representatives of several left-wing and democratic parties gathered outside Kandıra Women’s Prison in the western Turkish province of Kocaeli to demand the release of political prisoners. The gathering marked the anniversary of November 4, 2016, when the Turkish government launched a sweeping crackdown on the parliamentary representation of the Kurdish population with the arrests of then-HDP Co-Chairs Figen Yüksekdağ and Selahattin Demirtaş, along with several other members of parliament.




Tuncer Bakırhan, Co-Chair of the Peoples’ Equality and Democracy Party (DEM Party), had earlier visited Figen Yüksekdağ, who has been imprisoned for ten years, together with a delegation. Following the visit, party representatives and numerous supporters gathered outside the prison. Under the slogan “Freedom for political prisoners – for peace and democracy,” they demanded the release of those imprisoned.







Bakırhan: The political crackdown of 2016 continues to have repercussions today




Bakırhan described the arrests of November 4, 2016, as a “political coup” whose consequences have long since extended beyond the Kurdish opposition. He said the process had begun with the lifting of parliamentary immunity on May 20, 2016, a move that had also been supported by sections of the opposition at the time.




“On that day, a deep wound was inflicted on Turkey’s political history,” Bakırhan stated. He argued that the violations of rights committed at the time had since expanded to affect nearly all opposition forces. “What was done to the HDP back then is now being directed against all institutions and individuals engaged in opposition activities.”










“This is not just a peace process”




Referring to the ongoing Peace and Democratic Society Process, Bakırhan stated that the continued imprisonment of opposition politicians contradicted the declared objectives of political reconciliation. He stressed that anyone seeking to overcome social polarization must first address past injustices. This includes, in particular, implementing the rulings of the European Court of Human Rights (ECtHR) and Turkey’s Constitutional Court, he noted.




“For ten years, we have been standing outside these prisons and making statements. Hasn’t it been enough? In the eleventh year, our friends must once again be able to engage in democratic politics alongside us,” Bakırhan said. He stressed that Figen Yüksekdağ should be able to advocate her political position on peace outside prison. Selahattin Demirtaş, too, should be reunited with his people and his political colleagues, he said.




“This is not just a peace process. It is also a process of democratization,” the DEM Party Co-Chair emphasized. He remarked that prisons must be emptied for Turkey to achieve the rule of law, justice and democracy. Alongside Yüksekdağ and Demirtaş, he named several imprisoned politicians and activists, including Can Atalay, Osman Kavala, Bekir Kaya and Leyla Güven. He stressed that their place was not in prison but in society.




Left-wing parties demand an end to political prosecutions




Representatives of socialist parties also linked their demands for the release of political prisoners to fundamental democratic rights. Sezin Uçar, Deputy Co-Chair of the Socialist Party of the Oppressed (ESP), recalled the decade-long resistance against political persecution.




“Without freedom of expression, protest and organization, we can neither achieve peace nor build democracy,” she stated. Uçar said the ESP was demanding the release of all political prisoners, the repeal of Turkey’s Anti-Terror Law and the removal of all restrictions on freedom of expression, assembly and organization. She specifically highlighted those imprisoned in connection with the Kobanê and Gezi trials.













Levent Tüzel, Deputy Chair of the Labour Party (EMEP), described the Kobanê trial as a politically motivated prosecution. He pointed out that the HDP had been justified in calling for solidarity with the resistance against the siege of Kobanê in 2014. According to Tüzel, however, the protests at the time had been manipulated by paramilitary forces, with responsibility for the violence subsequently attributed to the HDP leadership. Tüzel criticized the lengthy prison sentences imposed as a result. He emphasized that the demand of peoples to live together in equality and freedom was at the heart of the current peace process.













Öztürk demands concrete steps from the government




Hakan Öztürk, Chair of the Labour Movement Party (EHP), called on the Turkish government to follow up its political statements and legislative measures with concrete action. Otherwise, he warned, the peace process risked losing credibility.




“If the reports that have been prepared and the promises that have been made were not merely empty words, they must now be put into practice. Otherwise, seriousness and trust will be lost,” Öztürk said.




Öztürk stated that the Kurdish movement and Abdullah Öcalan had made their contribution to changing the political climate. He said that this development must now also be reflected in Öcalan’s prison conditions and ability to work. In particular, Öztürk called for the establishment of the previously announced body for peace and political participation, which is intended to coordinate the further implementation of the process.




The EHP Chair also demanded the release of the politicians imprisoned in Kandıra, arguing that they had been deprived of their freedom through politically motivated court rulings and should be released immediately.

title: Kurdish writer Gülazer Akın released after 30 years in prison
content:
Kurdish political prisoner and writer Gülazer Akın has been released from Bünyan Women’s Prison in Turkey’s Kayseri province after 30 years of imprisonment. She was welcomed outside the prison by family members, representatives of the prisoners’ solidarity association TUHAYDER and numerous supporters. Akın, who had been imprisoned since November 1996, endured numerous health problems during her decades behind bars, completed a university degree and wrote several literary works.




Upon her release, Akın said she had not believed until the very end that she would actually be able to leave prison. The release of a fellow prisoner had previously been postponed by a decision of the Prison Administration and Observation Board. She therefore feared that her own release might also be blocked.




“As long as even one of our friends remains in prison, I will not feel that I have truly been released,” Akın said. She also welcomed the peace process that had begun: “We have matured and returned. A new process has begun. I said this before the board as well. A new process has begun, and I support it. There is probably nothing more beautiful than freedom.”




Following her remarks, Akın released a white dove as a symbol of peace.




TUHAY-DER calls for the release of political prisoners




During the welcome gathering, the prisoners’ solidarity association TUHAY-DER criticized the continued imprisonment of seriously ill prisoners and the repeated postponement of scheduled releases. Representatives of the association stated that genuine freedom could only be achieved when all political prisoners and Kurdish leader Abdullah Öcalan were released.




The decisions of Prison Administration and Observation Boards have faced criticism from human rights and prisoners’ rights organizations for years. These organizations accuse the boards of delaying the release of long-term prisoners for political reasons, despite their having met the necessary requirements for release.




Three decades behind prison walls




Gülazer Akın was born in 1975 in Ahlat, in the province of Bitlis. She joined the Kurdish freedom movement in 1993. On November 3, 1996, she was arrested in Istanbul and placed in pretrial detention. A Turkish State Security Court later sentenced her to life imprisonment on charges of separatism.




During her imprisonment, Akın was held in various prisons across Turkey. Despite health problems, she continued her education and graduated with a degree in public administration from Anadolu University.




At the same time, she devoted herself extensively to literature. Her experiences of imprisonment, social exclusion and women’s lives became central themes in her writing.




Writing against oblivion




Akın’s first novel, 

Tencerenin Dibi

 (

The Bottom of the Cooking Pot

), was published in 2013. The book was introduced by Turkish writer Adil Okay, who drew attention to the extraordinary circumstances under which she produced her literary work in an accompanying text.




Okay quoted from a letter Akın had written after 18 years of imprisonment. In it, she described how an entire generation had grown up behind prison walls while life continued outside:




“We were still almost children when we entered prison. Many of us grew up and matured while staring at walls. As the walls deteriorated, we grew more mature.”




Akın offered a particularly poignant account of her encounters with family members whose growth she could witness only during prison visits:




“When we entered prison, our siblings, nieces and nephews were still babies. Today, they are adults. We could only watch all of this through the small window of the prison. With every visit, we were amazed all over again and asked: When did you grow so big?”




According to Akın, this experience created an almost unbearable sense of injustice. Adil Okay praised her novel as a work written under conditions in which even colored pencils had reportedly been prohibited. Despite these restrictions, the writer developed her own literary voice to bring attention to experiences that were barely acknowledged beyond the prison walls.




Confronting patriarchal social structures




With her 2017 book 

Cinsiyetçiliğin Yaratımı

 (

The Creation of Sexism

), Akın also turned her attention to theoretical questions concerning women’s liberation. In the book, she examines sexism as a system of social domination and explores the significance of women’s self-determination in transforming social structures.




“We know that sexism is a male construct,” Akın writes. She emphasizes that women have both the right and the need to understand themselves, develop their abilities and independently determine their role in society.




She views women’s liberation not merely as individual emancipation but as a foundation for building a society based on solidarity and coexistence.

title: Ecocide continues in Şırnak: Hundreds of oak trees cut down
content:
Environmental destruction continues in the Kurdish province of Şırnak. Footage recorded by local residents yesterday in the Besta region shows hundreds of oak trees cut down across a vast area, leaving large sections of the forest stripped of trees.




While activities carried out under the guise of mining exploration on Mount Cudi and oil exploration on Mount Gabar for nearly a decade have already caused significant environmental damage, tree felling continues in the Besta region under the pretext of commercial activity.




According to reports, oak trees, some of them up to a century old, have been cut down by village guards under military supervision. Footage recorded in the Kaniya Kolanan and Dergê Gêzna areas showed numerous trees being cut down at their bases with chainsaws. The logging site is reportedly accessible only through a military checkpoint, and around ten people were said to be operating in the area with vans and chainsaws.




DEM Party Şırnak MP Mehmet Zeki İrmez shared the footage on his social media account, condemning the tree felling and tagging the Şırnak Governor’s Office and the Provincial Directorate of Agriculture.

title: Vigil in Geneva enters its 69th month: ‘Öcalan’s status must be officially recognized’
content:
A vigil by the Democratic Kurdish Community in Switzerland has been taking place in front of the UN headquarters in Geneva since 25 January 2021. Every Wednesday, activists stage a protest in front of the United Nations building to demand the release of Kurdish people’s leader Abdullah Öcalan. The action is carried out as part of the 'Dem dema azadiye' [Time for Freedom] campaign and is directed against the isolation of the Kurdish leader on the Turkish prison island of Imrali, the Turkish occupation attacks on Kurdistan, the massacres committed in Kurdish territories and the silence of the UN. Demonstratos call on international institutions to fulfill their responsibilities to secure Öcalan’s physical freedom.




This week's demonstration, which is held at a tent set up in Nations Square where the UN Office is located, began with a moment of silence in memory of those who lost their lives in the Kurdish freedom struggle.




During this week’s demonstration, participants from Kurdistan once again called on international institutions to fulfill their responsibilities in securing the physical freedom of Kurdish leader Abdullah Öcalan, who has been held in Imralı Island Prison since 1999.

title: German ambassador visits Amed Metropolitan Municipality
content:
The German Ambassador to Turkey, Sibylle Katharina Sorg, visited Amed (Turkish: Diyarbakır) Metropolitan Municipality. Accompanied by Embassy Secretary Nicole Gonsior, she was received by Serra Bucak and Emin Ay, the co-mayors of the DEM Party-run metropolitan municipality.

The discussions focused on the work of the local administration, ongoing projects in the city, and opportunities for mutual cooperation. No details were provided regarding specific initiatives or agreements.

The meeting was also attended by the municipality’s Secretary General, Serdar Bakıroğlu, and Deputy Secretary General, Muhabbet Erdoğmuş. The co-mayors thanked the ambassador for her visit.

title: Ağın: A united struggle is needed to democratise Turkey - Part One
content:
Writer and politician Ömer Ağın stated that the main obstacle to the Peace and Democratic Society Process was the state's failure to take concrete steps towards a democratic solution.




Ağın emphasised that democratic mass organisations, trade unions and professional associations must join the struggle for the process to advance, highlighting the importance of uniting around current democratic demands.




Ömer Ağın recalled the historical roots of the Kurdish question and the state's security-oriented approach, stating that a solution required time and mutual determination. Ağın said, "This process involves longstanding difficulties and deep-rooted problems. The Kurdish question is undoubtedly one of Turkey's most important and complex issues."




Ağın continued: "The issue has historical roots, and there are grievances that have accumulated on both sides from the founding of the Republic to the present day. The Kurdish people have no trust in the state, governments or the regime. Throughout the Republican period, almost every government has treated the Kurdish question as a security issue, a terrorism issue, and has attempted to suppress it through repression. This approach continues today. These attitudes remain deeply embedded throughout the system. Because this is a multidimensional issue, it is not easy to make progress or resolve the problem overnight. Everyone acknowledges this.




The Kurdish movement says so, and so do reasonable people. The Kurdish movement's own assessments also indicate that the issue can only be resolved through a process. It has been stated that this is merely the first step. Nobody expects everything to be resolved overnight. But what matters here is the approach being taken. Are there genuinely sincere intentions to resolve this issue? How do the parties view it? At what stage is society? What is society's ideological, political and organisational position? When we examine these questions, it is difficult to offer a particularly encouraging or reassuring assessment."




Ağın stated that he considered the Kurdish movement's approach to a solution sincere, emphasising its demands for dialogue and negotiations, the protection of democratic rights and an end to repression. 




Ağın said: "The Kurdish movement, the Kurds and the demands and aspirations of the Kurdish people are sincere. They genuinely want this issue to be resolved and to obtain their democratic rights. They want the repression and violence directed against them to end and the violations of their rights and values to be brought to an end. They are making efforts towards this goal, and their demands are sincere. The Kurdish movement has now recognised, in terms of its social values, organisational structure, ideological and political position and paradigm of struggle, that this issue can be resolved through dialogue and negotiations. It has understood that violence, repression and mutual conflict benefit no one. It believes that the Kurdish question can only be resolved through democratic and peaceful methods, within a framework of mutual rights and the rule of law.




There may be certain shortcomings on the Kurdish side and within Kurdish society in understanding, embracing and advancing the process. An adequate organisational structure may not yet have been established. Nevertheless, they are sincere in their ideas, paradigms and demands."




‘The process has become a whirlpool’




Ağın stated that the struggle for political power among Turkey's political forces had overshadowed the democratisation process, while parties' political calculations were slowing efforts to resolve the Kurdish question and secure common democratic gains for the peoples.




Ağın said: "This process has become a whirlpool. In Kurdish, a whirlpool is called 'gerînet'. It describes swirling water that draws in and engulfs everything around it. From a social perspective, the process appears to have entered such a whirlpool. Many people share this view.




I believe the Kurdish movement is aware of this. Because it knows that overcoming this situation will not be easy, it attaches importance to social values and shows patience in seeking to remove the obstacles to Turkey's democratisation. Today, there is the Republican People's Party (CHP), as well as the newly established party. The struggle and conflict for political power between these groups, particularly between the new party and the Justice and Development Party (AKP), have also turned into a whirlpool. Turkey's democratisation seems to have become almost entirely a struggle for power among these forces. For this reason, there is little evidence of a sincere approach or concrete steps towards democratisation. Pragmatic approaches and tactical calculations have come to the forefront.




Efforts that could contribute to the democratisation of Turkey, Kurdistan and the Middle East, and to common democratic gains for Kurds, Turks, Arabs, Circassians and all peoples, are progressing slowly. This is one of the main reasons for the current deadlock."




‘The state must take concrete steps’




Ömer Ağın pointed out that the state was dragging its feet over the process and had yet to take concrete steps. He stressed that the calls being made must be translated into practice.




Ağın said: "The government and the state, which have been slowing down this process, have not yet taken any serious steps. Looking at the current balance of power, there is little indication of a sincere willingness to take significant steps in the near future. Since the beginning of the process, Devlet Bahçeli has made various appeals in his speeches, such as 'Let them come and talk.' But how sincere are these appeals? How much influence do they have on the government? What is the state's overall position on this issue? These questions need to be examined seriously.




It is difficult to speak of any significant progress in practice because no concrete steps have been taken. A framework law has been introduced, and yes, this is something that should be regarded as important. But from this point onwards, the government's position, the statements of its spokespersons and the remarks of officials must be subjected to a test of sincerity. I do not believe that a particularly sincere approach has been demonstrated."




‘Democratisation cannot be achieved through the Kurdish people's struggle alone’




Ömer Ağın stated that a democratic solution to the Kurdish question would only be possible if different sections of society united around common demands.




Ağın continued: "A struggle limited to the Kurds cannot achieve results. It seems very difficult to overcome the obstacles facing this process through slogans based solely on their demands. Society as a whole, Turks, people living in western Turkey, democratic mass organisations, trade unions and professional associations must actively support this process. The democratisation of Turkish society and the successful, lasting continuation of the process cannot be achieved through the Kurdish people's struggle alone.




Those involved in politics in western Turkey, political parties and democratic mass organisations have not yet sufficiently recognised that resolving the Kurdish question through democratic methods would benefit Kurds, Turks and the Middle East, or that this is one of the fundamental issues in Turkey's democratisation. Nor have they reached the point of actively struggling for it. It also seems unlikely that they will mobilise solely around the Kurdish people's slogans or demands for certain forms of recognition of Abdullah Öcalan's status.




The demands of society in western Turkey and other sections suffering under the regime must also be brought together around the Kurdish question in a broader sense. Strategies and policies must be developed to achieve this. The demands for Mr. Öcalan's freedom, the recognition of the Kurdish people's demands, transparent negotiations and the free participation of democratic forces in the negotiation process are legitimate and entirely justified. Nevertheless, a large proportion of the Turkish population in western Turkey has not yet been convinced that this is the path towards democracy. This presents a problem. There is a need to broaden these demands and put forward more concrete proposals.




One of the most important issues is the situation in prisons. Kurds face serious difficulties. Many people have spent 30 years in prison and remain incarcerated despite having completed their sentences. People from the former ranks of the CHP, individuals associated with the newly established party, and the Mayor of Istanbul are also in prison. There are also people affiliated with religious orders who are imprisoned. In other words, prisons hold people from many different sections of society. This is a serious problem."
