title: Students in Kobanê reject incorporation of their university
content:
Students and staff at the University of Kobanê have rejected plans to incorporate their institution into the University of Aleppo. In a statement marking World Kobanê Day on November 1, they called for the university’s institutional autonomy to be preserved and for no decisions about its future to be made without the participation of its students and staff. They explicitly stated that they were not opposed to cooperation with other Syrian universities.




The statement was read out by student Gulistan Elî in front of the university building in Kobanê, in the presence of faculty members and students. It came in response to a recent decision by the Syrian Ministry of Higher Education to integrate the University of Kobanê into the state higher education system.




Opposition despite agreement with Damascus




Just on Saturday, the university administration announced the outcome of further negotiations with the Syrian government. According to the agreement, the University of Kobanê is to be incorporated into the University of Aleppo as a group of faculties while retaining its own administrative structures. title: Geothermal project in Varto: Court examines potential environmental damage
content:
A court-ordered site inspection has taken place as part of a legal dispute over a planned geothermal project on the border between the Kurdish provinces of Bingöl and Muş. A panel of experts appointed by the Bingöl Administrative Court examined the proposed drilling sites in the villages of Licik, Çermî, and Şorik in the Karlıova district. Local residents fear that the project will severely threaten their livelihoods and are demanding its cancellation.




The project, undertaken by the US-based company IGNIS H2 Energy, covers an area between Karlıova and Varto. Affected residents filed a lawsuit against the project in April. In July, the court ordered an expert assessment and an on-site inspection.




Concerns over water sources and agriculture




Numerous local residents participated in the inspection on Monday. The expert panel was accompanied by DEM Party MPs Ibrahim Akın and Sümeyye Boz, lawyers from the Diyarbakır Bar Association, and representatives of various environmental organizations from Kurdistan and Turkey.













Akın, who also serves as co-spokesperson for the DEM Party’s Ecology Commission, highlighted the local population’s ongoing resistance. He stated that the inspections would extend from Bingöl to the Varto region.

title: 29 women killed in Southern Kurdistan in ten months
content:
In the first ten months of 2026, at least 29 women were victims of femicide in Southern Kurdistan. Another 29 women died under suspicious circumstances, according to a recent analysis by the Roj News agency. Three women were killed in October alone.




On October 15, a 20-year-old woman was killed by her brother, who was eight years older than her, in the Domîz subdistrict of Sêmêlê district near Duhok. Five days later, on October 20, 30-year-old Kîjan Burhan was murdered by her father, who shot her three times, in Sulaymaniyah.




The third case was reported on October 29 in the village of Şêx Turab near Hewlêr (Erbil), where the body of a murdered woman was discovered. Four suspects were arrested, and police in Hewlêr launched an investigation.




Women’s organizations have long criticized domestic violence as one of the most serious social problems in Southern Kurdistan. They are calling for effective prevention and intervention measures aimed at preventing violence, protecting victims, and bringing about lasting changes in violent patterns of behavior.

title: ISIG: At least 678 migrants died on their workplace in six years
content:
Data compiled from reports by ISIG (Health and Safety Labour Observatory) show that migrant and refugee workers accounted for 4.8 percent of the 14,110 workers killed in workplace accidents between 2020 and the first nine months of 2026. Four workers were killed and another was injured when a tornado struck Antalya during the night of 26 October. Antalya Governor Hulusi Şahin said that the tornado had torn apart two containers housing workers employed at a residential construction site.




A judicial investigation was launched following the deaths of the four workers. Four people, including the construction contractor and site manager, were detained as part of the investigation.




Three of the workers were refugees




The workers who lost their lives were identified as Aycan Kılınç, Muhammed El Omar, Isa Elnevvah and Muhammed El Zeyn. The fact that three of the workers were Syrian brought renewed attention to the deaths of migrant and refugee workers in workplace accidents in Turkey in recent years.




Annual reports by ISIG provide information on deaths among migrant and refugee workers. According to ISIG reports, at least 678 migrant and refugee workers were killed in workplace accidents between 2020 and September 2026. The Observatory's annual reports show that a total of 12,374 workers were killed in workplace accidents between 2020 and 2025.

title: Fatma Ünsal Bostan: Security Council's role draws criticism
content:
The current stage of the Peace and Democratic Society Process aimed at resolving the Kurdish question, the linking of legislation passed by Parliament to decisions of the National Security Council, and the social and political dimensions of the process continue to be debated. Corruption and investment fund investigations, parliamentary disputes, match-fixing investigations and interventions against municipalities have also become major issues on Turkey's political agenda.




Political scientist Fatma Bostan Ünsal spoke to ANF about how different sections of society perceive the process, the prominent role given to the National Security Council and the impact of political developments on efforts to achieve peace.




‘Different sections of society perceive the process differently’




Fatma Bostan Ünsal pointed out that different sections of society define the Peace and Democratic Society Process in different ways, contributing to a lack of trust. 




Fatma Bostan Ünsal said: "We can see that different sections of society in Turkey perceive this process very differently, from its name to its content. One section, to which I belong and which unfortunately does not constitute the majority of society, calls it the 'Peace and Democratic Society Process' and expects corresponding changes in legislation and practice. However, a larger section, which is in power and therefore has the ability to introduce certain legislative and practical changes, calls the process 'Terror-Free Turkey'. This section approaches the issue within a security framework and appears prepared to make only very limited changes.




Alongside these two groups, another significant section of society is following the process while feeling that it is among those most directly affected by the country's increasing departure from democracy. This section does not trust political actors. Although more than two years have passed since the process began, it can be said that no policy has been pursued to bring these different perceptions and expectations closer together.




The recent division of the main opposition party through judicial intervention, alongside the perception that judicial interventions against municipalities are politically motivated, has fuelled widespread distrust towards the process."




‘The National Security Council's role on 28 February evokes negative associations’




Fatma Ünsal stated that the government's decision to give the National Security Council a prominent role in the process had created problems of trust within society and politics. Ünsal said: "The government is presenting the National Security Council as the principal institution in the process, in line with its understanding of the process as 'Terror-Free Turkey'. The National Security Council does not evoke particularly positive associations, especially because of its role in the 28 February process, when 'reactionism' was identified as the primary threat in the national security policy document known as the Red Book, and its involvement in the 'postmodern coup' that resulted in the fall of the then REFAH-YOL coalition government. The Council's prominent role in the current process is also being criticised because it has very limited channels for communicating directly with society."




‘The investment fund crisis could force the government towards transparency’




Fatma Ünsal also drew attention to the crisis caused by the investment fund fraud scandal within circles close to the government. She said that public pressure could force the authorities to become more transparent. 




Ünsal said: "The fact that both the perpetrators and victims of the investment fund fraud, involving billions of lira, largely come from circles close to the government has created a political crisis. The government, which has repeatedly managed to avoid transparency in the past, has been unable to close the matter because of public pressure surrounding the investment fund crisis. Hundreds of thousands of people close to the Justice and Development Party (AKP), many of whom belong to networks connected to government circles, remain outraged. They believed they would earn high returns through people they trusted, but their savings have largely disappeared because of negligence and abuses by those responsible.




The opposition's existing demand for transparency could now gain strength through the support of governing party voters, even if not its politicians, and could force the government towards greater transparency."




‘The opposition is on the brink of a fierce confrontation’




Fatma Bostan Ünsal stated that interventions against municipalities had caused major upheaval within the opposition and opened the way for an intense political confrontation with the government. She emphasised that the opposition needed to take steps to win public trust.




Ünsal said: "Interventions against opposition-run municipalities have caused major upheaval. The main opposition, which had enjoyed a degree of complacency within its own political space because it was not a genuine rival to the government, now finds itself on the brink of a fierce confrontation after gaining the strength to challenge those in power. As the late Özal once said, 'I have two shirts, one for celebrations and one for the gallows.' Politics in Turkey sometimes involves extremely high risks. What we have witnessed so far suggests that this is another such period.




This is a difficult period in which public support is vital. Proposals for changes aimed at winning public trust, such as an ethics law and amendments to party statutes that would give members a more active role, also have the potential to make Turkish politics more transparent in general. The success of the Student Movement in last week's elections in Serbia, which embraced transparency and distanced itself from both the repressive government and the existing opposition, offers the opposition a very clear indication of what it needs to do."

author: Unknown
title: Özgür Sevgi Göral: France’s dilemmas also exist in Turkey - Part Two
content:
ANF spoke to academic Özgür Sevgi Göral, who is currently in Paris and has participated in the demonstrations, about the historical foundations of the protests and their potential.




Part one of this interview can be read 

here

. 




When you compare these protests with the history of social movements and youth activism in Turkey, what similarities or significant differences do you see? Is the possibility of their influence spreading to Turkey limited, or what factors might increase that possibility?




This is a very difficult question. Youth movements in Turkey constitute a very broad field, and although I try to follow them, they are not my primary area of research. Therefore, I do not think I am in a position to compare the two countries in this respect. Perhaps I can offer just a few observations. Turkey has witnessed powerful youth movements, although they have been heavily suppressed, particularly over the past decade. We can assume that the racialised capitalist regime in which we live, and its various manifestations, have also generated considerable dissatisfaction among young people in Turkey. Moreover, even under Turkey's extremely harsh political conditions, youth movements have repeatedly emerged and made themselves visible over the past ten years. However, we know that for particular grievances or isolated political revolts to develop into powerful political mobilisation, there must be an accumulated history and tradition of struggle capable of protecting and developing itself. There must also be different political organisations operating at various levels, sometimes reaching agreements with one another and sometimes coming into conflict. I do not know to what extent such conditions exist or are possible in Turkey today, although there are certain emerging centres of struggle.




On the other hand, I think that rather than speaking of the protests spreading from one country to another, we can speak of a certain "simultaneity". Simultaneity, a concept frequently used in the literature on political and social movements, suggests that movements in different parts of the world during the same historical period can inspire one another in terms of political programmes, repertoires of mobilisation and demands, and that revolutionary ideas can travel across geographical boundaries. This could also apply to Turkey at a moment when the repertoire of street protests has some room to expand. However, the state's security strategy and policies against the accumulated experience of the Kurdish struggle, particularly the rapid criminalisation of forms of political violence and their framing through the concept of "terrorism", have unfortunately also proved effective among different political and social movements. Therefore, I cannot determine whether this wave of protests might produce rapid consequences for youth movements in Turkey through an effect of simultaneity, or what possibilities might exist for such a development. I am sure that my colleagues who are active in this field and study these movements have much more to say on the subject than I do.




Do these protests offer the prospect of lasting social and political transformation?




I think this question is extremely important, not only in relation to these protests but also in terms of the situation that widespread mass protests and uprisings have faced for some time. The latest youth uprising began on a broader scale than previous ones. However, in France and many other countries, it is debatable how successful such uprisings have been in producing concrete political and social transformation, despite all their potential. This movement also faces the dilemma your question points to. The central issue here is the dual nature of the demands of the groups driving the movement. There is a tension between those who prioritise short-term problems concerning the existing education system and those who focus on how wealth and resources should be distributed and on the broader prospect of anti-capitalist transformation. For now, it is difficult to say that this uprising has a programme and organisational structure based on a broader emancipatory perspective extending beyond its concrete demands. The government currently appears to have taken a step back by announcing that it will abolish Parcoursup, the university admissions system, in 2028. However, unless a strong and sustained bloc of political struggle can be established, it could introduce essentially the same system, based on exactly the same logic, under a different name.




This is not the only issue, however. There is also the risk that the uprising will be reduced to the presidential elections scheduled for April 2027. This risk is reinforced by the anger among young protesters at the possibility that Marine Le Pen, the leader of the far-right National Rally (Rassemblement National, RN), could be elected president, as well as by the presence of Jean-Luc Mélenchon, the presidential candidate of La France Insoumise (LFI, France Unbowed), whom the mainstream media has sought from the outset to portray as the person "behind the uprising". For the past 30 years, presidents from centre-right parties have been elected with votes cast to prevent the election of far-right or RN candidates. Yet these presidents bear primary responsibility for the enormous destruction highlighted by the youth uprising. Moreover, these political administrations have pursued policies so far to the right that they have competed with the RN in protecting the interests of the French big bourgeoisie. This has been evident in everything from racism against migrants and discriminatory policies to austerity measures controlling public spending and increased military expenditure. Processes of fascistisation have advanced under precisely those centre-right presidents who were elected to prevent RN candidates from coming to power. Therefore, although opposition to the RN and the anti-fascist emphasis in particular play a decisive role in the demonstrations, reducing the uprising of the suburbs, which demands a more profound transformation, to voting in the April 2027 presidential elections would dilute the movement's anger and enthusiasm.




On 23 October, one person was killed and five others injured in a racist attack in Trappes, near Paris. The racist attacker reportedly stated after being apprehended that he had targeted Black and Arab people because he wanted to "avenge shopkeepers whose businesses had been looted on 17 October". A copy of Mein Kampf and RN brochures and leaflets were found in the attacker's home. Far-right and fascist militias have also attacked demonstrations in some parts of France. Opposition to the RN will therefore understandably continue to influence the protests. However, directing this highly positive anti-fascist stance solely towards the April 2027 presidential elections risks alienating young people from the suburbs in particular. As I mentioned earlier, this is not simply a debate about electoral strategy. It also involves tensions over whether the movement will deepen through the institutions and timelines of institutional politics or through its own transformative potential. These two possibilities are certainly not necessarily opposed. However, the experience of the past 20 years is sufficient to demonstrate the negative consequences of reducing street movements to electoral mobilisation alone while setting aside all their transformative potential.




At today's demonstration against the racist attack in Trappes, Emmanuel Grégoire, the Socialist Party mayor of Paris, was booed while delivering his speech. Protesters also chanted, "Everyone hates the Socialist Party." The movement feels a very strong and, in my view, justified anger towards all the centrist parties, which have achieved almost nothing in the face of capitalism's enormous offensive over the past 30 years. Young people are no longer content merely to expose institutions such as schools and the police. By placing the question of equal access to public services at the centre, they want to redefine how resources are distributed and the limits of political participation. Whether the movement can produce lasting transformation will depend on the success of those who stand alongside these aspirations, demands, anger and the anti-capitalist core within the movement, who patiently engage with all the dilemmas arising from that core, and who have the political capacity to strengthen it. 




Finally, I would like to add that how the parliamentary left navigates this dilemma will also be critically important to its success. In a discussion of the economic programme proposed by LFI, Stathis Kouvélakis offers a detailed assessment that also examines the experiences of Greece and Spain. He emphasises the impossibility of reconciling the concept of "budgetary realism" with the idea of breaking away from austerity policies. Therefore, even parliamentary left movements that have achieved electoral success will face a similar dilemma. How they navigate it, and which class interests and social groups they prioritise in doing so, will be the most important criterion for achieving lasting political and social transformation.




How does the overall state of the world shape the debates and efforts to find a solution to the Kurdish question in Turkey? Does a world in turmoil create opportunities for a solution, or does it increase the risks?




The overall state of the world is characterised by the deepening of the 2008 economic crisis, the strengthening of far-right movements and processes of fascistisation worldwide, and a situation in which even the apparent credibility of the fragile consensus underpinning representative democracy has disappeared. Almost every concept is now discussed in terms of crisis, from the climate crisis to the crisis of democracy, from the crisis of masculinity to the crisis of the idea of living together. First came the conflict in Ukraine, followed by the ongoing genocide in Palestine, the war in Iran and the post-war process in Syria, which continues amid profound contradictions. The worldwide escalation of militarism and war economies forms the underlying mechanism driving processes of fascistisation. Such a world is very different from the early 2000s, a period often described as the golden age of conflict resolution. Moreover, even during that supposed golden age, the conflict resolution paradigm could be criticised in many respects for its limitations in producing profound and lasting transformations. The current political conjuncture therefore increases the risks. This is also part of the objective basis for why conflict resolution and peacebuilding processes are proceeding within such a constrained and narrow geopolitical framework.




Considering previous experiences of conflict resolution and examples from around the world, what kind of foundation, language and methodology are needed today to achieve a lasting, just and socially inclusive peace regarding the Kurdish question?




I think we have a tendency to be somewhat too generous in listing what needs to be done, and I do not believe this tendency is particularly useful. We can draw up a comprehensive list, but I see very little possibility of the proposals on that list actually being implemented. It seems to me that the real question is this: What can we do at a time when the comprehensive lists we produce in our reports, research and articles are largely unlikely to become reality? What comes to mind here is primarily what we call prefigurative politics, participating in movements that seek to build today the future we want to create. Of course, within a broader framework, the state can be pressured to take certain steps. In fact, such pressure should never be abandoned. However, I believe the current political circumstances can only be overcome through genuine, concrete and modest efforts in which movements for freedom and liberation rebuild themselves, turn towards society and seek to establish the foundations of the world they envision through the broadest possible alliances. These efforts mean shifting attention away from the bureaucratic mechanisms of representative politics towards everyday life and organising within society. 




For the current conflict resolution process to have meaning for broad sections of society, it must bring about a transformation in their lives. I believe this is the essential issue when we speak of making the peace process a process embraced by society. Civil society participation and contributions from "experts", although important in their own right, do not automatically mean that the conflict resolution process will be discussed by broad sections of society or produce politically and socially transformative outcomes. For example, the involvement of civil society organisations, experts and academics can, in certain respects, lead to an excessively technical approach to the process. It can allow a single political discourse, the language of conflict resolution, to become dominant and depoliticise the process by insisting that it must be conducted through the sterile language of certain experts. The only way to overcome all this is through political struggle that enables broad sections of society to believe that this process can provide the foundations for a shared life based on equality and freedom. Since the state will not provide these foundations, they will have to be built by all movements for equality, freedom and liberation, particularly the Kurdish Freedom Movement, by drawing on their capacities and establishing the broadest possible alliances. In fact, all the dilemmas we have discussed in relation to France are also present in Turkey, although, of course, in different forms.




Where do the efforts of young protesters in Paris intersect with those of people seeking peace and justice in the Middle East or Turkey? Where do you see hope and the possibility of a common struggle in a world engulfed in turmoil?




Amid economic crises, rapidly advancing processes of fascistisation, climate disasters and devastating impoverishment, people seeking peace, justice and freedom in many parts of the world face similar difficulties. I think two approaches could establish a connection between young protesters in Paris and young protesters in the Middle East. The first concerns the question of the future. Capitalism's inability to offer young people a future, or more precisely, the fact that the only thing it offers young people from the lower classes and children of broad sections of the working population is a future without prospects, is generally presented as a problem that needs to be corrected. However, this question of having no future actually means that capitalism, at its present stage, offers vast sections of society nothing but a series of disasters ahead. Rather than attempting to revise or reform this situation, I believe developing a politics around what an entirely different and radical vision of the future might look like could provide a perspective connecting people engaged in struggles across the world.




The second is the idea of the commune. One of the most prominent slogans of the youth uprising in France has been "Vive la Commune" (Long live the Commune). The possibility of a particular form of communal life, a social formation in which everyone is there for everyone and the pleasures of communal luxury can be experienced, undoubtedly seems very distant today. Nevertheless, both historically and under current political circumstances, this concept opens up important possibilities for different movements for equality, freedom and liberation to engage in discussion and develop political approaches. Ultimately, the struggle truly is endless, and despite all the difficult conditions, millions of people around the world refuse to abandon the streets. I believe this period also opens up certain possibilities for those who do not become consumed by the verbal satisfaction of appearing too clever to be fooled, those who strive to establish the broadest possible alliances and those who maintain a radical vision of the future. It seems to me that these possibilities will belong to those who are not afraid to remain engaged with difficult dilemmas, who work to expand the space available to them under all circumstances and who turn their attention carefully towards society.

title: Peace Mothers arrive in Ankara
content:
Members of the Peace Mothers’ Assembly, who set out from 24 cities demanding that Abdullah Öcalan’s physical freedom be secured, that prisoners be released, and that concrete steps be taken as part of the Peace and Democratic Society Process, have arrived in Ankara.




The mothers gathered at the headquarters of the Peoples’ Equality and Democracy Party (DEM Party) in Balgat.




The Peace Mothers will make a statement at Parliament Park to publicize their demands, then hold a tent vigil at Kurtuluş Park.




Buses from Istanbul, Izmir, Van and Amed




The Istanbul Peace Mothers’ Assembly traveled to Ankara by bus last night. 







Members of the Izmir Peace Mothers’ Assembly held a press conference last night at the Izmir provincial headquarters of the Democratic Regions Party (DBP), where they had gathered before setting off for Ankara. title: Independent Engineers and Architects: It is not natural disasters but greed and negligence that kill
content:
Heavy rainfall affecting many cities, particularly Istanbul, has once again exposed the inadequacy of urban infrastructure and the devastating consequences of profit-driven urban development policies. Flooding turned underpasses and tunnels into lakes, bringing transport and daily life almost to a standstill. Five people lost their lives in the floods. According to the governor's office, authorities recorded 1,277 flooding incidents, 15 landslides, 47 reports of people stranded, 13 fallen trees, and reports involving 76 vehicles, 808 homes and 280 workplaces.




The Istanbul Platform of Independent Engineers, Architects and Urban Planners spoke to ANF following the devastation, which has reached deadly proportions. The platform stressed that the real cause of the disaster was not the weather but a profit-driven and negligent mentality that disregards both nature and human life.




‘Disadvantaged sections of society are once again paying the price’




The platform drew attention to the political and social realities behind the destruction, which the government and business interests have sought to dismiss as a 'natural disaster'. It stressed that, as always, low-income and disadvantaged sections of society were bearing the heaviest burden. The platform described the profound social and spatial inequalities created by profit-driven planning decisions: “Construction that disregards a city's carrying capacity and ecological limits places the resulting costs on society as a whole, while concentrating economic gains in the hands of certain groups. However, these costs are not borne equally. People living in basement and ground-floor flats, low-income households, workers in insecure employment, those forced to work outdoors, people with disabilities and older people can be more severely affected by disasters. Disruptions to transport, loss of employment, damage to homes and workplaces, and reduced access to safe housing deepen social inequalities beyond the immediate physical destruction.”




‘The problem is not the rain but capital-driven urban planning’




The platform said: “The recent loss of life and flooding cannot be explained by heavy rainfall alone. Extreme rainfall is a trigger, but whether it turns into a disaster is directly related to how a city is planned and managed.” It stressed that urban infrastructure and architectural practices had increasingly departed from scientific principles, despite years of warnings from scientists, urban planners and engineers.




The platform pointed out that valley floors and streambeds had been opened to construction for profit, while natural water catchment areas had been covered with concrete and asphalt.




The platform identified the main factors contributing to flooding: “The rapid expansion of concrete and asphalt surfaces, the destruction of green spaces and the declining capacity of soil to absorb water cause rainfall to turn rapidly into surface runoff. Narrowing streambeds and allowing uncontrolled development in valleys and low-lying areas directly increase the risk of flooding. Inadequate stormwater drainage capacity, non-functioning pumping stations, missing drainage lines and the failure to maintain drainage grates and pipelines regularly make disasters worse. Transforming urban land from a public living space into an instrument of speculative profit, and maximising economic gains at the expense of ecological balance and the public interest, creates systemic vulnerabilities.”




The Istanbul platform stated that ecological balance had been sacrificed for the sake of capital accumulation: “The transformation of urban land from a shared social living space into an instrument of speculative profit drives the destruction of natural areas. Urban development strategies that maximise economic returns at the expense of ecological balance and the public interest deepen systemic vulnerabilities to disasters. The safe absorption of water into the soil following heavy rainfall has been obstructed. Valley corridors, underpasses and surfaces stripped of their permeability have become threats to people's lives.”




‘Ecological oversight and the public interest must take priority’




The platform stressed that routine maintenance and technical solutions are insufficient in times of crisis, and that the problem requires a fundamental change in mentality and the system itself. It stated that engineering, architecture and urban planning must serve the public interest and nature rather than profit.




The platform said that what was needed was not to watch the same scenes unfold after every disaster, only to forget them afterwards. It outlined lasting solutions that place people and nature at the centre of urban planning instead of yielding to pressure for profit: “Ecological planning must aim to ensure that green spaces are not concentrated solely in high-income areas but are equally accessible in every neighbourhood. People living in high-risk areas must be provided with access to safe housing, while urban transformation processes must be carried out without creating new hardships, forced displacement or housing crises. This is where the concept of ecological justice becomes important. Ecological justice requires not only the protection of natural resources but also ensuring that environmental risks and the costs of disasters are not imposed on particular sections of society. Making cities compatible with nature is also a struggle to build cities that are more equal, safer and more liveable.”




The platform emphasised that policies centred on nature had become a necessity as the climate crisis deepened: “The challenge is not simply to drain away water, but to implement an approach to urban development that respects the natural water cycle and places people and nature at its centre rather than the pursuit of profit. Because the kind of city we live in is not merely a question of engineering calculations, but also of the kind of life and future we choose to defend.”




‘A safe city is not a privilege but a fundamental right’




The platform stressed that the future of cities must be shaped not by the expectations of investors and capital, but by the limits of nature, ecological balance and human life. It emphasised that a solution was possible only through ecological urban planning.




The platform called for the implementation of sponge city practices, immediate protection of streambeds, the upgrading of infrastructure in line with climate scenarios, and greater transparency in planning processes to ensure that they serve the public interest.




The platform concluded its assessment with the following statement: “If the same areas of a city are flooded after every heavy rainfall, the same infrastructure problems keep recurring and people continue to lose their lives, we must question not only the rainfall but also the profit-driven, commercially motivated approach to urban planning that repeatedly produces these consequences.




Engineering must not be a technical instrument of capital, but a defender of life, nature and social equality. Living in a safe city is not a privilege, but a fundamental right to life that is non-negotiable for everyone!”

title: Aygül Yağış: Save our young people from drugs
content:
Alongside special warfare policies, drug use, betting, gambling, gang activity and incidents of individual violence are among the major social problems in Kurdistan. Field studies conducted by civil society organisations and bar associations indicate that addiction is becoming increasingly widespread, particularly among young people, while families continue to call for solutions. According to available data, the age at which children begin using drugs has fallen to as low as nine, while a significant proportion of users are first introduced to drugs through their friends.




Reports published in the media indicate that 71.2 percent of drug users were first introduced to drugs between the ages of 15 and 24, while 74.4 percent first obtained drugs from friends or people in their immediate social circles. The Turkish Green Crescent's 2025 Gambling Report also highlighted that the age at which people begin gambling has fallen to 15.




According to data from the Diyarbakır (Amed) Bar Association, lawyers were appointed to represent 2,173 people prosecuted for drug production and trafficking between 1 January and 9 September 2023. Lawyers were also appointed to represent 291 people accused of drug use or purchasing, accepting or possessing drugs for personal use.




Growing concerns include young people being drawn into addiction, the weakening of social ties and the increasing economic vulnerability of families, while special warfare policies continue to be systematically implemented in the region.




Aygül Yağış, who said that many families around her were struggling with similar problems, has been fighting for years to free her son from drug addiction. Yağış stated that young people were being drawn into drug use very quickly and found it difficult to overcome addiction. She drew particular attention to the targeting of young people and children from patriotic families.




‘We did everything we could, but we could not save him’




Aygül Yağış described the difficult experiences her son had endured because of drug addiction. She said that the family had searched for a solution for a long time but had been unable to achieve any results. Yağış, whose son struggled with addiction for six years, said: "Recently, almost everyone around us and in our families has been affected by these policies. The person closest to me who was affected was my son. Unfortunately, he went through a long and difficult period because of drug addiction and was eventually arrested.




My son was working in another city. When he returned here, he started using drugs. He began taking drugs while spending time with his friends. We did everything we could and tried every possible intervention, but we could not save him from addiction. Eventually, he completely lost control of himself. When he was under the influence of drugs, he was not himself and was constantly aggressive. When he came to his senses, he apologised to everyone. He was suddenly drawn into this situation, and before we could understand what was happening, he had become addicted."




‘Even his arrest did not free him from addiction’




Aygül Yağış said that her son sometimes told her about what he was experiencing. She explained: "Sometimes he would tell me, 'Mum, the police come and see us, then take notes and leave.' I repeatedly told him that this was not happening for no reason. Many investigations were opened against him after his arrest. From the day he started using drugs, I never once saw him in a good condition. We tried everything, but we could not persuade him to stop. He remained in this situation for six years and was eventually arrested.




I thought he might get better after his arrest. Even he used to say, 'Maybe I can overcome this if I go to prison.' But despite being imprisoned, nothing has changed in his condition. Moreover, it is not only my son. Many people around him are struggling with the same problem. All these people live here. We also see people coming here from other provinces to use drugs."




‘Everyone, from children to the elderly, is gambling’




Aygül Yağış pointed out that betting and gambling, as well as drug use, were becoming increasingly widespread among young people, placing families under economic and social strain. She said that families were worried about protecting their children and were being forced to send them elsewhere.




Yağış continued: "All mothers and families are now complaining about this situation. People are extremely afraid that their young people will be led down the wrong path. They do everything they can to protect them. Out of fear, they send their children to other places. Our young people need to be freed from this situation. It is not just drug use. Betting and gambling among young people are also spiralling out of control. Someone introduced my son to drugs by telling him, 'Take this to someone else.' Once he started using drugs, he could not give them up."




Yağış also described the difficulties faced by people who had accumulated gambling debts. She said, "I saw an elderly man crying because of his gambling debts. This is what people have been reduced to, and the situation is driving both families and young people into poverty."




‘Children from patriotic families are being targeted’




Aygül Yağış described these developments as part of special warfare policies, stating that young people, particularly children from patriotic families, were being targeted. She pointed out that young people were being pushed away from social relationships.




Yağış said: "Our young people need to be freed from this situation. Young people, particularly children from patriotic families, are being targeted. It is not only young people; mothers and fathers are also being targeted. The attitude is that young people should not throw stones, but they can do whatever else they want. That is why young people are being targeted. They do not even allow two young people to come together."







 







‘Necessary steps must be taken to find a solution’




Aygül Yağış appealed to all sections of society to take action against addiction, emphasising that political parties and public institutions must assume responsibility. She called for young people to be freed from addiction.




Yağış said: "Everyone must do whatever they can. Whether political parties or the state, everyone must make an effort to put an end to this situation. This is the only demand of our families: save these young people from this poison. We have had enough. Almost every family has a son or a child caught up in this poison. Save our young people from this poison. We do not want any mother or any young person to suffer."

title: ‘No independent investigations conducted into murders of journalist in the Kurdistan Region’
content:
The Metro Center for Journalists’ Rights and Advocacy issued a statement on the occasion of November 2, the International Day to End Impunity for Crimes against Journalists, designated by the United Nations (UN) in 2013.




The statement read: “In the Kurdistan Region, no independent investigations into the murders of journalists have been conducted because the judiciary is under the influence of the ruling political parties. Cases that have sparked widespread public outrage, such as the murders of Soran Mame Heme, Serdeşt Osman, Kawa Germiyani, Vedat Hüseyin, and Abdülstar Tahir Şerif, remain unsolved. Neither those who carried out the murders nor those who ordered them have been identified or brought to justice.”




Calling for the investigations into these cases to be reopened, the Metro Center drew attention to statements issued by UNESCO, stating: “Impunity for crimes leads to an increase in murders and violence and undermines the legal and justice systems. UNESCO warns that such impunity allows serious human rights violations and corruption to be concealed, causing harm to society as a whole. For this reason, the government, civil society organizations, and media outlets are being urged to uphold the rule of law and support international initiatives aimed at putting an end to such practices.”

title: Meral Beştaş: The process is facing a serious deadlock
content:
Peoples' Equality and Democracy Party (DEM Party) MP Meral Danış Beştaş spoke to ANF about the current stage of the Peace and Democratic Society Process aimed at resolving the Kurdish question, the decision to make implementation of the framework law conditional on a National Security Council decision, and the government's approach to the process.




Meral Beştaş pointed out that Kurdish demands for democratic rights and freedoms had been pushed into the background of political discussions. She said that a lasting solution required moving beyond a security-oriented approach, implementing legal reforms and taking concrete steps towards democratisation.




‘Political will must be translated into concrete steps’




Beştaş stated that although the framework law had passed through Parliament, the anticipated MGK decision required for its implementation had still not been issued. She pointed to the government's lack of political will in the process and said:




"I believe the fundamental issue here is the failure to translate political will into concrete and binding legal steps. Political will has been expressed during the process, and there have been important developments, including the framework law and, before that, the parliamentary commission. However, there has been a serious delay in establishing a legal basis for these developments, and the process is being prolonged. We can see this, and it is currently the most widely discussed issue among the public in Turkey.




On the one hand, the framework law is not being implemented because the National Security Council decision is still awaited. On the other hand, the failure to implement the parliamentary commission's report is creating uncertainty about how transitions will take place and when the law will be enforced.




We have always maintained that peace is achieved through reciprocal steps and mutual responsibility among institutions. The government must not postpone its own responsibilities. The state has the means to enact legislation, establish legal guarantees and remove obstacles to democratic politics. These responsibilities have legal, administrative and political dimensions. Yet we are witnessing an avoidance of these obligations.




There should actually be a simple measure: Which steps have been taken? Which have not? Which obligations remain unfulfilled? We need to examine the situation from this perspective, and these questions must be discussed transparently in public. Frankly, the government's constant introduction of vague conditions does not advance a solution. On the contrary, it prolongs the process even further. We must never lose sight of this.




When the 27 February call was made, neither the government nor the state had taken any steps. Nevertheless, Mr. Öcalan made that call unilaterally and fulfilled its requirements. As you may recall, there was considerable debate at the time. For weeks, experts argued that the call would not be followed and that Mr. Öcalan would not fulfil its requirements. But none of those predictions came true, and the steps were taken. This is a matter of building trust and demonstrating sincerity. Our demand, proposal and expectation are clear: rather than waiting for assessments by the security bureaucracy, political authorities must take concrete steps towards a democratic solution. We are being very specific about this. There is a saying: 'Actions speak louder than words.'




Political authorities make statements in different ways almost every day. Of course, that is not a bad thing. It is positive that these statements reach society. But everywhere we go, people ask very clear and concrete questions: Why are no steps being taken? Why are our prisoners still behind bars? Why are sick prisoners still waiting to die in prison? Why can people still not return to their country? Why have the doors still not been opened? Why has the Peace and Political Participation Coordination Board still not been established? So far, no satisfactory or convincing answers have been given to any of these questions."




‘A new decision-making mechanism has been established above Parliament’s authority’




Meral Beştaş stated that making the implementation of the law dependent on the assessment and confirmation of security institutions undermined parliamentary authority and democratic oversight. She recalled that the DEM Party had previously objected to leaving the process to the discretion of the security bureaucracy.




Beştaş said: "The law is before the Grand National Assembly of Turkey. Ultimately, the legislative body represents the highest expression of the people's will. We are all represented there, as are all political parties. However, the process is being left to the discretion of the security bureaucracy. In a sense, Parliament is being stripped of its authority, creating a form of tutelage. We openly objected to this and, from the very first day, expressed our criticisms and pointed out the many shortcomings of the framework law. At the same time, we said that we supported it in order to open the door and make participation possible. But we will never accept its misuse. It is being used negatively and interpreted in ways that undermine its purpose.




The National Security Council decision has now created a situation in which a new decision-making mechanism has been established above Parliament's authority. We are saying that a commission must be established immediately, not only within the National Security Council but also within the Grand National Assembly of Turkey. Monitoring bodies consisting of representatives of civil democratic organisations, activists, women and young people should also oversee and monitor the process. 




However, by insisting that this responsibility belongs exclusively to the National Security Council, they are placing the security perspective above everything else. Article 6 of the Constitution is very clear: sovereignty belongs to the nation. Article 7 establishes that legislative authority belongs to Parliament. Of course, the National Security Council is also a constitutional institution. Its role requires a separate and broader discussion. However, this institution cannot be given the authority to make binding decisions that subject the implementation of a law passed by Parliament to particular security assessments.




We maintain that the implementation of the law must be subject to oversight based on objective criteria, governed by legal rules, and that decision-making processes must be transparent. A structure must be established to ensure mutual responsibility and accountability throughout the monitoring process. We believe this mechanism should oversee the process. 




Unfortunately, the proposed commission has still not been established. The Speaker of Parliament makes statements to the press on this issue almost every day, on various occasions. Yet visits to political parties have still not taken place. Uncertainty continues to be prolonged over the structure of the proposed body, the extent of representation within it and the responsibilities of other political parties.




This further increases criticism of the democratic process, undermines trust and raises questions about sincerity. These are legitimate concerns and justified criticisms."




‘The process is a matter of democratisation and law’




Meral Beştaş pointed out that the process was not limited to disarmament and the cessation of conflict. She emphasised the need to take steps concerning political prisoners, the right to hope, the appointment of trustees and the expansion of democratic political space.




Beştaş drew attention to the deadlock in the process and said: "I would like to emphasise that, at the stage we have reached, there is a serious deadlock and the process is being put on hold and deliberately prolonged. This process is not merely about laying down arms and ensuring an end to conflict. It is also a process of resolving political and legal problems through democratic means and building a democratic society.




The priorities include enacting democratic legislation, implementing existing laws, issuing decisions that secure people's freedom, releasing prisoners, implementing the rulings of the European Court of Human Rights (ECtHR) and ending the practice of appointing trustees. We could extend this list even further. Are we now waiting for a National Security Council decision to implement ECtHR rulings? Are we waiting for a National Security Council decision to release prisoners?




The parliamentary commission's report is extremely important. It was adopted unanimously. The report contains various recommendations, while legislative proposals and packages are also on the agenda. MPs from the governing party have also signed the report. It addresses women's rights, equality and many other issues. Yet the authorities are acting as though none of these matters had ever been discussed, acknowledged or read. There is an attitude of ignoring and obscuring these issues. We have repeatedly stated that this approach must change. Unfortunately, no steps have yet been taken in this regard.




There is also a political dimension to the issue. The legal and political dimensions must be distinguished from one another. The fact that Abdullah Öcalan, the principal interlocutor and political actor in the process, is still being held on Imrali, that his meetings are being obstructed and that the outcomes of these meetings are not being reflected across all aspects of the process constitutes a serious problem. The political consequences of this situation are very clear.




We have been discussing the legal dimension for years, so I do not want to repeat the same points. However, there are also political questions awaiting answers. Which journalists and academics will be involved in the process? Has the Peace and Conflict Coordination Board begun its work? We expect steps to be taken on these issues and the obstacles preventing Mr. Öcalan from playing his role to be removed. Yet there has still been no explanation.




The process is being presented as normal, and messages of determination are being issued. We are told that the process is important and that it concerns Turkey's most significant unresolved issue. However, these statements never go beyond broad expressions that everyone can interpret as they wish. Frankly, no one can disregard the connection between the Kurdish question and the question of democracy. This is a matter of democratisation, democratic integration and law. All these dimensions must be addressed together. Kurds want to live in this country as equal and free citizens, just like everyone else. The political, legal and administrative obstacles preventing this must be removed.




There is no basis for assuming that these issues concern only Kurdish society or the Kurdish movement, or that they are limited to expanding the space for democratic politics. It is impossible to achieve a lasting and positive solution without recognising the underlying causes of the problem."




‘The Kurdish question is not a security issue, but a matter of democratic rights’




Meral Beştaş stated that treating the Kurdish question solely as a security issue had led to demands for democratic rights, including the status of Kurds and education in their mother tongue, being excluded from discussions. She emphasised that these demands must be negotiated and guaranteed to achieve lasting peace.




Beştaş said: "First of all, this is not a security issue. Viewing the Kurdish people's struggle for existence solely as a security issue means ignoring the historical and political reality of the question. This is a matter of identity, equal citizenship, mother tongue, representation and democratic rights. Removing weapons from the equation is, of course, extremely important, but it does not in itself constitute a democratic solution. We need to be clear about this.




These demands are not new. As I mentioned earlier, education in the mother tongue, the free use of the mother tongue in public life, strengthening participation in democratic life, democratising electoral processes and ensuring equal citizenship are demands that have been voiced and fought for over many years. Lasting peace cannot be built by excluding them.




The question of political status is also an important part of this discussion. Establishing a democratic system in which Kurds can organise freely with their own identity, express their political will and have a say in local government is one of the essential demands. What needs to be done is to address these demands as matters of democratisation and law rather than treating them solely within a security framework.




There is no insurmountable barrier between security concerns and democratic rights and demands. On the contrary, guaranteeing democratic rights is one of the fundamental conditions for lasting peace. The path to a dignified peace lies not in postponing these demands, but in negotiating them and providing guarantees for them. Our fundamental approach is clear: politics must replace weapons, law must replace conflict, and equality must replace denial.




As you also pointed out in your question, the continuation of the security-oriented approach and the continued use of the language of the period of conflict mean that the process is perceived not as a new beginning, but as a continuation of the war. If we fail to define the problem correctly and develop our language accordingly, we will move further away from a solution.




There is an issue we have repeatedly raised in our speeches: we must build the language of peace. To achieve this, Kurds, the democratic public and society as a whole must remain determined and continue their struggle. Rather than approaching the issue through the concepts of terror and terrorism, we must develop a language that accurately defines the question and is based on democracy and peace. There is no alternative to struggling to change this language and build peace.




The greatest source of support in this regard is the peoples of Turkey. The peoples, particularly the Kurdish people, must express their demands, struggles, positions and objections loudly and clearly. They must organise around these demands and struggle together with the broadest possible sections of society."

title: Women’s conference in Ankara criticizes stagnation in the peace process
content:
The stalled peace process in Turkey and the responsibility of politicians and society to achieve a democratic solution to the Kurdish question dominated the second day of the women’s conference in Ankara. Discussions focused on the lack of concrete political steps, the unequal conditions surrounding negotiations with Abdullah Öcalan, and how women from different social and political backgrounds could work together to achieve lasting peace. Participants made it clear that while they regarded an end to the armed conflict as a crucial step forward, they did not consider it sufficient in itself to guarantee peace in society.




The conference, titled “Women Discuss the Future Side by Side,” was initiated by 80 women and opened on Saturday with more than 500 participants. On the second day, female politicians, academics, and activists gathered at the Chamber of Civil Engineers to discuss political responsibility for peace, the role of parliament, and opportunities for grassroots organizing.




Buldan warns of deadlock in the peace process




Pervin Buldan, a DEM Party MP and member of the Imralı delegation, recalled the failed peace negotiations between 2013 and 2015 and the subsequent ten years of armed conflict. She emphasized that the most significant achievement of both the previous and current talks was the protection of human lives. At the same time, she pointed to the unequal conditions under which the political actors involved were operating. While President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan and MHP leader Devlet Bahçeli are able to carry out their political duties freely, she said, Abdullah Öcalan is attempting to advance the process from a prison cell. She explicitly expressed her gratitude to him for his efforts.




However, Buldan expressed concern about the current state of the talks. T”he Imralı delegation last visited Öcalan on September 13. There has been no further meeting since that day. So, there is something of a deadlock. Overcoming this impasse should not be left solely to the political negotiators. Women in this room can decide today that we need peace. They can become an organized force that puts pressure on the government and the actors involved in the process to ensure that it continues,” she said.




Buldan also proposed establishing dedicated women’s committees within the structures responsible for overseeing and monitoring the peace process. She stressed that women must come together not only in conference halls but also in public squares and on the streets.




Criticism over the delayed implementation of the framework law




Gökçe Gökçen, an MP from the YENI Party, criticized the government’s approach so far. She emphasized that the Kurdish question and the democratization of Turkey were inseparably linked, arguing that limiting the process to disarmament alone would be insufficient. “One side says that this is exclusively a matter of security and therefore calls the entire process a ‘terror-free Turkey.’ We, on the other hand, speak of a ‘democratic Turkey,’” Gökçen stated.




She stressed that laying down arms was important but must be accompanied by democratic reforms. Lasting social peace, she argued, required equality to become a lived reality and public confidence in justice to grow.




Gökçen was particularly critical of the delays in implementing the framework law passed by parliament on August 10. She said the text of the law had been presented only at the last moment, without allowing for a broad political debate. Unlike other political groups, her party was not invited to participate in the discussions, she added.




“Distrust of the process is, in fact, distrust of the government,” Gökçen said. She argued that the government had had numerous opportunities to take confidence-building measures but had failed to do so. She stressed that making the implementation of the law dependent on a decision by the National Security Council (MGK), thereby postponing it indefinitely, was neither politically nor legally justifiable.




“Peace is too serious a matter to be left to men and governments”




Former HDP MP Filiz Kerestecioğlu emphasized society’s responsibility in the peace process. Peace negotiations, she argued, should not be treated as a technical matter reserved for political decision-makers. “Peace is too serious a matter to be left to men and governments. It is also too serious to be treated as a purely technical issue. Society must be convinced of the process and actively participate in shaping it,” Kerestecioğlu said.




Responding to the frequently asked question of how women could trust the government in such a process, she said: “We don’t trust the government at all. Nor do we have to. What matters is trusting ourselves. The question is: Where do we stand in this process?”




Using a photograph from Cizre, Kerestecioğlu recalled the curfews and military siege imposed on Kurdish cities in 2015. She recounted the story of a woman she had helped transport for medical treatment at the time. Rather than being able to rely on the support of other women, she had been forced to seek assistance from then-Education Minister Nabi Avcı. She described the experience as an example of the isolation in which many Kurdish women had been left during the attacks. “When we say that women stand side by side, we must also be able to understand and empathize with that loneliness,” Kerestecioğlu said.




Buldan: “We must not pit the suffering of mothers against one another”




Pervin Buldan also addressed the human consequences of the conflict. She displayed photographs of Ceylan Önkol and Eren Bülbül, two children who lost their lives under different circumstances in connection with the war in Kurdistan. “Ceylan’s mother and Eren’s mother shed the same tears. We must not pit the suffering of these two mothers against one another,” she said.




One could spend hours discussing the Roboski massacre, unsolved political murders, and the injustices suffered by the Kurdish population, Buldan said. At the same time, she added, it was necessary to acknowledge that the conflict had affected people from different segments of society. “The silence of the guns alone is not enough to build lasting peace. We also need democratization and freedoms,” she emphasized.




In Buldan’s view, a new constitution could only be drafted on the basis of a broad social consensus. The current constitution dates back to the 1980 military coup. However, she stressed that overcoming the present deadlock in the peace process must take priority.




Arzu Yılmaz: Peace process is the result of historical changes




Political scientist Arzu Yılmaz placed the current developments within a broader political context. She argued that the peace process had not emerged from a voluntary rapprochement between the Kurdish movement and the AKP government, but rather from changing historical and regional circumstances.




“After all, the Kurds did not choose to make peace with the AKP either. It was not a free choice. Rather, both sides found themselves in a historical situation in which change became inevitable,” Yılmaz said. In her assessment, the process was also driven by state interests. Faced with profound transformations, the state is attempting to prepare for necessary changes, minimize risks, and safeguard its own interests, she added.




Yılmaz pointed out that conventional political concepts and approaches were no longer sufficient to understand these developments. “The crucial question, therefore, is which social forces will be able to help shape the impending restructuring,” Yılmaz said and pointed to the widening gap between politics and society, as well as growing social inequality. “Whether the current changes will produce a new social contract benefiting the broader population will depend largely on the influence of the women’s movement and other social struggles,” she added.




Hatimoğulları calls for a broad peace alliance




DEM Party Co-Chair Tülay Hatimoğulları echoed these arguments, calling on women’s movements not to allow political and ideological differences to become obstacles to working together for peace.




“How can we women build a peace alliance despite all our differences? Women on the right and left, women who wear headscarves and those who do not, liberals, politically organized and unorganized women – how can we all come together to form an alliance for peace?” Hatimoğulları asked.




Rather than focusing exclusively on past shortcomings, she argued, participants should discuss what they could build and organize together in the future. For her, this was the central task of the conference.




Message from Figen Yüksekdağ in prison




The conference also received a message of support from imprisoned former HDP Co-Chair Figen Yüksekdağ. Her written message from Kandıra Women’s Prison was read aloud by journalist Gözde Şeker. Yüksekdağ drew attention to wars, violence, and growing uncertainty about the future. Under these circumstances, she emphasized, it was more important than ever to build a society based on peace, freedom, justice, and democratic rights.




“Cooperation among women can serve as a bridge that brings together and unites different social and political forces,” she stated. The women’s movement, she said, possessed the experience and capacity to mobilize people who had suffered oppression and injustice in the struggle for peace and a democratic society.




Actress Füsun Demirel, who was unable to attend in person, addressed the conference through a video message. She noted that while male-dominated politics was primarily concerned with who had won the peace, women were focused on how to shape a shared future after the violence had ended. She summed up her message with the words: “Peace is in our hands.”

title: Humanitarian conditions deteriorate in Washokani and Al-Talae camps
content:
The humanitarian conditions of displaced families living in the Washokani and Al-Talae camps in Syria’s Hesekê Governorate have further deteriorated following recent rainfall and flooding. The Serêkaniyê Displaced Persons Committee has called for urgent shelter assistance ahead of winter season and for the process of returning families to their hometowns to be expedited.




Speaking to Shafaq News, committee spokesperson Mahmud Cemîl said that the tents in both camps had deteriorated and could no longer provide adequate protection against rain, cold weather and extreme heat. Cemîl said the committee had been requesting support and new tents from humanitarian organisations for seven years, but these requests had not been adequately addressed.




Returns should accelerate




Cemîl said that displaced families were facing administrative delays and various obstacles in returning to their hometowns. He called on the Syrian government to expand organised return convoys and increase the number of families able to return.




Cemîl also urged the Syrian presidential delegation overseeing the return process, international organisations and the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR) to support efforts to accelerate returns before winter conditions make life in the camps even more difficult.

title: 7,000-year-old architectural model discovered in Soran
content:
The General Directorate of Antiquities and Cultural Heritage of the Kurdistan Region has announced a significant archaeological discovery at Banahîlk Hill in the Soran district, northeast of Erbil.




In a statement, the directorate said that a rare model of an ancient building's roofing system, dating back more than 7,000 years and belonging to the Halaf culture, had been discovered. Describing the find as a first in archaeological history, the statement noted that it demonstrates the advanced engineering and architectural skills of communities during that period.




The discovery was announced to the public at a press conference held on 28 October at the Scientific Research Centre of Soran University. The archaeological project was carried out in cooperation with the Soran Directorate of Antiquities and Culture, the Autonomous University of Barcelona (UAB) and Salahaddin University.




The Halaf culture, dating approximately from 6100 to 5100 BC, was influential mainly across the lands of Southern Kurdistan (Başûr), Western Kurdistan (Rojava) and Northern Kurdistan (Bakurê Kurdistan). Known for its distinctive pottery decorated with geometric patterns and animal motifs, this culture provides important archaeological evidence of the prehistoric history of Mesopotamia and the Near East.
