title: Özgür Sevgi Göral: France’s dilemmas also exist in Turkey - Part One
content:
Academic Özgür Sevgi Göral said that a strong voice had emerged against inequality in Paris, adding, "Reducing the revolt of the suburbs, which demands profound transformation, to presidential elections would dilute the movement's anger and enthusiasm." Göral said that all the dilemmas facing France were also present in Turkey.




The streets of Paris have witnessed some of the most intense social mobilisation of recent times. Protests that began in September, led by high school students, grew into a mass movement day by day.




ANF spoke to Özgür Sevgi Göral, who is currently in Paris and has participated in the demonstrations, about the historical foundations of the protests and their potential.




Academic Özgür Sevgi Göral emphasised that the protests were rooted in a historical accumulation of struggles, saying, "This history includes the inequalities created by racialised capitalism and the many different forms of violence it has spread throughout everyday life."  Göral stressed the importance of the struggle, saying, "The struggle truly is endless, and despite all the difficult conditions, millions of people around the world refuse to abandon the streets."




Göral argued that the protests should be understood less in relation to 1968 and more in the context of the political mobilisation and suburban uprisings that emerged in the 1970s and 1980s and continued strongly throughout the 2000s. Göral also warned that directing the anti-fascist stance solely towards the April 2027 presidential elections risked alienating young people from the suburbs in particular.




Göral also assessed what kind of political ground, language and methodology were needed today to address the Kurdish question. Göral emphasised the importance of convincing broad sections of society that the current process could provide a foundation for a shared life based on equality and freedom and said: "Since the state will not provide this foundation, it will have to be built by all movements for equality, freedom and liberation, particularly the Kurdish Freedom Movement, by drawing on their capacities and establishing the broadest possible alliances. In fact, all the dilemmas we have discussed in relation to France are also present in Turkey, although, of course, in different forms."




You also participated in the demonstrations in Paris. What were your observations on the streets? What were the differences between the official narrative and the situation on the ground?




The high school protests in Paris are actually rooted in a particular historical background. This history includes the inequalities created by racialised capitalism and the many different forms of violence it has spread throughout everyday life. The more immediate historical background to this movement includes the severe class inequalities experienced during last year's extreme heatwaves in Paris, which claimed thousands of lives, particularly in schools in the suburbs. Even when temperatures reached 40 degrees Celsius, secondary schools were not provided with fans. There are also the structural inequalities associated with Parcoursup, the university admissions system, which separates students attending privileged high schools from those attending schools in working-class neighbourhoods, and the experience of collapsing public services, including education and healthcare, in suburban neighbourhoods.




The mobilisation began after the teachers' strike held in Paris and its suburbs on 29 September, which demanded greater public funding for public services. One of my favourite slogans, "The suburbs influence Paname, and Paname influences the world" (Paname is another name for Paris), resonated strongly. The blockades of high schools, which first began in Seine-Saint-Denis, gained strong support first in Paris's privileged high schools and then in higher education institutions. Saturday demonstrations in Paris, led by youth movements, attracted enormous crowds. Despite the extraordinary level of police violence, participation did not decline but continued to increase. According to figures from the General Confederation of Labour (CGT), 250,000 people participated in the Paris demonstration on 24 October, while more than 800,000 people joined demonstrations across France.




From the outset, the official narrative framed the wave of protests within a security paradigm. It categorically refused to discuss the profound structures of inequality highlighted by the demonstrations, the class, racial and ethno-political hierarchies that racialised capitalism has spread much more intensely throughout the suburbs of Paris, but also in the city centre, or to recognise the issue as a social problem. Instead, it described the demonstrations in terms of "protester violence" and refused to acknowledge police violence, declaring that police officers faced the risk of death because of the protesters. Moreover, it called on everyone to condemn this violence, which it characterised primarily as "damaging public property, looting shops and destroying everything." It introduced a political discourse that is fundamentally right-wing, confines social and political problems within a security paradigm and erases their actual substance. This discourse calls on everyone to express remorse and submit to this security-oriented approach. It also seeks to label those who refuse to comply as "undesirable" or "dangerous" protesters, thereby legitimising the police violence directed against them. This appeal was partially effective. All the centrist parties were quick to condemn protester violence without a moment's hesitation.




Elements of the reformist or parliamentary left that stand further to the left, such as La France Insoumise (LFI, France Unbowed), partly challenged this language but also adopted aspects of it, albeit selectively. The government therefore pursued an aggressive political strategy of separating acceptable protesters and their demands from those it considered unacceptable. The protesters on the streets, however, are not a single bloc. They consist of different groups. This discourse had little significant impact on those coming from the suburbs, who experience the fundamental violence produced by racialised capitalism every day in their bodies, their lives and their political imaginations. Other groups partly resisted this discourse and partly acted through certain compromises. Nevertheless, among the groups taking to the streets, opposition to this narrative appears stronger for the time being.




How would you describe the profile of the students taking to the streets? Are their demands limited to local policies, or are you seeing a broader critique of the system and concerns about a future without prospects?




I can only answer this question in relation to the situation in Paris. From what I have observed, the leading group consisted of young people living in the suburbs. Young people from Saint-Denis, Aulnay-sous-Bois and Seine-Saint-Denis raised a powerful voice against the inequalities they experience. The blockades of high schools and the erection of barricades began there. These students constitute the first group within the movement. They face enormous inequalities not only in their schools but also in their homes, the public services they rely on, and the lives they are building both today and for the future. There are currently three million millionaires in France, yet in that same country, one in five children cannot eat three meals a day because of the class inequalities they experience. This is the reality of life for young people in the suburbs of Paris. Therefore, what mobilised this group was both the conditions in their high schools and a broader anti-capitalist anger. I believe this is essentially the group that offers the broadest critique of the system and expresses the strongest reaction and anger against racialised capitalism, even though it does not have a comprehensive anti-capitalist programme or a strong political organisation.




The wave of protests subsequently spread to high schools in Paris, including the prestigious schools known for their privileges. Universities and higher education institutions then joined the solidarity demonstrations. For this second group, I think the specific demands concerning high schools, namely greater public funding, better facilities and the abolition of Parcoursup, the university admissions system, played a more prominent role. Of course, the immediate consequences of capitalism and the brutal violence it produces, particularly through the climate crisis and class inequalities, also feature in this group's political discourse. However, it differs somewhat from the strong emphasis of the suburban movement and its repertoire of political action, which at times includes self-defence against the police. Nevertheless, leading figures within this group also expressed the need for a break with the existing system and for a left capable of organising a broader programme of transformation. This second group became the more visible face of the protests, particularly through its appearances on television programmes and its prominent presence at demonstrations.




Over the past two weeks, the Yellow Vests (Gilets Jaunes) have also begun participating in the Saturday demonstrations. This group encompasses different political tendencies, including activists who maintain links with left-wing groups as well as others who hold right-wing or even racist views, although the latter are increasingly in the minority. The issue of police violence is what holds these three groups together.




How did protesters on the streets respond to the violence and the methods of police intervention?




First, let me provide some figures illustrating the extent of state violence. As of 15 October 2026, the Ministry of Justice reported that a total of 7,950 people had been detained, 85 per cent of whom were minors. According to historian Vincent Lemire's calculations, this figure exceeds the total number of detentions recorded over an entire year during the Yellow Vests (Gilets Jaunes) movement, when 6,730 people were detained.




As I mentioned earlier, the streets do not consist of a single, homogeneous group. Generally speaking, although everyone participating in the protests opposed framing the issue as a security problem, the political language and radical content of that opposition differed between groups. For young people living in the suburbs, police violence has a long and deeply rooted history. The illegitimacy of this violence, which has made their lives a living hell, is much more apparent to them. Moreover, they understand this violence as part of a broader critique of the system and capitalism.




At this point, I would like to briefly discuss the history of this violence, particularly in the suburbs. Police violence is deeply embedded in everyday life in these urban areas. It not only continually deepens segregation in schools but also creates a broader experience of social and ethnic-racial discrimination. Here, class and race, or racialised categories, are intertwined. Children from working-class communities living in the suburbs, particularly Black and Arab children, experience both racialised violence and class-based violence in forms that are interconnected and reinforce one another. The state describes political mobilisation in these areas as "urban violence" (violence urbaine). Although young people living there have been French citizens for generations, they are not regarded as genuine citizens. Discussions about the suburbs are consistently linked to immigration and racialised. Of course, there is also a large population of poor migrants living in the suburbs. However, even young people whose families have held French citizenship for four generations are described as "French on paper" and told that they are not truly French. This language of French racism also finds widespread acceptance in mainstream discourse. Class-based violence operates alongside widespread and deeply entrenched patterns of racism, including anti-Muslim racism.




Research in this field has shown that the term "urban violence" emerged in the 1990s following the Mas-du-Taureau uprisings in Vaulx-en-Velin. According to many researchers, the term serves to politically discredit protests and political struggles by reducing them to acts of violence and categorising those acts as "vandalism". For example, Didier Fassin, who researched the Anti-Crime Brigade (Brigade Anti-Criminalité, BAC) in Bobigny, Seine-Saint-Denis, argues that the category of "urban violence" serves to legitimise a state of exception that has become routine in the suburbs. Police violence, particularly violence used to suppress uprisings, is legitimised through this framework. On 6 December 2018, during the Yellow Vests movement, clashes broke out between police and high school students at Saint-Exupéry High School in Mantes-la-Jolie. The students were protesting the government's education reforms, including the Parcoursup system and changes to the baccalaureate examination. Police detained 151 students aged between 12 and 21 in a mass operation and forced them to kneel in the mud for hours with their hands held behind their heads. The incident came to light when footage recorded by a police officer, who could be heard saying, "Now that's a well-behaved class," circulated widely on social media. For young people from the suburbs and working-class neighbourhoods, neither police violence nor the struggle against the unequal practices of capitalism is anything new. Therefore, rather than viewing their opposition to police violence as a reaction limited to the present moment, we must understand it as today's manifestation of resistance to a deeply entrenched practice.




What are the similarities and differences between the events taking place in Paris and the youth protests of 1968?




The most important difference between May 1968 in France and the current wave of protests is that the youth movements of 1968 were accompanied by a powerful wave of working-class strikes. Today, trade unions are not a force standing behind the youth movement or advancing alongside it, and the movement is not developing in conjunction with a powerful wave of general strikes. The General Confederation of Labour (CGT) has called for a strike on 5 November, but that is all for now. Beyond this, although student unions in particular are involved in the protests, it is difficult to speak of a broader wave of strikes or calls for strikes.




On the other hand, I believe it is more appropriate to understand this movement in relation to the political mobilisation and suburban uprisings that emerged in the 1970s and 1980s and continued strongly throughout the 2000s, rather than comparing it primarily with 1968. Working-class neighbourhoods, known as the suburbs, have served as laboratories for the two main elements of what we might call the doctrine of "maintaining public order": managing and controlling the masses, and police violence. For example, the Flash-Ball, the predecessor of the LBD (Defence Ball Launcher), which is widely used in today's demonstrations and causes permanent injuries and disabilities among young people, was introduced throughout the national police force in 2002 at the initiative of then Interior Minister Nicolas Sarkozy, primarily for use in the suburbs to suppress uprisings. Consider the 2005 uprising, which is also familiar to the public in Turkey.




In Clichy-sous-Bois, a suburb of Paris, two young people, Zyed Benna, aged 17, and Bouna Traoré, aged 15, were electrocuted after hiding in an electrical substation while fleeing a police identity check. The suburban uprising that followed lasted three weeks. The government declared a state of emergency under a law dating back to 1955, and more than 4,000 people were detained. The statements made by then Interior Minister Nicolas Sarkozy, who said he would clean these neighbourhoods with a high-pressure Kärcher washer and described young people from the suburbs as "rabble" (racaille), remain central elements in the memory of that uprising.




In 2023, the killing of 17-year-old Nahel Merzouk, of Algerian and Moroccan descent, who was shot at close range by a police officer during a traffic stop in the Paris suburb of Nanterre, triggered another major uprising, particularly as footage of the incident spread rapidly on social media. The demonstrations were not confined to Paris. Just as they have today, they spread to major cities such as Marseille, Lyon and Lille. As in the current protests, the demonstrators were very young. The anger of young people from the suburbs targeted not only police buildings but also other symbols of the established order, including municipal buildings and schools. It would therefore be more appropriate to understand the current wave of protests, particularly its initial phase and the anger it contains against racialised capitalism, in relation to this history of uprisings.

title: İpek Er’s mother: My daughter was killed a second time
content:
“My daughter was killed a second time today.” With these words, Hikmet Kılınç, the mother of Kurdish woman İpek Er, who died in 2020, protested the recent acquittal of former gendarmerie officer Musa Orhan at a women’s conference in Ankara. Six years after her daughter’s death, she has leveled serious accusations against state officials and announced her determination to continue her fight for justice all the way to the European Court of Human Rights (ECtHR).




The protest follows a ruling issued on October 22 by a criminal court in Batman. Musa Orhan, who was sentenced to ten years in prison in 2021 for a serious sexual assault against İpek Er, was acquitted of the charge of incitement to suicide in a separate trial. According to Kılınç, the decision represents another setback in her years-long struggle to secure legal accountability for her daughter’s death.




Addressing more than 500 participants at the “Women Discuss the Future Side by Side” conference, Kılınç recounted her experiences since her daughter’s death. She accused state authorities of exploiting her hopes for justice and attempting to exert political pressure on her. “For six years, they told me: If you stay away from the Kurdish parties, we will ensure justice for your daughter. title: Shengal People’s Council call for the recognition of the city’s special status
content:
The Shengal People’s Council issued a statement regarding the democratic integration process underway in the city. The statement, which also marked World Kobanê Day on November 1, recalled that both Shengal and Kobanê were besieged by ISIS militants in 2014 and that a new phase of struggle had begun in both Rojava and Shengal after 12 years of resistance.




The Council welcomed the democratic integration process, describing it as the first time in more than a thousand years that a state had recognized the will of the Yazidi community and announced an agreement reached with the freely chosen representatives of the Yazidi people.




The Council further stated that democratic integration in Shengal encompassed not only the YBŞ-YJŞ and Êzîdxan Asayiş, but also all institutions of the Yazidi community.




“The integration of military forces into Iraq’s security institutions is not a project imposed from outside, but a process that has developed through the will of our people and guarantees the preservation of our achievements and lasting security for our community. Those who seek to portray this as a threat are themselves the ones attempting to profit from our community’s suffering and leave Shengal defenseless once again,” the statement said.




The Council pointed out that Shengal has been classified as a disputed territory for 23 years, yet the problems facing the Yazidi community remain unresolved. “We see addressing these historical and social issues together with the central government as the first step in this process,” it added.




The statement emphasized that the issue of Shengal concerns an entire community and its faith, and therefore cannot be reduced to a single armed force, nor can a solution be expected from any one force alone. It stressed the need to address the Shengal issue within the framework of the Iraqi Constitution and in cooperation with the Iraqi Federal Government.




Recalling that the Yazidi people have never accepted any agreement reached without regard for their will, the statement continued: “A genuine solution requires recognition of Shengal’s special status and local administration, as well as guarantees for our rights to self-governance and self-defense. These are the legitimate and natural rights of the Yazidi people. Shengal, the faith center of the Yazidi people, cannot be governed or protected against the will of the Yazidi community. We believe that a lasting solution lies in local self-government, and we demand recognition of this will. Our struggle for the recognition of local self-government will continue.”




The Council called on all relevant parties and individuals, particularly the KDP leadership, to respect the will of the Yazidi community and act accordingly: “The Yazidi cause is both a national and an international issue. No force or party has the right to downplay or distort this reality. They have attempted to frame the Shengal issue around whether or not Yazidis are Kurdish. This is a deliberate distortion and an agenda designed to obscure the truth. Through such agendas, they seek to divert attention from the will of the Yazidi community, create issues that do not serve the interests of the Yazidi people, and distract us from our fundamental demands.”




The statement further called on all Yazidi parties, organizations, women, and young people to set aside their differences and unite under one umbrella.




Amid these developments, the statement said, the 12-year period following the genocide against the Yazidis cannot be assessed without acknowledging the efforts of Kurdish leader Abdullah Öcalan and the Kurdish Freedom Movement.




“They came to our aid when we had been forgotten and saved our community from the most brutal genocide of the century. We have reached this stage through the philosophy of a free society. Today, the People’s Council, YBŞ, YJŞ, and all Yazidi institutions are products of these ideas and this philosophy. Following Leader Öcalan’s initiation of the democratic society process and development of the democratic integration project, negotiations with Iraq began. The stage we have reached today is the result of these efforts and initiatives. We call on all friends of the Yazidi people to continue supporting this process and contribute to a democratic solution,” the statement concluded.

title: The Kurdistan Region’s experience of government – III
content:
In the previous part of our series, we examined the common causes of government formation crises that have recurred in the Kurdistan Region over the past three decades, as well as the election process of 20 October 2024. This part examines the demands put forward by the Kurdistan Democratic Party (KDP) and the Patriotic Union of Kurdistan (PUK) in negotiations, the institutional vacuum created by the failure to form a government and the price the people are paying for it.




The KDP's demands




Iraqi media reported that the negotiating delegations of the two parties reached an agreement on 4 February 2025 on a draft joint government programme comprising nine sections and 15 articles. The programme covered parliament, finance, foreign relations, relations between Erbil (Hewlêr) and Baghdad, the peshmerga, energy and the judiciary. However, negotiations over the distribution of government positions lagged behind agreement on the programme.




The KDP's offer expanded over time. In April 2025, the PUK was offered only the ministries of Peshmerga Affairs and Finance. On 6 November 2025, however, the KDP announced that it had offered the PUK the parliamentary speakership, the vice-presidency of the Kurdistan Region, the deputy premiership, eight or nine ministries and "influential positions" within the security institutions.




Three issues remained outside the scope of the offer. A KDP representative announced on 8 October 2025 that the party would not hand over the Ministry of Interior to the PUK and would not negotiate on the matter. The KDP also refused to negotiate over the Security Council, which oversees the KDP's Parastin intelligence agency and the PUK's Zanyari intelligence agency, remaining under Masrour Barzani's authority. Masrour Barzani's position as prime minister and Nechirvan Barzani's position as President of the Kurdistan Region were likewise excluded from negotiations.




The KDP insisted that cabinet positions should be distributed according to the number of parliamentary seats held by each party. Masrour Barzani said in June 2025 that his party was "making serious efforts to form a government based on the majority". The KDP began adopting a more conciliatory tone from August 2026 onwards.




The PUK's demands




The PUK demanded the ministries of Interior and Natural Resources, the chancellorship of the Security Council and a written definition of the deputy prime minister's powers in April 2025. In the following months, its demands took shape around authority over either the Ministry of Interior or the Security Council, a senior executive position and the headship of the Presidency Office of the Kurdistan Region. The KDP also rejected the PUK's demand for the headship of the Presidency Office.




PUK officials stressed that the dispute was not about the number of positions. Deputy Prime Minister Qubad Talabani said on 31 May 2026 that the problem concerned the "philosophy of partnership". The PUK declared that it continued to insist on a 50–50 division of power and genuine partnership, and that it would not join the government until it was certain that the "mistakes of the past" would not be repeated.




The PUK's second demand concerned the decentralisation of powers. Qubad Talabani cited disparities in public services between Duhok and Germiyan, calling for greater authority to be granted to governors and mayors.




The PUK's position became more flexible in the autumn of 2026. Bafel Talabani addressed the KDP in a speech on 12 October, saying: "The PUK does not want to govern without you, nor can it govern without you."




The PUK-New Generation alliance




Bafel Talabani and New Generation Movement leader Shaswar Abdulwahid signed an alliance agreement on 2 July 2026. The agreement reportedly provided for the adoption of a regional budget law, full transparency over oil revenues, independent financial oversight, the reimbursement of part of the deducted salaries and marriage loans for young people. However, the agreement contained no provision specifying which party would hold the premiership.




The alliance with New Generation gave the PUK a combined strength of 38 parliamentary seats at the negotiating table, but did not commit New Generation to joining the government. On 24 June 2026, New Generation leader Shaswar Abdulwahid said that the next prime minister should come from the alliance. However, on 19 September, he announced that no discussions had taken place regarding participation in the government.




The deadlock between the two parties




Reports in August 2025 indicated that an agreement had been reached on the general framework. According to some sources, the proposed arrangement would leave the presidency, premiership, Ministry of Interior and Ministry of Natural Resources with the KDP, while the PUK would receive deputy positions with expanded powers, the parliamentary speakership, the ministries of Finance and Peshmerga Affairs. However, neither political party officially confirmed these reports.




Four issues were subsequently reported to remain unresolved: the powers of deputy officeholders, the choice between seat-based distribution and a 50–50 division of power, recognition of the PUK-New Generation bloc, and control over the Ministry of Interior and the Security Council. Statements from the two parties also contradicted each other. The KDP announced on 16 September 2026 that an agreement had been reached, while the PUK declared four days later that no agreement existed. The Kurdistan Islamic Union (Yekgirtû), Kurdistan Islamic Group (Komele) and National Stance Movement (Helwêst), which together hold 14 parliamentary seats, announced that they would not participate in any delegation formed by the two parties.




A parliament that cannot convene




Parliament has not convened since its inaugural session on 2 December 2024. Its leadership has not been elected, parliamentary committees have not been established and not a single law has been passed. Oversight institutions have also remained ineffective. Nevertheless, MPs continue to receive salaries for duties they are not actively performing.




The Kurdistan Region has not had a budget law approved by parliament since 2013. Expenditure is determined according to monthly salary transfers from Baghdad. The terms of the Commission of Integrity, the Board of Supreme Audit and the Human Rights Commission have expired without being renewed. Without a functioning parliament to question ministers, discrepancies in public spending also remain unanswered.




Institutions and commissions with expired mandates




The Council of Ministers' four-year term expired on 10 July 2023, while the mandate of the Kurdistan Region Presidency expired in June 2023. On 24 September 2023, Iraq's Federal Supreme Court dissolved the provincial councils that had remained in office since the 2005 elections. Municipal council elections have not been held since the early 2000s. The regional electoral commission was stripped of its authority, and the most recent elections were administered by Iraq's electoral commission. The Ministry of Natural Resources has been headed by an acting minister since May 2022, while the Minister of Finance submitted a resignation letter in October 2026.




The New Generation Movement applied to Iraq's Federal Supreme Court on 9 July 2026, requesting that the ninth cabinet be recognised as a caretaker government responsible only for day-to-day affairs from 10 July 2023 onwards. The case also includes a request to suspend oil, gas and electricity contracts signed after that date. The court postponed the hearing until 26 October 2026.




Thus, among the institutions whose mandates have expired, the only elected body still formally in office is the parliament, which remains unable to convene.




De facto dual administration




The unification of 2006 brought the ministries under a single administration, but the dual structure in revenue collection, security and local government remained intact. Asayish security forces and peshmerga units continue to operate along party lines, while the Parastin and Zanyari intelligence agencies function outside formal government oversight.




Non-oil revenues from Sulaymaniyah, Halabja, Raperin and Germiyan have been monitored through a separate portal established in July 2022. Each province covers its own salary shortfall.




The division within the security sector has also persisted. On 21 September 2026, the 80th and 70th peshmerga units were reorganised into the First and Second Regional Commands under the Ministry of Peshmerga Affairs. The failure to form a government is effectively reviving the dual administrative structure that existed between 1996 and 2006, without any formal declaration of division.




The salary crisis with Baghdad




Baghdad's policy of paying salaries through federal banks has progressed differently in the two areas. In December 2024, registration in the "My Account" system stood at 96 per cent in Erbil and Duhok, compared with 35 per cent in Sulaymaniyah and Halabja. Salaries for November and December 2025 were not paid. Salaries for June 2026 were paid after a 50-day delay, with deductions totalling 120 billion dinars.




Representation in Baghdad has also become divided. Nizar Amedi of the PUK was elected President of Iraq on 11 April 2026 despite a boycott by the KDP. The KDP subsequently boycotted the federal parliament. Baghdad's approach amid this institutional vacuum is being interpreted as an attempt to deal with the Kurdistan Region through individual provinces and parties rather than through a single regional authority.




Livelihood, public services and migration




Salary increases for public sector employees have been frozen since 2016. Two months' salaries went unpaid in 2025, and each employee has accumulated between 20 million and 100 million dinars in outstanding payments. The minimum pension in the Kurdistan Region is 220,000 dinars, compared with 500,000 dinars under federal law.




Economic losses worsened with the outbreak of the war involving Iran on 28 February 2026. The price of a cylinder of cooking gas rose from 8,500 dinars to between 30,000 and 33,000 dinars, while wholesale vegetable prices doubled. The Kurdistan Regional Government spokesperson put the cost of the war up to April at 1.5 trillion dinars. Public sector recruitment has been suspended since July 2024. The appointment of 775 unemployed doctors was not completed until September 2025.




Essential public services have also faced disruption. Baghdad reportedly supplied only half of the required medicines. A teachers' boycott in early 2025 prevented 600,000 pupils at 3,000 schools from attending classes for two months. An attack on the Khor Mor gas field on 26 November 2025 reduced electricity generation by approximately 80 per cent. The field has been attacked at least nine times since 2023, and four workers were killed in an attack in April 2024.




Migration has become one of the most visible consequences of the crisis. More than 148,000 people are reported to have migrated to Europe over the past decade, while 414 people lost their lives along the way.




Pressure on women and the press




Women have paid an even heavier price for the institutional vacuum. According to official figures, 44 women were killed in 2022 and at least 30 in 2023. The Kurdistan Regional Government stopped publishing statistics in 2024. In September 2025, the Council of Ministers instructed institutions not to disclose these cases to the public. A proposal to amend the domestic violence law has been awaiting parliamentary consideration since 2015.




Pressure on the press has also increased. The Metro Center recorded 315 violations against journalists in 2025, compared with 182 in 2024. Iraq fell to 162nd place in the 2026 World Press Freedom Index published by Reporters Without Borders.




After three decades




Nine cabinets have been formed in the Kurdistan Region since 1992, but their formation has never been governed by a constitution. Governments were established through agreements signed between the two parties, and as these agreements weakened, the time required to form a cabinet increased from 46 days to more than 720 days. The causes of the crises have remained unchanged: who controls the revenues, who commands the armed forces and intelligence agencies, and how the two parties are represented in relation to each other. The current deadlock also appears to centre on the Ministry of Interior and the Security Council.




The failure to form a government in the Kurdistan Region has become not an exception but a normal feature of the system. Frozen salaries, school boycotts, medicine shortages, suppressed protests, the migration of young people and the concealment of data on the killing of women are all consequences of the same institutional vacuum. Meanwhile, the federal judiciary has become the principal authority determining the Kurdistan Region's electoral system, salary payments and oil revenues.




The steps needed in the Kurdistan Region are concrete: convening parliament and electing its leadership, adopting the budget law that has not been passed since 2013, paying withheld salaries, removing the peshmerga, Asayish and intelligence agencies from party control, putting the constitution that has been pending since 2009 to a referendum, holding provincial council elections for the first time since 2014, and resuming the publication of data on the killing of women.




The cases scheduled to be heard by Iraq's Federal Supreme Court on 26 October 2026 will mark the next stage in the process of determining the legal status of parliament and the ninth cabinet. The meeting expected between the KDP and the PUK in early November will show whether the parties can reach an agreement before then.

title: Kurdish doctoral student imprisoned in Iran
content:
Matin Faramarzpour, a Kurdish cultural activist and doctoral student in philosophy at the University of Tabriz, has been sent to Mahabad Prison to serve a six-month sentence for “propaganda against the state”.




The Kurdistan Human Rights Network (KHRN) has reported that Faramarzpour, who is from Mahabad, was arrested on 28 October after appearing in response to a summons at the Enforcement of Judgements Office of the city’s Public and Revolutionary Prosecutor’s Office, and transferred to prison.




On 8 July, security forces violently arrested Faramarzpour in Mahabad’s Sheikh Shaltout Park, and he was provisionally released on bail several weeks later.




Branch One of the Islamic Revolutionary Court of Mahabad subsequently sentenced him to six months in prison on charges of “propaganda against the state.”

content:
Mithat Sancar, a member of the Imrali Delegation of the Peoples’ Equality and Democracy Party (DEM Party), made remarks on current developments during an interview with Medya Haber TV.




Stating that the Peace and Democratic Society Process had experienced a slowdown over the past two months, Sancar said that following the steps taken by the Kurdish Movement, the delegation needed to visit Imrali. He explained that the committee tasked with working with Abdullah Öcalan was the Peace and Politicisation Committee, emphasising that Öcalan's coordination was essential for the process to advance.




Saying that the process could not move forward through one-sided expectations and demands, Sancar stressed that the state needed to abandon its rigid stance in order to overcome the main obstacles.

Stating that Öcalan's aim was to unite the Kurds as a political subject, Sancar added: “Mr Öcalan has moved to the new facility built on Imrali. His agreement to move there should lead to an acceleration of the process.”

title: Turkish soldiers torture three women from Rojava at the border
content:
Turkish soldiers reportedly detained and assaulted three women at the border between Rojava and Northern Kurdistan, confiscating their money and personal belongings. According to the ANHA news agency, the incident occurred near the village of Qereman in Dirbêsiyê as the women attempted to cross the border from Rojava into Northern Kurdistan.




According to ANHA, the three women were stopped and tortured by Turkish border guards. No information is currently available about their whereabouts or state of health. No further details about the incident have been released so far.




Reports of mistreatment, violent pushbacks, and assaults by Turkish border forces continue to emerge along the Turkish-Syrian border. Human rights organizations have documented cases for years in which people attempting to cross the border have been beaten, shot at, or robbed of their personal belongings. Those particularly affected are people trying to cross the border due to war, persecution, or economic hardship.

title: ‘The National Security Council decision must be overcome and Mr. Öcalan’s status clarified’
content:
The peace process in Turkey, launched following the Call for Peace and a Democratic Society announced publicly by Abdullah Öcalan on 27 February 2025, approaches its second year.  As part of the process, the Law on Strengthening National Solidarity and Social Integration was adopted by the Grand National Assembly of Turkey on 10 August 2026, with 467 votes in favour. The bill stipulates that certain provisions could be implemented only after assessments by security institutions and confirmation of those assessments through a decision by the National Security Council (MGK).




The Turkish government’s failure to take concrete steps toward legal and political reforms as part of the peace and democratic society process is fueling growing debate and concern about the future of the process. Despite the steps taken by the Kurdish Freedom Movement since the beginning of the process, the state’s failure to fulfill its responsibilities remains one of the obstacles to building mutual trust and advancing a democratic solution.




DEM Party MP Sabahat Erdoğan Sarıtaş spoke to ANF about the current stage of the peace and democratic society process, the government’s responsibilities, and the steps that need to be taken.




‘The barrier posed by the National Security Council decision must be overcome without delay’




Criticizing the state for making the process dependent on administrative and security-oriented decision-making mechanisms, Sarıtaş stressed that the National Security Council (MGK) decision should not become an obstacle to progress. She stated:




“The fundamental issue that needs to be addressed here is not so much the institutional role of the MGK itself, but rather the fact that progress in the process has become dependent on an administrative and security-oriented decision-making mechanism. Of course, the state will have a timetable for the process, but this timetable should serve to advance and accelerate the ongoing process rather than hold it back. Over the past two years, the state and the government have largely played a role in slowing down the process. The perception that the steps the state needs to take are being held up by MGK decisions is becoming increasingly widespread in society. Therefore, we continue to emphasize on every platform that the barrier posed by the MGK decision must be overcome without delay.




For the peace processes to advance, the steps taken by the parties must build mutual trust and produce tangible results. When the steps taken by one party fail to elicit a response from the other, serious problems arise regarding the sustainability of the process. The announcements made by the leadership of the Kurdish Freedom Movement regarding their steps- such as the dissolution of its organizational structure, the destruction of weapons, and the withdrawal of armed forces from Turkish territory- are significant in terms of the stage the process has reached. These statements emphasized that the strategy of armed struggle against Turkey had been brought to an end and that democratic political struggle had been adopted as the guiding approach.




Following all these steps, the state’s responsibility is to clarify the legal and political conditions of the process, make implementation mechanisms operational, and take concrete decisions that will enable the transition to a new phase. One of the most important stages in achieving a final resolution in conflict resolution processes is the taking of reciprocal steps. When the parties adopt an approach based on reciprocity, it helps foster hope and support for a solution within society. Otherwise, confidence in the process weakens among the parties, particularly on the Kurdish side.




In short, the state has already delayed considerably in taking the concrete steps required of it. At this point, it must take the necessary steps urgently, without making any further excuses, to ensure the success of the process.”




‘The Kurdish Freedom Movement has taken the steps required of it’




Drawing attention to the commitment demonstrated and the steps taken by the Kurdish Freedom Movement since the beginning of the process, Sabahat Erdoğan Sarıtaş continued:




“The Kurdish Freedom Movement has fully implemented all the steps it committed to from the very beginning of the process. After fifty years, it has clearly demonstrated its determination to change and transform its methods of struggle and resistance. Trusting in Mr. Abdullah Öcalan’s paradigm and his ability to bring about a solution, the movement’s leadership made its decisions within a very short period and implemented them just as swiftly.




At the current stage, the movement has dissolved itself, laid down its arms, and completely withdrawn from Turkish territory. It is only natural that it should expect to see a concrete response to these steps. Likewise, the state must demonstrate signs that it is prepared to change its approach to the Kurdish question and undergo its own transformation in the process of resolving it. It can demonstrate this through the steps it takes and its approach to the process.




For example, we do not yet know how prepared the state is for the return of those who have been in the mountains, which is one of the most critical stages of the process. However, this requires comprehensive and realistic legislation. The relevant legal framework must also include provisions guaranteeing the security of returning individuals in every respect. Of course, this does not mean that everything can be accomplished in a single step or through a single law.




The foundational law passed by parliament last summer can be considered the beginning of this process. Mr. Öcalan’s words, ‘A journey of a thousand kilometers begins with a single step,’ perfectly capture the essence of the situation. That foundational law was the first step on this path—the legal path—and further steps must follow.”




‘Concrete steps strengthen trust’




Emphasizing that trust in peace processes cannot be maintained through statements alone and that messages must be backed by concrete action, Sabahat Erdoğan Sarıtaş said the state’s failure to take action has created uncertainty within society. Stressing the importance of implementing legal and political measures without delay for the future of the process, Sarıtaş stated:




“In peace processes, trust is not something that automatically endures once it has been established. Maintaining and strengthening trust requires that words be backed by action, that the parties fulfill their obligations, and that emerging problems be addressed in a timely manner. The state’s delay in taking the necessary steps is raising questions within society, particularly among those who have expectations regarding support for the process.




The concept of ‘concrete steps’ is, in a sense, the backbone of conflict resolution processes. Indeed, processes that lack such steps tend to follow an uncertain course. The state’s failure to take concrete action over the past two years has created an atmosphere of uncertainty surrounding the process. It is within the state’s power to dispel this uncertainty and strengthen public trust and support.




Since the peace and democratic society process began, it has actually been fairly clear what responsibilities each side bears. Even before the process began, Mr. Öcalan stated, ‘If the necessary conditions are established, I have the theoretical and practical capacity to move this process from a framework of conflict and violence onto a legal and political footing.’ Despite the state’s extremely slow pace in taking action, Mr. Öcalan has accomplished what he said he would do over the past two years.




At this stage, for us to be able to say that the process has now entered its political and legal phase, it must proceed on a sound footing, and the parties must have equal conditions for democratic negotiations. However, Mr. Öcalan’s status has still not been clarified. This is another factor deepening uncertainty and mistrust. It also demonstrates that the state has yet to fulfill this aspect of its responsibilities.”




‘Mr. Öcalan’s status must be clarified’




Stressing that Abdullah Öcalan’s role and status must be clearly defined for the process to advance on a political and legal footing, Sabahat Erdoğan Sarıtaş continued:




“Mr. Öcalan’s position that ‘We are committed to democratic politics’ remains valid to this day, despite all the difficult circumstances. On the other hand, when we look at the state, its actions over the past two years show that it still lacks a strategic plan or program for resolving the Kurdish question. What we see instead are signs of a predominantly tactical approach.




For example, while the bodies established to ensure the smooth progress of the process are expected to make clearer and more effective statements and take concrete steps, we often witness the state attempting to communicate its position through political advisers. The periodic statements made by the chief adviser to the president are the clearest example of this. This naturally brings us to the questions of who is recognized as a negotiating counterpart and what status they hold. Therefore, the relevant body must now formally declare that Mr. Öcalan will serve as the Coordinator for Peace and Political Transition.”




‘The state’s language must be geared toward peace and a solution’




Emphasizing the importance of all sectors, from state officials and political parties to the media and civil society organizations, adopting an approach focused on peace and a solution, Sabahat Erdoğan Sarıtaş stated:




“One of the most important aspects of such processes is the language and terminology used. If you have decided to resolve a prolonged period of violence through political and legal means, this also requires changing and updating your terminology to bring it into line with the spirit of the process. Therefore, it is crucial that everyone, from the highest levels of the state to political parties, the media, and civil society organizations, use language oriented toward peace and a solution. Unfortunately, we can say that the state has also fallen short in this regard so far.




The responsibilities of the state and the government are clear. The MGK approval we mentioned earlier, Mr. Öcalan’s status, accelerating legal reforms, the situation of political prisoners, the timetable for the return of those who have been in the mountains, and many other similar issues requiring action all fall within the state’s responsibility. Once these responsibilities are fulfilled, we will be able to make rapid progress toward lasting peace and a democratic solution.”

title: DEM Party in Mardin calls for fairer budget allocation
content:
The DEM Party has presented its demands for the ongoing budget deliberations in the Turkish parliament in Mardin. During a press briefing in the Artuklu district on Saturday, party representatives criticized the unequal distribution of public funds, growing poverty, and the economic consequences of decades of war policies. The event was held as part of the nationwide “Budget for Bread, Peace and Justice” campaign. Alongside party members, representatives of civil society organizations and other interested individuals attended the meeting.




Mehmet Ali Amak, co-mayor of Artuklu, drew attention to the financial difficulties facing municipalities. He emphasized that many of the city’s problems could only be resolved by providing local administrations with greater financial resources. “We have been in office for more than two years. Our financial situation prevents us from implementing everything we had planned,” Amak explained.




Military spending instead of investment




Nihat Gökalp, co-chair of the DEM Party’s provincial organization in Mardin, linked the budget campaign to the decades-long conflict over the Kurdish question. He stated that the region had suffered from a lack of economic investment while substantial state funds had been allocated to military purposes. “There has been an armed conflict for more than 40 years. During this period, the state suspended the rule of law. We did not accept this, and we will not accept it in the future,” Gökalp said. He also drew attention to political prisoners, many of whom remain behind bars.




Regarding the ongoing peace and democratic society process, Gökalp criticized the Turkish government’s failure to take the necessary steps, arguing that this was preventing the process from advancing at the expected pace.




Nilüfer Elik Yılmaz, co-chair of the party’s provincial organization, called for greater consideration of women and children in the state budget. She emphasized that bread, peace, and justice could only be achieved in a society where women could live freely.




“Children are going to school hungry”




DEM Party MP Beritan Güneş Altın stated that Mardin had been disadvantaged in the allocation of state budget funds for years. The city, she said, faces numerous social and economic problems that need to receive greater attention during parliamentary budget deliberations. “There are children in this city who go to school hungry. Our struggle for bread is a struggle for these children. While students are collapsing from hunger at school, the country is being shaken by financial scandals. When we look at the investment fund fraud scandal, we understand why working people are so poor,” Altın said.




Altın also criticized the renewed appointment of a government trustee to the Mardin Metropolitan Municipality. For the third time, she said, the democratically expressed will of the people has been disregarded. “The will of the people of Mardin has been usurped. The elected representatives must be reinstated immediately,” she demanded. The MP stressed that the impact of the trusteeship was no longer limited to local government: “This trustee has been imposed not only on a municipality but on every aspect of life.”




Altın pointed out that agriculture must also receive greater consideration in budget planning. Although Mardin has traditionally been an agricultural region, misguided political decisions have weakened production, she said, calling for additional funding for farmers and concrete measures to improve their economic situation.




Equal treatment in funding for religious communities




DEM Party MP George Aslan criticized the unequal distribution of state funds among religious communities. “While Turkey’s Directorate of Religious Affairs (Diyanet) receives substantial budget allocations, other religious communities are not given comparable consideration. They say we are brothers and sisters, but the budget is allocated to only one faith,” Aslan stated.




Aslan stressed that Mardin is often described as a city of diverse religions, languages, and identities. “This diversity must also be reflected in state funding. Budget funds must also benefit all religious communities on an equal basis.”




At the end of the event, journalists had the opportunity to ask questions and offer suggestions regarding the budget campaign and Mardin’s social and economic problems. The DEM Party announced that it would also hold discussions with civil society organizations as the campaign progresses.

title: Saturday Mothers commemorate the seven people killed in Mardin in 1995
content:
At their 1,127th vigil in Galatasaray Square in Istanbul, the Saturday Mothers commemorated seven people who disappeared and were murdered in October 1995 after being detained by Turkish soldiers and village guards in the Dargeçit district of Mardin. Three of the victims were minors. Although their remains were discovered in wells years later, the crime has gone unpunished.




The vigil focused on the cases of Davut Altunkaynak (12), Seyhan Doğan (13), Nedim Akyön (16), Mehmet Emin Aslan (19), Abdurrahman Olcay (20), Abdurrahman Coşkun (21), and Süleyman Seyhan (57). The joint statement was read by Gamze Elvan, the sister of Berkin Elvan, who was fatally injured by a police tear gas canister during the Gezi protests in 2013.




Abducted, murdered, and buried in wells




Following the arrests, the families made repeated but unsuccessful attempts to obtain information about the whereabouts of their relatives. At the time, the authorities claimed that those detained had been released after questioning and had subsequently “gone to the mountains.” An initial criminal complaint produced no results. It was not until the families and the Human Rights Association (İHD) submitted a renewed petition on May 29, 2009, that the public prosecutor’s office reopened the investigation.




Between 2012 and 2015, several excavations were carried out based on witness testimony. During these investigations, human remains were discovered in wells within a former military restricted zone. “These investigations brought to light the truth that had been denied for years. The people detained in Dargeçit had been killed and buried in wells,” Elvan stated. The bones recovered bore evidence of severe torture, she added.




Acquittals and statute of limitations




In the subsequent criminal proceedings, 18 defendants faced charges of intentional homicide. They included Hurşit Imren, the then-commander of the Gendarmerie Battalion in Mardin, Mehmet Tire, the Gendarmerie Commander of Dargeçit, as well as other military personnel and village guards. On July 4, 2022, the court acquitted all the defendants, ruling that insufficient concrete, clear, and convincing evidence had been presented to secure a conviction. Appeals against the acquittals were unsuccessful.




In May 2026, Turkey’s Court of Cassation ultimately dismissed the case on the grounds that the 30-year statute of limitations had expired. Gamze Elvan strongly criticized the decision: “The judiciary is continuing its tradition of using the statute of limitations as a tool to protect perpetrators and permanently entrench impunity.”




“Seven lives, seven hopes disappeared into that darkness”




Letters from the victims’ relatives were then read aloud. Abdülaziz Altunkaynak, whose son Davut was only twelve years old when he was abducted, recalled the night of October 29, 1995. “Thirty-one years ago, the lights went out in Dargeçit on a single night, and silence descended. Seven lives, seven hopes disappeared into that darkness,” he wrote.




Altunkaynak said that his son Davut had been denied the chance to live out his childhood, Seyhan Doğan’s school notebooks had been left unfinished, and the young men’s dreams for the future had been destroyed. Süleyman Seyhan, too, was unable to fulfill his hopes for his children. “We recovered the bones of our disappeared loved ones from the wells. But their murderers are still walking free, and the state rewards them with impunity,” Altunkaynak stated.




Relatives demand that the state confront its past




In his letter, Mehmet Seyhan described the abduction of his father, Süleyman Seyhan. He said soldiers and village guards entered the family home during breakfast and took him away in a military vehicle. He was subsequently murdered along with six other people.” Decades of attempts to cover up the crimes and the outcome of the criminal proceedings deprived the families of hope for justice through the courts. We expect the state to apologize to our families for the crimes of the 1990s. We call on the state to confront its own past,” Seyhan wrote.




Hazni Doğan, the brother of Seyhan Doğan, who was just 13 years old at the time, also addressed the gathering in a letter. He noted that the day of the vigil coincided with both his brother’s birthday and the anniversary of his mother’s death. He commemorated the Saturday Mothers who had died without ever being able to visit the graves of their disappeared loved ones. “We promise you that we will carry on the struggle for truth and justice that you have left us until the very end,” Doğan wrote.




The vigil concluded with the laying of red carnations in Galatasaray Square.

title: Hundreds demonstrate in Zurich, call for the achievements of the Rojava Revolution to be protected
content:
Around 1,000 people demonstrated in Zurich on Friday evening in defense of the achievements of the Rojava Revolution. Marking World Kobanê Day, they marched through District 4 in response to a call by a regional coalition. Through speeches, a message of solidarity from the Women’s Protection Units (YPJ), and a large-scale banner action, participants commemorated the resistance of Kobanê and drew attention to the current challenges facing the Democratic Autonomous Administration of North and East Syria.




In a communiqué, the Rojava Committee Zurich, which is part of the coalition, described the demonstration as an expression of militant international solidarity. The Committee stated that the resistance of Kobanê, twelve years after the battle against the terrorist organization Islamic State (ISIS), remains as significant as ever. “Especially in times like these, when the profit-driven logic behind the wars waged by those in power is once again being displayed so openly and brutally, the victory in Kobanê remains a symbol of hope and living proof that we can rely only on our own strength,” the committee declared.










https://video.anf-news2.com/live/firat/b1a51dbd_20261030235855_2026-10-30-zurih-1-kasim-dunya-kobane-gunu-icin-eylem-1.mp4










The future of the women’s revolution is at stake




The organizers recalled that, since 2012, a social alternative based on women’s liberation, ecology, and grassroots democracy has emerged in Rojava amid the Syrian war. People from different ethnic and religious backgrounds have organized together and participated in building the autonomous administration. For many people fleeing war and persecution, northeastern Syria had, for a time, become a place of refuge.




When ISIS attacked Kobanê in 2014, the resistance of the Kurdish self-defense forces sparked an international solidarity movement, which also gave rise to World Kobanê Day on November 1. According to the committee, however, this year’s mobilization took place under particularly challenging circumstances. “The agreement reached in January between the Democratic Autonomous Administration and the Syrian transitional government, along with the associated integration process, has fundamentally changed the political landscape. Numerous issues remain contentious or have yet to be negotiated.”













“The situation in Kobanê and the entire region shows that the future of the autonomous administration and the women’s revolution is by no means secure,” the statement said. “For this very reason, the historic resistance of Kobanê remains as relevant as ever. It serves as an example of sustaining resistance even under seemingly hopeless conditions, thereby creating the very foundations for social change.”













YPJ: Kobanê lives on in our struggle




During the demonstration through Zurich’s District 4, speakers emphasized the connection between the historic resistance against ISIS and the current struggles over the future of Rojava. Alongside international solidarity, they highlighted the need to bring different social struggles together. A special message from Rojava was delivered to the demonstrators. YPJ spokesperson Ruksen Mihemed conveyed greetings on behalf of the women fighters and the women of northeastern Syria:




“From Rojava, Western Kurdistan, on behalf of all YPJ fighters and all the women of Rojava, we send our greetings to everyone demonstrating in the streets of Switzerland today. Kobanê and the history written there will always remain alive.”




The memory of the resistance is not confined to the past, the spokesperson emphasized: “It is not merely a page in a history book. It lives on in our consciousness and in our hearts, in our daily work and in our struggle.”




An action at Piazza Cella also drew attention during the march. Activists unfurled a huge banner conveying their greetings to young people.













“Our solidarity must be put into practice here in Europe”




The Rojava Committee Zurich explicitly linked the demonstration to criticism of the economic and political conditions in Switzerland. International solidarity, it argued, must not be limited to public statements of support but must also be put into practice in places where wars are economically enabled and financed.




“We took to the streets today because our solidarity must be put into practice, especially here in Europe. The imperialist logic of capitalism—turning killing into a business—is financed and reproduced here in Switzerland,” the committee underlined.




In their statement, the organizers also condemned state repression and emphasized their determination to continue demonstrating publicly: “But we will take back our streets again and again. Your repression will not change that.”




The communiqué concluded with the slogans “Bijî Berxwedana Kobanê” (Long live the resistance of Kobanê), “Berxwedan Jîyane” (Resistance is life), and “Long live international solidarity!” as well as the demonstration’s central slogan: “Rojava is everywhere – resistance is everywhere."

title: ‘Labor struggle against capitalism and exploitation’ discussed at women’s conference in Ankara
content:
The second session of the “Women Discuss the Future Side by Side” conference, held at the Chamber of Civil Engineers (İMO) of the Union of Chambers of Turkish Engineers and Architects (TMMOB) in Ankara featured discussions under the theme “Labor struggle against capitalism and exploitation.”




The conference is organized at the initiative of 80 women, including journalists, writers, academics, politicians, and activists.




Ayfer Koçak, Co-Chair of the Confederation of Public Employees’ Trade Unions (KESK), said, “If we are to organize against exploitation, we must create a society in which workers can receive what they are entitled to, a society we call a ‘democratic society.’”




Sabahat Tuncel, an activist with the Free Women’s Movement (Tevgera Jinên Azad – TJA), stated that exploitation could not be eliminated without abolishing the capitalist system. “Because this system itself generates inequality and labor exploitation. Consequently, it exploits women’s labor even further. What we really need to focus on is how to eliminate this system.”




Tuncel continued: “As Marx said, ‘Workers are free only insofar as they can sell their labor,’ but even those conditions have now changed. Workers can no longer even sell their labor freely. title: Tahincioğlu: Pressure and access bans on the press are a wake-up call
content:
Pressure on the opposition press has increased under the Justice and Development Party (AKP) government, particularly over the past two years. The government has begun using various methods of repression against media outlets it considers critical of its policies.




Access to the website and social media accounts of T24, one of Turkey's most widely read news websites, has been blocked. A trustee was appointed to HALK TV, while the websites and social media accounts of Kurdish media outlets such as Mezopotamya Agency, Jinnews and Yeni Yaşam have frequently faced access restrictions.




Data released by the Dicle Fırat Journalists Association (DFG) for September 2026 showed that access to 3,492 pieces of online and digital media content had been blocked. During the same period, access restrictions were imposed on 15 news websites, while four websites were shut down.




Journalist Gökçer Tahincioğlu, a representative of T24, assessed the reasons behind the pressure on the press and its impact on journalism.




‘A government that has largely lost its narrative’




Tahincioğlu said that the government had largely lost its political narrative and stressed that the pressure on the press could not be attributed to a single cause. He added: "I don't think there is just one reason. If you look at the course of politics, you see a scattered and fragmented opposition, another opposition force facing obstacles to carrying out its role, and yet another opposition structure whose position in the elections remains uncertain. 




If you look at it from the perspective of a government that has largely lost its narrative and is experiencing economic difficulties at their most severe, you can also understand this opposition landscape. It would not be wrong to say that pressure on the media has increased as an extension of this fragmented political structure. Today, we are in an environment that is different even from the 2023 elections, one in which we feel pressure much more intensely. The media is not exempt from this pressure. On the contrary, it is among the most visible targets."




‘This is a turning point’




Tahincioğlu also addressed the access ban imposed on T24, describing the decision as a turning point for independent media. He said: "Given everything that has happened, it may not be entirely accurate to say that T24 is being singled out with particular persistence. However, completely blocking access to one of Turkey's leading independent news websites, especially on the basis of incomprehensible justifications that do not constitute offences under the law and even contain factual errors, after the website had already been targeted, is difficult to understand. But leaving aside whether it makes sense, it is possible to say that this marks a turning point. At the same time, this process serves as a warning, an alarm bell for independent media."




Tahincioğlu stated that government pressure had placed more than 95 percent of the media under the control of circles close to the government, pointing out that the public's right to access news was becoming increasingly restricted. He added: "Until recently, we were saying that 95 percent of the media was under the control of circles close to the government and that these outlets, far from going beyond the limits imposed on them, were voluntarily working to legitimise the government's criticised practices.




Today, those limits have narrowed even further. This also means that people are being deprived of news and must make extraordinary efforts to access information. Yet news should be information that reaches people and circulates freely. It should not be something people have to struggle to obtain. Of course, this environment is extremely advantageous for the government."




‘The divisions are deep and are not just a problem of today’




Tahincioğlu also assessed how different sections of society respond to the pressure on Kurdish media, saying that attitudes on this issue had not changed. He said: "I don't think this picture has changed. Those who criticise the repression continue to criticise it, while those who defend it as justified continue to do so, either openly or through their silence. Some people might be told, 'Look, now it has happened to you too,' but we can also say that these same people only regard what happens to them as a problem. Unfortunately, these divisions are very deep and are not just a problem of today."




Tahincioğlu pointed out that some sections of society consider the pressure on Kurdish media justified and said: "A large proportion of these actions are regarded as justified. Yet, at a time when efforts are being made to establish peace, perhaps everyone should reflect on these issues as well. However, there are deep divisions and deeply rooted habits. Abandoning these habits and looking at things from a different perspective is not easy. But without understanding and being understood, the chances of these processes succeeding are already very low." 




‘The problem goes far beyond the strength and influence of professional organisations’




Gökçer Tahincioğlu also addressed the position of press organisations and trade unions, stressing that professional organisations should be assessed individually rather than treated as a homogeneous group. He added: "We should not regard professional organisations as such a homogeneous group. However, the organisations that genuinely do their jobs properly, as we understand them, also have limited strength and influence. In an environment where most of the media operates within this structure, you cannot expect these organisations to have considerable strength or influence.mIn this respect, I think some professional organisations are being treated unfairly.




At this point, responsibility also falls, to some extent, on the public and political actors. When journalists have been reduced to such small numbers, both in terms of their presence and the platforms available to them, and journalism has been pushed so far into a corner, I do not think it is fair to criticise those who continue struggling. Unfortunately, the problem goes far beyond the strength and influence of professional organisations."
