title: Women’s conference in Ankara: There can be no peace without justice
content:
The “Women Discuss the Future Side by Side” conference, organized at the initiative of 80 women, including journalists, writers, academics, politicians, and activists, began in Ankara on. Saturday.




Following the opening speech, the conference continued with musical performances by İlkay Akkaya, Feryal Öney, Nurcan Değirmenci, and Selda Öztürk. More than 500 women from different cities are attending the conference.




Hikmet Kılınç, the mother of İpek Er, who died after being sexually assaulted and driven to suicide by Turkish specialist sergeant Musa Orhan in Siirt, is also among the participants. Showing her daughter’s belongings, photographs, and locks of hair, Hikmet Kılınç said, “I want justice for my daughter.”




The conference, consisting of three sessions, started with its first session, titled “Freedoms, democracy, justice, and equal citizenship.” Speakers at the opening session included politicians Gültan Kışanak and Zeynep Altıok Akatlı, Feride Eralp of the ‘I Need Peace Women’s Initiative’, writer Hidayet Şefkatli Tuksal, and political scientist Füsun Üstel.




Füsun Üstel: What we need is equal citizenship




Füsun Üstel drew attention to the legal reforms outlined in the fourth section of the report submitted by the Peoples’ Equality and Democracy Party (DEM Party) to the parliamentary commission as part of the ongoing peace process in Turkey.




Üstel stated: “What is being discussed here is a transitional legal framework. A wide range of demands are being put forward. These include equal citizenship for Alevis, addressing their demands in the context of freedom of belief, introducing certain amendments to the Political Parties Law and the Election Law, amending Article 42 of the Constitution, which governs the right to education, to enable the use of the mother tongue both in education and in various areas of public life, and finally, Article 66, which defines citizenship.




The demand for equal citizenship is based on a conception of citizenship that rests on a neutral and impartial relationship between the state and the individual. Citizenship, as we know, actually reflects an inherent tension. It is a status that both includes and excludes. Citizenship is a concept with both internal and external boundaries. In fact, it conceals existing inequalities.




The demand for equal citizenship alone is not enough. In an environment where rights and freedoms are being curtailed, public spaces are increasingly shrinking, and various forms of exclusion are being created, is equal citizenship sufficient? What we actually need is equal citizenship plus rights.”




Füsun Üstel pointed out that the demand for equal citizenship must also be critically examined from the perspective of women. She continued: “What does equal citizenship mean for women? Is the concept of equal citizenship broad enough to include women? Behind equal citizenship lie masculine norms, patriarchal structures, and hierarchies. At the local level, we are facing a major backlash against women. At the global level, we are also witnessing an alliance of right-wing, conservative, and authoritarian regimes against women. Therefore, we must not be content with the demand for equal citizenship alone. We can bring these issues to the forefront by discussing them as part of building peace and a democratic society.”




Gültan Kışanak: Freedom does not come with permission




Speaking after, Gültan Kışanak stated the following:




“Freedom is something that begins and ends with us. Freedom is not a space that opens up with the permission of those in power or of men. If you do not take action yourself, it will never happen. We cannot achieve equal citizenship without dismantling the patriarchal, capitalist, and colonialist system.




When it comes to equal citizenship, simply putting race, class, and gender into words is not enough. We have often discussed how the Kurdish question also stems from our inability to become ‘us.’ We believe that differences have points of intersection and that, by developing policies on this common ground, we can build our shared future. We will succeed.”




Hidayet Şefkatli Tuksal: We should focus more on what unites us than what divides us




Feminist writer Hidayet Şefkatli Tuksal emphasized that the women’s movement and the Kurdish women’s movement have been struggling together against policies of repression and violence targeting women in Turkey.




“We constantly say that we all come from different backgrounds. Instead of talking about our differences, we should emphasize what we have in common. We need to come together more often to learn from one another and discuss what we can do together,” she said.




Feride Eralp: There can be no peace without justice




Feride Eralp, a member of the ‘I Need Peace Women’s Initiative’, emphasized that genuine peace cannot be achieved without justice and equal citizenship.




Addressing İpek Er’s mother, Eralp said: “We are speaking here while looking at İpek Er’s photograph. Without justice, peace would mean that the violence of war continues to be inflicted on women’s bodies in everyday life. War is not just about weapons.”




Drawing attention to the relationship between domestic violence against women and state policies, Eralp continued: “It is no coincidence that the concepts of family, population, and security have been closely linked ever since the concept of citizenship emerged. Why is the declining population growth rate a cause for concern in Turkey? Because the supply of cheap labor will decrease. For example, there is talk of the Mecca Agreement. What will Turkey be able to offer Saudi Arabia, or how will it be able to claim, ‘I have NATO’s second-largest army’? Another reason is that the elderly population requiring care will increase. In a country like Turkey, women are expected to care for elderly family members within the household.”




Zeynep Altook Akatli: We must shape politics through the language of peace




Politician Zeynep Altıok Akatlı stated:




“I believe that we can grow by engaging with aspects of one another that we have not seen and ideas that we do not agree with, and that these differences can also teach us something.




As we speak about peace and embrace it with the same conviction, I want to address the language we adopt. Even in debates within the opposition itself, we see the influence of the government’s violent language and rhetoric. I want to talk about how a culture of violence has engulfed the culture of peace, making us forget that peace is itself a culture.




To truly internalize peace and the concept of equal citizenship, we must know, learn about, and keep alive the memory of the suffering that society has endured from the past to the present.




Being a woman in a patriarchal society is difficult. But when identities such as being a woman, being Kurdish, being Alevi, being a worker, being divorced, or being an atheist are brought together, they are treated as a ‘crime.’




We want to continue being women who speak of peace in a culture of violence that fiercely defends the right to be provoked by those who are different. That is why we must reshape the language of politics through women’s voices and rebuild its culture around the language of peace.”




The conference’s first session continued with contributions from participants, followed by a question-and-answer session.

title: The Kurdistan Region’s experience of government – II
content:
The expected outcome did not materialise following the elections of 20 October 2024. The two dominant political forces, the Kurdistan Democratic Party (KDP) and the Patriotic Union of Kurdistan (PUK), continue to insist on their respective demands. In this part of our series, we examine the government formation crises that have become all too familiar to the people of Southern Kurdistan (Başûr), their causes and the price paid for them.




Deadlocks from the first cabinet to the latest




Each crisis began with a different development, but all reached a deadlock over the same three issues: who would control the region's revenues, who would command the armed forces and intelligence services, and whether the two major parties would be represented equally or according to their parliamentary seats. In 1994, these disputes escalated into war; in 2015, they led to the closure of parliament; and after 2024, they resulted in a prolonged political deadlock.




First cabinet: 

The government was formed on 4 July 1992, 46 days after the elections of 19 May 1992. During this period, efforts were made to overcome allegations of electoral fraud and disagreements over equal representation, with 50 seats for each party.




Fifth cabinet:

 Following the elections of 30 January 2005, disagreements over the unification of the two administrations and the regional presidency delayed the formation of a new government for 462 days, until 7 May 2006.




Sixth cabinet:

 The government was formed on 28 October 2009, 95 days after the elections of 25 July 2009, following disputes over the transfer of the premiership to the PUK.




Eighth cabinet:

 The emergence of the Gorran Movement and the reduction in the PUK's parliamentary representation following the elections of 21 September 2013 led to a deadlock that was resolved after 270 days. The cabinet was formed on 18 June 2014.




Ninth cabinet: 

Following the elections of 30 September 2018, the end of equal representation and disagreements over the Kurdistan Region's ministerial legislation delayed the formation of the cabinet for 283 days, until 10 July 2019.




Tenth cabinet: 

More than two years after the elections of 20 October 2024, the Kurdistan Region's tenth cabinet has still not been formed because of disputes over the allocation of ministries and equal representation.




First cabinet: Equal representation, 50–50




The region's first government crisis began before the polls had even closed. Smaller parties accused the two major parties of multiple voting, while the KDP and PUK also accused each other of electoral irregularities. It was announced that 70 per cent of the problems had been caused by erasable ink. The initial count gave the KDP 51 seats and the PUK 49. The outcome was settled through three days of closed-door negotiations between the party leaders, after which the KDP relinquished one seat. The second round of the leadership election was also postponed and ultimately never held. As a result, the region had no elected president until 2005.




Under the 50–50 arrangement, every minister had a deputy from the rival party. The Director General of Public Security was from the KDP, while the Director General of Police was from the PUK. Of the supposedly unified 35,000-strong peshmerga force, 15,000 fighters belonged to each party. Real authority rested not with the elected parliament but with the political bureaux headed by Barzani and Talabani.




The government was established at a time when United Nations (UN) sanctions against Iraq coincided with Baghdad's embargo on the Kurdistan Region. The Ibrahim Khalil (Habur) border crossing on the Turkish border became the government's main source of revenue. From 1994 onwards, the KDP stopped transferring this revenue, which amounted to approximately $35 million annually, to the government. What the two parties were dividing was not a state but a shrinking pool of revenue. The civil war was fought over the terms of that division.




Civil war: 1994–1998




The KDP-PUK war began in Qaladiza (Qeladizê) on 1 May 1994. A total of 100 people from both sides were killed during May. Approximately 500 people lost their lives in clashes in Erbil (Hewlêr) in January 1995, and the city came under PUK control. By July 1995, the KDP controlled one-third of the territory and population, while the PUK controlled the remaining two-thirds. Parliament convened for the last time in May 1995.




The KDP-PUK civil war ended through mediation by the United States. However, the provisions concerning a joint government and elections were not implemented, and the dispute over revenue sharing remained unresolved. According to different sources, between 2,000 and 5,000 people lost their lives in the civil war, while some estimates put the death toll as high as 8,000.




Numerous attempts were made to halt the fighting during this period, but none produced a lasting solution. A temporary ceasefire was declared in June 1994, but clashes continued. An agreement was reached in France in July–August 1994, although it was never implemented. Barzani and Talabani signed a Pact of Alliance on 21 November 1994, but fighting resumed in December. A ceasefire reached in March 1995 collapsed in July of the same year. The Dublin talks in August–September 1995 reached a deadlock over the demilitarisation of Erbil and customs revenues. Iranian mediation efforts in late 1995 also failed to produce results.




The mediation efforts repeatedly stalled over the same two fundamental issues: the parties could not agree on how to share revenue from the border crossing or who would retain control of Erbil. Revenue sharing and territorial control had become preconditions for forming a government.




The two parties take 16 months to unite: 2005–2006




Sixteen months passed between the elections of 30 January 2005 and the formation of the unified cabinet on 7 May 2006. Parliament was unable to convene until four months after the elections. The PUK had reservations about the four-year term and powers of the regional presidency, while the parties could not agree on who would command the unified peshmerga forces or control the region's finances.




A solution was reached through a political trade-off between the Kurdistan Region and Baghdad. Jalal Talabani became President of Iraq on 6 April 2005. Under a compromise reached on 29 May 2005, Masoud Barzani became President of the Kurdistan Region and commander-in-chief of the peshmerga forces, while Adnan Mufti of the PUK became parliamentary speaker.




The negotiations took place between the parties rather than in parliament. The ministries of Interior, Peshmerga Affairs, Finance and Justice could not be brought under unified administration for at least another year.




Separate ministries and party-controlled armies




The unification agreement brought the ministries together but failed to unify the armed forces. The merger of the ministries was completed in February 2009. However, most of the approximately 120,000 peshmerga fighters remained under the control of the parties' political bureaux, serving in the PUK-affiliated Unit 70 and the KDP-affiliated Unit 80.




The security and intelligence services were officially unified under the Security Council in 2012, but in practice remained under party control. The continued division of the peshmerga forces was also the reason why the Ministry of Interior and security institutions became central points of contention in every round of cabinet negotiations.




The Gorran Movement and 17 February 2011




The 25 seats won by the Gorran Movement in the 2009 elections represented the first serious challenge to the two-party system. Gorran demanded the government's resignation in January 2011. On 17 February 2011, approximately 3,000 people marched in Sulaymaniyah (Silêmanî) against corruption and two-party rule. Two people were killed and at least 50 others injured on the first day when shots were fired from a KDP building.




The protests continued for more than two months. On 19 April, approximately 7,000 PUK-affiliated peshmerga fighters, Asayish security personnel and special forces were deployed to Sulaymaniyah. At least 10 people were killed and more than 250 injured during the protests.




The eighth cabinet: 270 days of negotiations




The elections of 21 September 2013 failed to give any party a majority. The KDP remained the largest party with 38 seats, while the Gorran Movement rose to second place with 24 seats. The PUK fell to third place for the first time, securing just 18 seats. The first reason for the delay was the internal crisis within the PUK, which had been left without effective leadership after Talabani suffered a stroke in December 2012. The second was the decision by 59 KDP and PUK parliamentarians to extend Masoud Barzani's presidential term by two years through Law No. 19 on 30 June 2013.




Following disputes over government positions, the Gorran Movement secured the ministries of Peshmerga Affairs and Finance, along with the parliamentary speakership, while the PUK received the deputy premiership. The ministries of Interior and Natural Resources, as well as control over security and oil revenues, remained with the KDP. Despite gaining ministerial positions, Gorran achieved greater visibility rather than substantial authority.




The 2015 salary and political crisis




Protests demanding the payment of salaries and Barzani's resignation began in districts of Sulaymaniyah and escalated into violence in October 2015. Three people were killed on 9 October when shots were fired from a KDP office in Qaladiza, while two others were killed in Kalar on 10 October. The KDP blamed the Gorran Movement for the protests. On 12 October, the parliamentary speaker was prevented from entering Erbil, and ministers belonging to Gorran were asked to resign. Parliament did not convene for 704 days, until 15 September 2017.




The political crisis coincided with the region's most severe financial crisis. Baghdad suspended the Kurdistan Region's 17 per cent share of the national budget, worth approximately $13 billion annually, in February 2014. Oil prices fell, while the annual cost of the war against ISIS exceeded $2 billion. By the end of 2015, salaries for approximately 1.4 million public sector employees were between three and five months overdue. In early 2016, the government introduced salary cuts of between 10 and 75 per cent under an "austerity" policy, promising to reimburse the withheld amounts at a later date. However, no timetable for repayment was established. A decade later, the deductions remain a subject of negotiation.




The referendum and 16 October 2017




A meeting of political parties chaired by Masoud Barzani on 7 June 2017 decided to hold an independence referendum. The Gorran Movement and the Kurdistan Islamic Group (Komele) did not attend, arguing that the necessary conditions were not in place. Parliament, which had been closed for two years, reconvened on 15 September without Gorran and Komele to give the decision legal status. The Turkish state and Iran opposed the referendum.




Iraqi forces and the Popular Mobilisation Forces (Hashd al-Shaabi) entered Kirkuk (Kerkûk) on 16 October 2017 in response to the referendum. Three-quarters of the territories that had come under Kurdish control after 2003, including Kirkuk, Khanaqin (Xaneqîn), Makhmour (Maxmûr), Shengal (Şengal) and the Mosul Dam, passed into Iraqi control. Oil production fell by half. Masoud Barzani stepped down as President of the Kurdistan Region on 1 November 2017. Five people were killed during protests over unpaid salaries that began in the Raperin region on 18 December 2017. The Gorran Movement and Komele withdrew from the government on 20 December.




The ninth cabinet and its crises: 283 days




The results of the 30 September 2018 elections were announced on 20 October, following a three-week delay. The KDP first reached an agreement with the Gorran Movement in February 2019, followed by an agreement with the PUK on 4 March 2019. The cabinet headed by Masrour Barzani was formed on 10 July 2019. For the first time, the KDP sought to make its parliamentary seat advantage the determining factor in the distribution of government positions. The same issue became one of the central disputes in negotiations over the formation of the tenth cabinet.




Baghdad suspended budget transfers in early 2020. The government introduced a 21 per cent salary cut on 21 June 2020. At least seven people, including a 13-year-old child, were killed during protests over unpaid salaries that began in Sulaymaniyah on 2 December 2020 and spread to other areas.




The two major parties came into conflict again in Baghdad in October 2022. Abdul Latif Rashid, who was backed by the KDP, became President of Iraq. Following the killing of a PUK colonel, Qubad Talabani began boycotting Council of Ministers meetings. The boycott lasted seven months and ended on 14 May 2023 following an appeal from the United States.




Divisions between the two major parties paved the way for decisions by Iraq's Federal Supreme Court that restricted the powers of the Kurdistan Region. In February 2022, the court ruled that oil exports from the Kurdistan Region were unconstitutional. On 30 May 2023, it annulled parliament's decision to extend its term. On 21 February 2024, it ruled that oil and non-oil revenues must be transferred to Baghdad and that salaries must be paid by the federal government.




Oil exports, which the Turkish state had halted on 25 March 2023, resumed under Baghdad's control after 917 days. The Kurdistan Region thus also lost control over its oil revenues.




Common causes of government formation crises




The 1993 Political Parties Law, which prohibited parties from maintaining military organisations, was not implemented following the outbreak of the KDP-PUK war. Even the ceremony marking the unification of the peshmerga forces in September 2026 failed to end the units' allegiance to their respective parties. As long as the peshmerga, Asayish security forces and intelligence institutions remained under party control, cabinet negotiations continued to revolve around the balance of military power. The party controlling the Kurdistan Region's revenues also determined its own influence within the cabinet. As revenues declined, the crises first affected salaries and then spilled onto the streets, as happened in 1994, 2015 and 2020.




The draft constitution adopted in 2009 was never put to a referendum. Political bargaining replaced constitutional foundations. The method of electing the regional president, along with the office's powers and term, has changed four times since 2005. The rules governing government formation were determined not by a constitution but by agreements signed between the two parties. Consequently, when these agreements weakened, no binding rules remained to replace them. Almost every crisis was either halted or deepened by external intervention, whether from Baghdad, Tehran, Ankara or Washington. No women negotiators were named among the delegations conducting cabinet negotiations since 1992, while women public sector employees and teachers were among those who paid the heaviest price for the crises.




The recurring cycle of crises has emerged from the combination of these factors. Once again, the formation of the tenth cabinet has been left to negotiations between the two party leaderships because there are no binding rules requiring election results to determine government formation, no security institutions independent of the parties and no written constitution.




The 20 October election process




The results of the elections, held two years after parliament's term had expired, were announced on 30 October 2024. A total of 136 electoral lists and 1,191 candidates, including 368 women, contested the elections. Salaries, the closed oil pipeline, electricity cuts and corruption dominated the election campaign between 25 September and 15 October.




The KDP won 39 seats, the PUK 23, the New Generation Movement 15, the Kurdistan Islamic Union (Yekgirtû) seven, the National Stance Movement (Helwêst) four, the Kurdistan Islamic Group three, the People's Front two and the Gorran Movement one. Five seats were reserved for minorities, including three for Christians and two for Turkmen. No party secured the 51 seats needed for a majority. The KDP won 35 of its seats in Erbil and Duhok, while the PUK secured 16 of its seats in Sulaymaniyah and Halabja. The refusal of the New Generation Movement, the third-largest political force, to join the government left the KDP and PUK dependent on each other once again.




Parliament convened on 2 December 2024, but its leadership has yet to be elected and no legislation has been passed. Nechirvan Barzani remains in office because a new President of the Kurdistan Region has not been elected.




The KDP and PUK have met dozens of times in an attempt to form a government. However, the parties have failed to agree on whether government positions should be distributed according to parliamentary seats or on the basis of a "genuine partnership". They have also disagreed over whether Masrour Barzani should remain prime minister or someone from outside the KDP should take the position. Masoud Barzani declared in May 2025 that there would be "no 50–50 arrangement". PUK President Bafel Talabani, referring to the combined number of seats held by the PUK and New Generation Movement, said on 1 June 2026: "We are 39 to 39. We want half of the government."




The main deadlock has centred on control of the security institutions. The KDP announced that it would "not hand over the Ministry of Interior to the PUK or negotiate over it". The PUK, meanwhile, is demanding either the Ministry of Interior or authority within the Security Council, which oversees the Parastin and Zanyari intelligence agencies. Public sector employees and the wider population are paying the price for the crisis.




More than 700 days have now passed since the elections of 20 October 2024, yet the tenth cabinet has still not been formed. The ninth cabinet, which took office in 2019, continues to govern the Kurdistan Region despite its term having expired 39 months ago. The cases scheduled to be heard by Iraq's Federal Supreme Court on 26 October will mark the next stage in the legal process concerning the dissolution of parliament and the legal status of the ninth cabinet.




In the next part of our series, we will examine the demands and disputes preventing the formation of a government in the Kurdistan Region, together with their impact on the population.







The Kurdistan Region’s experience of government – I

The Kurdistan Region is facing the consequences of its failure to form a government on every front, as the balance of power in the Middle East is once again being tested and the region faces the pr...

title: Iranian regime sentences Kurdish academic to nine years in prison
content:
The Iranian regime’s policies of repression and intimidation targeting the Kurdish population in Rojhilatê Kurdistan continue. Nebî Ûmêd, a university lecturer from the city of Malekshahi (Malekşahî), has been sentenced to nine years in prison for supporting protests held previously.




According to Kolber News, Branch One of the Ilam Province Court of Appeal charged Nebî Ûmêd with “acting against national security, organising gatherings and plotting against national security, and engaging in propaganda against the regime”. The court ruled that five years of his nine-year prison sentence must be served.




The violations of Nebî Ûmêd’s rights have not been limited to his prison sentence. He has been dismissed from his position at Payam Noor University, banned from leaving the country, had his passport confiscated and been prohibited from entering his hometown of Malekşahî.




Nebî Ûmêd is still living in Ilam and has not been allowed to return to his hometown.

title: Prof. Birdal: A system reliant on constant inflows was bound to collapse
content:
The repercussions of the investment fund fraud scandal, which also involves politicians from the Justice and Development Party (AKP), continue, while losses suffered by people seeking to invest their savings and fluctuations in the markets remain subjects of debate.




Professor Murat Birdal, an academic in the Department of Economics at Istanbul University, spoke to ANF about the causes of the fund crisis and its economic consequences.




‘The collapse in gold prices increased interest in funds’




Murat Birdal said that the fund crisis was linked to high inflation in Turkey, explaining that people had turned to investment funds to protect and increase the value of their savings. Birdal noted that savers had sought alternative investment instruments in response to high inflation and described how the situation developed.




Birdal said: "The main issue here is that people were trying to find ways to protect their savings against high inflation. Initially, deposit interest rates were very high, and people directed their money into bank deposits. As interest rates began to fall, people turned to instruments outside the Turkish lira, such as gold. However, when gold prices plummeted, interest in investment funds increased significantly.




Some of these funds are money market funds. They invest in relatively safer instruments such as Treasury bonds, corporate debt securities and reverse repurchase agreements. Others are unrestricted funds or equity funds. These funds were able to generate returns above interest rates through investments in shares.




In the case of the funds currently under scrutiny, investments in smaller companies outside the BIST 30 and BIST 100 indices were used to drive up share prices sharply. Some shares were even used as collateral after entering the BIST 30 and BIST 100 indices, allowing loans to be issued through money market funds that were supposed to be risk-free. In this way, risks from the stock market were transferred to money market funds. While share prices were being artificially inflated, inflows into the fund market and the flight from the Turkish lira accelerated.




The reason this system is described as a Ponzi scheme is that the mechanism could only survive through a continuous inflow of new money. The moment those inflows stopped, the system would collapse. When speculative movements in share prices began destabilising the market, Morgan Stanley issued a warning in June. Mehmet Şimşek had also previously spoken about the situation. The warning raised the risk of Turkey being removed from the Emerging Markets Index and was repeated twice more.




The Ministry of Economy then took action and issued a Fund Guide. Under the guide, funds were given a deadline to reduce their excessive concentration in particular shares. This forced funds to sell their holdings, triggering an exit from the market. In short, the system was bound to collapse at some point. Morgan Stanley's warning and the subsequent publication of the fund guide were what pulled the pin."




‘Banks and companies established an extensive marketing network’




Birdal said that banks and companies had actively promoted investment funds through advertisements on various platforms, adding that these marketing activities had influenced people's investment decisions. 




Birdal continued: "During periods of high inflation, people increasingly seek ways to protect the short-term cash they hold. Beyond this, however, an extensive marketing network was established through banks and financial YouTube channels.




Bank deposit customers were directed towards these funds by portfolio advisers at banks. They were encouraged with claims such as, 'Instead of earning 3 per cent a month on deposits, you can earn 33 per cent here,' or 'Funds from major companies offering guaranteed returns.' Academics promoted these products on television and YouTube.




Most importantly, a narrative was created suggesting that the AKP was behind the scheme. People acted on their trust in the government and in fund managers who emphasised their connections with politicians. Ultimately, the inevitable collapse was triggered by Morgan Stanley's warning."




‘A mechanism requiring constant inflows of money was bound to collapse’




Birdal stressed that the state had been forced to intervene but had also been negligent throughout the process. 




He said: "The state had to make this intervention. If the process of removing Turkey from the Emerging Markets Index had begun, foreign investors would have withdrawn their investments much more aggressively. Therefore, the warning from foreign investors prompted the state to take measures. In any case, this mechanism, which required a constant inflow of new money and could not continue indefinitely, was bound to collapse at some point.




There was serious negligence on the part of the state in allowing the situation to reach this stage.




The Capital Markets Board's (SPK) negligence in overseeing companies' initial public offerings, Borsa Istanbul (BIST) management's failure to monitor speculative movements, and the failure of the Banking Regulation and Supervision Agency (BDDK) and the Electronic Fund Trading Platform (TEFAŞ) to operate their oversight and control mechanisms, or their decision to ignore what was happening, all contributed to this situation.




This can be explained both by the pursuit of personal interests among certain circles within the party and by the contradictions inherent in the authoritarian regime. People within the system are reluctant to speak out even when they recognise wrongdoing."




‘The government will face growing difficulties ahead of the elections’




Professor Murat Birdal also assessed possible solutions to the fund crisis, outlining the measures needed in the short and long term. He said that a compensation plan for those affected by the funds was on the agenda in the short term, but highlighted uncertainties surrounding the scope of the arrangement and how the losses would be covered.




Birdal said, "In the short term, under the legislation passed by the government, payments are envisaged for those affected by the funds, particularly the large number of people with savings of less than one million lira, to enable them to recover their principal investments. However, it is unclear whether most of these funds have the resources to make such payments. The most critical question is whether these financial losses will be covered by the state budget or the Treasury. It is unacceptable for these losses to be covered by public resources while citizens are being told to tighten their belts."




Birdal noted that the stock market had suffered substantial losses in value and warned that the damage could exceed 90 billion dollars. He continued: "We may face losses exceeding the 90 billion dollars cited by Özgür Özel. Even major companies have lost 25 to 30 per cent of their value. Because share prices have fallen to their lower trading limits and buyers cannot be found, it will not be possible to convert the funds into cash and complete their liquidation in a short period.




In the longer term, the government will face considerable difficulties as the country approaches the elections. On the one hand, it wants to lower interest rates and stimulate the markets, while on the other, it must prevent the exchange rate from rising and fuelling inflation. When interest rates are reduced, money will not flow into bank deposits, and with confidence in the fund market also undermined, it becomes very difficult to increase demand for Turkish lira-denominated financial instruments. The extensive involvement of the bureaucracy and political establishment in this affair is deepening mistrust and imposing an extremely heavy cost on Turkey's economy."

title: Kamuran Reşîd: The greatest injustices occur in prisons
content:
Despite the steps taken by the Kurdish Freedom Movement as part of the Peace and Democratic Society Process, the Turkish government has yet to take any serious action. Human rights violations, unlawful practices and arbitrary measures in prisons continue to increase. Prisoners are being prevented from securing their release by Administrative and Observation Boards, which justify their decisions by citing "forced expressions of remorse" and claims that prisoners are "not ready to reintegrate into society". Political prisoners who have very little time remaining before their scheduled release are prevented from leaving prison through disciplinary penalties or other justifications and continue to be held behind bars.




Kamuran Reşîd, a member of the Rojava Prisoners Committee, spoke to ANF about the situation in prisons. Reşîd began by recalling that Abdullah Öcalan initiated the Peace and Democratic Society Process on 27 February 2025 and said: "The Call for Peace and a Democratic Society presents us with a new way of life, intellectually grounded in Abdullah Öcalan's ideas. Like a light, it opens the door to a new life. His call exposes the problems created by the existing global system and the deadlocks it has produced. Through this call, Abdullah Öcalan intervened in the current process of deadlock, crisis and collapse. He recognised that the existing system was no longer capable of managing the situation because a new crisis emerges every day. Crisis has now become part of everyday life.




The capitalist system can no longer respond to these problems. Although Abdullah Öcalan is imprisoned, he recognised these developments and considered intervention necessary. Rather than producing solutions to the problems of the Kurdish people and society in Kurdistan, the existing system responds through different methods each time. Sometimes through coercion, sometimes through division, and sometimes through forms of governance, it attempts to rule the Kurdish people and Kurdish identity by establishing domination and hegemony under different identities."




‘The state's approach is unacceptable’




Reşîd pointed out that no changes had been made to Abdullah Öcalan's circumstances following his call on 27 February 2025 and continued: "Not a single step has been taken towards Abdullah Öcalan's physical freedom. There has been no concrete development and no initiative has been undertaken. The state's approach is unacceptable. This approach represents a stance against both the process and Abdullah Öcalan. The determination demonstrated by Abdullah Öcalan is important to us. He wants to share his ideas freely with society. Once these ideas reach society, his original objective will have been achieved. The people must now embrace these ideas. Intellectuals and those who oppose the existing system must embrace Abdullah Öcalan's ideas. A struggle must be carried out on this basis, and his freedom must be secured.




Today, a law must be enacted to secure Abdullah Öcalan's freedom, and direct responsibility must be assumed. The Turkish state bears responsibility for this. Abdullah Öcalan's freedom is our fundamental issue. Öcalan is engaged in an intellectual struggle with the state every day to ensure that practical work can be carried out. He is conducting a very powerful struggle. He is also the one putting this work into practice. Obstacles are being created within the state's existing system. They do not want his call to be implemented on time and as required. Everyone's eyes are on Abdullah Öcalan. Everyone is asking, 'What will Abdullah Öcalan say?' He is the principal figure conducting discussions and negotiations and leading this process. Since the process began, Öcalan has conducted nothing in secret. The struggle is open and transparent. He expresses his views openly. The state has always denied us and treated us as though we did not exist. It refused to recognise the Kurdish people and Kurdistan and denied their existence. The struggle was carried out under these conditions. Many things were created out of nothing."




‘The situation of political prisoners is a serious issue’




Kamuran Reşîd, a member of the Rojava Prisoners Committee, spoke about the situation of political prisoners who have not been released from prisons in Turkey and Northern Kurdistan (Bakur), despite having completed their sentences: "The situation of our comrades held in prisons in Northern Kurdistan and Turkey is frequently raised and discussed. Civil society organisations also organise various protests. However, the legal and social initiatives undertaken so far have failed to secure the release of prisoners when they are due to regain their freedom. This shows that both civil society organisations and the structures representing the existing legal system face serious problems. In general, a significant proportion of our comrades who have not been released have been sentenced to aggravated life imprisonment or life imprisonment in Turkish prisons.




The release of political prisoners is prevented through various methods. Sometimes their sentences are extended. Until 1991, a life sentence corresponded to a prison term of 16 years. When Turgut Özal became President of the Republic of Turkey, he waged a major war against us. Through legal measures, he increased this term from 16 to 30 years. The Turkish state's aim was to ensure that a person would remain in prison for 30 years and would not survive. In other words, the intention was that 'they will remain in prison for 30 years and die'. According to the Turkish state's policy, either individuals would spend 30 years in prison and die there, or the state would eliminate the PKK movement within those 30 years. This was one of the main objectives of the struggle waged against our organisation. Today, there are political prisoners, sick comrades and comrades whose sentences have been extended. The Turkish state's approach and policies have continued in this way for a long time. We cannot consider these issues separately."




Reşîd said: "The Turkish state also violates its own laws. The law is disregarded when it comes to the freedom movement led by Abdullah Öcalan. There are prisoners suffering from cancer who are no longer physically capable of surviving in prison. Some of our comrades are war veterans who have lost parts of their bodies during the war and cannot live independently, yet they are still being held in prison. They need to be released and allowed to live outside prison. The Turkish state violates both the law and moral principles. We have also spent time in prison. Many of our comrades lost their lives and became martyrs while imprisoned alongside us. Some died inside prison, others while being taken to hospital, and others after arriving at hospital. Sometimes they were released for medical treatment but subsequently lost their lives. Many of our comrades became martyrs under different circumstances.




The state imposes a policy of submission on prisoners. As Duran Kalkan stated in his statement, if one of our comrades dies in prison, we will declare them a martyr. This means that there is a war taking place there. The struggle carried out by the freedom movement, namely the Kurdistan Workers' Party (PKK), in the mountains was aimed at stopping the war. The freedom movement made tremendous efforts to end this war. It did everything within its power to bring the war to an end. Despite this, our comrades remain imprisoned. The Turkish state is also waging a war inside prisons. Duran Kalkan's recent statement is a warning both to us and to the Turkish state."




‘Imposing repentance is an attack on human dignity’




Reşîd went on to emphasise that the policy of imposing repentance constituted an attack on human dignity and said: "A policy of repentance is being implemented against prisoners who have struggled for freedom, and repentance is being imposed on them. Let me be clear: if a person spends so many years in prison, they do so for their cause, their dignity and their humanity. Prisoners who struggle for freedom are fully aware of this. They are not there simply for their own existence. Political prisoners are conscious and knowledgeable people who are there for a cause. That is why they have no regrets. The Turkish state also knows that this is not a question of repentance. Nevertheless, it continues to impose its policy of repentance through different methods. It wants to devalue the cause and the struggle.




Some of our comrades have spent 34 to 36 years in prison. Imposing a policy of repentance is an attack on human dignity. Today, our comrades in prison lead dignified lives. Their lives are meaningful because they have a purpose. They have established their own system. Despite being confined within four walls, they maintain a life of the greatest dignity. Now let us look at society outside prison. Society is not at peace psychologically or intellectually. The existing system has made society emotionally, intellectually and psychologically unwell. Our people, civil society organisaions and political structures must now understand that leadership and a form of organisation are needed to resolve the problems imposed on society by the system and to enable people to lead meaningful lives.




Those who will provide this leadership are Abdullah Öcalan and our comrades in prison. Therefore, people must act without delay. They must put pressure on the state through their own efforts and actions. In the legal sphere, the European Court of Human Rights (ECtHR) has now become powerless. We submit applications, but they do not receive responses. Legal applications are made both from inside and outside prisons, yet no results are obtained. This is because legal changes are needed. The existing legal framework and legislation are insufficient to bring about the necessary changes. The process that has begun must not be regarded as an ordinary process. Abdullah Öcalan has written numerous books, developed many ideas and presented projects. A manifesto has been put forward, and we must act accordingly and put it into practice. A foundation has been established. We must focus on how to strengthen this foundation further and how to achieve practical results. Abdullah Öcalan brought about changes during the most critical and difficult periods. Now, wherever people are and whatever field they are involved in, they must put their actions into practice. Human rights associations and institutions supporting prisoners should gather outside prison gates. But this alone is not enough. Long marches should be organised, people should support one another, and solidarity should be strengthened. This is a democratic right. The violations committed against prisoners must be brought to public attention. The greatest injustices take place in prisons."




Kamuran Reşîd also commemorated the martyrs of truth who lost their lives in pursuit of the truth, as well as all those who became martyrs for this cause, on the occasion of the anniversary of the founding of ANF News Agency.

title: Bilmez: The right to hope is a legal right, not a privilege
content:
The political authorities' delay in taking the necessary steps regarding the Peace and Democratic Society Process has become a subject of debate. Since the process began, Kurdish political representatives and the Kurdish movement have emphasised that clarifying the status of Kurdish People's Leader Abdullah Öcalan and implementing the European Court of Human Rights (ECtHR) ruling on the right to hope are indispensable conditions for negotiations. However, tensions have arisen following indications that those sentenced before 2005 would not benefit from the Framework Law, as well as statements by Presidential Chief Adviser Mehmet Uçum that Öcalan's status as a convicted prisoner would not change and that the enforcement of his sentence would not be suspended. Ibrahim Bilmez, one of Abdullah Öcalan's lawyers, who submitted another application to the Council of Europe's Committee of Ministers last week regarding the right to hope, spoke to ANF. Bilmez emphasised that the right to hope is not a privilege but a legal right that Turkey is obliged to uphold.




‘The right to hope cannot be tied to the process’




Lawyers from Asrın Law Office also responded to statements by government representatives concerning the status of Kurdish People's Leader Abdullah Öcalan, the chief negotiator in the Peace and Democratic Society Process, and the conditions necessary for him to work freely. Ibrahim Bilmez, one of Abdullah Öcalan's lawyers, stressed that the ECtHR's 2014 ruling on the right to hope concerning his client must be considered independently of the process that has been underway for two years. Bilmez emphasised that Abdullah Öcalan has rights recognised under both Turkish and international law, but that these rights have not been granted to him. He recalled that one of the most important of these was the ECtHR's 2014 ruling on the right to hope.




Bilmez said: "The ECtHR has issued a ruling concerning the right to hope, and that ruling clearly states: 'You cannot sentence a person to imprisonment until death. If you keep someone confined within four walls without any hope of release, this constitutes a violation of Article 3 of the Convention. In other words, it amounts to torture.' Therefore, since the day this ruling was issued, it has effectively meant that Mr. Öcalan and everyone held under aggravated life sentences have been subjected to conditions amounting to torture. There is no doubt that this process must continue and reach a conclusion. It is a very important process. Ultimately, the peoples of Turkey need peace and a solution. Our client, Mr. Öcalan, also plays an important role in this process. However, linking the ruling on the right to hope concerning Mr. Öcalan to this process is not the correct approach. The right to hope is not a privilege but a legal right. Nor is this legal right limited to our client, Mr. Öcalan. It concerns everyone serving an aggravated life sentence."




‘Turkey has been evading the issue for 12 years’




Bilmez recalled that Abdullah Öcalan is one of the most important actors in the ongoing Peace and Democratic Society Process and continued: "Mr. Öcalan's position as an important actor emerged as a result of many years of great struggle and resistance. The state did not therefore decide on its own initiative to recognise Mr. Öcalan as its interlocutor. There are various reasons for this. Mr. Öcalan has the determination, strength and sincerity needed to resolve the issue. The Kurdish people and the Kurdish movement stand behind Mr. Öcalan. The state knows and sees this very well. We are therefore talking about an actor of this significance, yet we see that his rights are not being recognised. As I mentioned earlier, I am discussing this independently of the current process. Even if this process did not exist, the ECtHR ruling would still have to be implemented. We have submitted applications to the Committee of Ministers of the Council of Europe concerning the implementation of the ECtHR ruling on the principle of the right to hope. However, Turkey has failed to implement the ECtHR's ruling on the right to hope since 2014 and has continually delayed proceedings before the Committee of Ministers. Normally, Turkey should prepare and submit an action plan to the Council of Europe setting out the changes or improvements it intends to introduce regarding the right to hope. But Turkey has not implemented the right to hope for 12 years. In the action plans it has submitted so far, it has consistently evaded the issue and delayed taking action."




‘This is not an approach that contributes to a solution’




Bilmez recalled that the Gurban Group of cases, which concerns the right to hope and includes Abdullah Öcalan's case in the same category, was discussed at the September 2025 meeting of the Committee of Ministers of the Council of Europe. He said that Turkey had been given until June 2026 to take action. Bilmez pointed out that Turkey had once again referred to the ongoing process in relation to the right to hope and criticised its approach: "The deadline given to Turkey by the Committee of Ministers expired in June 2026. However, this time Turkey pointed to the ongoing process and stated that legal arrangements would be introduced and that the right to hope could be included within their scope. Yet the recently introduced Framework Law shows that those sentenced before 2005 are excluded. Turkey had already argued that aggravated life imprisonment was an exceptional punishment and claimed that it was imposed only for 'terrorism-related offences'. However, this is precisely the issue on which the ECtHR ruled against Turkey. The ECtHR says that there can be no exceptions. It says that you cannot impose such a sentence on anyone, even as an exception. That is the essence of the issue. But those defending Turkey's position constantly act as though they do not understand this. Now they refer to Framework Law, but we can see that the same mentality and the same approach continue there as well. Once again, an exception is being introduced, and once again Mr. Öcalan and others in similar circumstances, namely those sentenced before 2005, are excluded. Unfortunately, this is not an approach that contributes to a solution."




‘The Committee of Ministers must not approach the right to hope politically’




Bilmez stressed that the Committee of Ministers of the Council of Europe must not approach the right to hope from a political perspective, emphasising that it is, above all, a human rights issue. He recalled that the right to hope concerns not only his client, Abdullah Öcalan, but also thousands of other people. Bilmez said: "Last week, we submitted a Rule 9.1 communication to the Committee of Ministers and clearly set out our criticisms. We believe that the Committee of Ministers must not act politically and must fulfil the duty imposed on it by the Convention. We believe it should direct Turkey accordingly. Since 2014, we have submitted numerous Rule 9.1 communications, and we have repeatedly seen Turkey prolonging the issue or linking it to the Kurdish question. We have always told the Committee of Ministers that this approach is wrong." Bilmez also pointed out that Turkey had not prepared an action plan by June 2026, the deadline set by the Committee of Ministers. He said, "When the Committee of Ministers announced that it would reconsider the Gurban Group of cases on 3 December 2026, Turkey hastily submitted an action plan on 5 October 2026. As with its previous action plans, it once again failed to present any concrete plan regarding the right to hope."




‘The special isolation regime continues on Imrali’




Bilmez pointed out that his client, Kurdish People's Leader Abdullah Öcalan, continues to be held under conditions of isolation at Imrali F-Type High Security Prison. Bilmez said: "A special isolation regime is still being implemented on Imrali. Yes, there is an ongoing process, but as his lawyers, we have been able to meet our client, Mr. Öcalan, only three times during these two years. Our most recent meeting with him took place on 21 March, Newroz Day. Family visits should normally take place every week, but during this process, only four or five visits have been possible. Therefore, the conditions on Imrali still do not comply with the law. If we are talking about resolving the Kurdish question, Mr. Öcalan's conditions must be improved. This is a matter of reason and common sense. If such a major issue is to be resolved, you naturally have to establish appropriate conditions for the person you recognise as your interlocutor so that he can address the issue, intervene, speak with other parties, convey his message to society, persuade his own people and deliver the necessary messages to the peoples of Turkey. Unfortunately, these conditions have not yet been established."




‘Mr. Öcalan must regain his freedom’




Bilmez recalled that the Kurdish question concerns not only Turkey but the entire Middle East and continued: "There is someone like Mr. Öcalan who has the determination to resolve this issue. Mr. Öcalan has continued to live under those conditions of isolation for years with the aim of resolving this issue. He has no other objective. I can say this because I have witnessed it with my own eyes as his lawyer. Therefore, the necessary groundwork must be laid and the appropriate conditions established to resolve this difficult issue. Mr. Öcalan must also regain his freedom. That is why I believe statements that do not contribute to resolving the issue should be avoided. Statements should be more reasonable, more measured and more appropriate to the sensitivity of the process. Precisely for this reason, as a lawyer, I prefer to pay attention to the actions of government officials rather than Mehmet Uçum's statements. First, the Framework Law that has been introduced must enter into force, and Mr. Öcalan's conditions must be improved as soon as possible. Conditions must be created that allow him to act in accordance with the requirements of this process. And, of course, most importantly, he must regain his freedom."

title: Tuncay Yılmaz: We want to build a united front of resistance in Europe - Part Two
content:
ANF spoke to Tuncay Yılmaz, founding co-chair of the Socialist Refoundation Party (SYKP), about the outcomes of the Cologne meeting, the need for a common struggle, the situation of left-wing and democratic forces in the face of the rising far right in Europe, and the roadmap for the proposed alliance.




The first part of this interview can be read 

here

. 




On 17 October, 25 organisations from different political traditions came together in Cologne. Similar attempts to build alliances have been made in Europe before. Why has the need to establish a common platform for struggle emerged again today? What distinguishes this meeting from previous initiatives?




Organisations from different political traditions and social groups in Europe have come together at various times. Previously, there was the European Assembly for Peace and Democracy (ABDEM). We then extended the organisation of the Peoples' Democratic Congress (HDK) in Turkey to Europe, establishing a broad organisation under the name HDK Europe. This organisation later became the European Democratic Forces Union (ADGB) and continued its activities under that name. Most recently, ahead of the NATO summit, a joint initiative called PANEV was established against imperialist aggression, wars and NATO.




All these initiatives emerged from efforts to find ways for the forces of democracy, peace, equality and freedom to become better organised in Europe and pursue more effective political action against the enormous aggressive power confronting us.




The alliances we established at different times sometimes lost their effectiveness, both because of changes in the objective conditions in which they were formed and, to speak frankly, because of our own shortcomings. This is a reality, and we are aware of it. Indeed, this was one of the issues on the agenda of our meeting. We want to learn from our previous experiences.




However, the mistakes we made in the past or the changes we have experienced should not prevent us from bringing democratic forces together again and carrying out a common struggle. And indeed, they are not preventing us. One of the main motivations that brought us together at this meeting was the growing hostility towards migrants in the European countries where we live, the rise of the right, fascist movements coming to power and increasing state violence. The fact that laws targeting asylum seekers have reached almost inhumane proportions is also deeply concerning to all of us. We want to build a united front of resistance against all of this.




At the same time, however, all our attention, thoughts and concerns are focused on developments in Turkey. Looking at Turkey, we see a totalitarian regime being built step by step. Everyone who opposes it becomes a target. Presidential candidates are arrested. Selahattin Demirtaş has been imprisoned for years, as has Figen Yüksekdağ. Ekrem İmamoğlu was subsequently arrested. The Republican People's Party (CHP), which prides itself on being the founding party of the state, is also under serious pressure. Attempts are being made to divide the party, and many of its representatives have been arrested.




Alongside all this, a negotiation process has begun. It has not yet reached the stage of a peace process. However, this negotiation process has the potential to generate a collective strength capable of pushing back attacks on democracy through the positive developments it could bring to the country's political life. Despite this, we see that the political authorities are acting with appalling arbitrariness in this process as well.




To speak frankly, this process has been made possible by the determination and goodwill of Abdullah Öcalan and the Kurdish Freedom Movement. After all, decisions were taken to lay down arms and dissolve the organisation. These decisions represent a profound transformation in the movement's historical existence.




Despite this, the state continues to display an extremely indifferent and unserious attitude towards taking steps on these issues, potentially jeopardising the process. Its actions could allow the anti-democratic practices it maintains throughout the country to continue in different forms in this area as well. We can all see that, for months, instead of implementing the legal arrangements brought onto Parliament's agenda with broad support, the authorities have merely continued saying, "We want this as well, and we want that too."




Frankly, they are acting entirely with the mentality of a trader. Instead of seriously addressing such a fundamental problem facing the state, the regime and the country, and taking steps to resolve it, the process is being conducted through demands such as, "What did you get? What did you give? Do this as well, do that as well."




Considering all these developments, we see that, as social and political organisations in Europe, we cannot pursue a politics focused solely on protecting ourselves, withdrawing into our own circles and limiting ourselves to our own concerns. The Confederation of European Alevi Unions (AABK), the Kurdistan Democratic Communities Congress in Europe (KCDK-E) and many socialist groups are part of this alliance.




When we assess developments in Turkey, Europe, the region and the world together, the necessity of carrying out a common struggle against them becomes clear. I believe this is precisely why we were able to organise such a broad gathering on 17 October.




As the far right gains strength in Europe, hostility towards migrants, racism and war policies are increasingly being debated. Yet left-wing and democratic forces appear to be struggling to act together. What do you think are the main reasons for this fragmentation? What role could the alliance being established in Cologne play in changing this situation?




It is very clear that we are moving towards a major transformation of the international system established after the Second World War. Very negative changes are taking place both in the balance of power between imperialist centres and in the relations between the ruling classes and oppressed sections of society.




I would like to explain this through a few examples. The developments taking place today in the Middle East, Syria, Palestine, Lebanon, all four parts of Kurdistan and Iran are connected to tensions over which powers will control the world's trade routes, valuable minerals and energy resources. Essentially, the world is being redesigned. This is not limited to the Middle East. The restructuring process is creating tensions across the entire world.




Secondly, certain gains regulating economic and social life, which the capitalist-imperialist bloc was compelled to accept in some form during the existence of the Soviet Union, are now being rejected. For example, there are discussions in Germany about raising the retirement age to 70.




Why are young people taking to the streets in such large numbers in France? Why do they refuse to leave the streets despite such intense state violence? What are the fundamental demands that have brought the student movement in Serbia towards success? What lies behind the developments in Albania?




At the root of all this is the following reality: the ruling classes do not see a strong alternative or opposition capable of challenging them. Consequently, they are introducing measures aimed at securing as many advantages as possible in line with their own interests, both internationally and nationally.




The left, on the other hand, has frankly failed to create a comprehensive and renewed alternative. Without a coherent programme that society can embrace, internalise and stand behind, support for the left inevitably declines.




However, there are examples where this situation has been overcome. I believe these experiences offer important lessons about what we need to do.




Take Brazil, for example. Despite the support of the United States and major technology companies, from Elon Musk to Meta, Bolsonaro lost and Lula managed to win. The decisive factor was the creation of a common programme that brought together the demands not only of the working class but also of Indigenous peoples, poor peasants, young people and women.




In other words, movements that can bring together different sections of society opposed to the existing ruling system and unite them around a common programme can achieve success.




We see a similar experience in France. Yes, Macron remains in power, and the far right represented by Le Pen is in a strong position. However, the experience of La France Insoumise (France Unbowed) and the New Popular Front demonstrates that, despite all the risks, different opposition groups can come together around shared democratic demands.




What matters here is developing a programme capable of responding to society's most fundamental and pressing problems. People look at what you are concretely proposing to address the problems they face.




For example, the reason Elif Eralp has been able to come to the fore in Berlin against the Social Democratic Party (SPD), which enjoys the backing of major capital interests, is that she has developed a programme addressing society's fundamental problems. Similarly, the Communist Party's electoral victories over three terms in Graz, Austria, provide another example.




The existing system claims that it can set housing prices as it wishes and transform the healthcare system to the detriment of society. Society, in turn, is reacting against this.




In short, the left has not yet managed to develop a comprehensive response to this new situation confronting it globally. For this reason, a powerful global wave of the left has not emerged to counter the rising right. Nevertheless, there are important experiences demonstrating that such a development is possible.




‘We must build a bridge between the struggle in Europe and Turkey’




We discussed the contribution that the alliance we want to establish in Cologne could make from two perspectives at our meeting.




First, as people living in Europe, we are directly affected by the problems here. The housing crisis is our problem too. Changes to the healthcare system, environmental policies and attacks on social rights are also our problems. Therefore, through this alliance, we will become directly involved in social struggles across Europe.




Second, we need to provide strong support from the diaspora for the struggle in Turkey. However, this support cannot be achieved simply by saying, "We stand with those struggling in Turkey."




We must bring international social forces to a position where they can support the struggle in Turkey. We must embrace the struggle being waged in Turkey from Europe and create pressure on governments here and international institutions. Only in this way can we provide effective support for the ongoing struggle for peace and democracy in Turkey.




Of course, protesting developments in Turkey in the central squares of European cities is important. We cannot underestimate this. However, we must also recognise that this alone is not enough.




The most fundamental role our alliance can play is to build a bridge between internationalist struggles and the ongoing struggle for peace and democracy in Turkey. This is particularly important in bringing political and social forces in Europe together with the struggle in Turkey.




We have organisations with considerable experience and connections in this field. The diplomatic relations of the Confederation of European Alevi Unions, the connections of the Kurdish Freedom Movement and KCDK-E across Europe, and the ties established by socialist movements with socialist forces in other countries represent an important accumulation of experience and relationships.




Let me give you an example. You may have noticed that an organisation called the Anti-Imperialist League (AIL) was among those listed in the statement we published after the meeting. This is an internationalist bloc organised in 37 countries worldwide, including 14 European countries.




Representatives of this organisation also attended our meeting and stated clearly: "We attach importance to the revolutionary and democratic struggle in Turkey. We are aware of its significance for the Middle East. We know about the struggle of the Kurdish Freedom Movement and other democratic forces. We will closely follow this alliance and carry out joint activities, both to receive support from that struggle and to provide support to it."




This is precisely the point I am trying to make. I believe the alliance we have established will serve as an important bridge between international democratic and social forces and the struggle in Turkey.




You mentioned the rise of the far right in Europe and the left's inability to develop a strong alternative. However, this crisis is not limited to particular countries; it has an international dimension. Despite this, we see that internationalist struggle is not sufficiently strong. Some academics describe developments in Europe as the approaching footsteps of fascism. Why do you think internationalist struggle has weakened so much, and how can it be strengthened again today?




Let me continue in connection with my answer to your first question. As you know, world history has seen the experiences of the First, Second and Third Internationals. These Internationals were able to bring together progressive and communist forces from around the world. However, both after the collapse of the Soviet Union and even while it still existed, it had become clear that the communist international model of organisation was inadequate to meet the needs of struggles around the world.




This is because it is not possible to organise social opposition worldwide through an international organisation consisting solely of one communist party from each country.




Following the dissolution of the Soviet Union, new attempts were made. Social forums emerged first. You may remember the enormous gathering held in Porto Alegre, Brazil. This was one of the first significant examples of the search for new approaches.




The Occupy movements emerged later. The Gezi Resistance in Turkey can also be considered part of this category of social movements. Many experiences, from movements in North Africa to protests spreading across Europe and the Americas, were part of the search for new forms of struggle.




Today, we clearly need a new understanding of internationalist organisation. There are already many international organisations around the world. As far as I have been able to follow, there are various formations extending as far as a Sixth International.




However, they share a significant weakness. Some consist of communist parties that define themselves as continuations of the earlier communist international tradition. There are also Internationals organised around Trotskyist, Maoist and other ideological traditions. In other words, these organisations restrict themselves to particular political traditions and are open only to organisations emerging from those traditions.




The second fundamental problem is that, with one exception, almost all existing Internationals are based on communist, socialist or progressive political parties. They are essentially structured around party organisations.




Yet social opposition around the world today does not consist solely of political parties. One example that approaches this issue differently is the Progressive International. Alongside political parties, this organisation can also include social movements, labour organisations, women's movements, different intellectual formations and, most importantly, individuals.




Today, we cannot develop an adequate struggle against the rising right-wing and fascist movements around the world through an International consisting solely of political parties. Nor can we address this problem simply by strengthening one of the existing international organisations.




‘We need an International of Internationals’




I conceptualise this need as follows: Today, we need an International of Internationals.




In other words, we need an organisation capable of bringing existing international formations together while also including social movements that are not affiliated with any political party.




For example, Brazil's Landless Rural Workers' Movement (MST) represents a social struggle far broader than the existence of a political party. Or consider the student movement that has emerged in Serbia today. That is not a political party either.




We cannot tell all these forces of social opposition, "First, go and establish a party, then apply to our International, and we will examine your application and make a decision." Such an approach cannot meet the needs of social struggle. Nor can it create the conditions for internationalist struggle that you have pointed to.




We need a more dynamic and flexible network of internationalist relations, one that can bring together different forces of social struggle and enable them to act and organise collectively.




‘We must renew the old model of internationalist organisation’




This is undoubtedly not possible through the forms of internationalist organisation used in the past. We now have to renew that model. We must even open up channels of participation through which individuals can play an effective role.




Without distinguishing between small groups and large parties, and without excluding smaller movements, we must bring together all progressive, left-wing, socialist and democratic forces around the world against the existing capitalist and imperialist system and its destructive policies, which are once again calling fascism into service.




We face the task of establishing an International of Internationals capable of bringing the women's liberation movement, feminist movements, ecological movements and class movements together on a common platform of struggle.




This is the task facing socialists today. Recognising this reality, we must develop new forms of organisation that bring together our existing networks and unite different areas of struggle.




Important decisions were taken at the meeting held in Cologne on 17 October to establish a common platform for struggle. What organisational model do you envisage for this new alliance? What concrete steps will you take in the coming period?




We held discussions about two main issues at the meeting. Our first agenda item concerned the basis on which the alliance we want to establish should take shape. In other words, what should its political and social framework be? For example, can we focus solely on problems in Turkey? If we do so, can we be effective in our activities in Europe? No.




Or can we concern ourselves only with problems in Europe and say that developments in Turkey do not concern us? We cannot say that either. As I explained earlier, we are both directly involved in the struggles in Turkey and Europe and serve as a bridge between them. Therefore, the foundation of the alliance we establish must reflect this reality.




Our second agenda item concerned the kind of organisational model we should develop in light of the lessons learned from our previous experiences. Should this be a platform made up of political organisations? Or should we establish an assembly or congress structure that also allows individual participation, as was previously the case with HDK Europe? Should it take the form of a forum or a network?




We began discussing all these options. However, we decided not to make a final decision on the organisational model at the first meeting. Each organisation first needs to discuss this issue internally.




Furthermore, although we brought together a significant proportion of the organised forces in Europe through the participation of 25 organisations, we do not believe we have yet reached everyone we could potentially involve.




For this reason, we have set ourselves a one-month period. During this time, we will meet with other organisations and inform them about the alliance we want to establish. We will share the framework discussed at our first meeting. We want to determine the organisational model of this alliance collectively, together with the organisations and groups that will join us.




We will hold another face-to-face meeting in November. Meanwhile, our work and discussions are continuing. We have also assigned people to hold meetings with various organisations. Indeed, several more organisations have joined our initiative since the first meeting. We expect further participation.




The structure of the alliance we establish, its organisational model, the line of struggle it will pursue and its approach to politics will therefore become clearer at the forthcoming meetings.




‘We want to develop a common programme through broad participation’




We also held another important discussion at the meeting. Perhaps it would be more appropriate to advance this process through a conference with broader participation, rather than limiting it to discussions among representatives of political organisations.




In other words, we could organise a conference to discuss the question of reorganisation. This would allow us to develop a common programme and organisational model with the participation not only of political organisations but also of individuals, smaller groups and social groups active in different areas of struggle.




This approach also corresponds to the perspective I outlined earlier on how internationalist struggle should be reorganised. I believe an organisational model that brings together different forces of social struggle and enables their direct participation would be more effective.




We will evaluate all these options in the coming period. I can say that the meeting we hold in November will provide greater clarity on the path we will follow and how we will advance the process of establishing the alliance.
