title: From France to Kurdistan: How well do we understand society in transition?
content:
France occupies a special place in the political memory of the modern world. The Enlightenment, the Revolution of 1789, and the Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen gave freedom and equality universal significance. Yet proclaiming rights does not necessarily mean that all social groups can exercise them equally. The Republic’s promise of equality has repeatedly been put to the test by colonialism, class divisions, and discrimination against citizens with migrant backgrounds.




Against this backdrop, the words of jurist and statesman Robert Badinter, who lost his father during the Nazi occupation and played a key role in abolishing the death penalty in 1981, take on particular significance: “France is not the country of human rights, but the country where the Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen was proclaimed.” The gap between the historical legacy of these rights and contemporary social realities continues to demand critical examination.




The new language of the streets




The protests by students at French secondary schools, which began in mid-September and continued throughout October 2026, offer valuable insights into contemporary French society. Teacher shortages, long school days, overcrowded classrooms, poor conditions in school cafeterias, and anxieties about the future are among the students’ concerns. Some protest signs also reveal a sense of humor: the irony of a student complaining that his overloaded timetable leaves him no time to see his girlfriend may seem trivial at first glance. Yet these young people are questioning not only the conditions of their education but also the way their everyday lives are organized.




After five weeks of sustained protests, the government announced a plan on October 26 that included changes to the Parcoursup* higher education admissions system, reductions in class sizes, and the creation of additional university places. School and university student organizations considered these measures insufficient. The fact that problems raised for years only make it onto the political agenda following mass mobilization by young people highlights the difference between merely listening to the youth and genuinely responding to their demands.




Taking to the streets is nothing new in France. The country has a deeply rooted culture of protest, stretching from the revolutions and May 1968 to workers’ strikes and demonstrations against pension reforms. Today’s Generation Z, however, has a different relationship with traditional institutions. Digital communication tools make it easier to mobilize around specific demands in a very short time. Yet this is not simply a matter of new means of organization. Young people refuse to let others determine their lives and futures. They demand that their voices, living conditions, and expectations be taken seriously, and they want to play an active role in shaping their own future.




How well do we, who are intimately familiar with May 1968 and the political struggles of the past, truly know today’s French youth and the social realities in which they live?




We live in an age when access to information is easier than ever before. Yet having access to information is far from the same as understanding society as it is lived today. Young people who do not carry the political memory of previous generations can still fight against the injustices they experience themselves. Rather than judging them by the standards of the past, we must listen to them and understand what they have to say today.




Between solidarity and racist violence




The social reality of France cannot be understood solely through young people’s protests and their search for solidarity. In a country where the ideals of freedom and equality have a significant historical legacy, discrimination, exclusion, and racist violence also persist.




After the protests by secondary school students had dominated public debate, an armed attack in Trappes and La Verrière on October 23 once again brought another, darker side of France into focus. One person was killed and five others were injured, including a twelve-year-old child. President Emmanuel Macron described the incident as a “racist terrorist attack.” Investigations are underway on suspicion of a racist motive and terrorist offenses.




No direct causal link can be established between the students’ protests against their educational conditions and this attack. However, the fact that both occurred during the same period illustrates how social tensions can manifest in different ways. The growing influence of the far right in Europe is another social reality that cannot be overlooked. Economic insecurity, migration, and anxieties about the future can, under certain circumstances, foster solidarity, while under others they can encourage exclusionary identity politics.




The key is not to hastily interpret social developments through existing ideological frameworks, but to understand them in terms of their own causes and contradictions.




Neo-nationalism and youth in Turkey




The anxieties about the future experienced by young people in France raise the question of what political orientations similar forms of social uncertainty might produce in other countries. The neo-nationalism emerging among young people in Turkey is particularly revealing in this regard.




According to a study published in December 2025 by researcher Selin Gücüm at the French Institute for International and Strategic Affairs (IRIS), a survey conducted by GoFor and KONDA in February 2024 among people aged 18 to 30 found that approximately 39 percent of respondents identified as nationalist, while 44 percent identified primarily as Kemalist. These figures refer to all young people surveyed, not exclusively to those holding neo-nationalist views.




Neo-nationalism is not merely a continuation of traditional conservative nationalism. It is also found among segments of urban, secular youth who are critical of authoritarian forms of rule. Some young people who express concerns about economic insecurity and restrictions on fundamental freedoms simultaneously perceive refugees or the political demands of Kurds as threats to national unity and sovereignty.




Why does someone who demands freedom for themselves fail to recognize the freedom of others as part of the same principle?




This political orientation cannot be explained solely as a spontaneous reaction emerging among young people. One of its key historical foundations lies in the homogenizing conception of national identity that the Turkish state has repeatedly reproduced through the education system, official historiography, and security-related discourse.




Selin Gücüm’s study highlights another important aspect: Some young people with neo-nationalist views do not regard the “father state” as a sacred and infallible authority, but instead criticize it for its inability to provide social and economic security. However, this criticism is not accompanied by an equal recognition of different identities. According to the report, Kurdish, Circassian, and Armenian identities are tolerated in these circles only insofar as they remain within the framework of “Turkishness.” This is therefore a political orientation that, while differing from traditional state nationalism, does not fully overcome its homogenizing conception of national identity.




No simple contrast can be drawn between young people in France and those in Turkey. Rather, the crucial question is why similar anxieties about the future foster solidarity under certain conditions, while under others they encourage a politics that denies other people their rights.




A shared future and social transformation




Can Kurdish and Turkish youth come together in a common democratic struggle in the face of poverty, unemployment, and anxieties about the future?




Shared problems do not necessarily give rise to a shared political consciousness. The experiences of Kurdish youth, shaped by language, identity, and historical memory, serve as a reminder that equality cannot be achieved solely on the basis of economic demands.




Moreover, shared problems are not experienced to the same extent everywhere. A report by the Center for Kurdish Studies comparing data from the SEGE-2017 and SEGE-2025 socioeconomic development indices describes 16 predominantly Kurdish-populated provinces as a “region of inequality.” After nearly a decade, none of these provinces had managed to move up to a higher level of development; all remained in the bottom 16 positions in the nationwide rankings. This does not indicate absolute stagnation, but rather that their relative position compared with the rest of Turkey has remained unchanged. While the region moved marginally closer to the national average, the gap between it and Istanbul actually widened.




Economic performance continued to improve in some provinces, but their rankings in education and healthcare remained virtually unchanged.




In the 2019/20 school year, the preschool enrollment rate in the region stood at 36 percent, compared with 46 percent in the other provinces. Understanding the lived realities of young people requires recognizing these conditions as well.




Kurdish youth may have a strong sense of patriotism and a deep identification with their origins. However, this should not be equated with adopting the political and organizational patterns of previous generations. Embracing Kurdish identity does not require rejecting other identities and can be reconciled with universal values of freedom and equality.




Everyone engaged with the Kurdish question and the cause of Kurdistan can make an effort to speak directly with the young people around them. Equally important, however, is listening to their answers without trying to change them. Young people’s political and ideological views may differ from our expectations. Interpreting these differences as a rejection of patriotism or the historical struggle would be an overly simplistic conclusion.




The living conditions of Kurdish youth in the four parts of Kurdistan, in cities outside Kurdistan in Turkey, Syria, Iraq, and Iran, in the Caucasus, and in other regions of the world are by no means identical. Education, working life, migration, women’s demands for freedom, and technological change are reshaping their relationship with politics.




One of the central challenges facing the Kurdish freedom movement is passing on the legacy of its historical struggle to future generations. Yet methods that brought success yesterday may become a weakness tomorrow if they are no longer sufficient to understand a changing society and its new dynamics. Passing on this legacy does not mean imposing the language and organizational forms of previous generations on young people, but enabling them to give meaning to that legacy within the context of their own lives and in their own language.




We are living through a period of polycrisis, characterized by interconnected crises in which wars, economic crises, mass migration, technological upheavals, and political tensions mutually reinforce one another. Wars are no longer fought solely on the front lines, but also in the realms of economics, technology, and information. It is as though we are living on a simmering volcano. Beneath the events we perceive on the surface, deeper tensions are building.




At such a time, political movements that seek to drive social transformation and change society must question not only their political discourse but also their established ways of listening and organizing. It is these young people who will live through the future. We, meanwhile, are increasingly the bearers of experiences from the past. These experiences are valuable. Developing visions for the future, anticipating developments, and exploring possible paths forward are also among the responsibilities of political movements.




Yet the experiences and insights of the past do not give anyone the right to determine alone how the future should be shaped. The real challenge lies in finding ways to envision and shape the future together, without imposing historical experience on new generations against their will.




How well do political movements that seek to transform society truly understand society in transition? Perhaps the question we must first ask ourselves is even simpler: How attentively do we actually listen to the young people to whom we say the future belongs?




*Parcoursup: France’s national online platform through which final-year secondary school students and other prospective students submit applications to universities and other higher education programs.

title: Hatimoğulları: Alevis should play an active role in the peace process
content:
DEM Party Co-Chair Tülay Hatimoğulları called on the Alevi community to actively participate in the peace and democratization process in Turkey. At a meeting with representatives of Alevi organizations in Istanbul, she criticized the exclusion of Alevis from parliamentary deliberations and warned against leaving the future of the process solely in the hands of the government. Lasting peace, she argued, could only be achieved on the basis of equal citizenship, legally guaranteed fundamental freedoms, and the democratic restructuring of the republic.




The meeting took place at the Kazım Karabekir Cemevi in Istanbul’s Ümraniye district. Alongside representatives of Alevi associations and institutions, numerous other guests attended the event. Speaking here, Hatimoğulları emphasized that the process initiated by Abdullah Öcalan must not be understood as a power struggle between political camps. “We do not view peace in terms of one side winning and the other losing. Peace means building a shared life and giving one another our consent to do so. Genuine peace can only emerge when all 86 million citizens of this country can live in justice, freedom, and peace.”




Criticism of the exclusion of the Alevi community




The DEM Party co-chair recalled the decades of persecution, massacres, and assimilation policies targeting Alevis. Despite these experiences, she said, the Alevi community expanded its social and political organization in Turkey and Europe. Rather than allowing the history of injustices it suffered to paralyze it, the Alevi community drew strength from these experiences for its resistance and self-organization, she underlined. Hatimoğulları also addressed the massacres of Alevis in Syria by the Islamist forces of HTS, which have ruled the country since late 2024. She noted that international solidarity actions against this violence was warmly welcomed by the affected population.




Regarding the peace process, she particularly criticized the Turkish parliament speaker’s refusal to hear representatives of the Alevi community. “We have repeatedly asked the government why Alevis are not being heard. A faith community to which millions of people in this country belong cannot be ignored. Peace cannot be built without speaking to Alevis.” Remarking that the DEM Party has repeatedly insisted on their participation, she described Parliament Speaker Numan Kurtulmuş’s rejection of this demand as politically unacceptable.




Peace process amid state repression




Hatimoğulları spoke at length about the contradictions between the government’s official declarations of commitment to peace and its continued policies of repression. She pointed out that restrictions on freedom of expression, the persecution of opposition politicians, the imprisonment of critical voices, and the appointment of state trustees to opposition-run municipalities stood in the way of credible democratization. She also addressed questions that Alevi organizations had raised with the DEM Party: How can a peace process be advanced under conditions of severe state repression? Is there a risk that the AKP will exploit the process for its own electoral interests? And does participating in the talks mean politically aligning oneself with the government?




“These are all legitimate questions. As a party, we raise them with the same clarity as you do. The concerns and objections of the Alevi community must be taken seriously and discussed openly, Hatimoğulları stated. In this context, she also criticized the political instrumentalization of ongoing investigations and the unequal treatment of alleged financial crimes. “While opposition figures and smaller businesses are being targeted with considerable severity, the names of politically influential individuals allegedly implicated in the major investment fund scandal remain undisclosed.”




“If these were names from the opposition, wouldn’t they have published them on every front page long ago? But now they won’t even reveal the names. Why? Because the matter reaches into their own ranks. Despite the contradictions between the peace process and government policy, the democratic opposition must not abandon the struggle for a political solution.”




“We do not need religious brotherhood, but equal rights”




One of the DEM Party’s central demands is the legal guarantee of equal citizenship, Hatimoğulları said, rejecting a conception of social coexistence based on shared religious identity while ethnic, cultural, and religious differences continue to be politically subordinated. “Despite all these concerns and criticisms, we have no choice but to establish peace in this country. We do not need brotherhood based on the ummah, but solidarity based on equal citizenship. Religious brotherhood is not enough for us. We need equal rights, and this equality must be guaranteed by law.”




According to the DEM Party co-chair, Alevis must therefore not merely observe the process from the sidelines: “Their active participation is also necessary to prevent the government from determining its course and outcomes alone. If we manage to stand together at the heart of this process, take ownership of it, and move it forward, those who are carrying it forward will not be left alone. Peace will then no longer be left to the goodwill of this government.”




A democratic republic as a shared vision




Hatimoğulları reaffirmed that the demands of the Alevi community are an integral part of the DEM Party’s political program. These, she said, include recognition of religious and cultural diversity, a science-based education system free from state-imposed religious homogenization, and guaranteed access to education in one’s mother tongue. “Education policy, in particular, demonstrates how deeply state assimilation policies are embedded in social institutions,” she said, noting that the DEM Party opposes a homogenizing education system that excludes different identities, faiths, and languages from public life.




On the occasion of the 103rd anniversary of the founding of the Republic on October 29, Hatimoğulları emphasized the need for fundamental democratization of the political system. “The Republic must be the common home of all 86 million citizens. To achieve this, it must treat everyone equally and deny no one’s identity. What we need most urgently in Turkey today is the democratization of the Republic and the establishment of a democratic republic.”




Following her speech, the meeting with representatives of Alevi organizations continued closed to the press.

title: Iranian security bodies block medical leave for Kurdish political prisoner
content:
Iranian security bodies have blocked medical leave and access to adequate treatment for Fahim Ebadi, a Kurdish political prisoner in Orumiyeh Central Prison who suffers from diabetes, high blood pressure and high blood fat levels, the Kurdistan Human Rights Network (KHRN) has reported.




Iranian forces arrested Ebadi, who is from Orumiyeh and is serving a 45-month sentence, in the city around two years ago.




After several weeks of interrogation at the Ministry of Intelligence’s detention facility, he was transferred to Orumiyeh Central Prison, where he has remained since.




After several months in detention, a branch of the Islamic Revolutionary Court of Orumiyeh sentenced him to 60 months in prison on charges of “membership of opposition groups” in connection with membership of the Kurdistan Workers’ Party (PKK).




His sentence was subsequently reduced to 45 months after he waived his right to appeal and requested a sentence reduction.

title: Resistance against solar power plant project in Kulp on day 91
content:
Resistance against the planned solar power plant project.in the village of Cixsê, in the Kulp district of Amed (Diyarbakır), has continued for three months. For 91 days, residents have maintained a vigil in protest against the project, which threatens grazing lands, water sources, and agricultural livelihoods. An investigation by the Union of Chambers of Turkish Engineers and Architects (TMMOB) has now confirmed significant shortcomings in the environmental impact assessment. The organization is calling for the immediate cancellation of the project.




Representatives of the TMMOB Coordination Council in Amed presented their findings during a protest in Cixsê. The findings are based on a site inspection conducted on October 14, during which experts examined both the proposed construction site and the information contained in the environmental impact assessment documentation.




Grazing lands and water sources at risk




According to Filiz Kaçar, a member of TMMOB’s Energy and Ecology Commission, approximately 30 hectares of land within and around the project area are used as grazing grounds for livestock. The installation of solar panels, fencing of the site, and construction of access roads would fragment continuous grazing areas and significantly restrict their use. The commission is particularly concerned about the potential impact on local water resources. The affected area contains a pond and several streams that are important for supplying water to livestock. The planned construction work could damage these natural resources.




Cixsê is also an important center for silkworm breeding and cocoon production. Alongside livestock farming and crop cultivation, this sector forms a vital foundation of local livelihoods. According to the experts, habitats of migratory birds such as cranes, storks, and swallows would also be affected.




Significant shortcomings in the environmental impact assessment




According to Kaçar, TMMOB’s investigation found that key ecological and economic factors had been inadequately addressed in the project documentation. These include existing bodies of water, the traditional use of grazing lands, biodiversity, natural hazards, and the planned energy storage systems. The organization does not fundamentally oppose the expansion of renewable energy, but rather its implementation at the expense of local residents and their livelihoods. “The transition to renewable energy is necessary. But an energy transition that ignores nature and life is not sustainable. The solar project planned in Cixsê must be stopped immediately,” Kaçar stated.




Fatoş Nujen Ayhan of the TMMOB Coordination Council also criticized the economic interests behind the project: “Cixsê’s energy resources must be used and managed by the local population itself. We cannot allow corporations to exploit our resources and then sell the energy generated from them back to the people at high prices.”




Incorrect photographs previously discovered in environmental report




The new findings have intensified the dispute over the approval of the project. As early as September, it emerged that the environmental impact assessment report contained photographs that had not been taken in the proposed project area. The Amed Bar Association and the Association of Lawyers for Freedom (ÖHD) subsequently filed a criminal complaint against officials of the environmental consultancy Global ÇED and the construction company VBZ İnşaat. However, the public prosecutor’s office in Kulp found insufficient grounds for suspicion of document forgery and closed the investigation. The lawyers appealed the decision. Separately, the decision approving the environmental impact assessment is the subject of administrative court proceedings.




“Our land belongs to us”




The DEM Party also supports the villagers’ resistance. Berivan Turan, a member of the party’s provincial executive board in Amed, warned of the long-term social and ecological consequences during the protest. She stated that the loss of agricultural land and natural resources could exacerbate unemployment, poverty, and migration. “The people do not want a solar power plant on this grazing land. They have been expressing their opposition for months,” Turan said. She placed the resistance in Cixsê within the broader context of local struggles against the economic exploitation of natural resources in Kurdistan, citing the vigil in Arzoxlî as an example.




“We do not want to lose our cemeteries, our culture, or our memories. We will not allow any further plundering of Kurdistan. Yesterday we were in Arzoxlî; today we are in Cixsê. Our struggle continues,” Turan said.




Remarking The local population would not give up its livelihoods, she stated: “Our land belongs to us, and we will not give it to anyone. The natural environment of Cixsê is indispensable to us. We are resisting the solar project because we want to pass this heritage on to our children intact. We demand energy production that serves the people, not projects imposed against their will.”

title: Concern for at Least 14 Kurdish prisoners facing death sentences in Iran
content:
30 October has been declared International Day of Political Prisoners. A review of published human rights reports identifies at least 14 Kurdish political prisoners and protesters facing death sentences in Iran.




This list brings together reported cases and includes both initial court rulings and sentences upheld on appeal. Pakhshan Azizi, Hatem Ozdemir, Yousef Ahmadi, Pezhman Touberehrizi, Arman Marefati, Mohammad Faraji, Raouf Sheikh-Maroufi and Mohsen Eslamkhah are eight of these prisoners.




Earlier human rights reports warned that they could face execution. The reports described unfair and secretive proceedings, torture, pressure to obtain forced confessions, and violations of their right to defend themselves.




Hatem Ozdemir is a Kurdish citizen of Turkey imprisoned in Iran. Khosrow Mohammadnia, Masoud Toushmalani, Sirwan Shabani, Borzou Rezaei and Omran Amani are five others on the list. They were sentenced to death in connection with the January 2026 protests. The sentences against the first three were reported on 1 October, and Rezaei’s on 6 October. On 29 October, it was reported that 21-year-old Omran Amani had been formally informed of his death sentence at Great Tehran Penitentiary.

title: Human rights violations against Kurds continue in Iran
content:
The Iranian regime’s practices of detention, imprisonment and punishment targeting Kurds continue. According to information reported by the Kurdistan Human Rights Network (KHRN), a request for medical leave by Fehîm Ebadî, a Kurdish prisoner with diabetes held in Urmia Central Prison, has been rejected, preventing him from accessing medical treatment.




Ebadî was detained by Iranian regime forces in Urmia two years ago. He was sentenced to five years in prison on the allegation of being a “member of the Kurdistan Workers’ Party (PKK).” His sentence was subsequently reduced to 45 months.




Detained without a warrant




Mohammad Reza, who lives in the Malekshahi region of Ilam Province, was detained by Iranian regime forces and taken to an undisclosed location. According to KHRN, Mohammad Reza was detained at his family home in the early hours of the morning on 29 October, without the authorities presenting an arrest warrant. No information has yet emerged regarding the grounds for his detention.




Kurdish cultural activist arrested




Metîn Feremerzpûr, a Kurdish cultural activist and doctoral student in philosophy at the University of Tabriz, was also detained by regime forces on allegations of “propaganda against the state” and taken to Mahabad Prison. title: DEM Party delegation meets with prisoners: Rights violations continue in Aegean region
content:
A DEM Party delegation which included MPs Nevroz Uysal Aslan, Burcugül Çubuk, İbrahim Akın, Vezir Parlak, and Onur Düşünmez, met with prisoners held at Buca and Aliağa Şakran prisons between 26 and 29 October.




Speaking outside Şakran Prison, lawyer and MP Nevroz Uysal Aslan said prisoners’ access to social activities was being restricted, problems were occurring during conditional release procedures, and petitions were being left unanswered.




Aslan noted that some women prisoners at Şakran were being prevented from using the shared exercise yard, that the imposition of identity requirements continued, and that some detainees were being denied access to their rights to sports, outdoor exercise, and social activities.




She also stated that sick prisoners were facing obstacles in accessing healthcare, while letters, books, and publications in Kurdish were being delayed or withheld.




Referring also to the Peace and Democratic Society Process, Nevroz Uysal Aslan said political prisoners held in prisons should be released to pave the way for democratic politics and enable legal steps to be taken.




The delegation’s prison visits are expected to continue at Bodrum S-Type Prison.

title: Kobanê students: Our language is our existence
content:
Students in Kobanê protested against the Syrian Ministry of Education's decision to limit Kurdish-language education to three lessons. The students said that Kurdish was a fundamental part of their identity and existence and expressed their desire to continue receiving education in their mother tongue. 




We want to continue receiving education in our mother tongue




Eleventh-grade student Rehef Feysel Sedûn told ANF that they were not opposed to any language and that every people had the right to receive education in their mother tongue. Rehef Feysel Sedûn said, "I am the daughter of Martyr Abu Layla, and I have been receiving education in my own language for 11 years. We want to continue receiving education in our mother tongue. We already have Arabic and English lessons as well."







 







Rehef Feysel Sedûn pointed out that millions of Kurds had the right to receive education in their own language, stressing that mother-tongue education was a fundamental right of every people.




Rehef Feysel Sedûn, who wants to become a lawyer, said, "As Kurds, we also have the right to receive education in our mother tongue. I want to become a lawyer, and my dream was to do so in my own language. I want to fulfil my dreams in my mother tongue and defend my people in my own language."

title: Over 600 international personalities appeal to Council of Europe to act on Right to Hope for Öcalan
content:
International efforts to secure the implementation of the Right to Hope for Abdullah Öcalan, and to enable him to participate in the Peace and Democratic Society Process under free conditions, have entered a new phase.




As part of the international campaign “Freedom for Abdullah Öcalan, a Political Solution to the Kurdish Question,” a letter has been sent to the Presidency of the Committee of Ministers of the Council of Europe (CoE). According to information provided by the campaign organisers, the letter was prepared with the support of 620 signatories from 29 countries around the world.




The letter, sent ahead of the Council of Europe's Committee of Ministers' human rights meeting, scheduled to take place from 1 to 3 December 2026, calls for the implementation of the 2014 ruling by the European Court of Human Rights (ECtHR) concerning Öcalan.




According to information shared by the campaign organisers, the new letter has received the support of 58 elected representatives. The signing initiative also includes individuals affiliated with 30 political parties, 90 civil society organisations and 16 trade unions.




Politicians, academics, lawyers, trade unionists, representatives of women's organisations and human rights advocates from Austria, Germany, Italy, France, Belgium, Denmark, Norway, Sweden, Switzerland, Spain, Canada, the United States and other countries have signed the letter.




Among the signatories are 2022 Nobel Prize in Physics laureate Anton Zeilinger, philosopher Slavoj Žižek, Member of the European Parliament Özlem Alev Demirel, Nicola Fratoianni and Maurizio Acerbo from Italy, Bjørnar Moxnes from Norway, Carlo Sommaruga from Switzerland, Kadir Kasırga from Sweden, and Mertxe Aizpurua, a representative of EH Bildu from the Basque Country.




The list also includes numerous former and current members of parliament, municipal councillors, lawyers, academics, trade union representatives and representatives of organisations engaged in solidarity work with Kurdish institutions.




The letter, addressed to the Presidency of the Committee of Ministers, is as follows: 




"On behalf of the international campaign “Freedom for Öcalan, Political Solution to the Kurdish Question,” we call on the Committee of Ministers of the Council of Europe to ensure Turkey’s implementation of the “Right to Hope” in accordance with the European Court of Human Rights’ judgments in Öcalan v. Turkey (No. 2) and the related Gurban Group of cases. The international campaign started on the 9th of October 2024 with participation of undersigned social movements, trade unions, Nobel Laureates, lawyers, academics, youth, women’s organisations, NGOs, elected officials, and others in its third anniversary renews its demands for the release of Mr. Abdullah Öcalan for the success of the peace process. 




This is a decisive moment to support Turkey in fulfilling its obligations as a Council of Europe member state and advancing the ongoing Peace and Democratic Society process initiated by Mr. Abdullah Öcalan. Implementing the Right to Hope is the essential legal step toward ending the regime of extreme isolation imposed on Mr. Öcalan for the past 27 years and enabling him, as the principal negotiator, to participate effectively in the peace process.




The December 2026 meeting of the Ministers’ Deputies presents a crucial opportunity for the Committee of Ministers to reaffirm its commitment to the rule of law, democracy, and human rights through concrete action. A strong decision supporting implementation of the Right to Hope would help Turkey in breaking out of its current deadlock on such fundamental issues, while demonstrating international support for a peaceful and democratic resolution of the Kurdish question.




Mr. Öcalan’s Call for Peace and Democratic Society, announced on 27 February 2025, has had significant impact in Turkey and the wider region. It has contributed to reducing violence and renewed hope for democratic dialogue and peaceful coexistence after decades of conflict. However, for these hope to materialise significant changes domestically and the support of the international community are needed more than ever. 




Despite recent legislative developments, Mr. Öcalan remains imprisoned under conditions that severely restrict his fundamental rights and communication with the outside world. While some legal reforms have been introduced, they fall short of genuine democratisation and do not implement the ECtHR’s judgments. Most critically, they fail to address the legal status and working conditions of the peace process’s principal negotiator—an issue widely recognised as vital to the success of any sustainable peace process.




We therefore urge the Committee of Ministers to ensure the full implementation of the ECtHR’s 2014 judgment in Abdullah Öcalan’s case by recognising and enforcing his Right to Hope. This is the indispensable first step toward resolving his legal status and enabling his meaningful contribution to a democratic and peaceful resolution of the Kurdish question.




The Council of Europe has a historic opportunity to support one of its member states on the path toward genuine democratisation. We urge you to translate the Council’s principles into action by taking a clear and active decision at the December meeting.




We further call for Abdullah Öcalan’s release and for him to be granted full, free, and unrestricted conditions to participate meaningfully in the ongoing peace process."

title: Journalist Mavioğlu: Corruption in Turkey has become institutionalised plunder - Part Two
content:
Journalist Ertuğrul Mavioğlu spoke to ANF about how corruption has developed into a systematic structure over the years, the mechanisms through which public resources are transferred to capital and how this system is sustained through impunity.




Part one of this interview can be read 

here

. 




‘Football is not just football’




Mavioğlu discussed the controversies surrounding financial scandals, allegations of stock market manipulation, and match-fixing and betting investigations in Turkish football, saying that football could not be considered independently of the relationship between capital and politics.




Mavioğlu recalled the scandal publicly known as the “Fatih Terim fund”, arguing that the enormous sums of money circulating in football and the betting system had created an environment vulnerable to inadequate oversight.




Mavioğlu continued: “The most recent example was the scandal known as the Fatih Terim fund. A bank manager was imprisoned, and the scandal, which briefly occupied public attention, was eventually forgotten. Nothing clean can emerge from an environment where transfer fees worth millions of dollars are being discussed and the country's major capital owners dominate football clubs. And indeed, nothing clean does emerge.




Match-fixing is the most widespread example because football is also connected to the lottery and betting system. Wherever there is match-fixing, there is inevitably the mafia. And wherever the mafia operates, the conditions for violence, drugs and every kind of wrongdoing are already present.




This is why football is not just football. In Turkey, as elsewhere in the world, football is an industry in which all kinds of illegal activities are widespread and overlooked, yet it remains indispensable to the system. That is because football serves to manipulate the consciousness of millions of supporters.”




Mavioğlu cited historical examples of football being used by political authorities to influence society, drawing attention to the periods of António de Oliveira Salazar in Portugal and Francisco Franco in Spain: “People will remember the three-F formula associated with Portugal's fascist dictator Salazar and Spain's fascist dictator Franco. Salazar found a way to sustain his system through Football, Fado and Fatima, while Franco relied on Football, Fado and Fiesta. The only difference was that Salazar lulled the people through Fatima, meaning religion, while Franco used festivals and entertainment.




Perhaps that is precisely why Franco is said to have remarked, referring to stadiums, ‘I had three cradles built, each holding 50,000 people.’ When we consider all this alongside the fact that both Salazar and Franco remained in power for 36 years, we can better understand how the three-F formula invoked by these dictators provided a powerful source of support for fascism.




If we adapt this formula to Turkey, we should not overlook the possibility that the current government could continue making our lives miserable for at least another 11 years. Joking aside, Marx said, ‘Religion is the opium of the people.’ We cannot underestimate the significance of packed stadiums, alongside the government's firm reliance on religious arguments, just like Salazar. Perhaps this makes it easier to understand why football is not simply a game involving three referees and 22 players running around a pitch.”




‘Public tenders have become a means of transferring wealth to big capital’




Mavioğlu argued that corruption in public procurement had become normalised over time and that the allegations emerging today represented only a small part of a much wider system.




He drew particular attention to the growing use of the negotiated procurement procedure under Article 21(b) of the Public Procurement Law, arguing that a method intended for exceptional circumstances had become routine practice.




Mavioğlu said: “The most widely used method in public procurement is the negotiated procedure under Article 21(b) of Law No. 4734. In fact, the law requires extraordinary circumstances for this procedure to be used. In other words, negotiated procurement is subject to conditions such as natural disasters, epidemics, threats to life and property, sudden and unexpected events, security considerations and technical construction requirements.




However, particularly under AKP rule, open tendering has become the exception, while negotiated procurement has almost become the rule. This is because, under the negotiated procedure, the public institution issuing the tender invites whichever companies it chooses, and the negotiations become a staged exercise.




Very often, three different subsidiaries belonging to the same holding company are brought to the negotiating table merely to fulfil the formal requirements. The tender is then tailored to a predetermined company, with exorbitant prices accepted, and handed to big capital on a silver platter.”




Mavioğlu referred to World Bank data on the share of international public contracts awarded to Turkey-based companies, drawing attention to major public projects secured by companies such as Limak, Cengiz, Kalyon, Kolin, MNG, Makyol and Rönesans.




He made the following allegations: “According to a World Bank report, it is no coincidence that five of the ten companies receiving the most public contracts worldwide are based in Turkey. Limak ranks first globally among these companies. It is followed by companies close to the AKP, such as Cengiz, Kalyon, Kolin, MNG, Makyol and Rönesans.




The enormous public losses arising from these tenders are covered by taxes collected from the people. There is also a profound injustice here, and the universal principle of taxation has been completely reversed in Turkey. The taxes paid by major companies and holding groups account for just 12 per cent of total tax revenue.




This shows that people who earn less pay more tax, while those who earn more pay less. In other words, 88 per cent of the tax burden has been placed on the shoulders of the poor.”




Mavioğlu said that the alleged irregularities in public procurement were often not subjected to effective investigations and that journalists faced repression for reporting on these relationships.




He continued: “When we look back, all these organised activities that we describe as corruption are not even made the subject of investigations. And even when an investigation is launched, clearing those responsible for corruption remains the rule.




In short, an enormous machinery of plunder has been established, involving everyone who controls access to resources, from the highest levels of government to the lowest-ranking bureaucrats. They all benefit in one way or another, a new class of wealthy profiteers emerges, and those who report on these activities are silenced through detention, imprisonment or severe violence.




Yet, to borrow the words of Leonard Cohen's well-known song, ‘Everybody knows that the dice are loaded.’”




‘Oversight mechanisms have been rendered ineffective’




Mavioğlu argued that mechanisms overseeing the use of public resources had been progressively weakened under AKP rule, drawing attention to the supervisory functions of institutions such as the Court of Accounts and the Council of State.




Mavioğlu said: “Once the AKP government had consolidated its power, or entered what Erdoğan called its ‘mastery period’, it dismantled all oversight mechanisms. As a result, Court of Accounts reports no longer carry any weight, and the Council of State no longer issues orders suspending the implementation of decisions involving corruption, irregularities and profiteering taking place in plain sight.




This has enabled the government to use public resources freely for the benefit of a group clustered around the Presidential Palace, sometimes invoking the defence industry, sometimes disguising it as modernisation and progress, and sometimes justifying it with the claim that ‘there can be no economising on prestige’.”




‘The wealth of those close to the Palace continues to grow’




Mavioğlu cited public incentives provided to the defence industry and the growing wealth of certain figures operating in the sector, commenting on Selçuk Bayraktar and Haluk Bayraktar's inclusion on the Forbes billionaires list.




Mavioğlu continued: “Nobody dares to speak about it, but can it really be considered normal that Selçuk Bayraktar, Erdoğan's son-in-law and an armed drone manufacturer whose company received 600 million lira in state incentives in 2019, and his brother Haluk Bayraktar entered the Forbes list of dollar billionaires within just five years?




Selçuk Bayraktar, with a personal fortune of 1.2 billion dollars, and Haluk Bayraktar, with 1.1 billion dollars, made a rapid entry onto the Forbes list in 2024 with a combined personal fortune of 2.3 billion dollars. A look at the Forbes list shows that this resourceful pair have already increased their combined personal wealth to 5.1 billion dollars.




Leaving aside the much-discussed ‘gang of five’ and others like them, this example alone sufficiently demonstrates that the quickest way to make enormous amounts of money is to become part of the circle surrounding the Presidential Palace. That is because nobody outside the Palace knows how military contracts and expenditure are arranged or under what conditions.”




‘The struggle against corruption cannot be separated from democracy’




Mavioğlu linked the institutionalisation of corruption and plunder to policies targeting the Kurds, the weakening of oversight mechanisms and the suppression of democratic dissent. He said that the Peace and Democratic Society Process had significant potential to challenge this system.




He argued that the climate of conflict had made public opposition less visible and reinforced conditions that made it harder to hold the government accountable.




Mavioğlu said: “Just as every form of protest was drowned out by the sounds of guns and bombs, the relationship they established with society, based on never being held accountable, became increasingly institutionalised over time as oversight mechanisms were systematically eliminated.




The principle of separation of powers, which had appeared to function, however imperfectly, was completely discarded. Those who persisted in raising objections despite all the pressure were subjected to every kind of abuse to make an example of them.




In this sense, the success of the Peace and Democratic Society Process undoubtedly has the potential to shake the system of plunder. However, it would be unrealistic to expect this process to fix everything overnight, as though by waving a magic wand.”




Mavioğlu said that the struggle against corruption must be pursued alongside the struggle for democratic rights and freedoms, concluding: “Because they will never willingly abandon the system of plunder they have established, and they will persistently reject the democratic conditions that could serve as an antidote to the mafia-like system that has now become deeply entrenched.




That is precisely why it is now abundantly clear that we must make society understand the need to dismantle the existing system of plunder and build a united front of struggle against corruption as well as for democracy.”

As the Peace and Democratic Society Process continues in Turkey, investigations into financial scandals, match-fixing and betting operations in football, allegations of corruption in public tenders...

title: Attacker who shot Rojda Odabaşı cites ‘noise’ as motive
content:
Rojda Odabaşı, who was seriously wounded when Mazlum Çelebi shot her with a shotgun on the night of 23 August in Diyarbakır (Amed), continues her fight for justice. Odabaşı is still receiving treatment for injuries sustained in the armed attack by Çelebi, reportedly her downstairs neighbour. However, the attacker, who was arrested on the day of the incident, was released after 58 days in detention. Reacting to the release of Çelebi, who was indicted on charges of "intentional injury" and "damage to property", Odabaşı asked, "Did I have to die for him to be punished?"




First hearing scheduled for 8 April 2027




Mazlum Çelebi, who shot and wounded Rojda Odabaşı and damaged her vehicle, was detained on 23 August and remanded in custody the same day. The indictment prepared in connection with the incident seeks his punishment on charges of "intentional injury" and "damage to property". Çelebi reportedly justified the attack in his statement by saying, "They were making noise."




Following the preparation of the indictment, the court ordered Çelebi's release in a preliminary procedural decision issued on 23 October. Odabaşı subsequently requested a restraining order and protective measures, stating that her personal safety was at risk. The first hearing in the case is scheduled for 8 April 2027 at Diyarbakır 2nd Criminal Court of First Instance.

title: Tuncay Yılmaz: We want to build a united front of resistance in Europe - Part One
content:
As the rise of the far right, war policies, hostility towards migrants and attacks on democratic rights continue across Europe, political and social organisations from Turkey and Kurdistan are strengthening their efforts to build a common struggle. On 17 October, 25 organisations gathered in Cologne, Germany, and decided to establish a new alliance to unite their struggles for peace, democracy, equality and freedom. At the meeting, 20 organisations representing different political traditions declared their willingness to become founding members. The democratic resolution of the Kurdish question and the Peace and Democratic Society Process were also among the main issues discussed.




ANF spoke to Tuncay Yılmaz, founding co-chair of the Socialist Refoundation Party (SYKP), about the outcomes of the Cologne meeting, the need for a common struggle, the situation of left-wing and democratic forces in the face of the rising far right in Europe, and the roadmap for the proposed alliance.




On 17 October, 25 organisations from different political traditions came together in Cologne. Similar attempts to build alliances have been made in Europe before. Why has the need to establish a common platform for struggle emerged again today? What distinguishes this meeting from previous initiatives?




As you said, organisations from different political traditions and social groups in Europe have come together at various times. Previously, there was the European Assembly for Peace and Democracy (ABDEM). We then extended the organisation of the Peoples' Democratic Congress (HDK) in Turkey to Europe, establishing a broad organisation under the name HDK Europe. This organisation later became the European Democratic Forces Union (ADGB) and continued its activities under that name. Most recently, ahead of the NATO summit, a joint initiative called PANEV was established against imperialist aggression, wars and the NATO.




All these initiatives emerged from efforts to find ways for the forces of democracy, peace, equality and freedom to become better organised in Europe and pursue more effective political action against the enormous aggressive power confronting us.




The alliances we established at different times sometimes lost their effectiveness, both because of changes in the objective conditions in which they were formed and, to speak frankly, because of our own shortcomings. This is a reality, and we are aware of it. Indeed, this was one of the issues on the agenda of our meeting. We want to learn from our previous experiences.




However, the mistakes we made in the past or the changes we have experienced should not prevent us from bringing democratic forces together again and carrying out a common struggle. And indeed, they are not preventing us. One of the main motivations that brought us together at this meeting was the growing hostility towards migrants in the European countries where we live, the rise of the right, fascist movements coming to power and increasing state violence. The fact that laws targeting asylum seekers have reached almost inhumane proportions is also deeply concerning to all of us. We want to build a united front of resistance against all of this.




At the same time, however, all our attention, thoughts and concerns are focused on developments in Turkey. Looking at Turkey, we see a totalitarian regime being built step by step. Everyone who opposes it becomes a target. Presidential candidates are arrested. Selahattin Demirtaş has been imprisoned for years, as has Figen Yüksekdağ. Ekrem İmamoğlu was subsequently arrested. The Republican People's Party (CHP), which prides itself on being the founding party of the state, is also under serious pressure. Attempts are being made to divide the party, and many of its representatives have been arrested.




Alongside all this, a negotiation process has begun. It has not yet reached the stage of a peace process. However, this negotiation process has the potential to generate a collective strength capable of pushing back attacks on democracy through the positive developments it could bring to the country's political life. Despite this, we see that the political authorities are acting with appalling arbitrariness in this process as well.




To speak frankly, this process has been made possible by the determination and goodwill of Abdullah Öcalan and the Kurdish Freedom Movement. After all, decisions were taken to lay down arms and dissolve the organisation. These decisions represent a profound transformation in the movement's historical existence.




Despite this, the state continues to display an extremely indifferent and unserious attitude towards taking steps on these issues, potentially jeopardising the process. Its actions could allow the anti-democratic practices it maintains throughout the country to continue in different forms in this area as well. We can all see that, for months, instead of implementing the legal arrangements brought onto Parliament's agenda with broad support, the authorities have merely continued saying, "We want this as well, and we want that too."




Frankly, they are acting entirely with the mentality of a trader. Instead of seriously addressing such a fundamental problem facing the state, the regime and the country, and taking steps to resolve it, the process is being conducted through demands such as, "What did you get? What did you give? Do this as well, do that as well."




Considering all these developments, we see that, as social and political organisations in Europe, we cannot pursue a politics focused solely on protecting ourselves, withdrawing into our own circles and limiting ourselves to our own concerns. The Confederation of European Alevi Unions (AABK), the Kurdistan Democratic Communities Congress in Europe (KCDK-E) and many socialist groups are part of this alliance.




When we assess developments in Turkey, Europe, the region and the world together, the necessity of carrying out a common struggle against them becomes clear. I believe this is precisely why we were able to organise such a broad gathering on 17 October.




As the far right gains strength in Europe, hostility towards migrants, racism and war policies are increasingly being debated. Yet left-wing and democratic forces appear to be struggling to act together. What do you think are the main reasons for this fragmentation? What role could the alliance being established in Cologne play in changing this situation?




It is very clear that we are moving towards a major transformation of the international system established after the Second World War. Very negative changes are taking place both in the balance of power between imperialist centres and in the relations between the ruling classes and oppressed sections of society.




I would like to explain this through a few examples. The developments taking place today in the Middle East, Syria, Palestine, Lebanon, all four parts of Kurdistan and Iran are connected to tensions over which powers will control the world's trade routes, valuable minerals and energy resources. Essentially, the world is being redesigned. This is not limited to the Middle East. The restructuring process is creating tensions across the entire world.




Secondly, certain gains regulating economic and social life, which the capitalist-imperialist bloc was compelled to accept in some form during the existence of the Soviet Union, are now being rejected. For example, there are discussions in Germany about raising the retirement age to 70.




Why are young people taking to the streets in such large numbers in France? Why do they refuse to leave the streets despite such intense state violence? What are the fundamental demands that have brought the student movement in Serbia towards success? What lies behind the developments in Albania?




At the root of all this is the following reality: the ruling classes do not see a strong alternative or opposition capable of challenging them. Consequently, they are introducing measures aimed at securing as many advantages as possible in line with their own interests, both internationally and nationally.




The left, on the other hand, has frankly failed to create a comprehensive and renewed alternative. Without a coherent programme that society can embrace, internalise and stand behind, support for the left inevitably declines.




However, there are examples where this situation has been overcome. I believe these experiences offer important lessons about what we need to do.




Take Brazil, for example. Despite the support of the United States and major technology companies, from Elon Musk to Meta, Bolsonaro lost and Lula managed to win. The decisive factor was the creation of a common programme that brought together the demands not only of the working class but also of Indigenous peoples, poor peasants, young people and women.




In other words, movements that can bring together different sections of society opposed to the existing ruling system and unite them around a common programme can achieve success.




We see a similar experience in France. Yes, Macron remains in power, and the far right represented by Le Pen is in a strong position. However, the experience of La France Insoumise (France Unbowed) and the New Popular Front demonstrates that, despite all the risks, different opposition groups can come together around shared democratic demands.




What matters here is developing a programme capable of responding to society's most fundamental and pressing problems. People look at what you are concretely proposing to address the problems they face.




For example, the reason Elif Eralp has been able to come to the fore in Berlin against the Social Democratic Party (SPD), which enjoys the backing of major capital interests, is that she has developed a programme addressing society's fundamental problems. Similarly, the Communist Party's electoral victories over three terms in Graz, Austria, provide another example.




The existing system claims that it can set housing prices as it wishes and transform the healthcare system to the detriment of society. Society, in turn, is reacting against this.




In short, the left has not yet managed to develop a comprehensive response to this new situation confronting it globally. For this reason, a powerful global wave of the left has not emerged to counter the rising right. Nevertheless, there are important experiences demonstrating that such a development is possible.




We must build a bridge between the struggle in Europe and Turkey




We discussed the contribution that the alliance we want to establish in Cologne could make from two perspectives at our meeting.




First, as people living in Europe, we are directly affected by the problems here. The housing crisis is our problem too. Changes to the healthcare system, environmental policies and attacks on social rights are also our problems. Therefore, through this alliance, we will become directly involved in social struggles across Europe.




Second, we need to provide strong support from the diaspora for the struggle in Turkey. However, this support cannot be achieved simply by saying, "We stand with those struggling in Turkey."




We must bring international social forces to a position where they can support the struggle in Turkey. We must embrace the struggle being waged in Turkey from Europe and create pressure on governments here and international institutions. Only in this way can we provide effective support for the ongoing struggle for peace and democracy in Turkey.




Of course, protesting developments in Turkey in the central squares of European cities is important. We cannot underestimate this. However, we must also recognise that this alone is not enough.




The most fundamental role our alliance can play is to build a bridge between internationalist struggles and the ongoing struggle for peace and democracy in Turkey. This is particularly important in bringing political and social forces in Europe together with the struggle in Turkey.




We have organisations with considerable experience and connections in this field. The diplomatic relations of the Confederation of European Alevi Unions, the connections of the Kurdish Freedom Movement and KCDK-E across Europe, and the ties established by socialist movements with socialist forces in other countries represent an important accumulation of experience and relationships.




Let me give you an example. You may have noticed that an organisation called the Anti-Imperialist League (AIL) was among those listed in the statement we published after the meeting. This is an internationalist bloc organised in 37 countries worldwide, including 14 European countries.




Representatives of this organisation also attended our meeting and stated clearly: "We attach importance to the revolutionary and democratic struggle in Turkey. We are aware of its significance for the Middle East. We know about the struggle of the Kurdish Freedom Movement and other democratic forces. We will closely follow this alliance and carry out joint activities, both to receive support from that struggle and to provide support to it."




This is precisely the point I am trying to make. I believe the alliance we have established will serve as an important bridge between international democratic and social forces and the struggle in Turkey.







25 organizations in Europe seek to strengthen joint struggle and solidarity

25 political and civil society organizations from Turkey and Kurdistan have agreed to establish a joint alliance for struggle and solidarity in Europe. The initiative aims to bring together differe...

title: Kurdish businessman arrested in Belgium
content:
Businessman Muhsin Talay, who sought refuge in Belgium, has been arrested in Brussels on the basis of an Interpol notice issued at Turkey’s request. Talay, who was acquitted in a murder trial before a court in Amed (Turkish: Diyarbakır), is now in custody. His asylum proceedings in Belgium are still pending. His family warns of possible extradition to Turkey and calls on the Belgian authorities to grant him protection.




Murder accusation despite court acquittal




The arrest is linked to the murder of Murat Baycan, who was killed under unclear circumstances in Amed in 2005. Baycan is alleged to have worked as an informant and agent for the Turkish intelligence service (MIT). Muhsin Talay was accused of involvement in the killing but was acquitted in the subsequent proceedings before the 4th High Criminal Court in Amed.




According to his family, Talay continues to be linked to the murder despite his acquittal. The allegations are reportedly based on a report by the Turkish intelligence service (MIT), even though the evidence presented during the trial was discredited. The family accuses the Turkish authorities of seeking to prosecute and sentence Talay again on this basis.




Talay was reportedly subjected to repeated pressure from MIT during the court proceedings. Fearing mistreatment and renewed prosecution, he eventually left Turkey and applied for asylum in Belgium.

title: YJK-E and KON-MED launch campaign against femicide and patriarchal violence
content:
The Kurdish Women’s Association in Germany (YJK-E) and the Confederation of Kurdistan Communities in Germany (KON-MED) are launching a nationwide campaign against femicide, patriarchal violence, and the structural oppression of women on November 1. Under the slogan “We are intensifying our social struggle against femicide and patriarchal mindsets,” seminars, educational programs, and public events are planned through International Women’s Day on March 8. The campaign will focus on developing democratic family structures, promoting gender equality, and protecting women’s lives.




In their joint statement, the two umbrella organizations criticize the fact that women are subjected to violence in all areas of life, even in a country like Germany, which professes a commitment to fundamental democratic values and human rights. According to the organizations, a total of 105 women have been killed since the beginning of 2026, with Kurdish women accounting for approximately ten percent of the victims. “These women are not just numbers. Each of them had a life, dreams, a family, children, and a future that was taken away from her,” the statement reads.




Patriarchal violence does not begin with femicide




YJK-E and KON-MED do not regard femicides as isolated acts of violence, but as the most extreme consequence of patriarchal power structures deeply embedded in society: “Women are particularly likely to experience violence within their own families or intimate relationships. The belief that men have the right to control women’s clothing, social contacts, employment, or way of life forms a fundamental basis of this oppression.”




“As long as a mindset that teaches boys superiority and girls obedience remains unchanged, the roots of violence will not be eliminated,” the organizations say. The campaign therefore explicitly addresses the social conditions in which gender-based inequality emerges and is passed down through generations. Economic dependence, traditional gender roles, and the expectation that women should tolerate violence for the sake of family unity are among the structures that must be overcome.




As an alternative, the organizations advocate the concept of a democratic family, in which equality, mutual respect, and shared decision-making form the foundation of family life. Children should be able to grow up as free individuals, regardless of their gender. “No tradition, no concept of family, and no social value takes precedence over a woman’s right to life,” YJK-E and KON-MED emphasize.




Calls for investigations into deaths in refugee accommodation facilities




Another key focus of the statement is the situation of refugee women and young people in Germany. Many people who have fled war, persecution, and violence face isolation, discrimination, psychological distress, and inadequate protection in accommodation facilities. The organizations are particularly critical of deaths in refugee accommodation facilities that have officially been recorded as suicides. They call for transparent investigations into the circumstances of these deaths, as well as independent inquiries where there is evidence of neglect, violence, or other criminal offenses.




“No one should be made invisible because they are a refugee, and no death should ever become normalized,” the statement reads. The organizations stress the need for dignified accommodation conditions, safe spaces, psychosocial support, and reliable access to legal advice. Women and young people, in particular, must be protected from violence and social isolation.




Women’s freedom as a shared struggle across borders




The organizations also place their initiative within the broader context of the Kurdish women’s freedom struggle. They recall the genocide perpetrated by the Islamic State (ISIS) against the Yazidi population of Shengal and the systematic abduction and enslavement of Yazidi women. They also explicitly address the threats to the achievements of the women’s revolution in Rojava, as well as state repression and death sentences imposed on women in Iran and Rojhilat (Eastern Kurdistan).




“Although the forms and circumstances of violence differ, protecting women’s lives, autonomy, and freedom is a shared responsibility,” the organizations declare. In Germany, YJK-E and KON-MED call in particular for the expansion of women’s shelters and counseling centers, effective measures to prevent femicide, and consistent support for women who have experienced violence or are at risk of it. They stress that the protection of women must not become a political issue only after a murder has occurred.




Nationwide educational activities through March 8




Through their campaign, the two umbrella organizations aim to bring the issue of patriarchal power structures more prominently into public debate. Nationwide seminars and educational programs are planned, focusing particularly on what constitutes a democratic family, how such family structures can be developed, and their significance for women’s freedom. November 25, the International Day for the Elimination of Violence against Women, will serve as a major focal point for mobilization. On this occasion, efforts will be made to raise awareness of the various forms of gender-based violence and the living conditions of women affected by it.




The initiative is explicitly aimed not only at women but at society as a whole. “Violence against women is not just a women’s issue, but a problem that concerns society as a whole. Therefore, the struggle against it must also be a collective social struggle,” YJK-E and KON-MED say.




The campaign is set to continue until March 8. Its goal is to create a society in which women can live without fear at home, in the workplace, on the streets, and in refugee accommodation facilities, and where their right to self-determination is fully recognized. “We defend life against femicide! We defend women’s freedom against patriarchal mindsets! Jin, Jiyan, Azadî!” the joint statement concludes.

title: Iranian regime sentences Van resident Cenk Demir to 5 years in prison
content:
The Kurdistan Human Rights Network (KHRN) stated that a regime court in the city of Urmia had sentenced Cenk Demir, originally from Van (Wan), to five years in prison on charges of “membership in opposition groups.”




According to the statement, Demir was arrested in Urmia approximately eight months ago. After being questioned for months at a security detention centre in the city, he was transferred to Urmia Central Prison.




It was reported that, following the announcement of the verdict, Demir was transferred to the Ershad ward, where political prisoners are held.
