title: The Kurdistan Region’s experience of government – I
content:
The Kurdistan Region is facing the consequences of its failure to form a government on every front, as the balance of power in the Middle East is once again being tested and the region faces the prospect of major changes. Two political forces remain determined to secure their respective demands in the government formation process: the Patriotic Union of Kurdistan (PUK) and the Kurdistan Democratic Party (KDP). In this series, we look back at the history of government formation in the Kurdistan Region, beginning with its first government.




The Kurdistan Front after the Raperin uprising




Following the First Gulf War and the Raperin (uprising) of March 1991, the Iraqi government withdrew its administrative institutions from much of the region in October 1991, following United Nations Resolution 688 and the establishment of a no-fly zone north of the 36th parallel by the allied powers. The administrative vacuum left by the withdrawal was filled by the Kurdistan Front (Bereya Kurdistanê), marking the beginning of a period of de facto autonomy for the Kurds.




The Front was established in 1987–1988 by the KDP, PUK, the Kurdistan Democratic People's Party (KPDP) and the Kurdistan Socialist Party-PASOK (Kurdistan Democratic Independence Party). By 1992, it had developed into an eight-party umbrella organisation with the participation of the Iraqi Communist Party, the Kurdistan Toilers' Party, the Kurdistan Socialist Party (KSP) and the Kurdistan Islamic Movement. The Assyrian Democratic Movement was also among the Front's constituent organisations.




A committee established by the Front held negotiations with Baghdad over autonomy. Election Law No. 1, adopted on 8 April 1992, provided for the distribution of 100 parliamentary seats through proportional representation, with five additional seats reserved for Christian lists. An electoral threshold of 7 percent was introduced for the 105-seat parliament.




The KDP received 437,879 votes, securing 45.27 percent, while the PUK won 423,833 votes, or 43.82 percent. The Kurdistan Islamic Movement fell below the electoral threshold with 5.08 percent. The Kurdistan Socialist Party, the Iraqi Communist Party and the Kurdistan Democratic People's Party also failed to enter parliament.




Following the initial count, the KDP secured 51 seats and the PUK 49. However, objections led to the KDP relinquishing one seat, leaving the parliament evenly divided, with 50 seats for each party. The region was governed by an eight-member Presidential Council comprising four representatives from each party. Parliament convened on 4 June 1992, and Cewher Namiq Salim was elected its speaker.




By a majority vote, parliament adopted a decision defining relations with Baghdad on the basis of a “federal union within a democratic and parliamentary Iraq”. This decision would become the first document establishing the federal status later enshrined in the 2005 Iraqi Constitution.




First cabinet: 1992–1993




The first cabinet, formed by Fuad Masum of the PUK, received a unanimous vote of confidence from parliament in Erbil (Hewlêr) on 4 July 1992. The post of prime minister was allocated to the PUK, while the deputy premiership went to the KDP. Of the 15 ministries, six were allocated to each party. The Iraqi Communist Party, the Assyrian Democratic Movement and an independent representative received one ministry each.




The cabinet had no foreign affairs or defence ministries. The Minister of Peshmerga Affairs effectively served as defence minister. Ankara, Tehran and Baghdad did not recognise the government. The post of justice minister remained vacant when the cabinet was announced. Two notable features of the first government were the appointment of poet Şêrko Bêkes as culture minister and Kafiye Süleyman's position as the only woman in the cabinet.




Second cabinet: 1993–1996




The cabinet formed by Kosret Resul Ali of the PUK, who was elected prime minister in April 1993, received a vote of confidence on 25 April 1993. The distribution of ministries between the parties remained unchanged, except for the Ministry of Justice, which was allocated to the Kurdistan Unity Party.




Clashes and the division of the region




Clashes between the KDP and PUK began on 1 May 1994. The joint government effectively collapsed when the PUK took control of Erbil in 1994. The KDP captured Sulaymaniyah (Silêmanî) on 9 September, while the PUK recaptured the city on 13 October 1996.




The region was subsequently divided into two administrative areas. Erbil and Duhok came under KDP control, while Sulaymaniyah and Germiyan were controlled by the PUK. Despite numerous negotiations between the parties, a unified administration could not be established until 2006. Throughout this period, the region continued to operate under a dual-administration system.




Third cabinet: 1996–2006




Erbil administration (KDP, 1996–1999):

 The KDP established its own cabinet under Roj Nuri Şaweys in September 1996 after taking control of Erbil. As most PUK parliamentarians did not attend, parliament continued to convene in Erbil with 67 of its 105 members.




Sulaymaniyah administration (PUK, 1996–1999):

 Following the division of the region into two distinct administrative areas, the PUK maintained its government in Sulaymaniyah under Kosret Resul Ali. The administration governed a population of 1,442,797. Jalal Talabani subsequently appointed Barham Salih as prime minister in place of Kosret Resul through Decree No. 9, issued on 20 January 2001.




Fourth cabinet: 2001–2006




Erbil administration (KDP, 1999–2006):

 Nechirvan Barzani's 23-member cabinet received parliamentary approval on 21 December 1999. The cabinet governed the Erbil-Duhok area, which had a population of 1,868,391.




Sulaymaniyah administration (PUK, 2001–2004):

 Jalal Talabani appointed Barham Salih as prime minister in place of Kosret Resul through Decree No. 9 of 20 January 2001. Salih headed a 19-member cabinet. He subsequently moved to Baghdad on 28 June 2004 to serve as Iraq's deputy prime minister. The Sulaymaniyah administration remained under PUK control between 2004 and 2006.




The reunification period: 2002–2006




Party leaders Barzani and Talabani met in Shaqlawa (Şeqlawa) on 8 September 2002 and established four joint committees. Parliament convened for a joint session in Erbil on 4 October of the same year. Twenty-nine new parliamentarians, including 28 from the PUK and one from the KDP, were sworn in. Parliament was thus reconstituted with 51 KDP members, 49 PUK members and five Assyrian-Chaldean representatives.




In the Iraqi elections held on 30 January 2005, the Kurdistan Democratic Patriotic Alliance, comprising the KDP, PUK and several other parties, won 25.73 per cent of the vote and secured 75 of the 275 parliamentary seats. Jalal Talabani was sworn in as President of Iraq on 7 April 2005.




Parliamentary elections were held in the Kurdistan Region on the same day, with 111 seats contested. The KDP won 40 seats, the PUK 38, the Kurdistan Islamic Union (Yekgirtû Islami) nine, the Kurdistan Islamic Group (Komele) six and the Toilers' List one. Parliament convened on 4 June 2005. Masoud Barzani was elected President of the Kurdistan Region in a vote held on 12 June 2005.




An agreement signed by the two parties during an extraordinary parliamentary session in Erbil on 21 January 2006 allocated the first term as prime minister to the KDP and the parliamentary speakership to the PUK. The agreement provided for the two positions to rotate between the parties after two years. The KDP and PUK each received 11 ministries, while the remaining ministries were allocated to other parties.




The parties also agreed to merge the separate ministries of interior, finance, justice and peshmerga affairs established by the two administrations within one year. However, the merger was not completed until 2009. The structure of the peshmerga forces, which remained affiliated with the two parties, continued until September 2026.




Fifth cabinet: 2006–2009




The first unified cabinet received a unanimous vote of confidence from all 111 parliamentarians on 7 May 2006. Newşirwan Mustefa, who left the PUK in 2006, contested the parliamentary elections held on 25 July with the Gorran Movement. In its first election, Gorran secured 23.72 per cent of the vote and won 25 seats. The joint Kurdistan List formed by the KDP and PUK received 57.37 per cent of the vote, with its representation falling to 59 seats, including 30 for the KDP and 29 for the PUK.




Masoud Barzani won the regional presidential election, held by direct popular vote on the same day, with 69.6 per cent of the vote.




Sixth cabinet: 2009–2012




The premiership passed to the PUK in accordance with the agreement between the two parties. Masoud Barzani tasked Barham Salih with forming a government on 30 September 2009. Salih's cabinet received a vote of confidence on 26 October 2009. Barham Salih reduced the number of cabinet members from 42 to 21, forming a government composed of representatives from the KDP and PUK.




Seventh cabinet: 2012–2014




The premiership returned to the KDP, with Nechirvan Barzani elected prime minister on 17 February 2012. His cabinet received a vote of confidence on 5 April 2012 and was sworn in the following day. The PUK and KDP, which held a parliamentary majority, passed Law No. 19 on 30 June 2013. The law extended Masoud Barzani's term as President of the Kurdistan Region, which was due to expire on 20 August 2013, until 19 August 2015.




In the elections held on 21 September 2013, the KDP won 38 seats, the Gorran Movement 24 and the PUK 18. The Kurdistan Islamic Union (Yekgirtû) secured 10 seats, while the Kurdistan Islamic Group (Komele) won six. Four opposition parties also entered parliament with one seat each. Turkmen and Assyrian-Chaldean representatives secured five reserved seats each, while Armenians received one reserved seat.




Eighth cabinet: 2014–2019




Government formation negotiations continued for eight months following the elections. The five parties holding a parliamentary majority agreed to allocate the premiership and Ministry of Interior to the KDP, the parliamentary speakership and the ministries of Peshmerga Affairs and Finance to the Gorran Movement, and the deputy premiership to the PUK. The cabinet was sworn in on 18 June 2014.




ISIS captured Mosul in June 2014. On 3 August 2014, KDP peshmerga forces stationed in Shengal withdrew from the area, and ISIS launched its genocide against the Yazidis. Thousands of Yazidis were massacred, while women and children were abducted.




The KDP accused the Gorran Movement of responsibility for attacks in which KDP offices were set on fire during protests over salaries in October 2015 and announced that it no longer recognised the parliamentary speaker. Ministers were prevented from entering their ministries and were replaced by other appointees. The Gorran Movement declared that appointments made without consulting parliament were illegitimate. Parliament did not convene between October 2015 and 15 September 2017.




The Gorran Movement and Komele formally withdrew from the government on 20 December 2017 amid renewed protests over salaries in Sulaymaniyah. The eighth cabinet subsequently continued as a KDP-PUK government until 2019.




Ninth cabinet: 2019–present




Masrour Barzani's cabinet, comprising representatives from the KDP, PUK, Gorran Movement, Turkmen community and Christian community, received a vote of confidence on 10 July 2019. Vala Ferid of the KDP was elected the first woman speaker in the history of the Kurdistan Parliament on 18 February 2019. She was succeeded by  Rewaz Faiq of the PUK on 11 July 2019. The PUK began boycotting Council of Ministers meetings on 26 October 2022. The boycott ended on 14 May 2023 following a meeting between Masrour Barzani and Qubad Talabani. The Gorran Movement decided to withdraw from the government on 10 October 2024.




The Kurdistan Parliament extended its term by one year in October 2022. Elections were postponed four times, with dates set for 1 October 2022, 18 November 2023, 25 February 2024 and 10 June 2024. On 30 May 2023, Iraq's Federal Supreme Court ruled that the extension of parliament's term was unconstitutional, invalidating all parliamentary proceedings conducted during the extended period. As parliament had also lost its authority over the electoral commission, the elections were administered by Iraq's Independent High Electoral Commission. A further ruling by the same court divided the Kurdistan Region into four electoral constituencies: Erbil, Sulaymaniyah, Duhok and Halabja. The ninth cabinet's four-year term expired on 10 July 2023.




In the next part of this series, we will examine the deadlocks encountered in previous government formation processes and the latest electoral process.

title: Karayılan commemorates fallen guerrillas from Shengal
content:
Murat Karayılan, a member of the Central Headquarters of the People’s Defense Forces (HPG), has issued a statement commemorating seven fallen Kurdish guerrilla fighters from Shengal. He paid tribute to their contribution to defending the Yazidi population against the terrorist organization Islamic State (ISIS) and to establishing independent self-defense structures in Shengal. Karayılan also commented on the talks between the Iraqi government and the leadership of the Shengal Resistance Units (YBŞ). He welcomed the prospect of integrating the YBŞ into the Iraqi army, provided that the units retain their local character and remain permanently responsible for protecting the population.




In his statement, Karayılan recalled the genocide perpetrated by ISIS against the Yazidis in August 2014, which the Yazidi community refers to as the 74th Ferman, as well as the role of the Kurdish guerrillas in defending Shengal. He regards the YBŞ and YJŞ forces established during that period as a crucial achievement in the struggle to prevent another genocide.










https://video.anf-news2.com/live/firat/7ec6516d_20261029095010_2026-10-29-navenda-nuceyan-murat-karayilan-peyama-ji-bo-malbaten-sehiden-sengale-1.mp4











The full statement reads as follows:




“With our greetings and respect to our people in Shengal!




Seven of the fallen fighters whose deaths we are announcing and whom we wish to commemorate came from Shengal. In honor of them all, we remember our comrades Agir Botan and Çiçek Öcalan with respect and gratitude, and bow before their memory. We renew our pledge to our fallen comrades to remain faithful to the path of our common cause until the very end.




On behalf of the leadership of the Kurdish movement and the HPG Central Headquarters, I extend my condolences to the families of our martyrs and to the entire population of Shengal, particularly the Yazidi and Arab peoples. I hope that our people will duly recognize the significance of these martyrs. We firmly believe that they will follow in their footsteps, preserve their memory, and give them a dignified welcome.




“The 74th campaign of extermination did not go unpunished”




Dear Families!




Our Yazidi people have been subjected to 74 fermans throughout their history. Each of these campaigns of extermination involved massacres and genocide. Yet not a single one was ever brought to justice. Whoever committed these crimes went unpunished.




However, we know that the 74th campaign of extermination did not go unpunished, thanks to the ideas and philosophy of Rêber Apo [Leader Abdullah Öcalan] and the awareness he instilled in us. Once again, massacres took place. More than 12,000 of our people were killed or taken captive. ISIS had a far-reaching objective: it sought to completely eradicate the Yazidi faith. But the guerrillas of the Kurdish freedom movement, acting in accordance with Rêber Apo’s vision, could not stand by and watch. As soon as they learned of the attacks, they decided to intervene and immediately mobilized.




As is well known, attempts were made to prevent this intervention. But that was not all. At the time, no one was able to stand up to ISIS. Even states fled in the face of its advance. The intervention and resistance in Shengal gave courage to many other forces. ISIS continued its attacks because it could not tolerate being met with resistance. However, it had no experience in mountain warfare and was unable to prevail against our guerrillas. It failed to occupy the mountains.




By contrast, ISIS had experience in urban warfare. It therefore considered Kobanê our weakest point and attacked the city in an attempt to take revenge. Our movement responded to both the attacks on Shengal and those on Kobanê. Even at that time, it was declared that these crimes would have far-reaching consequences—not only in Shengal and Kobanê, but everywhere.




The crimes committed against Kurdish and Yazidi women and the victims of the campaign of extermination did not go unpunished. ISIS’s system of rule was dismantled. The city of Raqqa, which it had declared its capital, became the scene of its defeat. The fighters of the Apoist movement pursued ISIS all the way to Baghuz and brought an end to its system of rule.




The reason for this was the atrocities ISIS had committed in Shengal. In other words, the crimes did not go unpunished, and the blood of the victims of the campaign of extermination was not forgotten. History did not repeat itself. The campaign of extermination did not go unanswered.




“The responsibility for defending Shengal was entrusted to the YBŞ”




To prevent a 75th campaign of extermination in the future, the necessary precautions were taken, including by the young people of Shengal themselves. During the war, the YBŞ and YJŞ were established. The steps taken under the leadership of comrades Mam Zeki, Hesen Seid, Dijwar Feqir, Zerdeşt, Berxwedan, Dilgeş, and Bêrîvan were intended to secure the future of our Yazidi people. The aim was to establish an independent defense force capable of preventing further campaigns of extermination.




This is where the significance of the YBŞ lies. It consists of young Yazidis and members of the Arab population associated with them, capable of defending itself against all forms of attack and provocation, protecting both its members and the wider population. It is not a temporary force, but a permanent, preventive, and reliable self-defense structure.




The YBŞ and YJŞ were established on this basis. Their formation was also made possible by the efforts of our fallen comrades. Their aim was to prevent another campaign of extermination, secure the future of the Yazidi people, and create the conditions for them to protect themselves without depending on others. This was in line with Rêber Apo’s vision. Although there were shortcomings, the work was carried out on this basis. The YBŞ continues this work. It was entrusted with this responsibility.




After we, as the HPG, withdrew from Shengal, responsibility for defending the region was transferred to the YBŞ, including at the level of its command structures. We are convinced that it will continue to preserve this legacy and fulfill its mission in the future.




“The guerrilla intervention was historic”




Our esteemed people, we lost comrades in Shengal. The guerrilla intervention was a historic and honorable undertaking. We are proud of our martyrs. We witnessed young people from Shengal, the daughters and sons of this community, joining our ranks. They wanted not only to fight in Shengal but also to come to the mountains of Kurdistan to stand alongside their comrades.




These remarkable young people joined us, and some of them fell in battle. This is a source of honor for you. The young people of Shengal came to support the guerrillas. This is something deeply valuable and honorable. Just as we are proud of them, you have every right to take pride in them as well. I wish to express my appreciation to the families of these fallen comrades and to the mothers of those young people who came from Shengal to the mountains of Kurdistan and lost their lives in battle, in recognition of the legacy they have left behind.




We commemorate them with deep respect and profound admiration. For us, this carries both an ideological significance and the meaning of a bond forged through blood shed together. It is a deep, meaningful, and firmly rooted comradeship. We firmly believe that all our people and the families attach the same importance to these values.




“The agreement on the YBŞ is a step in the right direction”




We have learned that talks are taking place between the YBŞ leadership and the Iraqi government. We have also learned that an agreement has been reached to grant the YBŞ official status as a local and autonomous defense force, enabling the people of Shengal to protect their own region.




Such an agreement is appropriate. Our people should also welcome it in this spirit. Our fundamental concern is to prevent a 75th campaign of extermination and ensure that the necessary precautions are taken. If the YBŞ is integrated into the Iraqi army under this agreement while retaining its permanent responsibility for defending Shengal as a local force, it will be able to fulfill their role. This would be a sound and appropriate decision.




In this way, the legacy of our martyrs could also be preserved. We firmly believe that the members of the YBŞ and YJŞ, together with our esteemed people in Shengal, will be able to safeguard the achievements made possible by the efforts of our martyrs and continue to pursue the cause for which they stood.




Once again, I extend my respect and condolences to our esteemed families. Şehîd namirin – The martyrs are immortal.”

title: Bar associations file criminal complaint against deforestation in Gabar and Besta
content:
The bar associations of Siirt and Şırnak have filed criminal complaints over the ongoing deforestation in the Gabar and Besta regions. They are demanding an immediate halt to the tree felling and criminal investigations into those responsible. The complaints target both individuals involved in the deforestation and public officials suspected of bearing responsibility.




According to the environmental and urban development commissions of both bar associations, the relevant complaints were submitted to the public prosecutors’ offices in Siirt and Şırnak. They concern tree felling carried out between April 20 and July 29, 2025, which reportedly continued beyond that period.




The lawyers are calling for investigations into suspected illegal tree felling, the unlawful transportation of timber and other forest products, and possible complicity in these activities. They are demanding that prosecutors identify those responsible, initiate criminal proceedings, and order examinations of the affected logging and storage sites to secure evidence.




At the same time, the bar associations are demanding full disclosure of the official permits and environmental decisions authorizing the logging operations. These include any environmental impact assessments, information on the number and species of trees felled, transportation documents, and reports on environmental inspections conducted

author: Unknown
title: Kurdish protester wounded by IRGC sentenced to prison and fined
content:
Milad Ebrahimi, a 31-year-old Kurdish man from Kamyaran, Kurdistan Province, who was shot and wounded by Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) forces during the December 2025–January 2026 protests, has been sentenced to one year in prison and fined four billion rials on charges of “disturbing public order”.




The Kurdistan Human Rights Network (KHRN) has reported that Branch 101 of the Kamyaran Criminal Court Two tried Ebrahimi in mid-October. He was notified of the verdict on 25 October.




IRGC forces shot Ebrahimi in the lower back with live ammunition during protests in Kamyaran on the evening of 8 January 2026.




He was taken to a medical facility in Sanandaj, the provincial capital, where he underwent surgery before returning home to recover.




Ministry of Intelligence forces arrested him on 1 February, despite his need for further hospitalisation because of an infection caused by his gunshot wound, and took him to the ministry’s detention facility in Sanandaj.




He was denied access to a lawyer and medical care during his detention and was provisionally released on bail on 27 February.

title: Broad support for resistance against solar project in Arzoxlî
content:
Resistance against the controversial Zenkar-2 solar energy project in the Arzoxlî village of Amed (Turkish: Diyarbakır), is gaining further support. On the eighth day of the vigil against the development of communal grazing lands, a delegation from the Democratic Institutions Platform visited the protest camp in the village. Following a joint march from the village square to the vigil tent, representatives of political parties and environmental organizations called for the complete cancellation of the project.




Ruçem Vefa Elyakut, co-chair of the DBP’s provincial branch in Amed, praised the local community’s struggle. “The people of Arzoxlî have been putting up dignified resistance for days,” she said. She placed the conflict within a long history of displacement and economic exploitation of Kurdish lands. “The mentality that sought to dominate this land has tried to drive its people away. Today, it wants to plunder this land using the same methods. We will never accept that.”




Construction work resumes despite ongoing court proceedings




At the center of the dispute is the “ZENKAR-2 Solar Power Plant and Energy Storage Facility” project developed by the company Zenkar. The company was granted a 49-year electricity generation license for two planned solar power plants equipped with energy storage systems. The facilities are to be built on land that is essential to the local population’s agricultural and livestock activities. Legal proceedings are ongoing against the reclassification of communal grazing lands, the zoning plans, and the favorable environmental impact assessment decision for Zenkar-2. A court-appointed panel of experts concluded that implementing the project in its current form would be unsuitable.













Violent clashes had erupted in March when the company first attempted to enter the site. Five villagers were injured, one of them seriously, during an operation by Turkish police and gendarmerie forces. Fifteen people were temporarily detained. On October 21, the company once again entered the disputed land under the escort of security forces. Since then, residents have been holding a vigil to protest the continuation of construction work and restrictions on their access to communal grazing lands.




“Thousands of years of natural habitats are being sacrificed for profit”




During the solidarity visit, Sabri Kılıç, co-spokesperson of the Amed Ecology Council, criticized the increasing commercialization of natural resources essential to sustaining life. He argued that solar and hydroelectric power plants, mining projects, and oil extraction were part of a broader development trend that increasingly disregarded the needs of local communities. “Land, water, mineral resources, sunlight, and wind are being turned into commodities in the process of capital accumulation,” Kılıç explained. “Mining, oil, hydroelectric, and solar energy projects in our valleys, mountains, and plains are destroying our habitats, which have existed for thousands of years, through policies aimed at maximizing profits.”




Kılıç particularly criticized the role played by the police and military. During the assault in March, he said, they had been deployed not to protect the population but to enforce the company’s interests. “The security forces, whose duty is to protect the people, attacked them as though they were the company’s private security personnel.”




Kılıç pointed out that the planned solar park threatens the agricultural use of the land and, with it, a vital source of livelihood for the village community. He warned of the potential displacement of residents and long-term ecological damage. He also emphasized the historical significance of the area, arguing that it should be officially recognized as a protected cultural heritage site.













Resistance to be expanded




Ruçem Vefa Elyakut stressed that preserving the grazing lands is inseparable from the population’s right to live in their homeland and have a say in its future. “This is our land, our life. We inherited it from our ancestors. We will never allow profiteers and those in power to plunder this land and this heritage,” the DBP politician declared. He vowed that the resistance would continue until the project was stopped.




The Democratic Institutions Platform also announced that it would support the people both through legal action and in their protests. Kılıç called on the relevant authorities to halt the project and protect the livelihoods of local residents. “As the Democratic Institutions Platform, we will support the legal proceedings, stand alongside the people in their practical and legitimate resistance, and expand the resistance.”




The rally concluded with the slogan: “Long live the land, long live labor, long live the resistance!”

title: DEM Party: The Republic must be updated
content:

title: Journalist Mavioğlu: Corruption in Turkey has become institutionalised plunder - Part One
content:
As the Peace and Democratic Society Process continues in Turkey, investigations into financial scandals, match-fixing and betting operations in football, allegations of corruption in public tenders and links to the criminal underworld have once again brought relations between politics, capital and criminal networks into focus.




Journalist Ertuğrul Mavioğlu spoke to ANF about how corruption has developed into a systematic structure over the years, the mechanisms through which public resources are transferred to capital and how this system is sustained through impunity.




Mavioğlu also discussed the current stage of the Peace and Democratic Society Process, saying that the state had failed to take concrete steps towards democratisation despite the measures taken by the Kurdish Freedom Movement. He argued that the struggle against corruption could not be separated from the struggle for democracy, as the weakening of oversight mechanisms and the suppression of public dissent had facilitated the plundering of public resources.




‘The state aims to dismantle the Freedom Movement’




Mavioğlu assessed the current stage of the Peace and Democratic Society Process in light of the steps taken by the Kurdish Freedom Movement and the state's response, saying that the process was still in its early stages.




He criticised the framework law passed by parliament for being limited to disarmament and for making its implementation dependent on verification by the security bureaucracy.




Mavioğlu said: “We are still at the very beginning of the Peace and Democratic Society Process. The main reason is that, despite a series of important steps taken by the Kurdish Freedom Movement, the state has yet to take any clear and concrete action. Parliament passed an extremely inadequate framework law and, at the same time, handed over its authority to the security bureaucracy. In other words, for the law to come into force, disarmament must first be established and verified. It is not yet clear how long this will take.




Another issue is that the law is limited solely to disarmament and contains nothing concerning democratisation or the collective rights of the Kurds. Although the Kurdish side has accepted this as the first step on a thousand-kilometre journey, statements from the state offer no glimmer of hope regarding democratisation. Meanwhile, anti-democratic practices continue with undiminished intensity and severity.




Yet the government does not need any new legislation to abandon the appointment of trustees, which amounts to the usurpation of the people's will, or to stop effectively condemning sick prisoners to death. Nor does it need legislation to end the repression and intimidation of journalists, attempts to reshape the opposition through bribery and pressure, or the violent suppression of protests demanding rights. Nevertheless, everything continues as before.”




Mavioğlu argued that the state's decision to call the process a “Terror-free Turkey” process was not merely a matter of terminology, claiming that the state aimed to dismantle the organised structure of the Kurdish Freedom Movement.




Mavioğlu continued: “In other words, the state's description of this process as a ‘Terror-free Turkey’ process is not a mistake in terminology. The state's real objective is not simply to disarm the Kurdish Freedom Movement. Various statements make it clear that there is an attempt to impose surrender by demanding that the movement dismantle its organised structure. It is therefore possible to say that, from the state's perspective, this process has nothing to do with democracy.




On the other hand, the Kurdish Freedom Movement has not left the Peace and Democratic Society Process entirely at the mercy of the state from the outset. In fact, because they know that the Turkish state will not take democratic steps of its own accord, they regard the transition to democracy as a process of struggle.




Seen from this perspective, it is possible to answer your question with both yes and no. If you simply wait for the state to act, you will continue to live under repression and coercion. But the more you struggle, the greater your chances of securing democratic rights.”




‘Corruption and impunity fuel social decay’




As investigations into financial scandals and allegations linking politics to corruption have once again come under scrutiny in Turkey, Mavioğlu argued that corruption had developed into a systematic structure, citing examples spanning several decades.




Mavioğlu said that successive governments in Turkey had long pursued policies protecting the interests of the capitalist system. He described the transfer of public resources and society's savings to big capital as a defining feature of this system.




Mavioğlu said: “Right-wing politicians have been in power in Turkey for many decades, including during periods of military rule. This essentially means that every party and coalition that has come to power, even when using populist rhetoric, has regarded protecting the capitalist system as its primary duty.




The examples range from the fictitious trade scandal involving Yahya Demirel, the nephew of Süleyman Demirel, to the bloodshed unleashed by those responsible for the 12 September military coup to meet the demands of the capitalist class and their destruction of freedoms. They include the bankers' scandal, people's savings being wiped out by bank collapses, the Missing Trillion case, Islamic capital groups abroad defrauding thousands of people under the guise of ‘halal earnings’, the Central Bank making 128 billion dollars disappear by selling foreign currency at artificially low exchange rates, and the countless manoeuvres undertaken to protect the wealth of the rich through the exchange-rate-protected deposit scheme. There are many more cases of corruption and profiteering, whether we can recall them all or not.”




Mavioğlu said that the transfer of income and capital had become fundamental to the functioning of the system, drawing a direct connection between deepening poverty and policies of impunity: “Because the system itself is built on the transfer of income and capital, the primary function of every government is to create the conditions for big capital to absorb the savings of poor and middle-income people. Otherwise, more than 90 per cent of people living in Turkey would not be condemned to lives below the poverty line, nor would more than 60 per cent be living below the hunger threshold.




Although almost all of these are serious crimes committed against the people, impunity is the prevailing principle. After a while, they become part of everyday life and are normalised. This situation also fuels a culture of getting rich quickly and embeds moral decay in every part of society.”




‘The stock market transfers wealth from small investors to big capital’




Mavioğlu said that investigations into investment funds and allegations of stock market manipulation had raised further questions about financial oversight mechanisms. He argued that the stock market operated in the interests of big capital.




He claimed that small investors' savings were transferred to big capital through insider trading, capital increases and market manipulation.




Mavioğlu said: “The real issue we need to focus on is the fact that the stock market is, in reality, a system of robbery. To call things by their proper names, the history of the stock market is the history of manipulation by big capital. Just as in gambling, the house always wins. This includes everything from the enormous profits made through insider trading, using privileged information, to the absorption of investors' savings through capital increases. These are all common practices.




Some people will remember how Tansu Çiller once gave the convenient answer ‘I made it on the stock market’ when asked to explain how she had accumulated such wealth and made investments in the United States. Yet nobody can consistently bet on the right horse without inside information. In a market dominated by foreign investors and enormous corporations, you might occasionally win by chance, but most of the time you lose.




Because the stock market is a mechanism for transferring capital from small investors to large investors, oversight systems must also function as compliant cogs in this machinery. To put it in terms they would understand, robbery is inherent in the very nature of the stock market.”




Mavioğlu said that people responsible for financial oversight had themselves been implicated in allegations surrounding the recent investment fund investigation. He criticised the failure to intervene despite unusual market activity: “Didn't the information emerging from the latest investigation into investment fund fraud show that the very people who were supposed to oversee the process were already involved in it? Even the most oblivious people were aware of the abnormal movements in the shares concerned. Isn't it obvious how we should interpret the fact that the fraud was not prevented despite all the warnings?




This means clearing the way for profiteers connected to the government, or those holding power themselves. Even after the scandal broke, doesn't the fact that figures from the Justice and Development Party (AKP), who were among the main actors in the scheme, were not arrested despite this blatant crime suggest that many more profiteers are being concealed behind the scenes?”

author: Unknown
title: Shengal is at a historic turning point
content:
Shengal is now at a historic turning point. Shengal’s existence and integration bring with them a comprehensive unity with Iraq. The integration of the collective will and the genuine integration of people’s everyday lives represent the first concrete step towards bringing the two communities together in a shared life, while preserving their mother tongues and native cultures. The political reality and future represent a historic stage in which this social unity is translated into a political reality.




The coming together of the two communities through their respective cultural values and their ability to live in their mother tongues forms the cornerstone of this process. This political and cultural integration carries a force that connects with the reality of Abdullah Öcalan’s life and unites the entire society around this collective will.




This historic process expresses the will of the people of Shengal to determine their own future and live on an equal footing with Iraqi society, while also laying the foundations for building a shared future, peace and stability.




A shared political future aims to strengthen the political and social status of the Shengal region within Iraq as a whole and to permanently enshrine the people’s right to self-determination on a constitutional basis.




The integration process enables people of different faiths and identities to develop practices of coexistence based on social peace and tolerance. It is clear that the harmony fostered by integration will contribute to preserving regional stability and establishing lasting peace in Shengal and the surrounding areas.




The integration of security and administrative structures also involves reorganising the region’s security and administrative mechanisms so that they are aligned with the collective will of the people.




Socio-economic development and the integration of services will also improve people’s living standards by strengthening the region’s infrastructure, healthcare and education services.




Historical memory and recognition of identity




This process also entails preserving historical memory and acknowledging the truth, demonstrating respect for the region’s past and enabling its people to look towards the future with confidence in their own identity.




Shengal’s legal status and administrative structure within Iraq as a whole are being balanced within a framework of mutual respect and shared interests with other communities in the region. The key to the success of this process lies in the people’s will and their ability to shape their own future through their own collective decisions, across every area, from infrastructure to education.




Democratic Participation and Representation:

 The process is based on a participatory model of democracy that ensures different segments of society are represented equally and effectively within governing institutions.




Pluralistic Representation and Participatory Politics:

 The integration process has been designed to ensure that the will of all social groups, religious communities and women’s councils living throughout Shengal is reflected at the highest level in governing institutions. Rather than a narrow structure of power, this approach demonstrates a commitment to implementing an egalitarian, participatory political model that develops from the grassroots upwards. In this way, every individual’s voice can be represented in the process of governance.




The Principles of Justice and Equal Citizenship:

 The integration process is based on establishing justice in the region and fully safeguarding the constitutional rights of all ethnic and religious groups. This is intended to guarantee equality before the law for every segment of society and peaceful coexistence within a democratic legal order.




Distinctive Education and Cultural Preservation:

 The integration process guarantees the restructuring of the region’s education system in accordance with the principle of education in the mother tongue, as well as the transmission of cultural heritage to future generations. This is a critical step towards protecting and strengthening local identity.




Socio-Cultural Development and Social Welfare:

 The integration process also encompasses development programmes designed to strengthen the region’s social fabric and improve people’s well-being. Raising standards in education and healthcare and improving infrastructure are essential to establishing the foundations for a stable life.




Historical Memory and the 2014 massacre:

 The people of Shengal continue to carry the profound pain of the massacre and atrocities they endured in 2014. The systematic violence inflicted on women and children has been etched into the community’s collective memory. The steps being taken today demonstrate that this process is part of the struggle to confront that historical trauma. This struggle is being carried forward in dedication to the memory of the heroic martyrs, with the aim of safeguarding the community’s future through this resolute stance.




This process reflects a historic reality in which the suffering experienced, and the struggle waged in Shengal are intertwined with the cherished memory of those who lost their lives. The continuation of the struggle and its achievements symbolise how these sacrifices have strengthened the collective will of the people and helped lay solid foundations for the future.




Constitutional guarantees and legal status




Securing an autonomous and legally recognised status for Shengal within Iraq would ensure that the people’s democratic rights are protected within a constitutional framework and that Shengal can integrate with Iraq through its own administrative institutions.




Democratic Governance:

 Removing all administrative and legal obstacles to governing Shengal through its own councils and autonomous structures would enable the collective will of the people to be reflected in political decisions.




The Functioning of Local Government:

 Local councils and committees in Shengal make decisions through the direct participation of the people and carry out their administrative functions in accordance with democratic principles. This structure aims to ensure that the needs of the community are met as effectively as possible.




Historical Justice and Social Healing:

 The steps being taken for Shengal are vital not only for establishing its political status but also for recognising what happened in 2014 and achieving historical justice. Being able to look towards the future with confidence requires confronting the painful truths of the past and drawing strength from them to reinforce the collective will of the people.




Democratic Autonomy and Rights:

 This process also represents the people’s determination to secure their own governing institutions and rights within a framework of democratic autonomy, with constitutional guarantees.




Self-Governance and Social Organisation:

 The model of social organisation initiates a process through which Shengal can establish its own administrative structures and popular assemblies, putting political and administrative autonomy into practice.

title: Iran sentences three protest detainees to death, whereabouts unknown
content:
Branch 23 of the Islamic Revolutionary Court in Tehran has sentenced three men arrested during the December 2025–January 2026 protests to death on charges of “espionage.”




An informed source who spoke to the Kurdistan Human Rights Network (KHRN) said that the men, named Mehdi, Amir-Reza and Vahid, were notified of their sentences in Greater Tehran Central Penitentiary on 26 October.




The source added that on 28 October, the three political prisoners were summoned to the prison’s guard office on the pretext of being transferred to Ghezel Hesar Prison in Karaj, but were taken to an undisclosed location.




Security forces arrested the three men during the protests in Tehran and transferred them to the Greater Tehran Central Penitentiary after a period in detention. Their case was referred to Branch 23 following their indictment on charges of “espionage”, the source said.




At the time of the report, their transfer to Ghezel Hesar Prison remained unconfirmed, with no precise information available about the trial proceedings or the latest status of their cases.

If Öcalan is not free, any laws that are passed will be meaningless,” Teke said.




Demands for Öcalan’s freedom and improved prison conditions




The Peace Mothers are demanding that Öcalan be granted a legally and politically recognized status that would enable him to participate actively in the peace process. title: Zeynep Karayılan: Peace process cannot be one-sided
content:
Discussions continue over establishing a legal framework for disarmament and the return of members of the Kurdish Freedom Movement as part of the Peace and Democratic Society Process, launched with the aim of achieving a democratic solution to the Kurdish question. Two years into the process, the National Security Council (MGK) has yet to issue the decision required to implement the framework law passed by parliament on 10 August with the support of 467 MPs.




The law, published in the Official Gazette on 16 August, requires security agencies to verify that disarmament has taken place, with their findings subsequently confirmed by an MGK decision before the mechanism established under the law can be activated. The absence of concrete steps towards implementation, despite parliament beginning its new legislative year and the MGK holding a meeting, has drawn criticism.




Zeynep Karayılan, Co-Chair of the Diyarbakır (Amed) Branch of the Association of Lawyers for Freedom (ÖHD), spoke to ANF about the legal dimensions of the process, the shortcomings of the framework law, expectations for democratisation and the steps that need to be taken.







 







‘Implementation of the law requires an MGK decision’




Zeynep Karayılan said the implementation of the law had been made conditional on assessments by security institutions and an MGK decision, reflecting the continued treatment of the Kurdish question through the framework of security policies.




Karayılan said: “For the mechanism established under this law to become operational, the security forces must first determine that the organisation has laid down its arms. This must then be confirmed by a decision of the National Security Council and published in the Official Gazette. In other words, the verification and confirmation mechanism must first be activated before the provisions of this law can take effect.




We have repeatedly said that this law is deeply inadequate, that numerous problems will arise in its implementation and that, far from resolving the Kurdish question, it once again places security-oriented policies at its core. Nevertheless, despite all its shortcomings, we, Abdullah Öcalan and the Kurdish Freedom Movement have regarded this law as a starting point.”




‘The Kurdish side takes historic steps, but the government lacks transparency’




Karayılan said negotiations aimed at resolving the Kurdish question were particularly important after a century of policies of denial and destruction and 50 years of conflict. She added that the emergence of a basis for dialogue carried historical significance, particularly in light of the policies pursued over the past decade.




Karayılan said the Kurdish Freedom Movement had taken and implemented significant decisions as part of the process, while the government had failed to take corresponding concrete and transparent steps.




Karayılan said: “Following the Collapse Plan implemented over the past 10 years, sitting down at the negotiating table is extremely important, as is demonstrating the political will to pursue a solution. Mr. Öcalan is undoubtedly the principal architect of this process. The Kurdish Freedom Movement has also supported the process and, from the very beginning, made and implemented a series of historic decisions. Just recently, it issued a unilateral statement announcing the evacuation of camps near the Turkish border. In doing so, it once again demonstrated its determination to pave the way for the process.




However, looking at the other side of the negotiating table, we see from the government's statements that the process is still being approached primarily through security and disarmament. Although two months have passed since the law was adopted, there has been no official explanation of how the verification and confirmation mechanism is being implemented. Councils convene and meetings take place, but no official information is provided about their content. The government is not conducting the process transparently.”




‘Toxic language and uncertainty undermine public trust’




Karayılan said uncertainty surrounding the progress of the process and the language used in the media were weakening public confidence in peace. She said the Kurdish question could not be treated solely as a matter of disarmament or ending the conflict.




Karayılan said: “The media uses extremely toxic and hostile language. Both this language and the current uncertainty and prolonged period of waiting are undermining public confidence in the process. The government and sections of the opposition must stop reducing the Kurdish question to security-oriented policies and disarmament.




The Kurdish question is not simply a matter of disarmament or ending the conflict. Of course, removing weapons from the equation is important, but it would be wrong to reduce the issue to that alone. A lasting solution requires recognition of the political, cultural and collective rights of Kurds, the removal of obstacles to democratic politics and the introduction of appropriate legal reforms.”




‘A non-discriminatory and inclusive framework law is needed’




Karayılan said more comprehensive legal provisions were needed to guarantee the disarmament and return processes, criticising the existing framework law for categorising individuals and types of offences.




She said freedom of expression, thought and association must also be guaranteed to pave the way for a transition to democratic politics.




Karayılan continued: “To provide legal guarantees for the disarmament process and pave the way for returns, what was needed first and foremost was a non-discriminatory, inclusive framework law based on a democratic solution. The process should not have been divided into categories based on types of offences, historical periods or particular individuals and groups. This categorical approach creates obstacles to the transition from armed struggle to democratic politics.




What was needed was a comprehensive legal framework that would enable disarmament and participation in democratic political life, clearly define the conditions for return and provide legal guarantees. Such a law needed to cover not only the conditions for disarmament but also freedom of expression, thought and association, the right to participate in democratic politics, the right to a fair trial and the legal status of those returning.”




‘The process cannot continue through one-sided sacrifices’




Karayılan said restrictions on freedom of expression and association continued in Turkey, while the space for democratic politics was shrinking. She argued that people who had laid down their arms could not be expected to return under such conditions.




Karayılan said, “At this stage, it is unrealistic to expect those who have laid down their arms to return while restrictions on freedom of expression and association continue intensively in Turkey and the space for democratic politics is being narrowed. It is no longer sustainable to carry out this process through one-sided sacrifices. The steps taken must be reciprocated, and the government must assume concrete responsibility for democratisation and legal guarantees.”




‘

Öcalan’s legal status and the right to hope are central to the process’




Karayılan said Abdullah Öcalan's legal status and working conditions were among the central issues in the process. She said conditions must be established to enable Öcalan to play an effective role in facilitating the transition from armed struggle to democratic politics.




Karayılan recalled that implementing the judgments of the European Court of Human Rights (ECHR) was an obligation under international law for Turkey.




Karayılan said: “Mr. Öcalan's legal status is one of the central issues in this process. To create the conditions for a transition from armed struggle to democratic politics and make returns possible, he must be provided with the communication and working conditions necessary to fulfil his role in the process.




In this regard, the ‘Right to Hope’ is one of the most fundamental issues that must be addressed. It is essential to implement the judgments of the European Court of Human Rights, fulfil Turkey's obligations under international law and guarantee the Right to Hope in domestic legislation.”




‘Steps can be taken without introducing new legislation’




Karayılan said not every step towards democratisation required new legislation. She pointed out that measures such as ending the appointment of trustees, removing obstacles to prisoners' release and freeing ill prisoners could be implemented under the existing legal framework.




Karayılan said: “The law that has been adopted is currently stalled pending an MGK decision. However, there are many steps that can be taken outside this law, and in some cases without even introducing new legislation. For example, ending the appointment of trustees, stopping the arbitrary extension of prison sentences, releasing ill prisoners and lifting restrictions on freedom of expression and association are measures that would pave the way for democratisation without waiting for another decision.




These issues were also included in the report prepared by the commission established within parliament. Nevertheless, no steps have been taken to implement them. All of these are priority measures that the state must take to ensure the process progresses in a constructive manner.”




‘Truth and reconciliation commissions must be established’




Karayılan said lasting peace could not be achieved simply by ending the conflict, but must be supported by the recognition of democratic rights and a process of confronting the past. She called for a new social contract based on equal citizenship.




Karayılan also called for the establishment of Truth and Reconciliation Commissions to address the consequences of past conflicts.  Karayılan concluded: “Legal measures must be taken to establish positive peace. A new social contract based on equal citizenship must be developed, and the cultural, political and social rights needed to address the structural dimensions of the Kurdish question must be recognised. Truth and Reconciliation Commissions must also be established to confront the consequences of the conflict.




The commitment to lasting peace must not remain merely a declaration of intent. It must be supported by concrete legal reforms and reflected in everyday social life. Most importantly, all of this must happen without delay. Peace will become lasting only through the gradual building of mutual trust, coexistence and social solidarity.”

title: Resistance against solar power project in Amed: “We will not give up our land”
content:
In the village of Arzoxlî (Turkish: Kervanpınar), in the Sur district of Amed (Diyarbakır), resistance against two planned solar power plants continues. For around a week, villagers have been maintaining a vigil in tents on the proposed project site to prevent the destruction of their communal grazing lands. Women are at the forefront of the resistance, fearing for their livelihoods and determined not to surrender the land to the energy company.




The company Zenkar plans to build two photovoltaic facilities, ZENKAR-1 and ZENKAR-2, with associated energy storage systems in Arzoxlî. The projects cover areas of approximately 22.7 and 31.3 hectares, respectively. They are designed to have a combined electricity generation capacity of 33 megawatts and an energy storage capacity of 33 megawatt-hours. The affected areas include communal grazing lands used by villagers who depend primarily on livestock farming, as well as sites of historical and cultural heritage.




Expert report raises doubts about environmental compatibility




A lawsuit challenging the positive environmental impact assessment decision for ZENKAR-2 has been filed with the Administrative Court in Amed. Following a site inspection on July 16, experts concluded that the project’s impact on agriculture, livestock farming, water resources, residential areas, and cultural heritage had not been adequately assessed. In its current form, the project was therefore deemed unsuitable for implementation.




Although the legal proceedings are still ongoing, company employees entered the proposed construction site on October 21, accompanied by the Turkish gendarmerie. In response, villagers established a protest camp. Since then, women in particular have maintained a vigil under the slogan “Em herîya xwe nadin” – “We will not give up our land.” “We came here with the manure of our animals on our shoes. We have no livelihood other than livestock farming,” the women say. They intend to continue their protest until the company withdraws.










https://video.anf-news2.com/live/firat/f00c9dd0_20261027140608_26-10-2026-amed-arzoxli-kadınlar-mucadele-kararli-topragimizi-gese-kurban-etmeyecegiz-1.mp4













‘If livestock farming disappears, we cannot stay’




Leyla Aslan, one of the protesting villagers, fears that the construction of the solar power plants will force residents to leave their homes. “If this solar power plant is built, we will no longer be able to raise animals or earn a living here. Then everything will be over. They will push us to the point where we have no choice but to leave our village. What would be left for us here if we no longer have animals, land, or health? We do not want to leave. We will surrender neither this land nor our lives to them.”




Their resistance is directed against the destruction of grazing lands and the threat to water resources. Aslan criticized state authorities for supporting the company instead of standing by the villagers. “Rather than standing behind the company and helping it, the state should come and help the villagers. We want this problem to be resolved before it leads to conflict, and we want to ensure that people’s land is not taken away from them.”













Criticism of the gendarmerie’s involvement




Gülşen Birer, who is taking part in the protest vigil in solidarity with the villagers, sees the actions as another example of the destruction of natural habitats and the appropriation of land in Kurdistan. She is particularly critical of the gendarmerie accompanying the company despite the ongoing legal proceedings. “We are here to protest against the long-standing destruction of nature and the seizure of land and property in Kurdistan. We stand with the people. The villagers do not want the companies, the gendarmerie, or the excavators. Not even the legal requirements are being observed,” Birer stated.




Instead of protecting the rights of the population, the security forces are defending the company’s interests, Birer underlined. “It is the company that is being protected here, and those who own the capital are being supported. Today, the security forces serve as a shield for these companies. We will not allow this. We will not allow this destruction to continue.” Birer also criticized the failure to adequately consider the potential impact of the large-scale facilities on public health and local living conditions. “We women are the ones who protect life. We are here to defend our own lives, and that is why we are fighting.”
















We women are at the forefront




Bahar Çiftçi from Arzoxlî also believes that the solar power projects threaten the very existence of the village. The residents have few sources of income other than livestock farming. Losing their communal grazing lands would deprive them of this livelihood as well. “We are demanding our rights. Our lives belong to us, and we will not surrender them to anyone. Everyone here is unemployed, and now they are targeting our livestock farming too.”




Çiftçi describes the protest as a struggle for the right to remain in their homeland: “We came here with our shoes covered in animal manure. They want to take away our lives, seize our land, and drive us out of here. We women are leading the way. Whatever happens, we will stay here and resist. If the grazing lands are lost, there will be no livestock, no work, and therefore no way to earn a living. Our means of survival are being taken away from us. That is why we have no choice but to resist.”

content:

title: Argentine Human Rights League calls for freedom for Öcalan
content:

In its letter, the human rights organization, founded in 1937, pointed to the Kurdish leader Abdullah Öcalan’s 27 years of imprisonment on the Turkish prison island of Imrali. It said that Öcalan has spent most of this time in solitary confinement and was sentenced to aggravated life imprisonment without any ordinary prospect of release. title: Students in Dêrik demand constitutional recognition of Kurdish
content:
In the city of Dêrik in Rojava, students have once again protested against the education policies of the Syrian transitional government. They are demanding that Kurdish be officially recognized in the Syrian constitution and that the right to education in their mother tongue be guaranteed.




The demonstrators initially gathered outside the school administration building in Dêrik. They then marched to the headquarters of the regional administration, where they met with regional director Şero Şero and presented their demands.




Şero stated that he supported the students’ rights within the framework of a new, democratic Syria. He said the regional administration would forward their demands to the relevant authorities.




The protest concluded with slogans calling for the right to education in the mother tongue and the official recognition of the Kurdish language.

title: Nazan Üstündağ: Democratic integration does not mean being absorbed into the state
content:
According to sociologist Nazan Üstündağ, the democratic integration of Kurdish society must not be confused with adapting to existing state structures. Rather, she says, it involves legally recognizing Kurdish life in its entirety while strengthening society’s independent capacity for political action. Speaking to ANF, Üstündağ emphasized that the development of a democratic society must not wait for state reforms.




The academic made these remarks on the sidelines of a conference on democratic integration organized by Akademî Kurd in Zurich. The concept is one of the central topics of discussion in the ongoing peace and democratic society process. It is closely linked to Abdullah Öcalan’s concept of a democratic society and the question of how relations between the Kurdish population and the Turkish state should be shaped in the future.










https://video.anf-news2.com/live/firat/90c73c27_20261025134559_2026-10-25-zurih-nazan-ustundag-sosyolog-demokratik-entegrasyon-devletle-butunlesme-degildir-1.mp4













Bringing Kurdish life out of illegality




Üstündağ defined democratic integration as both a legal and a social process. The decades-long exclusion of the Kurds, she said, extends far beyond political prohibitions or state repression. “Rather, everyday aspects of life have also been marked by the denial of rights and criminalization. The Kurds have repeatedly been pushed into illegality in various ways. I do not mean this only in political terms, but also in relation to social life: access to healthcare, electricity, employment, and income. One could say that they have been pushed into a kind of illegality in their everyday social lives.”




Üstündağ pointed out that: “Democratic integration therefore also means ensuring that Kurdish life receives legal recognition in all its dimensions. Interactions with state institutions must no longer be characterized by criminalization but must instead be based on rights and equal access to social resources. However, this legal equality is only one aspect of the process. Equally important is that Kurdish society itself defines the forms of exclusion it experiences and determines how they can be overcome.”




A democratic society emerges through self-organization




In Üstündağ’s view, democratic integration cannot be achieved solely through legislative reforms or political negotiations: “It must also emerge from social discussions, collective organization, and the development of independent alternatives. This will happen through social organization, by engaging in discussions within society, sharing experiences, and developing demands based on them. Sometimes, these processes will give rise to alternative forms of production, alternative ways of life, and alternative spaces.”




Üstündağ identifies two interconnected dimensions of the current process: the democratization of state structures on the one hand, and the independent development of a democratic society on the other. For this very reason, she says, social development must not be made dependent on the pace of state decisions. “The fact that the process of democratizing the state is progressing slowly must not mean that the development of a democratic society should also proceed slowly. This is the most important issue.”




“Democratic integration never means becoming one with the state”




Üstündağ draws a fundamental distinction between democratic integration and the notion of a harmonious unity between state and society, free of contradictions. “Even under changing political conditions social interests and the state’s claims to power will continue to come into conflict. Democratic integration can never mean merging with the state to become a single entity. For we know that fundamental contradictions exist between the state and society, and that there will always be tensions between them.




The crucial task, therefore, is not to eliminate these contradictions but to develop new ways of addressing them through democratic means. While the conflict in the past was largely shaped by armed struggle, society itself must increasingly emerge as an active political force in the future.




Of course, society has always been active. But we must make it even more active, enable it to become a stronger actor in this struggle, and mobilize society at every level. That is what I understand by democratic integration. This also means beginning now to consider how social conflicts can be organized and addressed through civilian means. People must develop new ways of representing their own interests and exerting democratic pressure.”




Alliances must emerge from below




Üstündağ also emphasizes that the social dimension of democratic integration must not be limited to the Kurdish population: “Other population groups in Turkey also experience exclusion and are pushed into legally precarious living conditions by existing political and economic circumstances. This could give rise to shared interests and new forms of solidarity-based organization. What matters, however, is that such alliances are not formed exclusively at the level of political leadership.




Of course, we must forge alliances and build relationships, but above all, these must be alliances from below, not from above. In Turkey, it is not only the Kurds who have been pushed into illegality. This affects many people and social groups. This can also create common ground.”




As an example, the sociologist points to people who, because of their living conditions, are forced to rely on informal or criminalized means of making a living. She states that the common struggle for legal recognition and social participation must bring different population groups together. According to Üstündağ, such alliances are among the indispensable foundations of democratic integration.




Social transformation even in the face of state resistance




Asked whether democratic integration could also be developed against the will of the state, Üstündağ rejects a rigid opposition between social resistance and state transformation. The two processes, she argues, can influence one another. “Against the state and at the same time with the state. I do not believe these two things necessarily exclude each other. After all, we have seen over many years that, through our actions against the state’s will, we have also been able to bring the state to a certain point.”




Üstündağ continued: “The past five decades of Kurdish resistance have demonstrated that social movements can bring about change even when their achievements do not initially receive formal legal recognition. Political terminology, social representation, and public debate can be transformed through sustained resistance, eventually putting pressure on state institutions to adapt.”




“Legal reforms and independent social organization must therefore be considered together. However, the political starting point must not be the expectation of concessions from the state. Our goal must be to understand ourselves, represent ourselves, and develop our own voice through democratic means,” Üstündağ concluded.

title: Students in Rojava oppose the incorporation of their universities into state institutions
content:
The planned incorporation of the universities of Rojava and Kobanê into Syria’s state higher education system has met with resistance from students in Rojava. The Union of Patriotic Students rejects the recent decisions by the Syrian Ministry of Higher Education and warns that they threaten to undermine academic self-governance and Kurdish-language higher education. At a gathering at the University of Rojava in Qamishlo, the organization declared that it would not accept any decision that jeopardizes the educational structures built up over the years or the rights of students.




The dispute stems from two decisions by the Syrian Higher Education Council, announced on October 27. Under these decisions, the University of Rojava in Qamishlo is to be incorporated into the state-run Al-Furat University, while the University of Kobanê is to be placed under the University of Aleppo. Their faculties will henceforth fall under the authority of the respective state universities. Restrictions on the admission of new students are also planned for certain degree programs.




Kurdish-language education under renewed pressure




The decision comes amid growing disputes over the future of the Kurdish-language education system in Rojava. In late August, the Syrian Ministry of Education stipulated that Kurdish would be included in the state curriculum only as a subject taught for three hours per week. Permission to teach other subjects in Kurdish was granted only as a temporary measure.




While an independent education system with Kurdish as the language of instruction has been developed in Rojava over the years, students now fear that the future of higher education in their mother tongue is also at risk. They believe that incorporation into state universities could lead to existing degree programs being restructured, merged, or abolished.




At the gathering in Qamishlo, attended by numerous students, a statement read out in Kurdish and Arabic said: “These decisions will have a serious impact on us, as we have studied in our mother tongue, Kurdish, throughout our entire school education. The right to continue higher education in the same language is a fundamental academic right. Attempts to interfere with departments and faculties where education is provided in the mother tongue are an attack on the foundations of academia and a threat to our academic future. We will never accept this decision.”




“Integration does not mean assimilation”




The Students’ Union recalled that the establishment of independent universities in Rojava around ten years ago marked a historic step forward. For the first time, thousands of young people were given the opportunity to pursue higher education in their hometowns and in their mother tongue. These achievements must not be undone by administrative decisions, the organization said, particularly rejecting potential interference with existing faculties and degree programs.




“The abolition, merger, or restructuring of academic departments in this manner constitutes a clear violation of fundamental human rights and international conventions that guarantee the right to education in one’s mother tongue and the free, independent administration of educational institutions,” the Students’ Union declared.




The union demands that changes to the higher education system not be decided without consulting those directly affected. “Any transitional phase must be organized fairly and respect the identity of each university. Integration does not mean assimilation. Throughout the integration process, educational, logistical, legal, and academic criteria must be taken into account transparently. Otherwise, we will be faced with injustice and a betrayal of students’ rights.”




Recognition instead of dismantling independent structures




The Students’ Union emphasized that it welcomes official recognition of the universities in principle. However, it said, such recognition must not come at the expense of their autonomy or Kurdish-language degree programs. “Our wish has always been, and remains, for our university, built through dedicated efforts over the past ten years, to receive full recognition and continue fulfilling its mission without its academic programs being dismantled.”




The union pointed out that the people of Rojava have a legitimate right to universities that meet their academic needs while preserving their linguistic and cultural identity. It stressed that neither the efforts invested in establishing these universities nor the right of students to continue their chosen degree programs should be sacrificed for the sake of administrative restructuring.




In conclusion, the Union of Patriotic Students called on the Syrian transitional government, the Ministry of Higher Education, and all institutions involved to review the decisions and establish binding guarantees to protect the existing educational structures. “As a students’ union, we remain fully committed to our position and will continue our struggle for our rights by all means at our disposal. The achievements of the universities must be safeguarded, and young people’s right to higher education in their mother tongue must be protected,” the statement said.

title: Kurdish athlete arrested after summons in Kermanshah, taken to undisclosed location
content:
Mohammad Nasseri, a Kurdish athlete who manages a bodybuilding gym in Harsin, Kermanshah Province, has been arrested after reporting to a prosecutor’s office in Kermanshah in response to a summons on charges of “propaganda against the state”.




The Kurdistan Human Rights Network (KHRN) has reported that Nasseri was arrested on 26 October after reporting to Branch 16 of the Investigating Office at Kermanshah’s Public and Revolutionary Prosecutor’s Office and was taken to an undisclosed location.




He had received the summons in recent days.

title: YJA Star guerrillas: Martyr Bêrîtan is the torch of our struggle
content:
