title: History repeats itself for the Turkish state
content:
The Justice and Development Party (AKP) government has recently been forming a number of alliances. While the AKP and the Nationalist Movement Party (MHP) defend these agreements, the opposition has criticised them. Various reasons have been put forward to explain these alliances. However, given that they involve the Middle East and its surrounding region, the first question that comes to mind is their connection to war. Military historians define war as the continuation of politics by other means. From this perspective, it is clear that these alliances risk drawing Turkey into the war in the Middle East.




In fact, the alliance with Saudi Arabia and Pakistan has already drawn Turkey into the war. According to incoming reports and assessments, Turkey has become involved in the ongoing war in Yemen. The Turkish state has sent its armed drones and the specialists who operate them to Saudi Arabia, from where attacks are being carried out against the Houthis in Yemen. As is known, the Houthis are supported by Iran. Turkey has therefore effectively entered into a war with Iran. On the one hand, it claims to oppose the war being waged by the United States and Israel against Iran, while on the other, it is waging war against the Houthis in Yemen.




Turkey is trying to play every possible side to suit its own interests. By participating in the war against the Houthis, it has placed itself in an anti-Iranian position. The Houthis are also enemies of Israel. Turkey has therefore effectively adopted a position favourable to Israel. Supporting Iran while acting against it, appearing to oppose Israel while pursuing policies that favour it! Turkey is pursuing a policy riddled with such contradictions. To use a familiar expression, it has recently been pressing every button. It is well known that those facing difficulties and crises resort to trying everything. Turkey believes that it can salvage something by acting this way, but in reality, it is gambling.




Neither Iran will forget Turkey's position nor will Israel begin to view Turkey favourably simply because it has attacked Yemen. Turkey's apparent opposition to the war against Iran is entirely connected to its hostility towards the Kurds. It opposes the war because it believes the Kurds could benefit from it. Indeed, when Devlet Bahçeli calls on the Kurdistan Free Life Party (PJAK) to lay down its arms, he is expressing hostility towards the Kurds rather than concern for Iran. Iran knows very well that, despite Turkey's approach, Ankara ultimately wants Iran to be weakened. Turkey believes that a weaker Iran would allow it to become more influential in the region.




By forming an alliance with Saudi Arabia and Pakistan, Turkey is not merely positioning itself against Iran. It is also antagonising India. India, like China, is emerging as a rising power. India also maintains strong relations with Israel. There is a considerable possibility that Turkey's new alliance will leave it worse off than before, losing what it already has while pursuing something more.




It is well known that Enver, Talat and Cemal Pasha brought a devastating defeat upon the Ottoman Empire by entering the war alongside Germany, which they believed to be a powerful ally. The AKP government may be calculating that closer relations with Saudi Arabia will bring in petrodollars and enable it to overcome its economic problems. Yet the attraction of these petrodollars could drag Turkey into all kinds of disastrous situations. The alliances being formed demonstrate precisely this danger.




Every political alliance causes concern among certain states and political forces. The alliance with Qatar, Pakistan and Indonesia will unsettle not only India and Iran but also other countries. Turkey's agreement with Libya on maritime jurisdiction has already caused concern in Europe, Greece, Israel and Egypt. Antagonising Europe in this way will cost Turkey dearly. Egypt is already deeply dissatisfied with Turkey's policy towards Libya, and this dissatisfaction will now increase. Turkey has already antagonised Israel, Southern Cyprus and Greece. It has thus created further opposition on another front.




If war is the continuation of politics by other means, then the alliances Turkey is forming indicate that it is moving towards war.




Two years ago, faced with the war in the Middle East and the prospect of changing political balances, Turkey sought to end its war against the Kurdish Freedom Movement and protect itself from the dangers that might emerge. It pursued a policy of strengthening the domestic front as the Middle East was being reshaped. Indeed, the authorities consistently presented their involvement in the Peace and Democratic Society Process as an effort to strengthen the domestic front. Turkey now appears to have abandoned its policy of ending the war against the Kurds to avert these dangers. The state's failure to take any steps, despite the Kurdish Freedom Movement having taken every possible step, already indicates a change in policy. Its recent pursuit of alliances is a concrete expression of this shift.




The AKP and MHP government now appears to be seeking to overcome the threats it perceives in the Middle East through external alliances rather than by strengthening the domestic front. On the one hand, it is exerting pressure on forces opposed to it; on the other, it is sidelining the Peace and Democratic Society Process. In short, it is doing everything that could weaken the domestic front. This clearly shows that strengthening the domestic front is no longer its policy. Instead, it has adopted an approach based on suppressing domestic opposition through external alliances while seeking to counter threats from abroad.




The Ottoman Empire weakened and retreated in the face of the West during the 19th century because of internal conflicts, particularly those involving the Kurds. At the beginning of the 20th century, it gambled on an alliance with Germany and lost. The Turkish state is now repeating this historical experience. By refusing to accept the hand extended by the Kurds, it is making a historic mistake. The only way to rescue Turkey from this impasse is to take steps that will advance the Peace and Democratic Society Process. Turkey's future also depends on the policy it pursues in this regard.




Source: Yeni Yaşam newspaper

title: The AKP cannot function without war
content:
It is becoming increasingly clear with each passing day that the process initiated by Kurdish leader Abdullah Öcalan through his February 27, 2025 Call for Peace and Democratic Society amounts, in a sense, to a disruption of the established game. To the domestic and international powers that divided Kurdistan into four parts, imposed genocide on the Kurds, and have benefited from the Kurdish question and the contradictions and conflicts it has generated, the message was effectively: “I will not play the game you want and impose on me. I will play my own game.” In this way, Öcalan has challenged the politics of war and moved toward adopting a politics of peace.




This new strategy and policy developed by Abdullah Öcalan has undoubtedly shocked and bewildered the forces that have tied themselves to, and benefited from, the strategy of conflict arising from the Kurdish question. It appears that the AKP is among those most taken aback. Indeed, under present conditions, when Turkey’s interests and democratic future lie in a politics of peace, the AKP remains unable to break away from its entrenched politics of war and militarization. It has failed to respond positively as required to the peace process initiated by Öcalan. The steadily increasing violence, judicial repression, and police pressure across all areas of life in Kurdistan and Turkey are manifestations of this. By sending military equipment to Saudi Arabia for use against the Houthis in Yemen, preparing to deploy troops, and developing new military alliances in the region, the AKP demonstrates that it cannot function without war and is unable to abandon its politics of war.




As of October 29, the Republic of Turkey will have completed its 103rd year since its founding and will be entering its 104th year. If the period that began with the fascist military coup of September 12, 1980, is to be defined as the “Second Republic,” then the AKP’s quarter-century in power undoubtedly constitutes the central ruling force of this period. It could also be put this way: The “Second Republic” process initiated by the military junta headed by Kenan Evren found its true ruling power under Tayyip Erdoğan’s leadership. In other words, the “Second Republic” was shaped by the mentality of Kenan Evren and Tayyip Erdoğan. Its only difference from the First Republic was the incorporation of political Islam, which had previously been excluded from the state under the label of “reactionism,” into the state apparatus. Thus, the “Second Republic” continued and intensified its hostility toward the Kurds and communism.




Let us look back and recall this recent history. The Evren–Özal alliance, which laid the foundations of the September 12 regime, became the driving force behind this transformation of the Republic. It was primarily Turgut Özal who carried this forward, developing the political line inherited from Menderes and Demirel, albeit with cautious and hesitant steps. When the same Turgut Özal sought to pursue a similar approach toward the Kurds, however, that intention cost him his life. Necmettin Erbakan attempted to advance the process initiated by the Evren–Özal alliance, but his approach to the Kurdish question was also deemed unacceptable, and he was pushed aside. Having drawn the necessary lessons from all these developments, Tayyip Erdoğan became the most skillful and thorough practitioner of the mentality and policies of September 12.




Tayyip Erdoğan’s nearly quarter-century in power should also be examined in two distinct periods. During the first period, when he was still engaged in a fierce power struggle with the secularist forces of the Republic, he was compelled to forge both covert and overt alliances to consolidate his strength. To succeed in this struggle, he pursued a policy of presenting himself as generally “pro-peace.” Indeed, during this period, whenever elections approached, he requested a ceasefire from the PKK and secured electoral victories by ensuring that elections were held in an atmosphere of ceasefire. In the second period, after neutralizing the secularist forces within the Republic, he fully aligned himself with the Turkish Republic’s deeply entrenched anti-Kurdish and militaristic policies. He donned a military uniform and sought to fulfill the role of commander-in-chief. During this period, he undoubtedly adopted a strategy of winning elections by escalating both domestic and external conflicts.




In its current form, the state and the AKP government have merged and become fully integrated. Some intellectuals and politicians describe this situation as the “AKP State,” a characterization that is, in fact, not entirely inaccurate. Ultimately, the AKP State, having incorporated political Islam and operating in an environment where the socialist movement has also been weakened, has concentrated its entire militaristic orientation on the “war against the Kurds.” As a result, an AKP political strategy has emerged that feeds on this war and has tied its survival to it, regardless of Turkey’s overall trajectory. An AKP administration has thus taken shape that depends on the war against the Kurds for its existence and can easily sustain itself through it.




In recent years, however, two developments have disrupted this seemingly smooth course:




- The US-Israeli war plans and actions aimed at establishing a new hegemony in the Middle East have come to threaten Turkey’s future.




- The announcement of the peace and democratic society process, aimed at protecting Turkey from this threat and overcoming it.




Having become incapable of surviving without war, the AKP finds itself at an impasse, unable to find a way forward in the face of the peace and democratization process initiated by Abdullah Öcalan.




The AKP’s new political approach that has emerged under these circumstances is striking and must be properly understood. Notably, it makes no mention of peace or democracy. Instead, it employs a deceptive method that subsumes and effectively erases everything under the concept of a “Terror-Free Turkey,” devised by some of its advisers. Likewise, the steps involving a “Parliamentary Commission” and a “Framework Law” have become two magic wands shielding the AKP from the demands of the peace and democratic society process. By relying on these measures, the AKP creates the impression that it is doing everything necessary to advance the process, while in reality attempting to conceal its political stance, which fundamentally opposes peace and favors war. Above all, this deception must be clearly recognized and exposed.




It appears that the AKP government has sought to use the peace and democratic society process initiated by the Kurdish side as leverage against the United States and Israel, ultimately seeking to reach an agreement with them—or, more precisely, to surrender to them. Indeed, this surrender was realized at the NATO meeting held in Ankara in July. Through the “Mecca Agreement,” Turkey has now effectively joined the Abraham Accords in a covert manner, aligning itself with the US-Israeli war bloc as a means of ensuring its own survival. Thus, even if it does not engage in war domestically, it will seek to sustain and operate the war machine it has built by participating in conflicts abroad.




In fact, it cannot be said that the war within Turkey has come to an end either. Yes, since the ceasefire declared by the PKK on March 1, 2025, there have been no armed confrontations on the Kurdish front. Nevertheless, the AKP government has intensified economic, political, judicial, and police repression against the Kurds and Turkey’s society to such an extent that its actions have become far more destructive than armed warfare. In other words, it continues to expand and implement the seven-dimensional special warfare strategy outlined by İlker Başbuğ in 2009. Through the appointment of government trustees, it is attempting to seize control of almost all municipalities. It is imposing restrictions on the press reminiscent of the reign of Abdülhamid. It is said that the age of drug use in Kurdistan has fallen to as low as five. Prisons are overflowing, and even those who have served their full sentences are unable to secure their release. Prostitution, femicides, and other forms of pressure and violence against society have reached extraordinary levels.




According to a statement by Sezai Temelli, deputy parliamentary group chair of the DEM Party, military expenditure under the heading of “defense” has increased by 60 percent. While arming itself to such an extent, the AKP government simultaneously demands and expects complete disarmament from the Kurds. This contradictory approach—arming itself while demanding that the Kurds disarm—is troubling the minds of everyone living in Turkey today.




It is abundantly clear that the AKP cannot function or govern without war. The war machine it has built is spreading bloodshed and death all around it. Escalating violence against society and the opposition domestically, combined with participation in wars alongside the US-Israeli bloc internationally, forms the foundation of the AKP’s current policies. There must be no illusions about this. The AKP has long since abandoned the policy of transforming Turkey into an alternative model of life and society through peace and democratization. Instead, it has joined the world of US-Israeli hegemony, a world that destroys societies and nature. It is evident that Turkey can have no future under the current AKP government. Yet a Turkey without the AKP could be a much better place.




Source: Yeni Özgür Politika

title: Hozat: Turkish authorities increase pressure on opposition to prevent broader support to process
content:
KCK Executive Council Co-Chair Besê Hozat spoke to Medya Haber TV about the current stage of the process, the women’s freedom struggle, practices in prisons, and regional developments.




Part one of the interview can be read 

here

. 




The government’s operations against municipalities continue. New trustees are being appointed. Most recently, a trustee was appointed to Halk TV. Many digital media accounts have been shut down, and some are being blocked. Attacks on newspapers are rampant, and arrests are on the rise. Overall, there are intense attacks directed at the press and media workers. It is as if the government is carrying out purges against those who do not align with it. What do these attacks signify at a time when the democratization of the republic is being debated?




That’s a good question. What is this state doing to prevent the process from becoming a societal movement? It is implementing a policy of oppression and hostility in the prisons. There has been no change in Rêber Apo’s [President Abdullah Öcalan] conditions to date. Isolation continues. While Rêber Apo took the initiative in this process, drove it forward, and brought it to this level, there is still no change in his conditions. Journalists were supposed to visit him, but it was prevented. The committee was supposed to go, convene, and work; that did not happen. His status was supposed to be formalized, but it didn’t happen. He was supposed to freely lead this process. There were supposed to be advisors, academics, and politicians visiting him. None of the things our leader demanded have happened. It’s a similar situation in prisons.




In order to prevent this process from gaining broader societal support in Turkey, the Turkish authorities are intensifying pressure on the opposition. They are attacking the press. There are particularly intense attacks on the opposition media. Dozens of journalists are being detained, arrested, and threatened. Yesterday, they held a very impressive march. I believe journalists marched in ten cities to voice their protests. I salute them. It’s truly very meaningful. These efforts need to develop further. There is intense pressure on the opposition press, on the opposition itself, and on workers. There is extremely intense pressure on all segments of society in Turkey that criticize this government or express dissatisfaction with it. This also prevents the process from becoming a social movement on the Turkish front. To prevent this process from becoming a societal movement – to prevent society from taking ownership of it – they are doing nearly everything in their power.




Like I said, there is currently intense pressure and oppression on the Turkish front as well. There is a policy of intense pressure targeting all opposition democratic, opposition liberal, and opposition groups. They do not want the truth to reach the public. That is why they’ve intensified the pressure on the opposition media so much. They don’t want the public to know the truth. Especially now that this funding crisis has come to the fore. The opposition media covered it extensively. A fierce wave of attacks has been launched. They also don’t want the government to be criticized for this process or for the truth to come to light.




And as a result of this intense attack, the process is not gaining traction among the Turkish public. It is blocking progress, and concerns regarding the state and the government on this issue are deepening even further. What kind of process is this? Can this process develop without democratization? That is the fundamental principle and philosophy of this process. It is the democratization of Turkey. Turkey cannot resolve the Kurdish issue without democratization. And Turkey cannot democratize without resolving the Kurdish issue. Turkey must embark on a democratic process. In this sense, the current government must take democratic steps. It must pursue very serious democratization in every legal, political, and social sphere. The opposite is happening. Increasing authoritarianism and an even more intense policy of repression and oppression are running rampant across all segments of society that oppose the government. Anti-democratic policies are intensifying and deepening. This process will neither become part of the social fabric nor develop in this manner. The development of this process depends on Turkey’s democratization. Currently, there are no signs of this.




The US has withdrawn from Iraq. Southern Kurdish forces have voiced their concerns about the upcoming period. They have indicated that a process similar to that of 2014 could unfold. Is there truly such a danger? How can these dangers be averted? What should the Kurdish forces do?




The US has withdrawn its ground forces from Iraq, as well as from Southern Kurdistan. As far as we know, only a small number of officials, playing an advisory role, remain. However, the US has not withdrawn from Iraq. It is not realistic to assess the situation that way. It is a hegemonic power. It is in the midst of a major war with Iran. It has a decisive influence in shaping the region. And the war continues to deepen. A stable order has not yet been established in the region. Therefore, the US remains in the region; the US is in Iraq. There is no question of any such withdrawal. It has military influence, political influence, and economic influence. It also has significant military bases in areas close to Iran. There are command centers directing this war right within the region itself. In that sense, it would not be realistic to describe this as a complete withdrawal. Because the US continues to have plans and interests in the region. The US has not relinquished its global hegemony. It is a hegemonic power. Whoever is the hegemon in the region becomes the hegemon of the world. That is a fact. Therefore, these dynamics continue.




Trying to strengthen the central states in the region is the nature of US policy. It sees its interests here. Tom Barrack’s statements, as well as Trump’s, have made this clear. They indicate that attacks may occur in the coming days. Current practices also point in that direction. We saw this in its Syrian policy. Something similar is unfolding in other countries as well – in Lebanon, and now in Iraq, too.




Of course, this situation poses a threat to the Kurds in Iraq – particularly regarding the status of the Kurds and the federal Kurdistan region. The strengthening of central governments naturally creates a threat and a risk for the status of Kurdistan as well. In order to eliminate these dangers and risks, democratic unity of the Kurds is needed. Truly, the only thing that will eliminate all these dangers from the Kurds’ perspective is the democratic unity of the Kurds – their democratic national unity. Therefore, every Kurdish organization – regardless of its structure or political orientation – must analyze the situation very carefully, recognize it, and be forward-thinking. They must understand that the only solution is democratic Kurdish unity and, on this basis, must change, transform, and take action. The development of such a process in Southern Kurdistan – and it playing an effective role in the matter of democratic Kurdish unity – is also linked to the overall democratization of the administrative system in Southern Kurdistan.




If the process of democratization develops within the governance model of Southern Kurdistan, then – in conjunction with other Kurdish organizations, institutions, and the civil society – such a problem will truly cease to exist for the Kurdish community. A strong national consciousness, spirit of unity, and sense of solidarity have emerged within society. There is significant social cohesion and unity. The problem lies within political organizations and structures. If a process of democratization develops in this regard and a democratic Kurdish unity takes shape, these threats to South Kurdistan can be averted. Democratic Kurdish unity is an urgent necessity.




Trump and Barack have stated that new attacks on Iran could occur in the coming days. The Tehran administration has lost a significant amount of power. What kind of change do external powers foresee in Iran? How can Iran find a way out of this process? And, most importantly, how should the Kurds respond to it?




The policy of international powers toward Iran is either to subdue the Iranian regime or to overthrow it. This is the framework within which the policy is developing. Iran has been severely worn down by the war waged against it so far. It has truly weakened. Of course, the US has also found itself in a serious impasse, particularly regarding the Strait of Hormuz. In that sense, these powers have also faced difficulties—that is also a reality.




There is also a serious situation of weakness and contraction within Iran itself. To some extent, Iran’s current stance is providing a pretext for such interventions. If Iran were to democratize internally, if it were to respond to the demands of the people in Iran – including the demands of women – and undergo such a fundamental reform based on democratization, it could very easily repel these attacks. Even if the attacks were to occur, they would not achieve their goals. They claim to have the support of the people, but that is not the case. There is serious discontent and backlash within society. There is no point in deluding oneself. The policy of executions is leading to support for these attacks from many parts of society. The policy of executions generates serious anger and a serious anger and backlash – among the Kurdish community, within Iranian society, and in the international community. This, in turn, has a very serious negative impact on Iran.




The path forward is democratization. The struggle strategy developed by Kurdish organizations in this regard is very appropriate. The democratization of Iran based on local democracy is the most appropriate strategy. Kurdish organizations are waging a struggle on this basis. This must be carried out together with all the people of Iran, in conjunction with the democratic social dynamics within Iran, and in solidarity with the people.




It appears that Turkey has embarked on an intensive diplomatic effort. It signed the Mecca Alliance and joined the Badr Alliance. Furthermore, just a few days ago, it announced that it had renewed the agreement it had previously made with Libya regarding the Mediterranean. However, some countries, such as Israel and Egypt, have expressed their concerns regarding the agreement with Libya. Given these developments, what scenarios might emerge for the region in the future?




Turkey is attempting to fill the vacuum created by Iran’s weakening in the region. Clearly, the US and NATO have, to some extent, cleared the way for Turkey in this regard. The Mecca Alliance, the Badr Alliance, and the Libya Agreement were all established with some degree of US and NATO approval. None of this would have happened without them. However, a counter-front is naturally emerging in response to this. This has ever existed since the past. Israel, Greece, Egypt, and Southern Cyprus are increasingly forming a bloc against the defense and military alliances Turkey has been developing.




There is a major struggle for hegemony in the region. The region is undergoing a process of redesign. Turkey also wants to have a place in this reshaping; it wants to carve out a space for itself. In this sense, the decision to act in full alignment with NATO was made through the NATO agreement. Turkey has fully shifted its course toward the US and NATO. On the basis of representing US and NATO interests in the region, both the US and NATO have opened the way for Turkey to some extent. All these alliances and agreements have developed somewhat on this basis. In a way, this also demonstrates just how difficult, how weak, and how helpless Turkey’s situation is. In a sense, it has surrendered to NATO and to the US It is currently pursuing a policy in the region based on US interests. This Mecca Alliance was essentially formed in this way, against Iran. The US wanted this. And Turkey is trying to benefit from it as well. Within this framework, it is trying to carve out a place for itself in the region by relying on these alliances. Taking a stand against the Houthis also means opposing Iran.




Although they are striving to pursue a more coordinated and closely aligned policy on the Kurdish issue – and even though Turkey is making a serious effort to draw Iran toward that line, particularly on this matter – it is becoming clear that they will face serious conflicts over this issue in Yemen and in their regional policy. This is because Turkey, as a whole, is seeking to end Iran’s hegemony in the region and to consolidate its own position in the areas Iran has vacated. It’s a matter of Israeli hegemony versus Turkish hegemony. In this way, Israel and Turkey exist as two hegemonic powers in the region; in fact, over the past year, we have seen these two powers assert themselves even more. The mutual rhetoric is developing partly as a result of this. This led Turkey to face problems with Iran regarding the hegemonic dynamics in the region. That is clear. Even if they try to maintain harmony regarding the Kurdish issue, they will face problems in regional hegemony and regional politics. Because Turkey is pursuing a hostile policy toward Iran on this matter. As I said, it has surrendered to NATO and the US. It is trying to eliminate Iran’s influence in the region and position itself accordingly. But Turkey cannot ensure its own security in this manner.




There are deep fault lines in Turkey. One of these fault lines is the Kurdish issue, another is the Alevi issue. And there are many other social issues, such as the issue of women’s rights. They are very deep, very serious, and fundamental problems. Without resolving these fundamental issues on a democratic basis, Turkey cannot secure its survival, its future, or its very existence. Nor can it become a power in the region. It cannot become a lasting power. Periodically, by developing such military alliances and defense pacts, it has secured itself and guaranteed its existence; indeed, it has many such aspirations in the region as well, striving to establish itself as a hegemonic power. However, if Turkey does not resolve its internal problems – if it does not resolve these fundamental, historical issues, namely the Kurdish and Alevi issues – Turkey’s existence cannot be guaranteed. With this strategy and these interventions, Turkey will face serious challenges both at home and abroad. The reason Turkey has brought this process to an almost standstill, is precisely these developments in the region. It is trying to manage this situation in its own way through various means. But it is not able to manage it. These are very deep-rooted problems, and Turkey has been experiencing a civil war for over 50 years. If Turkey does not resolve this issue on a democratic basis, this civil war will deepen and throw Turkey into a completely different place. It should not delude itself. I find this important. Only by resolving the Kurdish issue and the Alevi issue, and by becoming democratic – only then can Turkey emerge unscathed from this storm.




There is a popular movement in France that was initiated by high school students and is gradually spreading. There have been periodic protests of this kind in France in the past as well. What do you think is the fundamental reason for the emergence of such movements at the very heart of capitalist modernity?




The system of capitalist modernity has been in a systematic crisis for the past 100 years, and it has especially deepened over the past 50 years. It is in a state of turmoil. The current social upheaval has turned into an explosion. It began primarily led by students but has now become a widespread social movement, spreading across Europe – especially in France and Italy – and has become a social uprising spreading everywhere. The streets are ablaze. This is the stage the crisis of capitalist modernity has reached. This system of exploitation – this multi-layered colonialism – has created a serious rift in society by diverting the economy’s resources, all of society’s resources, toward militarization, war, so-called defense, security, and the wealthy class. The rich have grown richer and richer. One segment – a tiny handful – has been condemned to deep poverty, while other segments of society have been condemned to deep poverty. This is the root cause of the current uprisings in Europe. The demand for social rights is at the heart of it. For instance, all resources are being diverted to military spending and such. They are flowing to the bourgeoisie, the upper bourgeoisie – in short, the wealthy class. A deep chasm has opened up between the poor and the rich. This is the deep crisis of capitalist modernity. This is the point to which the colonial system has arrived.




Now Turkey is capitalizing on this. It claims that it would be the center of democracy in these countries and points to the people’s plight, trying to gain some advantage for itself. Turkey’s situation is far worse than that of European countries. For years, Turkey has kept itself afloat through anti-Kurdish sentiment and the Kurdish issue. By militarizing society and fostering nationalism and racism, these regimes perpetuate themselves and stay in power. That is precisely why they leave the Kurdish issue unresolved. It is a fundamental form of capital – the capital of power. It has been turned into the law of maintaining power. There is no such intense issue in Europe right now. That’s why society is doing what it’s doing. Otherwise, in Turkey too, the exploitation of labor, the exploitation of women, social exploitation, and genocide are at their peak. Last time, a retired police officer committed suicide during protest actions. There are many suicides. Everywhere there is labor exploitation, poverty, and hunger. It’s rampant. Now, because Turkey is waging the biggest war, these resources are going toward the war. These resources are going toward militarization, leaving society hungry, destitute, and deprived of every right and freedom.




This is emerging as a systemic crisis, and Turkey is a part of this system. It is manifesting as a systemic crisis. And I believe this affects the entire world. These issues are not limited to Europe; they affect the whole world. Because this is a systemic crisis of capitalist modernity. It is a crisis of the nation-state system. It is a social explosion triggered by the Third World War. It is a state of upheaval. It is the outward manifestation of a crisis in this form. And these issues will not be limited to that region either. It in-fact began in the Middle East earlier. Now it is spreading everywhere, and the system is truly facing a downward spiral. This system is too much for this society to bear. Society can no longer bear it. It cannot bear this colonial and oppressive system.




It is very intense everywhere, and young people are leading the way. This is important. Huge crowds are in revolt, on their feet. This needs to become much more organized everywhere. With a program and strategy, a genuine alternative to capitalist modernity can emerge. That is why a program is important in the struggle, and strategy is important. Organized power – along with its program, strategy, and struggle strategy – is crucial. If this social popular movement, this movement of the peoples, can achieve this, it can gradually bring forth such an alternative to the system. These things are important.




In fact, the “democratic nation” and “confederal system” project developed by Rêber Apo is the remedy and alternative for the entire world. The alternative of democratic modernity against capitalist modernity… It is a genuine solution project that addresses the needs of the entire society, of the peoples, and of women.

title: DBP and DEM Party: We will be in Varto on 2 November
content:
The Varto (Gimgim) district organizations of the DBP and DEM Party set up a stand in Kox Square as part of the legal proceedings against the geothermal power plant project.




Speaking in a press conference, DBP District Co-Chair Aziz Oral said that the project threatens not only the natural environment but also the living spaces and cultural existence of the local population.




Oral pointed out that potential water pollution could affect agriculture and livestock farming, as well as a wider area of the Euphrates basin via the Murat River. He emphasized the need to protect nature, water resources, and the right of future generations to life.




The DBP and DEM Party called on residents to gather in the village of Xwarik on 2 November for an expert inspection related to the planned geothermal power plant (JES) project in Varto.

title: Iranian director Jafar Panahi sentenced to 5 years and 1 month in prison
content:
Iranian director and screenwriter Jafar Panahi was sentenced to 5 years and 1 month in prison in a case heard by Branch 26 of the Tehran Revolutionary Court. The court ordered the confiscation of all his movable and immovable assets, banned him from social media activities for two years, and prohibited him from leaving the country.




According to a report by HRANA, citing Emtedad, Panahi’s lawyer, Mostafa Nili, stated that the verdict had been issued in his client’s absence. Nili said Panahi learned of the ruling after his bank accounts were frozen.




Lawyer Nili said that although his client returned to Iran on March 30, 2026, the case file listed him as being outside the country, and he had not been notified of the hearing date. Nili also stated that an arrest warrant had been issued for Panahi on May 20, 2026, and that the director currently faces three separate legal cases.




Panahi had previously been sentenced to one year in prison in a separate case on charges of “propaganda against the regime.” He was also given a two-year travel ban and prohibited from joining political and social organizations. His request for a retrial was rejected in June 2026.

author: Unknown
title: "Women, Justice and Memory" vigil in Amed: “Rojda is not alone”
content:
Women’s organizations have once again protested against patriarchal violence, femicides, and impunity for perpetrators outside the courthouse in Amed (Turkish: Diyarbakır). The “Women, Justice and Memory,” organized by the Network Against Violence, entered its fourth week on Tuesday. Alongside representatives of political parties and civil society organizations, Rojda Odabaşı also took part in today’s demonstration. She had survived an attack in late August when a neighbor shot at her with a shotgun in her apartment.




The participants carried photographs of murdered women and a banner reading “Women hold vigil for justice and memory,” chanting “Jin, Jiyan, Azadî,” “Femicide is political,” and “Long live women’s struggle.”




ÖHD: Rojda’s safety must be ensured immediately




The demonstration focused on demands for protection and justice for Rojda Odabaşı. The suspect had been released late last week following the armed attack on her. Aycan Diril, from the Women’s Commission of the Association of Lawyers for Freedom (ÖHD), criticized the decision and called for a thorough investigation into the case. “We demand that Rojda’s safety be ensured immediately, that the decision to release the suspect be subjected to effective judicial review, and that every aspect of the attack, including possible intent to kill, be investigated. We will continue to follow this case. Rojda is not alone,” Diril declared.




The lawyer emphasized that the vigil was intended not only to commemorate women who had been killed but also to highlight the responsibility of state institutions. This week, the focus was on seven women who were killed or died under unclear circumstances between October 18 and 26. Representatives of the participating organizations shared their stories.
















Killed despite protection orders




Criticism of the state’s failure to protect women from violence was particularly evident in the cases of Sevda Dinler and Perihan Akbulut. Both women were killed despite having already obtained protection orders against the suspected or eventual perpetrators. Sevda Dinler, a 22-year-old graduate of a vocational school of health sciences, was shot dead with a hunting rifle on October 21 in the Kozan district of Adana. According to media reports, she had rejected Gamber Fidan’s advances and had subsequently been threatened and stalked by him. A protection order had been issued against the man. Following the killing, he was arrested and placed in pretrial detention.




Perihan Akbulut, a 61-year-old mother of five, was stabbed to death in the street the following day in Yeşilyurt, in Malatya. She sustained eight stab wounds. A protection order had also been issued against her husband, Hasan Akbulut. The perpetrator died in hospital after attempting suicide while being pursued by police.




“Femicide is not an unforeseeable event. Previous violence, threats, persistent stalking, and applications for protection orders are often warning signs. When a woman is killed despite a known risk to her life, it must also be investigated whether state authorities fulfilled their duty to protect her,” the statement said. The activists linked this criticism to the economic conditions that can prevent women from leaving abusive relationships. They opposed political attacks on alimony rights and highlighted the lack of security regarding housing, income, and caregiving responsibilities.




Femicides and unexplained deaths




The vigil also commemorated Melek Altınboğa and Aliye Aker. Melek Altınboğa, a 30-year-old mother of one, was killed with a hunting rifle by her husband, Murat Altınboğa, on October 18 in the Akören district of Konya. The couple had been married for just four months. The perpetrator subsequently injured himself with the same weapon. Women’s organizations criticized media reports that reduced the murder to a domestic dispute, thereby downplaying the patriarchal violence involved.













Aliye Aker, 27, was shot dead on October 21 in Osmaniye by Salih Aker, whom she had married just 20 days earlier. The man subsequently took his own life. The activists emphasized that a perpetrator’s death following a femicide did not absolve the authorities of their duty to investigate possible failures to protect the victim and the circumstances surrounding the crime.




Particular attention was also paid to 26-year-old lawyer Özge Penbegül, who was shot dead on October 22 in her apartment in Menemen, near Izmir, by her fiancé, Aykut Erol. The man, who worked as a police officer in Hakkari, subsequently took his own life. The network emphasized the particular responsibility of state institutions when armed public officials commit violence against women. They underlined that wearing a uniform must not shield anyone from scrutiny or accountability for such acts.




Alongside these femicides, the women highlighted two unexplained deaths. Remziye Damar, 61, was found dead in her apartment on October 20 in Kızıltepe district of Mardin. The activists warned against prematurely classifying her death as suicide. They demanded that possible circumstances involving violence and coercion also be investigated.




Kazakh national Aisulu Bekmakhanova (26) died after falling from a great height in Istanbul’s Şişli district. The exact circumstances remain unclear. The network called for a thorough investigation and emphasized that women’s protection and access to justice must not depend on their nationality or residence status. In this context, the activists once again criticized Turkey’s withdrawal from the Istanbul Convention.




Bucak: Rojda demands justice for herself and other women




Following the commemoration of the seven women, Rojda Odabaşı herself addressed the gathering. She demanded justice and appealed to the media and women’s organizations to support her struggle. Amed co-mayor Serra Bucak praised Odabaşı’s courage: “Rojda has stated with great courage and clarity that she wants justice. She is demanding this justice not only for herself but also for other women.”




Bucak called on the women of the city to join the vigil and maintain pressure on the judiciary. “I appeal to all women in Amed: Come here every Tuesday, to stand before the institution that fails to hold the perpetrators accountable.”




The fourth vigil ended with a minute of silence in memory of the women who had been killed.

title: Trial begins in Leipzig over knife attack on Kurdish woman
content:
Proceedings began today, 27 October, at the Leipzig Regional Court in a case concerning the stabbing and serious injury of a 31-year-old Kurdish woman on a tram on 26 January 2026. The 21-year-old Syrian defendant, Ahmed A., faces charges including aggravated assault, threats, robbery and insult.




According to the indictment, the defendant, Ahmad A., and another person who is being investigated separately insulted and attacked the Kurdish woman aboard tram line 16. The attackers reportedly threatened Kurds, saying, “We will kill all Kurds.”




During the incident, the woman was injured by knife blows and her thumb was severed. It was later surgically reattached at a hospital. She reportedly sustained permanent restrictions in movement and loss of sensation in her hands and fingers, and continues to receive psychological treatment.




Defendant denies anti-Kurdish motive




Speaking in court, the defendant, Ahmed A., admitted to attacking and robbing the victim but claimed that he had no personal issue with Kurds or with the woman he attacked. He said he had consumed alcohol on the night of the incident and had become involved in a knife fight on the tram.




The victim previously told the German newspaper 

Taz

 that she believed she had been attacked because of her Kurdish identity. “Their problem was that I was Kurdish. They didn’t need my money,” she said.

title: At least 87 people executed in Iran in 20 days
content:
The wave of executions in Iran continues. According to the “No Execution Tuesdays” campaign, at least 87 people have been executed in just 20 days. Death sentences have also reportedly been handed down to numerous other prisoners. The protest movement, which has been campaigning against the death penalty and the Iranian regime’s execution practices for more than two and a half years, is now continuing its actions in 66 prisons. On Tuesday, the campaign entered its 144th week.




In a statement, participants warned of the scale of state repression as hundreds, possibly even thousands, of prisoners in Iran are awaiting execution. “The regime uses the death penalty not only to kill people but also to spread fear throughout society and silence opposition voices. Each execution also leaves families in deep grief.”




The campaign highlighted the large number of executions carried out during the Iranian month of Mehr, which lasted from September 22 to October 19. According to the campaign, this development demonstrates how systematically the regime uses the death penalty as a tool of intimidation. “Yet history has shown that no gallows can tear the desire for freedom and equality from people’s hearts. No repression can silence forever the voices of those who fight for their rights,” the statement said.

author: Unknown
title: Convicted rapist Musa Orhan acquitted of charge of inciting suicide
content:
Turkish former non-commissioned officer Musa Orhan, who was sentenced to ten years in prison for raping 18-year-old Kurdish woman İpek Er, has been acquitted in a separate criminal case. On October 22, a court in Batman ruled that it could not be proven that Orhan had incited the young woman to take her own life. The acquittal came despite her suicide note, incriminating witness testimony, and his previous conviction for serious sexual violence. Orhan remains free and has yet to begin serving his prison sentence.




The case of İpek Er sparked outrage far beyond Kurdistan in 2020 and became a symbol of impunity for sexual violence committed by uniformed state personnel. Women’s organizations and the Kurdish women’s movement protested against Orhan’s repeated release from custody and the Turkish judiciary’s handling of the young woman’s case. Even his subsequent conviction did not change the fact that the former soldier remained free.













İpek Er reported being held captive and raped




İpek Er had met Musa Orhan online. In the suicide note she later left behind, she described how the professional soldier, who was stationed in the district of Beşiri at the time, had held her captive for several days, drugged her, and raped her. author: Unknown
title: Swedish Social Democratic Party seeks to strengthen cooperation with DEM Party
content:
Following the confirmation of the Swedish election results, DEM Party co-chairs Tülay Hatimoğulları and Tuncer Bakırhan sent a congratulatory message to Swedish Social Democratic Party leader Magdalena Andersson.




Magdalena Andersson, who is currently working to form a government in her country, sent a letter addressed to the DEM Party co-chairs.




The letter, shared by the DEM Party Press Office, reads as follows:




“Thank you for your letter and congratulations on behalf of the Peoples’ Equality and Democracy Party. The election results were very close, and this period requires patience, dialogue, and determination. We are doing everything we can to form a government that works for social justice and equal opportunities—ideals that you, too, continue to champion.




At a time of increasing polarization, we must demonstrate that social democracy can deliver results for ordinary people while offering a genuine alternative to the forces seeking to divide us. We deeply value our friendship with the DEM Party. We stand in solidarity with your demands for peace, justice, and democracy in Turkey and look forward to further strengthening our cooperation, both bilaterally and through our shared international platforms.”

title: Hêzil Özgür: Bêrîtan’s struggle is the story of the free woman
content:
YJAStar (Free Women’s Troops) guerrillas marked the 34th anniversary of the founding of the women’s army with a ceremony and cultural program in the mountains of Kurdistan. The event centered on the legacy of guerrilla commander Bêrîtan Hêvî (Gülnaz Karataş), who fell on October 25, 1992, during the Southern War. Her resistance against surrender and the attacks on the PKK at the time became a defining reference point in the development of an autonomous women’s military organization within the Kurdish freedom movement.




The event began with a speech by Hêzil Özgür from the YJA Star Central Headquarters. Other women guerrilla fighters reflected on Bêrîtan Hêvî’s significance for the women’s freedom movement and the development of a collective identity. The commemoration featured cultural performances and concluded with group dances.




“The women’s army was founded on Bêrîtan’s legacy”




Hêzil Özgür began by recalling the difficult years of 1991 and 1992, when the Kurdish freedom movement was experiencing growing support while simultaneously facing massive military attacks. Particularly large numbers of young women joined the guerrilla forces during this period, she noted. “In those years, participation increased across all sections of society, and the number of female comrades in particular grew significantly. The guerrilla’s influence in Kurdistan grew stronger by the day

title: Altun: Government must end delaying release of prisoners
content:
Kenan Altun, who had been imprisoned for 30 years, was released from Maltepe No. 1 L-Type Prison in recent days. Altun spoke to ANF about the Peace and Democratic Society Process, saying it had generated great enthusiasm among the people and that prisoners had also strongly embraced the process.




Altun said the Kurdish people had embraced the process, but certain approaches adopted by the government were raising concerns. He added that the situation in prisons was deepening these concerns, pointing to the importance of prison conditions for the progress of the process.







 







‘Prison practices are raising concerns about the process’




Altun drew attention to practices in prisons and said: “It is genuinely difficult to make sense of these practices and explain them to our people. The situation of our imprisoned comrades who have spent many years behind bars, particularly our elderly comrades, is deeply troubling for all of us. One example is Ali Rıza Yurtdaş, who was held in the prison I have just left. He is 84 years old. Despite being referred to the Forensic Medicine Institute several times during this process and having medical reports, he was arbitrarily declared ‘fit to remain in prison’. This is just one example. There are many others.

title: Journalists call for united struggle against repression
content:
Censorship, access restrictions and repressive policies targeting the press and media workers are intensifying, but journalists continue their struggle for a free press in the face of these obstacles. As the public's right to information comes under attack, growing pressure on journalists is deepening restrictions on freedom of expression and press freedom. Free press workers, however, continue to resist these pressures and bring the truth to the public.




Evrensel newspaper reporter Elif Ekin Saltık and Dicle Fırat Journalists Association (DFG) Co-Chair Selman Çiçek spoke to ANF about the mounting pressure on the media. They said the repression affects not only journalists but also democratic politics, freedom of expression and the public's right to information. The journalists pointed out that the longstanding repression of the Kurdish press has now expanded to include other opposition media outlets. They called for solidarity and a united struggle against the obstacles facing free and multilingual journalism.




‘The attacks initially targeted the Kurdish press’




Evrensel newspaper reporter Elif Ekin Saltık said that repression in the media had continued for many years, initially targeting the Kurdish press and the Free Press. title: MSD condemns the attack in Gire Spi: Return of IDPs is an inherent right
content:
The Syrian Democratic Council (MSD) strongly condemned the recent attacks against forcibly displaced Kurdish families returning to Tal Abyad (Gire Spi) in the Raqqa countryside. Returning civilians—including women and children—faced death threats, physical assaults, and property destruction. These violent acts were accompanied by racist slogans targeting Kurdish national identity.




MSD stated that this incident is a grave crime against unarmed civilians, a flagrant violation of the January 29 agreement, and a direct threat to social peace and the right to safe return.




The MSD holds the Syrian Transitional Government fully responsible for protecting civilians, safeguarding their property, and immediately stopping these abuses to prevent their recurrence. It calls for an independent, impartial, and public investigation to reveal the facts, hold both perpetrators and instigators accountable regardless of affiliation, and end systemic impunity. Furthermore, the MSD demands decisive action against hate speech and racial incitement to ensure that no citizen is targeted based on national identity.

title: Şener: Flood disasters are not caused by heavy rainfall alone
content:
The floods that followed heavy rainfall in Istanbul last week have once again brought the destruction of the city's ecosystem and unplanned urbanisation into focus. The increasing spread of concrete development, the destruction of natural areas and the disruption of ecological balance are also heightening the risk of disasters.




At least four people lost their lives in the floods. The devastation in Ayazağa, where construction has expanded alongside the destruction of the Northern Forests, has renewed criticism of Istanbul's urban development policies.




Umut Şener from Polen Ecology spoke to ANF about the floods in Istanbul and the consequences of the destruction of the city's ecosystem.




‘The underlying problem is the city's lack of drinking water’




Umut Şener pointed out that ecological destruction in Istanbul has a long history and discussed the environmental problems the city has faced over the centuries.




Şener said, “In the case of Istanbul, it is possible to trace the transformation of nature as far back as antiquity. The environmental problems inherited by the Ottomans when they conquered Istanbul, following centuries of Roman and Byzantine rule, and the measures introduced to address them, demonstrate just how far back this history extends. title: PJAK spokesperson Awdanan: Region preparing for new phase of war
content:
Kurdistan Free Life Party (PJAK) spokesperson Rêwar Awdanan commented on the course of the war between Iran, the US and Israel, as well as developments across the region.




PJAK spokesperson Rêwar Awdanan noted that the Islamic Republic of Iran had suffered devastating defeats in the 12-Day War, the 40-Day War and the Strait of Hormuz War. “Despite this, it continues to act stubbornly and ignores the advice of figures such as Karroubi, Khatami, Zarif and Rouhani. They even view agreements such as the Treaty of Turkmenchay as beneficial to the stability of the system. Negotiations and the Islamabad Agreement were not enough to extinguish the flames of war, because the concessions demanded by each side are unacceptable to the other,” he said.




Negotiations failed to prevent war




Stating that all indications point to preparations for a new phase in the US-Israeli war against the Islamic Republic of Iran, Awdanan said: “The Strait of Hormuz War and the naval and air blockade imposed on Iran demonstrate the reality of the full-scale and intense war we are facing. title: Seventh denial of release for Nedime Yaklav
content:
In the fourth week of its ongoing protests against the blocking of women prisoners’ releases at Sincan Women’s Closed Prison, the Ankara Democratic Institutions Platform made a statement in front of the Ministry of Justice. The protest highlighted the seventh denial of release for Nedime Yaklav, who has been imprisoned for 34 years.




Speaking on behalf of the platform, Nesil Çifçi stated that although there were insufficient social and sporting activities available in the prison, Nedime Yaklav’s failure to participate in these activities had been cited as grounds for denying her release. “Postponing prisoners’ freedom on the basis of facilities that the institution itself fails to provide is not justice; it is oppression,” she said.




Nesil Çifçi stated that, according to data from the Lawyers for Freedom Association (ÖHD), the release of 90 prisoners had been blocked over the past three months. She called for an end to the arbitrary obstruction of prisoners who have become eligible for release and demanded that sentence enforcement practices be revised in accordance with human rights principles.

title: Bakırhan: 'Peace and Politicisation Council’ must be established immediately
content:
With Abdullah Öcalan’s “Call for Peace and a Democratic Society”, the process entered a new phase. The Kurdish Freedom Movement announced its decision to dissolve itself, burned its weapons and withdrew its forces. However, the state’s delays in taking legal and political steps in response to these moves have increased questions and concerns about the future of the process.




Speaking to ANF, DEM Party Co-Chair Tuncer Bakırhan said that trust must be established for the process to move forward and called on the government to take concrete steps. He stressed that the verification and assessment report must be published without delay, that the National Security Council (MGK) must adopt a decision, and that implementation of the Framework Law must begin. “Now it is the government’s turn,” he said.




At last week’s parliamentary group meeting, you pointed out that the government was ‘coming up with a new condition every week and a new pretext every month’. Why is the government dragging its feet? What arguments is it putting forward at the moment?




The way to build trust and establish a future through the “Peace and Democratic Society Process” is for both sides to take reciprocal steps. title: Besê Hozat: Abdullah Öcalan’s status must be formalized for the process to move forward
content:
KCK Executive Council Co-Chair Besê Hozat spoke to Medya Haber TV about the current stage of the process, the women’s freedom struggle, practices in prisons, and regional developments.




This is part one of the interview. 




25 October marked the 34th anniversary of the martyrdom of comrade Bêrîtan (Gülnaz Karataş), who played a pivotal role in the development of the Kurdish freedom struggle and particularly the women’s resistance movement. What impact did the change she pioneered have on Kurdish sociology?




To begin with, I commemorate all the martyrs of the revolution and the struggle for freedom represented by comrade Bêrîtan with respect, love, and gratitude. Comrade Bêrîtan holds a special place in our struggle. Her place and importance are particularly unique from the perspective of the women’s freedom struggle. Comrade Bêrîtan is a symbol of resistance and of the struggle for freedom. Comrade Bêrîtan’s stance, character, and her resistance – the noble stance she took against the impositions of collaborationists, traitors, and capitulationists, as well as against the line of surrender – have had a tremendous impact on organizing women and on the development of women’s self-defense. Her influence on Kurdish women, in particular, has been immense.

title: HPG and YJA-Star guerrillas: Bêrîtan embodies the truth of struggle
content:
People's Defence Forces (HPG) and Free Women's Units (YJA-Star) guerrillas commemorated commander Bêrîtan Hêvî (Gülnaz Karataş) on the anniversary of her martyrdom.




YJA-Star guerrilla Agirî Efrîn spoke about Bêrîtan Hêvî's martyrdom, saying: “I was inspired by comrade Bêrîtan, and it was on this basis that I joined the movement. Today marks the 34th anniversary of her martyrdom. Comrade Bêrîtan was a commander of the women's army, and Abdullah Öcalan developed the women's military organisation following her martyrdom. Her personality is like a light for us women. I had the opportunity to visit the Martyr Bêrîtan Academy myself, which was a great privilege. As a woman, comrade Bêrîtan showed me the right path. She understood Abdullah Öcalan and put his ideas into practice, and for this we owe her a great deal.







 







Comrade Bêrîtan made history through her resistance against the occupiers. No one would knowingly throw themselves off a cliff, but comrade Bêrîtan did so for a cause. In a short period of time, she had embraced and embodied the idea of the free woman. The position of women in society and within the party is different, and we can see this very clearly. The women's army belongs to all women. Women from every nation have a place in our military organisation. Every woman who recognises the importance of her freedom joins the ranks of the women's army. author: Unknown
title: Two Kurdish women missing after being detained
content:
The Voice of Iranian Prisoners Organisation issued a statement concerning two Kurdish women detained in Rojhilatê Kurdistan (East Kurdistan).




The statement said that 17-year-old Perya Nasirî was detained by Iranian intelligence forces at her school in Nexede on 21 October. Six days after her disappearance, her fate and whereabouts remained unknown.




It also stated that Sedrî Bexşî, 43, from the village of Weştape in Bokan, had been held at the Urmiye Intelligence Directorate since her detention a month earlier and was facing serious security-related threats.




After being detained over posts shared on digital media platforms, Sedrî Bexşî had been allowed only one brief telephone conversation with her family, according to the statement. Iranian intelligence forces reportedly threatened the family with severe punishment if they publicised her detention in the media.




According to the report, Iranian Revolutionary Guard forces raided Sedrî Bexşî’s home in the village of Weştape a month ago, using eight armoured vehicles. Following a search of the house, they seized her phone.

title: Families in Washokani Camp stage protest: We want to return to our homes before winter
content:
Families who were forcibly displaced from Serêkaniyê and Til Temir and are living in Washokani Camp staged a protest today. Blocking the Til Temir–Hesekê road, the families demanded to return to their homes as soon as possible.




The protesters stated that they were facing numerous difficulties in the camp and that no organization was providing them with assistance anymore.




Camp resident Mûsa Mihemed from the village of El Menacîr, said that no organization was helping them anymore and that their living conditions were poor. He explained that winter was approaching and that when it rained, water poured through their torn tents, leaving them exposed to the rain. He demanded that they be enabled to return to their homes as soon as possible.




Another resident of the camp, Cabir Ebdulrehman, said: “I am from the village of El Kêf in Til Temir. We are organizing protests because we want to return to our homes as soon as possible. Our situation is difficult, theft has increased, there is chaos, and we have no means of making a living. We want the return convoys to include all displaced people.”




Mihemed Ebdulrehman, from the village of El Kinêhir in Til Temir, stated: “The return convoys only include people from certain areas. We want to return to our village before winter arrives.”

author: Unknown
title: 25 organizations in Europe seek to strengthen joint struggle and solidarity
content:
25 political and civil society organizations from Turkey and Kurdistan have agreed to establish a joint alliance for struggle and solidarity in Europe. The initiative aims to bring together different political currents and strengthen resistance against the rise of right-wing and fascist forces, imperialist war policies, and state repression. At the same time, the participating organizations intend to support the peace and democratic society process in Turkey and advocate for a democratic solution to the Kurdish question.




The agreement stems from a meeting held on October 17 at the Cologne headquarters of the Federation of Alevi Communities in Europe (AABK). Representatives from various political traditions and social movements gathered at the invitation of eight organizations. In a joint final declaration issued today, the participants reaffirm their determination to preserve their organizational independence while establishing a lasting foundation for joint political action.




Against militarism, fascism and imperialist war policies




In their declaration, the organizations describe a world marked by growing international tensions. They warn that wars and conflicts driven by imperialist centers of power are increasing the risk of a broader military confrontation, potentially escalating into a new global war over the redistribution of power and resources. title: Panel discussion on Jineolojî and self-defense in Marseille
content:
A panel discussion and commemoration event focusing on Jineolojî and the formation of women’s armed forces was held in Marseille, France, organized by the Association of Martyrs’ Families (KOMAW), the Marseille Arîn Mîrkan Women’s Council, and members of Jineolojî Provence. The event, held at the Marseille Kurdish Democratic Community Center, was attended by numerous Kurdish women from the region, as well as representatives of French internationalist women’s movements.




The event began with a minute of silence in memory of the martyrs of the Kurdistan freedom struggle, represented by Bêrîtan (Gülnaz Karataş), described as an immortal commander of the Kurdish women’s struggle, as well as international women revolutionaries who lost their lives defending life.




This was followed by a video presentation highlighting Bêrîtan’s commitment to the principles of women’s freedom and the resistance of Kurdish women in their struggle for liberation. During the screening, chants of “Şehîd namirin” (“Martyrs are immortal) frequently echoed through the hall.

title: Girê Spî Committee calls for the protection of families trapped in Regional Directorate building
content:
A group of Kurdish residents from Girê Spî, who were returning to their homes at the invitation of the Girê Spî Regional Directorate, were attacked while entering the building earlier today.




The Girê Spî Committee for the Forcibly Displaced reported that more than 100 Kurdish families were under siege inside the Regional Directorate building.




The committee described the attack against Kurds as an assault on their safety and their legitimate right to return. It called for the protection of the families and for an immediate investigation into those responsible.




The committee stated that it had been coordinating with relevant parties and following up on efforts to enable forcibly displaced families to return to their homes and properties. These efforts have so far yielded no results, it added.




The committee emphasized that the Regional Directorate officials must fulfill their responsibilities to protect the residents against such attacks.




Drawing attention to the plight of more than 100 Kurdish families, including women and children, trapped inside the Girê Spî Regional Directorate building, the committee called on the relevant authorities to intervene immediately to protect the residents from further attacks.




The committee stated that anyone wishing to return to Girê Spî should contact and coordinate with the committee so that their return can be organized

title: Temelli: Steps toward democratizing the Republic must not be delayed
content:
At a press conference held in Parliament, DEM Party Deputy Parliamentary Group Chair Sezai Temelli addressed the peace and democratic society process. He called for the opportunity presented by the process to be seized and for the necessary steps to be taken without delay.




“The democratic resolution to the Kurdish question is the most important step toward comprehensive democratization and the democratization of the Republic,” Temelli said.




Temelli pointed out that the Kurdish question has remained unresolved throughout the Republic’s 100-year history, and that its democratic resolution is of critical importance for the democratization of the Republic.




He emphasized the need to guarantee freedom of the press and expression, protect human rights, and end political bans.




Drawing attention to the continued imprisonment of political figures in Turkey, Temelli cited Figen Yüksekdağ and Selahattin Demirtaş, who are imprisoned in connection with the Kobanê trial, as well as Can Atalay.




Criticizing the Turkish state’s failure to implement rulings of the European Court of Human Rights, Temelli stated that the Republic must embrace democracy and freedoms.

content:

title: Özcan Yaman: No liberties, democracy or peace without free media
content:
Journalists took to the streets in several cities on Saturday, 24 October, to protest against the detention and imprisonment of journalists, the appointment of trustees to media outlets and access restrictions imposed on news websites and social media accounts.




The protests were organised following calls by the Dicle Fırat Journalists Association (DFG), the Mesopotamia Women Journalists Association, the Journalists' Union of Turkey (TGS), the Journalists Association of Turkey (TGC), the Press Council, the Confederation of Progressive Trade Unions of Turkey Press Workers' Union (DISK Basın-Iş), Haber-Sen and the Contemporary Journalists Association (ÇGD). Protesters demanded the release of imprisoned journalists and an end to interference with press freedom.




Journalists and members of the public gathered in front of the Bull Statue in Kadıköy, Istanbul, before marching to Kadıköy Pier Square, chanting slogans. They demanded the release of their colleagues, an end to the appointment of trustees and guarantees for the public's right to information.

How do war policies undermine class solidarity between Turkish and Kurdish workers? You frequently visit workplaces and meet workers. Have you observed this in practice?




One of the most important realities we observe on the ground is that workers face very similar economic problems. Workers in Antep, Başpınar, metal factories and the logistics sector talk about inadequate wages, long working hours, workplace accidents, job insecurity and obstacles to trade union organising. Workers living in different cities and belonging to different identities share many of the same problems. But the existence of common problems does not automatically lead to a common struggle.




That requires organisation, trust and shared experiences. War policies and nationalist polarisation undermine precisely these foundations. The conflict of interests between workers and their employers is pushed into the background. title: Camcı: Urban Commune must be established to combat poverty
content:
Deep poverty in Diyarbakır (Amed) is reflected in unemployment, precarious working conditions, food insecurity and difficulties accessing basic necessities. According to 2024 data from the Ministry of Family and Social Services, 196,530 households in the city received social assistance, with the total amount reaching 4.47 billion Turkish lira. These figures reveal that poverty is not merely a matter of individual income loss but a structural problem affecting different aspects of social life.




Field research conducted in the Bağlar and Sur districts of Diyarbakır also reveals the tangible effects of deep poverty on neighbourhoods. Approximately 93 per cent of the women who participated in the research reported reducing their food purchases, while 95 per cent said they had cut spending on clothing. Many families are forced to take on debt to meet their basic needs.




Children living in damp homes affected by water leaks and inadequate heating are reportedly experiencing health problems. The fact that 196,530 households in Diyarbakır received social assistance in 2024 further illustrates the scale of poverty across the city.

content:
The new academic year has begun under the shadow of security-oriented policies, alongside chronic problems such as inadequate student grants, safety concerns in dormitories run by the Credit and Dormitories Institution (KYK), dysfunctional democratic mechanisms and sexism on campuses. Together with the Council of Higher Education's (YÖK) instruction to address the theme of “Terror-free Turkey” in the first lecture, it reflects the government's efforts to tighten its control over universities.




ANF spoke to Sude Şener from Labour Youth, Yasin Incekara from the Revolutionary Youth Union (DGB) and Özcan Berber from Student Activity about the new academic year, the government's security policies at universities and how students plan to organise in the coming period.

content:

KNK Co-Chair Ahmet Karamus spoke to ANF about the work to be carried out following the conference. He highlighted the importance of political contacts in South Kurdistan (Başûr), establishing a commission involving all four parts of Kurdistan and the diaspora, and preparing a joint roadmap.




Karamus said efforts to secure observer status at the UN should be developed with the participation of different political and social groups and coordinated through joint diplomatic work.




Karamus explained that the idea for the conference had emerged at a KNK congress and was followed by approximately a year of preparations. title: Turkish military blocks protest against solar power plant in Amed
content:
Resistance against the planned “Zenkar 2” solar power plant continues in the province of Amed (Turkish: Diyarbakır). For four days, residents of Arzoxlî (Kervanpınar), a village in the Sur district, have maintained a protest vigil in a tent after company employees entered the project site accompanied by Turkish gendarmerie and police forces. Meanwhile, legal proceedings are ongoing against the favorable environmental impact assessment decision for the project, which includes both a photovoltaic power plant and an energy storage facility.




On the third day of the protest, villagers gathered in front of their tent and set off together toward the site where the company had begun its work. Chanting slogans such as “We will prevail through resistance” and “If you remain silent, you will be next,” they marched toward the project area.




Soldiers stopped the protest march and prevented residents from entering the site. The demonstrators then returned to the protest tent, where they are continuing their vigil. They emphasize that their resistance is not directed against solar energy itself. Rather, they criticize the fact that the facility is planned for grazing land that is essential for livestock farming and, consequently, their economic survival. The construction of the solar power plant threatens to deprive them of a vital source of livelihood.

A liter of diesel, which we need to cultivate our fields, now costs more than 100 lira,” the people explained.

title: PJAK member remains forcibly disappeared following arrest by IRGC
content:
More than three months after Khaled Barzanji, a Sanandaj-born member of the Kurdistan Free Life Party (PJAK), was arrested by the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) Intelligence Organisation in the village of Uch Tappeh, Bukan, his fate and whereabouts remain unknown. Despite repeated enquiries by his family, security and judicial authorities have refused to acknowledge his detention.




The Kurdistan Human Rights Network (KHRN) has learned that on 10 July 2026, IRGC forces surrounded a garden house in the village of Uch Tappeh in Bukan and arrested Barzanji along with two other individuals who owned the property.




The identities of the two other detainees remain unknown, although one of them was reportedly released after some time.




Since his arrest, Barzanji has been denied access to a lawyer and all contact and visits with his family. Despite repeated visits and enquiries by his family to judicial authorities and security agencies in Bukan and Orumiyeh, the authorities have denied any knowledge of his arrest or whereabouts.




On 22 October 2026, PJAK issued a statement confirming the arrest of its member and stating that no information about his fate had been obtained.

title: Gamze Çakan: Silence of guns is not enough
content:

ANF spoke to film critic Gamze Çakan, founder of the Independent Cinema platform, about the relationship between cinema and peace.




What can the relationship between cinema and confronting the past teach us about the current peace process?
